units.t: FOREWORD

Steingrímur Hermannsson asked me only one question before we signed the agreement for the publication of this book: "By the way, didn't you do quite well in Icelandic in secondary school?" He already knew by then that this would be my first book, that I had never voted for the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), and that we were doubtless on opposite sides of many issues in Icelandic politics.

A biography always bears the mark of being told from the vantage point of a single individual. In that sense it can never be neutral. I was nonetheless determined to write an impartial account, setting Steingrímur's opinions aside, and from the first day I considered it my principal task to ensure that the biography of Steingrímur Hermannsson would not become a one-sided heroic tale in the tradition of the royal literature of the Middle Ages, the sagas of bishops — or, for that matter, the conventional biographies of Icelandic politicians. Steingrímur said, unprompted, that this was how he too wanted the work to be done.

I soon discovered that Steingrímur wanted to tell his story without dodging questions about anything that might be considered sensitive, whether it came from the political arena or from his own personal story of fate. In his biography he offers deeper insight into conflicts in his private life and behind the scenes of politics than I know of in any comparable book. Steingrímur does not apologize for himself, and he wants to leave behind what we might call a true biography. Whether I have succeeded in mastering the material and putting it decently into a book, others will have to judge.

When Steingrímur Hermannsson suddenly disappeared from the political stage in the spring of 1994, he had behind him fifteen years as chairman of the Progressive Party, almost as long a tenure as a government minister, and seven years as prime minister in three governments. The prime minister's son who never intended to go into politics thereby concluded

one of the most colorful careers in Iceland's political history with hardly less commotion than when it began in 1971, when the election bombshell that has come to be known by the name of the green peas burst with a resounding bang.

Over his nearly 25-year career, Steingrímur was the most diligent of all Icelandic politicians in admitting mistakes or shortsightedness. More than once, and more than twice, he said he had been "duped" in matters that had not turned out as well as one might have wished. No one placed greater emphasis on the fact that Steingrímur Hermannsson was imperfect and human than Steingrímur Hermannsson himself.

Steingrímur is tenacious and ambitious. He has the ambition and the hunger for distinction to match almost anyone, and he therefore takes it badly not to be at the front of the pack. He is considered a skillful negotiator, easy to talk to, and is renowned for compromise. He speaks plainly and in a down-to-earth manner, and during his long political career he was a daily presence in radio and television news broadcasts and on the pages of the newspapers. He had a reputation for never turning a journalist away, and he regularly produced statements and retorts that were considered variously dubious, awkward, or cunningly clever. When he was confronted in a television debate over the fact that working people lived in such straitened circumstances that rice porridge was on their tables every night of the week, he replied without hesitation that he thought rice porridge was good food. When the leaders of the labor movement delivered more than 34,000 signatures in protest against the government's emergency legislation abolishing the right to collective bargaining, he knocked the weapons from their hands by remarking that the signatures lacked home addresses, which was most unfortunate. The right to collective bargaining was mentioned only in passing in some of the news reports about the handover.

At the same time, Steingrímur was one of the most energetic critics of his own government's policies. He was tireless in his criticism of interest rates and loan terms while serving his second term as prime minister, even though both could be traced back to the policies of his own previous government. The same can be said of the quota system in the fisheries, which he has criticized sharply, and in recent years Steingrímur has expressed doubts about power plants and heavy industry after having spent nearly thirty years of his life fighting for those very causes, long in opposition to his own party and its leadership. There is no hero in the biography of Steingrímur Hermannsson where these matters are concerned. There is, however, a politician who is unafraid to change his mind when he hears sound arguments for doing so. This makes his story full of contradictions that are exciting to grapple with.
Despite the contradictions, no politician was more popular among the nation.

When Steingrímur Hermannsson went into his last election in 1991, 40% of the nation wanted him to remain prime minister — more than twice as many as those who said they would vote for the Progressive Party. He enjoyed as much support for the office as Davíð Oddsson and Þorsteinn Pálsson combined.

The pictures from Steingrímur's political career are many and varied. Unlike most leaders from that arena, he did not enter politics until his late thirties — around the same time that he declined to take part in founding a company that would go on to become one of the most flourishing in the country. By then he had already endured heavier blows and greater difficulties in his private life than most people face in a lifetime. He championed gold prospecting and heavy-industry ventures in his position as director of the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins), pushed for the import of the first computer, founded an ice factory and the first hamburger restaurant in Iceland, along with numerous other businesses with mixed results. He brought Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson into the Progressive Party, represented Iceland at the United Nations General Assembly, and was involved in founding the contracting company Íslenskir aðalverktakar. He traveled the world on behalf of Vilhjálmur Þór and the Federation of Icelandic Cooperatives (Sambandið), and took part in building the Fertilizer Plant at Gufunes. He was called "Big Red" during his student years in the United States, practiced wrestling, and corresponded with his father, the prime minister, in letters where criticism, sound advice, and words of encouragement were never in short supply. All of this played a part in shaping the man the nation knows best as Steingrímur Hermannsson, prime minister.
Dagur B. Eggertsson
Chapter One
FRAGMENTS OF MEMORY FROM CHILDHOOD

Today is 19 March 1945, the First Day of Summer. Nearly two years have thus passed since I meant to fill in this gap in my diary. My name is Steingrímur and I am the son of Hermann Jónasson, who was prime minister from 1934–1942, and Vigdís Steingrímsdóttir. My grandfather Jónas was Jónsson. He died in the summer of 1942, and I was then at Syðri-Brekkur, where he died. He was a farmer and a carpenter. His wife was named Pálína Björnsdóttir, and grandmother is still alive and lives at Syðri-Brekkur. My other grandfather, Steingrímur, was Guðmundsson. He died in 1930. He was also a carpenter and lived on Álftanes and later in Reykjavík. His wife was Margrét Þorláksdóttir, and she is my grandmother. [She is] also alive and lives with us.

So read the opening words of my diary. I began keeping it in my fourteenth year. It is almost as if I had intended them to serve as the introduction to this biography. In fact, I did not put them on paper until two years after my diary-keeping began, under the heading "An Overview of My Life up to 15 January 1943."

I kept diaries for many years after this. Those writings accompany me into this book, together with the numerous letters and personal notes I have in my keeping — minute-books, papers, and books that have accumulated over the years. My whole life is stored in boxes, in orderly rows arranged by year and event. I have always been a great collector. I call on all this as witness, especially where memory fails or where it matters most that the story be told correctly.

One knows little of the course one's life will take when diary fragments are put together in one's fifteenth year. My father became prime minister again after this was written, and I myself later still. Few things were further from my mind in the spring of 1945. I never intended to go into politics.
Denni and Dolly

I was born on 22 June 1928 in the heart of Reykjavík, at Amtmannsstígur 4, probably around midday. An acquaintance of mine has it from a nationally known astrologer that it is highly significant to be born on that long day, especially near midday. When he informed me of this, I actually knew nothing about the time of my birth. Some time later, however, I met a woman in Keflavík who said she was born the same day, in the morning. The midwife went from her mother straight to mine.

I have a sister who is one year younger than I, born on 12 September 1929. Her name is Pálína, but she was never called anything but Dolly. It is as if fate had not intended our parents to have more children. Mamma and Pabbi lost a daughter before I was born. She lived only a week. That sister of mine was named Herdís and was born on 12 May 1927. Later they lost another child, Dolly's twin sister. She died on the second day of her life. We were all born at home on Amtmannsstígur.

Probably no one understands what it is to lose one's children without experiencing it oneself. My mother later said that the grief that came with losing her two daughters was the only thing in her life that truly wounded her. She watched over my sister and me all the more closely because of it.

At home I was usually called Denni. Why, I do not know. The riddle of the name has only ever preoccupied journalists, never me. I was christened after Steingrímur, my maternal grandfather. I believe the name Denni came from my mother, and she almost never called me anything else. My father more often called me Steingrímur, especially among strangers and when I was being scolded. At home I was Denni, or "my Denni," and there was nothing strange about that, it seemed to me.

Well into my youth I stumbled over certain words. It was as if my tongue could not keep up with my mind when much was at stake. Some of my childhood friends recall that I would bite my lip and put all my energy and concentration into getting the words out when it was at its worst. For a long time I was a person of few words, polite and quiet in other people's houses — at least in front of the grown-ups. On the playgrounds, however, I did not spare
the noise; I was boisterous and, as I recall, quite a handful. I was ruddy, strongly built, and big for my age. Play-fighting, sports, and tests of strength were my favorites.

The stammer loosened as time went on, and the speech impediment was gone before I entered secondary school. My self-confidence grew accordingly. A shyness about speaking in front of a large group stayed with me longer, though, and I worked hard to drive it out of myself.

I must have been quite a handful in my childhood. My sister, at any rate, found me pushy and unruly, and what she remembers best is that I dragged her around by the hair. I don't remember it myself, but it may well be true. I was certainly no angel.

I describe my sister in only a single sentence in my diary: "She is rather pretty." I was 16 then. She would surely have been pleased to hear it. She probably never did — not from me. Dolly took little part in us boys' games in those years. She was much more reserved than I, and my overbearing manner often got on her nerves. We were never really close, though we were fond of each other. Nor were we ever real playmates. She was not as ambitious as I was and was happiest with dolls and needlework. Dolly attended the Women's College (Kvennaskólinn) and did well. After that she went to study at a school of home economics in Norway. Later she married Sveinbjörn Dagfinnsson, who was permanent secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture. I believe it is a happy marriage. Their children are Hermann, Vigdís Magnea, Lóa Kristín, and Dagfinnur.

We siblings were raised with great affection, and my mother's forbearance was quite exceptional. My father, on the other hand, was the one who delivered the serious reprimands, often at my mother's request. That was his role in our upbringing.

On one occasion I was told to be home by a certain time. Before long I disobeyed. When I finally turned up at home, every door had been locked and no one answered when I knocked. So I took a ladder that stood in the yard by the Prime Minister's Residence and climbed up to the balcony. There I broke a pane in the door, went into my room, and locked myself in. Pabbi came running and wanted to talk to me, but I would not let him in.

In the morning I got a dressing-down from my father. I was called in onto the carpet in his office, as was usual on such occasions. Punishments sometimes took the form of a ban, but most often of a reprimand; I was never beaten or spanked. My father usually ended the talking-to by patting me on the head and saying:
“Do this now for me, Denni dear. Otherwise you’ll make your mother so sad.” I came home on time after that scolding, at least for the next month or so.
My upbringing, however, was characterized above all by the fact that I was trusted. My father later described it this way in a letter to me while I was staying in the United States:

I have, it seems, quite often been reproached by outsiders for how much I let you have your way. It could spoil you. I have no faith in that, and I will keep to the rule I have followed until now, of trusting you. I have wanted you to be able to grow like a straight tree.
A Proposal in a Letter

My parents met after Pabbi began studying law at the University. Among the law students in those years was Sigurður Jónasson, who was for a long time a great friend of my father’s. He rented rooms on Amtmannsstígur, in my mother’s home, which later became my birthplace. Sigurður is said to have invited my mother along when the schoolmates went out to enjoy themselves. Their gathering place in those days was the Mensa in Lækjargata. Soon my parents became well acquainted, and many people have remarked to me that my father was fortune’s favorite, since my mother was considered one of the most promising catches in town and much sought after. She was working then at the National Bank (Landsbankinn) on Austurstræti, and he at the town magistrate’s office at Suðurgata 4. Sigurður Jónasson presumably had to move out of Amtmannsstígur 4 after my parents married. My mother had had her own sorrows before she met my father. I did not learn of that until I had myself come to know heartbreak firsthand. My father then wrote me these lines:

Your Mamma has her sorrows too. She was engaged to a man [...] but he proved unfaithful to her. She broke off [the engagement]; she felt life was worth nothing. She has borne her sorrows and disappointments with me; but she has come through it all – and I think I need not describe her love to you, for she now seems content as long as I and you children are doing well.

My mother would probably never have told me this story, and I would never have asked. She was not that kind of woman. Her love was silent and warm. Between my parents there developed a special equilibrium that nothing could shake, no matter what happened. Of course no marriage is without its setbacks, but it seemed to me that my parents
grew ever more firmly and securely bound together as the years passed. My father put it this way in a letter:

It has not all been free of sorrow between me and your mother, but of that I will say no more. But this much is certain: after everything, there is no one in this world I hold dearer – and with the years that has become unshakable; one of the few things that are.

My father’s ideas about love were in a certain sense down-to-earth, but true nonetheless, as will be recounted later. The warmth of their relationship is easy to read in my father’s descriptions from the years I was staying in the United States. She was his greatest strength:

Last evening (night), when I had gone to bed, your mamma and I talked a little about you. She said she would write to you, but then said: “The worst of it is, one never knows what is for the best in these matters – you know that, and so do we both.” Then she patted me on the head and said good night, and she fell asleep, but I lay awake a little while and thought, as I have often thought before, what an enormous thing it is that this frail woman is many times stronger than I.

About my father’s marriage proposal there is a story that reveals him no less than it does the changed customs of the age. He recounted it to me in a letter so that I might consider “whether there might not be something sensible to be found in it.”

When I met your mother in the summer of 1923, I was reading for my law examination. I did not know then what she would say to my proposal. I wrote her a letter and told her how things stood, adding that if she refused, I would take it very hard and it would disturb my studies; if she accepted me, that too would delay me in my studies. I therefore thought it best to receive no answer until after my examination in the month of February 1924. – So I read for the examination and took it after 2½ years (having also taught for 1 year), the third-highest law examination result at the University. – Much has happened since then, of course, but naturally it is clear to me that I owe more to no person than to your mamma, and after the experience of all these years, I cannot imagine a more perfect person.

The occasion for these writings of my father’s was his worry that I intended to marry at an inopportune point in my studies. Much had changed in those matters since my parents wed. When my father finished his studies he was completely indebted,

and that being so, marriage was out of the question. He therefore worked himself to the bone for a year and a half until the debts were paid in full. My mother had to wait in the meantime. They tied the knot on 30 May 1925.

My parents’ close acquaintance thus came about through the doing of Sigurður Jónasson. He figured prominently in the family’s story, and so this singular man deserves a fuller account. Sigurður was the life of the party in his student years and indeed long afterward. He was a big man and imposing in stature, but he was given to drinking to excess. On one occasion he is said to have sat at Hótel Borg, neighing terribly and declaring himself to be a horse. To prove his point he began devouring the tulips that stood on the tables there. Jóhannes of Borg is then said to have appeared with a bridle, which he put on Sigurður, led him out onto Austurvöllur and tethered him to a post. Sigurður also claimed that he could leave his body and there enjoy the assistance of a deceased physician in another world. From there he received numerous magnificent ideas, many of which would bring him money. Once he showed up tipsy at a meeting with my father and said he had spiritual sources confirming that a ship of gold was to be found in Húnaflói. My father was not exactly thrilled. I, on the other hand, was.

Sigurður sat on the town council for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) at the same time my father sat there for the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Sigurður was one of the town council’s foremost enthusiasts for harnessing the Sog river and for other large-scale projects. Despite his various flaws, my father relied on him greatly for good works and, among other things, persuaded him to turn his back on his old comrades and take a seat on the Progressive Party’s list in the town council elections of 1938.

Sigurður was a man of enterprise with a great deal in circulation. He had in fact become a man of considerable wealth by the beginning of the war thanks to profitable dealings. He did a great many unusual things. He bought Geysir in Haukadalur and gave it to the nation in order to save the hot springs from the hands of foreigners. No less princely was his gift to the Icelandic state of Bessastaðir as a presidential residence — he even threw in the balance of a savings-bank book to cover the debts encumbering that ancient chieftain’s seat.
Marrying Up in Means

My parents made a prenuptial agreement upon their marriage, as was common when girls from well-to-do families married men of lesser means. These agreements were often made at the initiative of the girls’ fathers, who wished to secure for their daughters separate ownership of the assets they brought into the household, and thereby a measure of financial security. My father was not unfamiliar with such
agreements, for they were recorded and witnessed at the town magistrate’s office, where he was a deputy.

The prenuptial agreement shows that my mother contributed nearly all the furnishings of the household and, in addition, a deposit in a savings book with the National Bank of Iceland (Landsbanki Íslands), a total of 29,103 krónur, which was a considerable sum. There is a long list of the items in her separate ownership: oak furniture for the dining room, eight chairs, a buffet and a cabinet. Two made-up beds, nightstands, wardrobes and linen cupboards, plus a towel rack for the bedroom. A bureau, two upholstered chairs, a divan, a table and a carpet for the sitting room, along with silverware, tablecloths and kitchen utensils, towels and curtains, to name but some of it. Everything was conscientiously entered in the books in my father’s handwriting, like the other prenuptial agreements during his time as deputy.

I cannot imagine how he felt inside while writing this out. This was something most of those who married “above themselves” in means had to accept. What my father brought to the household he had earned by his own labor. He came from poor people.

Grandfather Steingrímur had made his money building houses, for he was a prolific master builder. His family traced its roots to Skagafjörður; he was of the so-called Steingrímur line (Steingrímsætt) from up north. In Reykjavík he built many beautiful houses. It suffices to mention the Women’s College (Kvennaskólinn) and Thor Jensen’s house on Fríkirkjuvegur, the old Teachers’ College (Kennaraskólinn), where the offices of the Teachers’ Union (Kennarasambandið) are now, and Jón Þorláksson’s house on Hverfisgata. Some of these houses he owned and rented out. My mother sometimes recalled that he would often send her and her sister down to the Women’s College with the bill for the rent.

Shortly after word got out that I was working on my biography, I received a lovely letter from Helgi Falur Vigfússon, who lives in Sweden. We have never met, but he wrote that his grandfather had worked with my grandfather Steingrímur on the construction of these houses. He included one of the best descriptions of my grandfather that I know of, though I have heard many. The letter says: “Steingrímur was true and whole, cautious yet enterprising, loved and respected by all for his fine qualities, instructive and encouraging, and among friends cheerful and merry.”

Grandfather Steingrímur was generally very well liked. I benefited from this when I began dabbling in carpentry. Once I sought materials for building from Kristján the wainwright. He had a workshop on Grettisgata and a great deal going on. His answer I shall never forget: “Hermann’s son gets no stick of wood from me. It is quite another matter for the grandson of the late Steingrímur. He can have all the wood he wants.” Kristján disagreed with my father in politics.
Some time ago I came into possession of the remains of a chest of drawers that is said to have been
the journeyman’s piece of Grandfather Steingrímur. It must once have been a treasure, but it was in very poor condition. I restored the chest of drawers and it is a great favorite of mine.

Grandmother Margrét was Þorláksdóttir, from Þórukot on Álftanes. She was of the Húsatóftir line (Húsatóftaætt). Grandmother was forceful and managing, kept everything well organized and maintained a good home. During her married years many apprentices trained under Grandfather and took their meals with the couple. When Grandfather Steingrímur died in 1930, my father made the decision on Grandmother’s behalf to sell most of their property. The money was deposited in a savings book. Grandmother Margrét thus had enough to live on for the rest of her days. She lived with us the whole time after my grandfather’s death. She had a flat of her own in the Ministerial Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn) and later in our house at Tjarnargata 42, where she had a separate entrance.

I was a great favorite of this dear grandmother of mine. She often slipped me a króna, or even a five-krónur coin, and told me to nip down to the Uppsalir cellar shop (Uppsalakjallari) and get myself something. I would go and usually get chocolate or some other sweets. A five-krónur coin bought a great deal of goodies. She also gave me a violin that Grandfather had owned, intending for me to learn to play it. Grandfather was apparently a fine violinist and as a youth played for dances on Álftanes. I had no idea how to handle an instrument and remember only once trying to get a sound out of the violin. I broke three or four strings. Grandmother took the violin and gave it to another of her grandchildren, Magga, my mother’s niece, who owns it still. Now I sorely regret losing that violin, for my children could doubtless have gotten the hang of it much better than I did. The violin is among the most beautiful-sounding of instruments.

Grandmother said I had inherited my interest in carpentry from Grandfather Steingrímur. She therefore gave me a splendid chest that held his old carpentry tools. They were handmade, and a special place was skillfully fitted out for each and every one of them in the chest. When the family moved to Tjarnargata 42 in my teenage years, the chest was kept in the garage while the interior of the house was being painted. When someone went to fetch it, not a trace was to be found. The chest had vanished. Numerous tradesmen had had it before their eyes for days on end, but no one claimed to know what had become of it. I greatly mourned the loss of that fine piece.

When Grandmother Margrét had grown infirm, she had no choice but to move to the Grund old people’s home. Those were heavy steps for her. She would rather not have gone there, even though we lived a short distance away and Mamma visited her daily. Grandmother, however, needed nursing care, so there was nothing else to be done. Grandmother Margrét died after I had left to study in the United States. When I said goodbye to her in late summer she said: “We shall probably not see each other again, Denni dear.” She proved right about that.
My Mother

My mother’s full name was Vigdís Oddný Steingrímsdóttir. She was born on 4 October 1896 and was thus a scant three months older than my father. From her parents she received a traditional upbringing which I think could fairly have been called strict. In photographs of the sisters from their childhood years they are usually very well turned out, wearing fine hats. Mamma seldom spoke of her growing-up years.

My mother was an unassuming woman, free of all pretension. Early in the day she usually wore what was called a morning gown. This was a knee-length dress or apron tied behind the back with a belt. If she went out on an errand in town, or guests arrived, she changed into Danish dress. That was what ordinary suits were long called, to distinguish them from Icelandic dress, which meant the upphlutur or the peysuföt costume. Grandmother Margrét always wore Icelandic dress. That was the everyday clothing of her generation. When my mother dressed up, I thought her exceptionally elegant. She would then wear either fine dresses, which she bought on her travels abroad, or the skautbúningur festival costume, which she wore on ceremonial occasions.

Mamma was dark-haired, with gentle eyes. She was, however, by no means without temper or opinions. There was no mistaking it when she was displeased about something. Then her face could take on a sterner look. Yet very few ever saw her lose her temper. She did not parade her feelings and was restrained in her bearing. She bore all sorrow in silence.

She was both prudent and intelligent, and her prudence showed itself in many things. She often let Pabbi believe he was deciding something that she had in reality long since decided. She always took care to include him in the deliberations. I remember, for example, how she let him think he was being allowed to choose the upholstery for the chairs in the living room. In reality she had chosen it long before. This shrewdness of my mother’s proved better provisions for the road in politics and coalition government than almost anything else. There, many a piece of upholstery must be chosen, and everyone wants to have their say.

My mother graduated from the Commercial College (Verslunarskólinn) in 1913 with high marks. Studying came easily to her. I heard this myself from an old teacher of hers, Bogi Ólafsson. He taught me English in secondary school and lived across from us on Tjarnargata. It sometimes happened that we walked together on the way home from the Secondary School (Menntaskólinn). When I was in the second year I caught scarlet fever. I was immediately placed in quarantine, as was the custom in those days, and was out of school for some time. A little while later, Bogi called to me one day across the street:

“Steingrímur! Come here and speak with me.” He always used the formal form of address. “You have been absent a long time. I suggest you visit me in the near future. We shall catch up on the English.” The progress must have been somewhat slow in coming, for on one occasion Bogi hurled my exercise book at me and snapped: “You are a damned dolt and no mistake. What a difference there is between you and your mother.” Then he added: “She is one of the best students I have ever known.”

After finishing her Commercial College examination, my mother went to Denmark, which was uncommon for young women in those years. She stayed there for two years, first studying at a well-known school of home economics and then working in a bank. She was good with languages, spoke good English and passable German. Danish she spoke fluently. This was unusual in that day, especially among women.

My mother was religious and proceeded on the assumption that all people were good. It was in her nature to trust people, and she would regularly speak up in someone’s defense if she heard them spoken ill of. She had a rich gift for making high and low alike feel welcome. She was sociable and enjoyed having visitors. Much often rested on her and the household where politics was concerned. Her women friends were frequent guests as well. She called those gatherings ladies’ parties (konuboð). Not seldom did I manage to sneak some of the waffles and cakes that were usually on the table on those occasions.

My mother worked a great deal in women’s organizations, took part in founding the Housewives’ School (Húsmæðraskólinn) in Reykjavík in 1942 and sat on its board until 1974. Around the same time she established a prize fund at the school. It is named after her mother, Margrét. She built the fund up with steady contributions, and from it prizes were awarded each year to the students who excelled in the housewifery department.

The home was her place. Crowds of people visited her there all her life, among them relatives from the numerous Húsatóftir clan (Húsatóftaætt). My mother and grandmother were very devoted to their kin. Various others also sought out their company. The discussions at the kitchen table were wide-ranging. Issues were analyzed to the marrow, stories were exchanged, and people were weighed and measured. Politics was often discussed. My mother had definite opinions about it. Especially if she felt the Conservatives or the Communists were behaving badly.

The discussions were generally calm in tone. My mother was very quick with words, and there were not many who could hold their own against her when she was in full flow in the kitchen. That was her parliament chamber. She never sought any direct involvement in politics in the public arena, and she never spoke at meetings. It would not have occurred to her.
She was nonetheless active in the national federation of Progressive Party women, which one might say was founded in the living room at home in 1945.

My mother formed a protective wall around the family and my father. Once I had come to years of discretion, I regularly exchanged views with my father on national affairs. When I was living abroad I wrote him, among other things, sharply worded letters criticizing his government. I would then receive reprimands from my mother, in which she pointed out to me the difficult position my father was in. He had to mediate between irreconcilable viewpoints, and I ought to support him in that. This was in the days of the left-wing government. No doubt much of what my mother said was right. I was young and categorical.
A Housewife with All Her Heart

Keeping house and the work of a housewife were for my mother not a burden or an obligation but an ambition and a life’s work. Nor was the task an ordinary one, for countless banquets and a ceaseless stream of guests came with my father’s leadership role. The household chores were manifold in a large home. My father never touched them. He seldom looked into the kitchen except to find out what was for dinner once he had grown hungry. Then Mamma would usually chase him out good-naturedly and tell him not to meddle in the cooking. On mountain trips, Pabbi and I usually carried food prepared in advance. Those outings were rarely so long that he had to cook for himself. I cannot remember ever seeing him preparing food. I believe my father likewise never washed up or cleared away after a meal, and he once remarked that he knew nothing of such things. Nor would my mother hear of it. In this respect I am little better myself, and I very rarely wash up, though I know how.

In his later years my father valued my mother’s contribution more highly than that of most others, and he strongly pressed her qualities upon me when the time came for me to choose a wife. About her he said in a letter:

Self-denial, moreover, is not always a torment; – a fitting challenge and self-denial is often one of the highest pleasures in life, and without it a man gets nowhere – and does not become a man. When do you think your mamma feels better than in self-denial and struggle for you children and me – even though none of us has fully appreciated it? And after she has prevailed she feels best – though she may be tired. But this has also distinguished her as a woman whom all respect for her strength of character. After the duties and the struggle, the joy of rest and play first becomes true pleasure.

In my childhood, Mamma was the shelter and Pabbi the hero. To tell the truth, I believe it was one of the greatest strokes of fortune in my life that my mother worked at home. She looked after the household superbly. Her cooking was famous. She was renowned for her dexterity, her sewing and needlework. Most of the clothes we children wore she sewed herself, and it was a matter of great pride to her that we were well dressed. She also loved the arts and played the piano. In much of what my mother did one could see that she had an artistic gift.

The division of labor between my parents was clear-cut, and that was how they both wanted it. I learned this once and for all. During my secondary-school years, we siblings once went with our parents east to Hallormsstaður. Pabbi was then an ordinary member of parliament in the opposition. Mamma fell ill and was fetched in haste by an airplane that landed on Lögurinn. Pabbi went with her to town. It turned out to be a stomach ulcer. Nothing displeased my mother more than having this mentioned. She never spared herself, and the ulcer flared up again.

I became very interested in this and read a great deal about the disease, especially about diet. In a book by a Swedish physician I came across the sovereign remedy kruska. It was a coarse-grain dish with wheat bran, oatmeal and raisins. Not unlike what is called muesli today. I made kruska for Mamma and the rest of us. The whole family ate kruska, and I am convinced that it did my mother, at the very least, a great deal of good. That is where my interest in healthy eating was kindled, and it has stayed with me ever since.

I also read that too much strain could cause stomach ulcers. When we moved from the Prime Minister's Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn) to Tjarnargata 42, there were no longer any girls to help Mamma. The stream of guests, however, was hardly any smaller. On one occasion, when there had been an unusually heavy flow of visitors, I had a word with Pabbi. I pointed out to him that there might be a connection between the stomach ulcer and excessive strain. The ulcer could flare up again if the burden on Mamma became too great. My father said I was probably quite right about that. The next morning I met Mamma, and, contrary to all custom, she called me Steingrímur. I understood at once that she was in a heavy mood, which was very unusual. She called me into the sitting room and said: "Steingrímur, I understand you have been meddling in matters between me and your father." I flinched but admitted it. Then she said, more firmly than she had ever spoken to me before: "I do not want you, Steingrímur, interfering in how we divide our duties between us. When I married your father I was determined to make him a good home. I want no interference in that and I refuse to accept any." I trudged out.
Even though my mother had grown up in considerable affluence, nothing was ever spent

on unnecessary things in the household. Mamma was very careful with money. She received a fixed portion of Pabbi's salary every month. He never concerned himself with how she spent that money. I later found out that she set a considerable part of it aside. In 1949, when I had come to the United States, I wanted to buy myself a car. I had earned some money and wanted to use it, but I was somewhat short. Among other things, I sold my stamp collection, and I regretted it deeply for a long time. It was a very good one. Among other things, it contained envelopes from the Italian squadron flight, which now sell for a hundred thousand krónur apiece. My collection, however, went for a pittance, so I was still short of money for the car purchase.

I wrote home to find out whether I could get a loan. My father, however, was against the purchase and thought I had no need of a car. I therefore expected to bid farewell to the dream of buying a car. So I was both astonished and delighted when a check from my mother lay inside a letter that reached me shortly afterwards. My father knew nothing about it. He told me later that she had set this money aside from the housekeeping funds. When my mother died, she left behind a savings book. In it one could see that in this way she had accumulated considerable sums as the years went by. From there had come various things that she had contributed to us children.

My mother had an older sister, Sigríður. They were close friends. In their younger years they went camping a good deal, which was unusual then, especially for girls. Once they traveled by ship up to Borgarfjörður and climbed Baula together with their girlfriends. On another occasion they set out on quite a long cycling tour around the South of Iceland. Some delightful photographs survive from it. Among other things, they had to wade across several rivers. My mother was always a great lover of the outdoors.

Sigríður studied photography and married Björn Rögnvaldsson, a master builder whose family came from Skagafjörður. They lived on Bergstaðastræti, diagonally up from the house my parents built at Laufásvegur 79. Sigríður and Björn had four children. Margrét is the eldest, and then twin sons were born to them who were about my age. We were considerable playmates, but I largely lost contact with them when I went to the Menntaskólinn. My relationship with their sister Magga and Sigurður Úlfarsson, her husband, on the other hand, was close for a long time and is still good.

My aunt Sigríður died in childbirth in 1935, far before her time, but the child survived. My mother took her sister's death very hard, and Grandmother took this newborn grandchild of hers into foster care. It was a boy who was christened Sigurður Birgir, and he stayed with us until his father Björn remarried. Siggi has now passed away.
My Father

My father, Hermann Jónasson, was born at Syðri-Brekkur in Skagafjörður shortly before noon on Christmas Day, December 25, 1896. He was the son of Jónas Jónsson and Pálína Björnsdóttir. I came to know Pabbi's parents, Grandpa Jónas and Grandma Pálína, well, because I spent some six summers in the countryside at Syðri-Brekkur. I describe them later in this book.

My father was a man of medium height, stockily built, muscular and well proportioned, handsome in appearance and striking in countenance. His bearing and demeanor were thought to testify to firmness and strength of will, to borrow the wording from a description by Karl Kristjánsson, member of parliament and an old schoolmate of his, who also described my father's manner well when he said that he did not toss greetings far and wide around him, but was considerate and warm in his greetings to all who approached him in peace.

Many people remember my father for various pranks or high spirits. Competitiveness, playfulness, and an insistence on having time for himself and his family were the three things his colleagues in parliament felt characterized him. They often told me stories of how he was apt to jump flat-footed up onto the meeting table in the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) caucus room, and many had at the ready stories of his wrestling bouts with Karl Kristjánsson in there.

It is not strange that these traits stand out in many people's minds. I witnessed it when Pabbi and a visiting policeman competed at jumping flat-footed onto the cabinet table in the Government Offices (Stjórnarráðið). It was impossible to tell them apart until they had stacked two or three books on top of the tabletop to increase the height. There are countless stories of this kind. Ólafur Thors remembered my father for disappearing in the middle of a government-formation meeting — in order to take a bath! Ólafur said he had readily agreed to it. The Progressive Party's parliamentary group awaited the outcome of the meeting impatiently, and some were astonished when Pabbi arrived rather late to meet the parliamentary group with wet hair.

When Pabbi was born, however, he did not keep anyone waiting. The story goes that the birth happened so quickly that there was no time to fetch help. My grandmother, Pálína, therefore had to make do with the assistance of a woman nearby who lived on one of the parcels of the farm at Syðri-Brekkur. At that time three households shared the property. Grandma no doubt guided her herself, though, for she was by then already a widely renowned and thoroughly experienced midwife, besides being the mother of four children. She practiced midwifery continuously for fifty-two years, longer than most other midwives in this country.
When I stayed with Grandma Pálína and Grandpa Jónas and the other folk at Syðri-

Brekkur in my childhood years, I heard numerous stories from my father's formative years in Skagafjörður. He grew up among six siblings in a turf farmhouse at the beginning of the century. Means were scant and dreams could be costly. Especially if one's will was set on education. The couple at Syðri-Brekkur could only afford to support one of their four sons through schooling. The choice fell on my father, although he was the youngest. Higher education was probably never mentioned in the same breath as his two sisters. For his studies he enjoyed the support of the whole family.

My father's mind was always set on learning. He was bookish all his life and owned, among other things, a good collection of poetry books. He drew on them a great deal, but no less on translated novels and other writings. The Sagas of Icelanders and Hávamál were dear to him, and he thought highly of Stephan G. Stephansson. In his letters he frequently quotes from what he has read, and he often expounds on lines of verse or the substance of poems. He himself composed verses and poems, many of which are good, and some became famous throughout the country.

To pay for my father's schooling, his father was forced, among other things, to ask Rannveig of Svaðastaðir, a neighbor in the district, for a loan. Rannveig was no stranger to such dealings and counted debts owed by 109 farmers in the district and beyond when she died. She granted the loan grudgingly and set the condition that my father, once his studies were finished, should see to it that Greenland was won back from the Danes! Pabbi enjoyed telling this story later, even though he never fulfilled the promise.

Later, students of little means often sought help from my father, who smoothed their path to the utmost of his ability. To many of them he gave financial support by standing personal surety or issuing promissory notes. He was probably mindful of how painful it is to have one's future depend on others, for he made it a rule to tear up the promissory note as soon as such meetings ended. Nor do I ever know of him pressing for payment from these debtors of his.
Coatless in the Great Frost Winter

Whatever has been written about my father's upbringing in other books, his childhood was no bed of roses. In the most difficult moments of my life I benefited from the experience he had stored away. In his letters he instilled courage and optimism in me with recollections from his own life. In one place he says of his childhood:

By far my hardest time was my childhood – since then everything has steadily improved. "I think the hymn of praise to the delightful childhood is one of the greatest life-lies there is. It is like the thawing season of spring, the rivers

and the brooks overflow, tearing everything apart and shredding it. Everything lies gaping in wounds. Then comes the summer (the years of manhood) and heals everything, clothes it in flowers and grass, creates balance in the life of nature." Something along these lines were the words of Bernard Shaw, that great sage who died recently at 93 years of age. My life experience accords with the words of that wise man.

My father would have told this to no one but those closest to him, and nothing here is exaggerated. Few things were further from his nature than recounting his own hardships, still less exaggerating them. In most people's minds he has been first and foremost a hard-driving wrestling champion, competitive and playful. Yet he also had other sides, better hidden, rich in feeling, and a sensitive soul. They emerge clearly in his recollection from his youth in which he recounts his misfortune in love. The description is drawn from his letter to me, written nearly half a century after the events:

When I was at the lower secondary school in Akureyri I was by far at the top of the 1st and 2nd forms. Þorsteinn Jóhannesson, the pastor at Vatnsfjörður, was next. I then fell so much in love with a girl in Akureyri that school and studies vanished from my mind. I withdrew from school, – I, the boy who was then inspector scholae and chairman of most of the school's societies.

Poverty and lack of money meant not only scant means, worn clothes or poor fare. A destitute man could not marry, for it was not thought fitting to offer a prospective wife a life of complete uncertainty or hardship. My father hardly knew which way to turn. The account continues:

I did go back to school, however, and took a rather good, but not excellent, examination. I spoke with the girl; I wanted her to wait for me. She was half-undecided although she loved me, and I thought I loved her and would never love any other. I could not marry, had nothing to live on, and wanted to try to continue [my schooling]. When I rode Móskjóni, my brother Siggi's horse, north along the street in Akureyri on my way home from school that spring, I wept over my fate, rode so hard that I was to be arrested, but no one could catch me. When Móskjóni came at a gallop into the turn onto the bridge over Glerá, he skidded like a car in too sharp a turn, but by pure chance his feet found purchase on a stone and he made the bridge. – That is why our last hour did not come in Gljúfrin. When I came home I was a paralyzed man. But misfortune still pursued me – as I thought – I lost my best friend, him
drowned in Héraðsvötn – and in the autumn, when I was to go to school, everything at home burned.

That summer my father had worked night and day to earn money for his journey. He had taken every job that came his way — on the farm, as a hired hand, on bridge construction, and in the herring. He intended to get an education and be able to provide for a wife. After the hayfields had been mown and others were enjoying their rest, he stood on the meadow strips with his scythe aloft, sometimes in water up to his arms, wrestling with the stubborn mowing. In this way he earned himself an extra shilling. After all this toil, one can only imagine how he felt as he watched his childhood home burn and the fruits of his labor, the savings kept there, vanish in the flames. Everything he had scraped together, which was to pay for his studies at the Menntaskólinn in Reykjavík, burned. In a single night the dreams seemed turned to ashes. My father went south nonetheless:

I went south with 137 krónur and knew no one. I sold the clothes off my back, went without an overcoat all through the great winter of 1917–18. I fell ill from cold (everything in my room stayed frozen for three months of the winter) and from wretched conditions just when I was to begin studying for the examination. Still I struggled through — with a fever, a swollen head covered with sores: through the exam. Then when I came south after one year and intended to enter the sixth form [and] had begun the examination [...] it went badly. Then I met a schoolmate from the north who informed me that the girl had married up north. And my son, your father was then no greater a man than this: he went home to his dark little room on Lækjargata, got into bed and wept – abandoned the examination and lay in bed for two days. – But then a certain book lay on the table, the Biography of Skúli the Magistrate (Æfisaga Skúla fógeta), and I leafed through it [and] began to read; then this thought seized me: "You, Hermann, meant to make a man of yourself, and you are bending under the difficulties; – if you compare your trials with the trials of this man, you will see that you are no man at all – straighten yourself up." I got up, ate that evening, and once again chance intervened. I then met Kristinn Guðmundsson, later a doctor, and we decided to study together. During the winter I told him my story, which I then believed was the greatest tale of woe there ever was. – Since then we have been inseparable friends. I recovered completely and have long since become convinced that everything that had happened to me was the greatest blessing God has granted me.

My father completed his matriculation examination and enrolled in law at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands). He studied law in an astonishingly short time, three and a half years, and graduated with high first-class honors in 1924. By then he was 28 years old. After finishing his law degree he took a position as deputy to the town magistrate in Reykjavík, Jóhannes Jóhannesson. They became good friends even though Jóhannes was a convinced conservative. Shortly afterwards, however, there entered the scene the greatest shaper of destiny in my father's life, Jónas Jónsson of Hrifla.

Jónas was Minister of Justice and rarely hesitated over matters. He pushed through changes to the law on the office of town magistrate in Reykjavík and split it in two: the offices of city attorney (lögmaður) and chief of police. His opponents believed that by this he wanted to oust Magistrate Jóhannes for political reasons, and it is certain that Jónas let the magistrate understand that he would not get an office even if he submitted an application. Björn Þórðarson, a staunch Progressive, was appointed city attorney.

My father was the only applicant for the position of chief of police and was appointed at the beginning of 1929. No one criticized that appointment, and my father does not appear to have taken a party-political stance at that point in the story. As evidence of this, Magistrate Jóhannes urged Ólafur Thors to get my father to take the top seat on the Independence Party candidates' list in the town council elections a year later. It was not until later that my father's rapid rise began to arouse people's envy.
Wrestling King of Iceland

My parents knew of each other for some time before their acquaintance began in earnest. They first met when my father competed in the King's Wrestling Match (konungsglíma) at Þingvellir in 1921. My mother was there with her parents. The King's Wrestling Match was held on the occasion of the visit of King Christian X. Earlier that same year my father had thrown all his rivals in the Iceland Wrestling Championship (Íslandsglíman) and won the honorary title Wrestling King of Iceland (Glímukóngur Íslands). He was therefore invited to the match along with most of the country's best wrestlers. Everything went the same way there: my father threw everyone, and most people expected him to receive the king's cup. After the match, however, it was announced that it had not been a competitive bout, and that Guðmundur Kr. Guðmundsson would receive the prize for the most beautiful wrestling in the judges' opinion.

My father took this badly and believed there had been foul play. Others thought so too, and it became much talked about. My father won both honor and fame throughout the country for his feat, even though the king's prize went to another. Some time later he was presented with a beautiful silver cup from the Icelandic Wrestling Federation (Glímusamband Ísland
(Glímusamband Íslands) with the inscription: "The victor in the King's Wrestling Match at Þingvellir 1921." That cup I have at home.

My father never competed in glíma wrestling after this, although he was not old. He did not, however, hold these events against Guðmundur. He became our neighbor on Laufásvegur, and they were good friends — indeed, they were nearly the only Progressive Party men in that neighborhood. Guðmundur lived with his family on Bergstaðastræti. He had a son named Haukur, who was one of my best friends in those first years of my life. He died on his sickbed only six years old. It was a great sorrow.

Whenever my father was mentioned in public, it was invariably brought up that he was a wrestler or wrestling king. His political opponents were foremost in this, along with foreign newspapers. I think few things annoyed my father less. On the contrary, he drew from wrestling entertainment, play, and even a philosophy of life and good counsel. He had himself had to fight, and in the struggle of life a line is drawn between those who hold out and those who falter:

Life has never been and will not be – the proofs of that are plain now – any game, but a struggle, and those who do not understand that in time go under. [. . .] – I used to compete in wrestling matches in former days. Some of my many wrestling companions lost heart at a fall – or a knee-touch\ – and gave up hope of good or acceptable results. None of these men has turned out well; – they have all, when facing headwinds, lost courage in life, where everyone takes "falls" and knee-touches many times in the endless wrestling match of life. Other competitive wrestlers hardened in the match if they suffered a setback. They have also proved to be that way in the struggle of life – all of them became men, some with limited talents – but vigorous characters. "Talent and education are like a sharp and gleaming sword, but character is the hand that holds the sword" – and now forgive an old man's boasting, my son. As for me, it was the case in competitive wrestling that my opponents were reluctant to wrestle with me after I had suffered a setback. There was laughter among the athletes when one good wrestler said, when he was to wrestle a match against me – after I had fallen: "I want to fall; throw me at once." – My accidental fall was matched in their
\ Hnéskítur (knee-touch) was the term used in glíma when one of the wrestlers fell to his knee.
match against the fall my main opponent received from me. We came out equal. We wrestled to a decision and that went quickly.
In this long letter he spoke thus about the course of his life:

I have made countless blunders, my son, and taken many "falls" since then; it is not for me to blame others though they might meet with some "accident". – Everyone takes falls and scrapes his knees in life's wrestling match, deservedly or undeservedly, and it is not that which decides. The other thing is the main point, it settles the match – in glíma or in the struggle of life – whether the man, when he stands up again, is more determined than before – or slackens and gives up. The latter is the unforgivable thing.

In my eyes it has always been obvious on which side of the ridge my father landed. He always stood up; that he proved with his life. But it was no less important to him to instill courage in me and to draw out the fighting spirit, the competitiveness or the stubbornness in me. He gave me rules for living with encouragement rather than reproach, as he recalled in this letter:

That is why I think my heart has seldom been gladder than when you, after falling off a horse above S. Brekkur (do you remember?), stood up and said: "I am not afraid" – and showed that you meant it – got back in the saddle and held your own. Also when you, after illness before the matriculation examination, with little studying beforehand and not very high winter grades, "stood up" and made an effort that I shall never forget and that awakened great admiration among your classmates at the matriculation exam. They have often spoken of it to me.

I admired my father greatly and took him as my model. He truly was a great champion. At some point a comrade of his said that Pabbi had been a warrior, and a great hero he would have been had he lived in ancient times. When he wrestled he usually threw men with the first move. This was often criticized. People felt it did not make for enough of a match. He would often take wrestling holds on people long after he stopped competing, even as if involuntarily. Not everyone appreciated such falls. During radio debates in one of the hardest-fought election campaigns on record, in 1937, the men of the Progressive Party (framsóknarmenn) and of the Independence Party (sjálfstæðismenn) each had a room of their own at their disposal in the broadcasting house. Ólafur Thors happened to walk into the Progressives' room and bantered a bit with my father. They took each other by the shoulders, and in no time at all

Ólafur lay flat on the floor. He sprang up at once and grew angry over it. This gave rise to some newspaper coverage, and Morgunblaðið maintained, among other things, that my father had assaulted Ólafur!

Perhaps it is not strange that the wrestling champion loomed large in the public mind where my father was concerned. It is distinctive traits that set people apart. In the political arena, too, what people think attracts less notice than what is done. In politics my father was not much given to spending a long time on things. It was sometimes said that he took on the big issues and drew the main lines, while Eysteinn saw to trimming off the corners and following up closely. Eysteinn Jónsson was a man of great precision and always on the go. I came to know that later. He was apt to telephone at seven in the morning if he had gotten an idea.

My father could be hard-hitting. When he got angry he could curse people vigorously, as happens. On the rare occasions when he was in such a mood he was apt to call people "a damned wretch" or something in that vein. Then Mamma would often say: "Oh, Hermann dear, he really can't be that bad." My mother handled matters entirely differently. Many would say that she was the better half in their marriage, for she was always making allowances for people. She herself never swore.

My father's impulsiveness could also show itself in impatience. When he phoned for a taxi and was told that it would come in five minutes, he began to grow restless once a minute beyond that had passed. Then he would want to call and hurry things along. More often than not Mamma tried to calm him with something like "perhaps the poor man had gotten a flat tire".

My father was a man of tremendous exertion in everything he undertook. When he picked up a shovel he went at it so furiously that I have never seen anything like it. Once he allowed me to sit behind the wheel of the car at the forestry plantation south in Fossvogur. There was a stream there and a road running alongside. I can have been no more than 10 years old. As ill luck would have it, I backed the car so that one rear wheel went over the edge of the road and it was stuck fast. Pabbi scolded me for my clumsiness but seized a beam that was lying there, thrust it under the car, and we both heaved on it. Nothing moved, and he evidently felt I was only in the way and said: "Move aside, Denni dear." Then he let out a tremendous roar and up came the car. Then I understood what is meant when it is said that champions and gods change shape and run berserk.

Despite his forcefulness my father was not inflexible. Indeed it seems to me that his political career was characterized above all else by his frequently having to steer between skerry and wave. He wanted to remedy the Depression without resorting to the nationalization that was nonetheless on the platform of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn),

of the coalition partner in the government. He led governments on behalf of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), yet often had to go against the will of Jónas from Hrifla, who was for a long time the party's chairman and one of its foremost leaders. My father was the chairman of a centre party because, as he himself said, no accord was conceivable between the parties furthest to the right and to the left "unless a strong centre party mediated between them".
The Heart of Reykjavík

At first the family lived under the wing of my mother's parents on Amtmannsstígur. Amtmannsstígur 4 was a two-storey timber house clad in corrugated iron which Grandfather Steingrímur had built. Long after we had moved away from there it burned to the ground along with two neighbouring houses, and six more houses were damaged in the fire. The blaze occurred on 17 November 1946.

My first memories are from this house. I feel as though I sat on the knee of my grandfather, who died when I was two years old. My grandfather Steingrímur was a slender man with a grey beard. The part of the house I remember best was the staircase between the floors, which I found utterly remarkable. Grandfather had built it, along with much else, indoors and out. The banister was very beautifully curved and made of mahogany. It was a work of art, for grandfather was a master craftsman. He had a carpentry workshop in a shed out at the back.

Reykjavík was still being born during my growing-up years. The settlement lay "within Hringbraut", as people said — that old Hringbraut which was a real ring and ran where what is now called Snorrabraut lies, along the sea round to the west, to the spot where Hringbraut now begins by the JL building, and then east until the ring closed. Outside this area there was hardly any continuous settlement, only farmsteads. The streets were at best gravel roads. Cars were few, but horses drew the cart that collected the rubbish from every house. It was poured into tubs which were carried out to the cart and tipped into it. It was great sport to feed these horses bread. The ash heaps were by Vatnsmýrin, where the BSÍ bus terminal now stands. East of that area was the so-called Turn-of-the-Century Garden (Aldamótagarðurinn). There the people of Reykjavík were allowed to grow vegetables. No young lad was worth tuppence unless he stole turnips from there.

The building of the Reykjavík Grammar School (Menntaskólinn í Reykjavík) was the focal point of my childhood surroundings at Amtmannsstígur. Not only was it much taller and larger than the other houses, but the school green and the area around the school were also our main playing field. On the school grounds I got my first scrapes. In the diary this alone is written about the years at Amtmannsstígur:

I broke my leg when I was at Amtmannsstígur, probably about 3–4 years old. It happened when I was sliding on a belly-sled on the green by the Grammar School and got my leg caught under the iron bars of the fence below the green.

There, brainy schoolboys strutted about sucking on pipe stubs to try to look dignified, and comely girls had become a more common sight among the students than before. These people were to inherit the land and were preparing themselves for it. Yet it so happened that instead of the young people embracing the virtues and traditions of their elders, there was a spirit of rebellion in the school and much unrest. The main characters on the stage were two men, Jónas from Hrifla and Pálmi Hannesson. Jónas was one of the foremost leaders of the Progressives, the most powerful minister in the government, and unafraid to appoint his party men to any position whatsoever. When he got the power to do so, he chose a young natural scientist, Pálmi Hannesson, over a great many far more experienced teachers and schoolmen and made him rector of the school. Pálmi was an old schoolmate of my father's and later sat with him in parliament for the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Pálmi's appointment met with strong opposition inside the school and outside it, especially in Reykjavík, and people divided sharply into camps along political lines. The life courses of both Jónas and Pálmi became thoroughly interwoven with my story, and no less with my father's.

I was of course oblivious to all this as I walked or ran about the school grounds in those childhood years of mine. The young people who met one's eyes were grown-up people in fine clothes. The boys wore ties and the girls skirts. That was part of the schools. No doubt I gazed with curiosity at these people without becoming in any way aware of the turmoil in the school's life.

My parents built their first private home on the corner of Laufásvegur and Barónsstígur, at Laufásvegur 79, opposite the old Teachers' College (Kennaraskólinn), which my grandfather built. The construction work was overseen by Björn Rögnvaldsson, Mamma's brother-in-law. There we had much more room than at Amtmannsstígur, but we did not live there long, for in July 1934 my father became prime minister in the "government of the working classes". Then we moved to Tjarnargata 32, the Ministerial Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn).

Besides Grandmother Margrét, her foster-daughter also lived with us. My grandmother and grandfather had taken her in when she was very young. She was never called anything but Stella or Stella Steingríms, though that was not her correct patronymic. Her real name was Ingibjörg and she was the daughter of friends of my grandfather and grandmother. Stella was born on 8 October 1913 and was thus fifteen years older than I. I was very fond of her. She worked for my father at the office

of the Chief of Police and lived with the family from the time she lost her mother right up until she married. Her husband was Leifur Þórhallsson and they had two children, Steingrímur and Þórhallur. Stella died of cancer long before her time.

My father was one of the few who cultivated a garden in those years. He planted at Laufásvegur and no less at the Ministerial Residence. The trees standing there along Suðurgata were all planted by him. He always had a great interest in forestry. In Fossvogur he obtained land for afforestation, and there he pursued tree-growing. This was in all about 26 hectares which he received on hereditary lease. That meant that the state could take the land back whenever it needed to. My father was not allowed to sell the leasehold right, mortgage it, or dispose of it in any other way on his own. The conservatives' newspapers criticized this arrangement severely. They said that a fortune was being handed to the Chief of Police, since it would be a simple matter to sell the land for a hundred thousand krónur, which in those days was a considerable sum. In Fossvogur he established extensive forestry, and from there I have many good memories of working at my father's side. He was a farmer in the city.
The Depression Years in Iceland

In Iceland there was a depression, as elsewhere in the world, when I was growing out of my baby shoes. It left no country untouched except, so it seemed, the Soviet state of the revolution. Some therefore sought their ideals there, and the communists went from strength to strength. Unemployment soon became widespread. The Depression hit many people hard, and the liberalism of the nineteenth century sang its swan song, both in the minds and hearts of the people who had been cheated of their livelihood, and of the others as well. I believe my family lived fairly well. Grandfather was among the busier master builders in the town and owned houses and building lots. My father became Chief of Police before the Depression and thus had secure employment and certainly a decent income. I assume he could afford to build at Laufásvegur without plunging himself into heavy debt. He never wanted to be in debt. After he became prime minister his income increased further. Relative to the lowest wages, I believe a prime minister's income then was higher than it is now. Income disparity in society, however, has on the whole increased greatly from what it was then. In my opinion it has become far too great.

I believe the poverty of his early years largely determined my father's political stance. He was ill content with the unequal distribution. Destitution left a deep mark on his ideas and outlook on life. He regarded it as his chief task in politics to work the nation out of the Depression and to even out living standards in the country. He

was, on the other hand, never taken with nationalization, which the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and the socialists were fighting for at that time. He wanted private parties to be allowed to fend for themselves. He believed that companies should first and foremost think of their employees and the public. The common good was his chief aim.

During the Depression my father was worried not least about the towns and was called one of Jónas from Hrifla's "town radicals". The countryside fared better than the towns in this period. In the towns there was unemployment which many found hard to bear.

I never knew the poverty my father grew up with. I never remember suffering any want, and I had every option open to me. I have been told that I grew up with a silver spoon in my mouth, and perhaps there is a little something to that.
Police Batons on Laufásvegur

Probably all boys dream of being able to tell their friends that their dad is a cop. I could do better. My dad, you see, was the Chief of Police. I doubt that anyone on our street thought cabinet ministers or members of parliament as impressive as police chiefs and cops. Even my friends found Pabbi hardly as impressive after he became prime minister as when he was Chief of Police.

My best friends were Árni and Haukur. Haukur was, as mentioned before, the son of Guðmundur Kr. Guðmundsson, who was a Progressive like Pabbi. They were the exceptions that proved the rule, for on Laufásvegur the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) was the rule. Árni was the son of Árni J. Árnason, but I do not know where Árni's parents stood in politics. We kept up our friendship for a long time and still do. Once the two of us were down on the street when our adversaries came along. They were acting belligerently. My father was then Chief of Police and his car stood in the driveway. We ran there and got rubber batons out of the car. We then turned to face the pack of boys and swung our terrible weapons with hideous yells. The boys fled at once, panic-stricken, with cries and shouts: "They've got police batons! They've got police batons!" We won that battle. Árni became a leading figure in sports and an enterprising businessman. Among other things he founded and ran the firm Austurbakki, but he now lives in Florida. It is good to visit there and play golf with Árni.

I was young when my father was Chief of Police. Still, I remember that I was sometimes allowed to visit him at the police station. It was then in Arnarhváll but moved in 1935 into the old telephone exchange in Pósthússtræti, where previously the Children'

s School of Reykjavík (Barnaskóli Reykjavíkur) had been. The policemen of that era were many of them giants in strength. Lárus Salomonsson stuck in my memory. He was the brother of Gunnar, who displayed feats of strength all over the world, but Lárus was no lesser strongman. He often picked me up with one hand and hoisted me up towards the ceiling. That was of course a small matter, but I was at once hugely impressed by these men of might. In those days the police force in fact had need of all its strength, for there were quite a few scuffles in the town. The Gúttó Battle (Gúttóslagurinn) became by far the most famous. I do not, however, recall my father ever coming home injured, but I was so young then that of course it may have happened.

My father had in fact himself been made to feel the strength of these policemen of his. When he was made Chief of Police he was no doubt something of a kitten in their eyes. Things came to a head when he wanted to get them to take up gymnastics. These strong men considered they had no business doing physical training, and naturally they reckoned themselves fully a match for this stripling. My father hit upon the plan of calling the men into his office one after another and challenging them to glíma wrestling. He threw them all. From then on everyone showed up for gymnastics, the Chief of Police included.

Once my father called for Árni and me. He took us into the car and drove down to Vatnagarðar. There were then many aeroplanes on the sea there. We were thrilled by this adventure. It was the mass flight of the Italians. It attracted enormous attention. An Italian air fleet came here under the leadership of Italo Balbo, the Italians' minister of aviation and air marshal. He later became governor of Libya. My father met Balbo. I do not remember whether I saw him, for it was the aeroplanes that captivated my mind. There were about 20 of them.

Aeroplanes later became one of my chief interests when I began to build models. I still have the model books my father gave me. In them were all the main fighter planes in exact proportions and measurements. I built many types of aeroplanes. They could fly forward on rubber bands that drove the propeller. The hardest part was making the propeller precisely enough for the balance to be right. Later it became possible to get ready-made propellers. This was long before models came ready-made in plastic. But the drawings were precise and good. I sawed cross-sections out of plywood and glued thin strips of balsa wood onto the outside. Finally I covered the fuselage and wings with greaseproof paper. The planes could then be painted, and the insignia of the main air forces could also be bought — swastikas and the British roundels. We would then try to fly these off the balcony. Some glided passably. They seldom lasted long. Most of the models ended their journeys with crash landings of varying dignity in the garden.
"Did you land a blow on him?"

On Laufásvegur I felt the brunt of the so-called "eider duck affair" (kollumálið). Politics in those days was harsh and personal. In these matters the Progressives, with Tíminn and Jónas from Hrifla at the head of the column, were certainly no laggards behind anyone. Kristján Albertsson took Jónas on in single combat in his paper Vörður and paints this picture there:
Tíminn has taunted men with their poverty, their lack of money, their unemployment, with old age, with bodily defects, with insanity, time after time when the fury was at its greatest pitch.

Unfortunately this is an all too true testimony about the politics of that era. What I felt most, though, was what broke over Pabbi. It was no polite banter. Þorkell Jóhannesson, editor of Nýja dagblaðið, the Progressives' Reykjavík daily, summed up in this way the terms of abuse that the conservatives' papers, Vísir and Morgunblaðið, had rained down on Hermann Jónasson before the elections of 1934:
They have called him a "boor", a "fool", a "traitor to his country", a "stupid coxcomb", a "liar", an "idiot before the whole nation" some 40 to 50 times in the past year.
Þorkell added that the conservatives "scarcely possess a term of abuse which they have not used about H.J."

I was in my sixth year when this was written. In the papers it was asserted that the Chief of Police made trips out to Örfirisey to shoot eider ducks, which were protected. In the wake of this, one of the conservatives' candidates brought a charge. Pabbi was convicted in the lower court. He himself had in fact done the bidding of Jónas from Hrifla in a rather similar case. As Minister of Justice, Jónas ordered criminal proceedings against Magnús Guðmundsson for alleged financial misconduct. It fell to Pabbi to judge the case. He convicted Magnús, who by then had become Minister of Justice. That verdict was handed down the same day the Gúttó Battle was fought. These were times of strife. The Supreme Court overturned both of these verdicts.

The fury of politics did not pass us by. Even the kids were political. I was nicknamed "duck-killer's son" (kollubanasonur) and was in constant scuffles. Once I came home with a bloody nose. My mother did not like the look of things. She asked my father, who came home shortly afterwards, to step in and speak with the parents. My father looked at me and asked: "Did you land a blow on

him?“ I thought so. “Did he get a bloody nose?” “Yes,” I thought so too. “Then this should be all right,” said Pabbi. These were my first political battles. After this I put great emphasis on striking back at these opponents of mine, repaying like with like and refusing to come out the loser. These clashes stayed with me for a long time. Perhaps one could say that in them I received my political baptism of fire.

In the eider-duck affair, witnesses came forward who claimed to have recognized Pabbi from 300 meters away. They could not repeat that feat when it was re-staged.
