The eider duck was also supposed to have drifted ashore, but the wind blew in the opposite direction. Many people found that a strange piece of drift. The newspapers of the Progressives (framsóknarmenn) never called the case anything but the false-witness affair. I asked Pabbi myself whether he had shot the eider duck and he said that was an absurdity. In my mind that remains, together with the verse he composed. Pabbi was a fine versifier and the verse became famous across the whole country in an instant:
My life is nothing but a search for a wild swan. But I, as the whole nation knows, am only a duck-slayer.
Chapter Two
THE YEARS IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S RESIDENCE

I was in my sixth year when my father became prime minister, and what I remember most is that at first I was not at all pleased about moving away from my companions on Laufásvegur. I soon acquired new playmates, though, and friends at the primary school. From my first acquaintance with the Prime Minister's Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn) I remember how big and grand the house seemed to me. I liked the look of it. At that age, however, I had little idea of what being prime minister involved. What I did know was that my father had been travelling a great deal ever since he was chosen to stand for election in Strandir. I later heard many stories of those journeys when I myself stood for election in the Vestfirðir. Most of them are wreathed in considerable glory.

The atmosphere of the household changed thoroughly once we came to the Prime Minister's Residence. The bustle increased, and parlour maids and a chauffeur joined the household staff. His name was Arreboe Clausen; he was dignified in bearing and wore a remarkably fine hat. Arreboe had been known to take a drop now and then, but he got back on an even keel once he had a steady job, and he was a superb driver. He stood high in my esteem, and indeed in that of many others. Countless stories circulated about this dashing, elegant man. One of the most famous tells of the time my father lent the minister Skúli Guðmundsson a car and driver. Skúli always went hatless and was nothing like as dignified as Arreboe. Some said the reason was that Skúli's hat had blown into the grave of his first wife, while others insisted that Skúli had forgotten to take off his hat while the burial rites were read over his wife's remains and regretted it so deeply, once it was pointed out to him, that he vowed never to put on a hat again. On this trip of theirs, Arreboe and Skúli came to Klaustur, where they were given refreshments and lodging for the night. Arreboe, of course, was wearing the fine hat, and naturally everyone assumed he was the minister.

He was therefore shown to the seat of honour, and he is said to have held forth at great length while Skúli sat quietly by. The misunderstanding was not corrected until it was time to show the distinguished minister to the better bed for the night.

I had a lot to do with Arreboe, since his sons, the twin brothers Örn and Haukur, were among my best friends. They were rarely called anything other than the Clausen brothers or the Klásens. They lived in a basement flat at Vonarstræti 8 and later became nationally famous sportsmen and international champions in their disciplines. Their enthusiasm for sport was kindled early, and the same was true of me. Our friendship has lasted a lifetime, and probably few stand closer to them than I do. In those years I was one of the very few who could tell the twins apart, and I was sometimes brought in to intervene when they came to blows, which they did both often and even ferociously, being men of strong temper. Örn was stronger, but on the other hand Haukur was the faster runner. These were my first efforts as a mediator.

Of my other companions from primary-school days, Pétur Guðmundsson, airport director at Keflavík Airport, and Björn Þorláksson are among the most memorable. Björn was always called Bjössi, or Bjössi Þorláks, and came from staunch Conservative stock. Bjössi and I went together all through primary school and grammar school, but our paths parted soon after we finished our matriculation exams. We have nevertheless always remained on good terms.
The “Red Bloc” against the Conservatives

When my father was persuaded to stand for election, it was against Tryggvi Þórhallsson, who had been one of the foremost leaders of the Progressives (framsóknarmenn). He had recently broken away from the party and was now running in the name of the Farmers' Party (Bændaflokkurinn). Tryggvi was immensely popular in Strandir, and unseating him was no easy task. He was admired both inside the party and out for his eloquence and imposing presence. Admittedly, Tryggvi was suffering from some illness when this took place. My father therefore did not relish going up against this previously unchallenged leader. But he was a fierce competitor once the fight was on.

The people of Strandir laughed at the duck-slaying affair, since many of them had probably shot themselves an eider duck for the pot when the need arose. Indeed, some have maintained that the affair carried my father to power because it drew to him “attention mixed with sympathy”. That is surely too great a simplification. The elections in Strandir proved historic.

When I myself stood for election in those parts, many people told me that my father had managed to unseat Tryggvi because he reached the young people. They were taken with him, with his energy and his manliness. Thus I heard stories of

how he had walked over mountains and moorlands to meet people. One morning, when meetings were to be held in Árneshreppur later in the day, he had vanished from his bed when someone came to wake him. Shortly afterwards a man was seen standing at the very top of Kálfatindur, the highest mountain in those parts. Many found this symbolic, and it was much talked about. When the meeting began, everyone of course knew that Hermann Jónasson had climbed the highest peak while others lay sleeping. Yet no one expected my father to win. It was therefore one of the most talked-about results of the 1934 elections that he unseated Tryggvi. That surely played its part in making him prime minister, even though he had not previously sat in parliament.

My father began his political career on the Reykjavík town council. Elections were held in January 1930. By then he had become chief of police. The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) had two men elected: my father, who headed the list, and Páll Eggert Ólafsson. I once asked my father why he had not headed the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) list in those elections, as he had been invited to do, as I have mentioned before. He replied that he could not reconcile himself to the party's priorities. The Independence men put the value of wealth above the value of man. They thought of the companies rather than of their employees and the general public. That was contrary to my father's outlook on life. Ólafur Thors himself said the reason was that Jónas had already got to him.

My father was considered radical in his younger years and was counted among the “town radicals” (bæjarradíkalar) of Jónas from Hrifla. The town radicals sprang from Jónas's vision. He had gone to Britain and immersed himself in the politics there. My father and Jónas have been called “the innermost clique of the town radicals”, together with Eysteinn Jónsson, whom Jónas summoned south and made director of taxation. Eysteinn was at first the closest collaborator of Hrifla-Jónas. Later he became a kind of sworn brother of my father in politics. By then he and Jónas had drifted apart.

The political ideas of Hrifla-Jónas had a lasting influence. He founded the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), which was meant to become a workers' party. He also played a substantial part in founding the Progressive Party, which was to be a liberal party, a middle-class party, but to base its power on the farmers and the countryside. Jónas was nonetheless one of those men who wanted the Progressive Party to establish itself in the towns. My father's first candidacy in Reykjavík was part of that policy in action. Jónas was an incredibly far-sighted man.

The town radicals were concerned for the welfare of the working class in the towns and wanted changes in Icelandic society in the direction of the modern welfare state. Opposition to the Conservatives was another recurring thread in their thinking. The Conservatives

were the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and the Farmers' Party of Tryggvi Þórhallsson. In a speech at the party congress before the parliamentary elections of 1934, Hrifla-Jónas wanted the vote to be a choice between the conservative parties on the one hand and the Progressive and Social Democratic parties on the other. Those parties he called the democratic parties. Their opponents answered by naming these parties “the Red Bloc”.
The Government of the Working Classes

Jónas from Hrifla received the Progressive Party's undivided mandate to take charge of forming a government after the 1934 elections. He was most interested in cooperation with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn), while he called the Farmers' Party and the Independence Party the chief adversaries and warned against a “dictatorship of conservatives and Nazis”. The Social Democratic Party responded well to the idea of forming a government but flatly refused to have Jónas at its head. And there matters stood. Jónas then pointed to my father in his place, and he and Eysteinn were subsequently entrusted with forming a government. My father became prime minister, Eysteinn finance minister, and the Social Democrats' minister was Haraldur Guðmundsson, who became minister of industries. This was the Government of the Working Classes. It operated on the basis of the first coalition agreement ever made in this country. It was entirely in the spirit of international currents that involved more extensive planning in the running of states and enterprises than had been known before.

I consider the Government of the Working Classes to be among the more remarkable governments in the history of Iceland. It is my opinion that it has not been given sufficiently thorough treatment. Great feats were accomplished in those years. It was an incredible effort amid utter destitution. The government worked to establish herring factories, schools around the country, and public education. In those years a drive was launched to build roads throughout the whole country. They were laid not only to improve transport but also to provide employment. The Government of the Working Classes also tried, with its limited means, to build up the beginnings of a welfare system despite unemployment and hardship. To achieve its goals, compulsory civic labour was even resorted to.

After my father became prime minister in the 1950s, I criticized certain elements of this government's legacy in letters to my father, among them the monopoly position of the Milk Marketing Board (Mjólkursamsalan). It rested, among other things, on the so-called milk marketing laws enacted by the Government of the Working Classes. It is, however, very far from true, as has sometimes been claimed, that the milk laws together with the meat laws were the sole contribution of the Progressives and my father to the government's programme. That list would be long if everything were counted.
Just as the Social Democratic Party made my father prime minister

the Independence men lifted me into the same chair half a century later. At that time the Independence Party was the largest in parliament, and it was natural that the party's chairman, Geir Hallgrímsson, should become prime minister. Opinions about Geir's chairmanship were, however, divided within the Independence Party's parliamentary group. Some wanted to depose him as chairman. That would have been difficult for them if he sat in the prime minister's chair. For that reason the message came from the Independence parliamentary group that they preferred a Progressive to preside, with the Independence Party receiving more ministers in return. Geir delivered the message to me himself. I could clearly sense that this weighed heavily on him, for we had expected nothing other than that he would become prime minister. I felt the Independence Party treated Geir Hallgrímsson badly. He was the finest of men and one of the best colleagues I have known in my political career. Geir was foreign minister in that government, which was under my premiership. But that is a story of later times.

Relations between Jónas from Hrifla and my father soon began to cool after my father became prime minister. There were often little clique meetings in my father's office. His acquaintances from the party frequently dropped in on him. When I grew older I was sometimes allowed to sit and listen.

As my father and Eysteinn grew in stature, they no longer walked the same path as Jónas. Their ways parted over methods of work, not ideals. The disputes over men and issues that followed were simply the consequences of a breach of trust. When trust ebbs away, men stop talking to each other, and at the same time the will to compromise diminishes. Then matters are brought to a head, and these men did so without hesitation. A more unscrupulous adversary than Jónas can hardly be found.

Jónas demanded to know about everything that went on. After he and my father drifted apart, Jónas practically tried to spy on his words and thoughts. He telephoned the chauffeur Arreboe Clausen, whom he knew well, and wanted to know what was said in the back seat of the ministerial car. Arreboe replied: “It's the strangest thing, Jónas my friend. Since I started driving this car my hearing has deteriorated so much that I never hear a word of what is said in the back.” I think this story describes them both well. Arreboe never betrayed a trust.

It was not strange that the breach of friendship was hard both for the young men and for Jónas. Jónas had not only got my father to stand for the town council but also played the midwife's role in bringing him into national politics. Jónas introduced him to the leading men of Strandir at a party congress in Reykjavík in 1932, worked on the matter, and when the loose ends had been tied up he sent one of his mysterious telegrams north: “The house will be built on the foundation you laid.” My father thus owed his advancement to him to a considerable degree.

Jónas had also taken Eysteinn under his wing, made him his assistant and later got him into parliament. One of the things Jónas knew better than most others was how to get young people to work with him. That was the fiery spirit in him. On the other hand, he found it very hard to tolerate anyone overshadowing him or holding independent opinions. My father once said to me that, unfortunately, he and Jónas simply had not been temperamentally compatible. Jónas had wanted to decide everything and to hold men by the hand. Pabbi never wanted to discuss this history of conflict much. He was saddened by how it turned out. Nor did my father ever want to speak ill of Jónas beyond this: that it had been impossible to work with him. I know that Eysteinn said the same.

I never knew Jónas from Hrifla personally. In my mind he is one of the greatest generators of ideas of his time. He saw far ahead of others that the time had come to reshuffle the party system as the struggle for independence was reaching harbour. Like many geniuses, however, he had tremendous flaws, not least his temperament and his reluctance to let others receive fair credit. His career as minister of justice was altogether extraordinary. His methods of work became his downfall.
The Prime Minister's Residence, Tjarnargata 32

When we moved into the Prime Minister's Residence, Grandmother Margrét and Stella, her foster-daughter, moved with us and lived there in their own quarters, as I have mentioned before. The house had been imported from Norway and was owned by Hans Ellefsen, a Norwegian fishing-industry magnate. Originally it stood at Sólbakki in Önundarfjörður, where the member of parliament Einar Oddur Kristjánsson now lives. Ellefsen ran a whaling station there. The whales moved, however, and Ellefsen followed them with his station east to the fjords. The story goes that he thereupon sold the house to Hannes Hafstein. They were good friends, as became famous, for the purchase price is said to have been merely nominal — some say one króna. Hannes had the house moved to Reykjavík and lived in it during his time as minister.

A few years ago I was sent a photograph from Norway showing the old house where it stood by Önundarfjörður. An acquaintance of mine had come across it and obtained a copy. It shows that the house was added to when it was erected on Tjarnargata. A storey was built beneath it and the wings extended to the west. My father was the last prime minister to live in the house with his family. Since we moved out nearly nine years later, the residence has not been a dwelling, though the name has remained. The Prime Minister'

s Residence has been used by ministers for receptions of many kinds, banquets and various other purposes. In what was once my parents' bedroom, Davíð Oddsson, for example, had his temporary office in 1997 while the Government House (Stjórnarráðshúsið) was being renovated.

The main entrance is, and was, on the northwest side, and steps lead up to the front door from Tjarnargata. The first room on the left, on the Tjarnargata side, was my father's office, which was never called anything but the kontór. There he received numerous visits from comrades and members of parliament of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Karl Kristjánsson, member of parliament, was a great friend of Pabbi's. He came often, and they were apt to wrestle. These were often mighty struggles, for Karl was both agile and strong. On one occasion my father wanted to test whether Karl could escape from his famous heel-hook, a move he executed better than other men. The bout ended in a great tumble. They landed on the corner table of the office, which was smashed to pieces. My mother then came and broke up the match. Karl did not manage to counter the heel-hook that time.

Among my father's other guests, Eysteinn Jónsson should be named first. The members of parliament Gísli Guðmundsson, Skúli Guðmundsson, Páll Zóphaníasson and Páll Hermannsson also came quite often. Þórarinn Þórarinsson, editor of Tíminn, was a frequent visitor, especially after my father became chairman of the Progressive Party, for in those days the party newspapers were truly party newspapers, in effect under the direct control of the chairman and the secretary. If something in Tíminn annoyed my father, he would telephone and give Þórarinn a thorough scolding. They were, however, good friends.

No doubt most of the leading men of the Progressive Party visited the home in those years, at the Prime Minister's Residence and later at Tjarnargata 42. The one exception was Jónas Jónsson from Hrifla. He came only as an invited guest to official banquets.

Beyond the kontór was the so-called middle parlour. Next came the red parlour, or the ladies' parlour, as it was sometimes called. In earlier times the custom was that after dinner the men went into the middle parlour and smoked cigars while the ladies sat in the red parlour. Later these rooms were combined. These rooms were beautifully furnished and were forbidden territory for us children. Beyond the red parlour was a small conservatory, which has now been altered. I think that is a pity. It was a delightful room, though its architecture probably did not harmonize with the rest of the house. Among the flowers stood three chairs and one table. People withdrew there if they wanted to talk in private. All this was on the Tjörnin side of the first floor.
Opposite the two formal parlours is the dining hall. It seats up to forty people and is a very stately banqueting room. There the family ate

together in the evenings. The staircase up to the upper floor leads from the entrance hall. Between the dining room, the living room, and the staircase there was a short passage out to the kitchen wing, which faced the garden.

On the second floor were bedrooms, a little sitting room that my grandmother had for herself, and my mother's needlework room. The Danish royal couple stayed in my sister's and my rooms when they visited Iceland in 1937. We had been sent to the countryside that spring. I believe the queen slept in my room. Above the kitchen wing was Grandmother's bedroom and the room of the parlour maids who helped in the household. There was also a special kitchen nook that Grandmother and they had to themselves.
The attic was one open space except for two rooms at the south end. One of them was something of a junk room, but the other I took over for carpentry. Laundry was hung up in the attic now and then.

Under the whole house is a cellar, which one went down into by the kitchen. There was a large, unpartitioned space, a cellar entrance, and several rooms. In the west end is a room that was usually kept firmly locked. It was the house's wine cellar, which I believe is still used for the same purpose. As in other houses in Reykjavík, some years there were rats about in the cellar. Once I came upon a rat that was stranded on the steps leading up from the cellar door. I helped it up into the garden, and it made off in some haste once it got there. If this had been in a fairy tale, it would no doubt have repaid me later for sparing its life. But the Ráðherrabústaður rat did not bow even once, and I never saw it again.

After I became prime minister I naturally came often to the Ráðherrabústaður. On my first visit I went through the whole house, up to the attic and into my old room. Soon I began to think about maintaining the house. I had the floor in the banquet hall renewed, and the north side. I never had the financial means that my successor Davíð Oddsson has. He has had the whole house thoroughly renovated inside and out. He deserves thanks for that. I did not consider myself entitled to take so much money for the work from the budget. I planned to fix the house up little by little.
Parties and gatherings of friends

The home was entirely given over to politics. Much more than homes are today. Pabbi was often travelling around the country. Though Mamma of course backed him up loyally, I would not be surprised if she had wished he were more at home. In those days one did not dash off by plane to Akureyri and back in an evening. It took, for example, two days to get north to Skagafjörður to Grandfather
and Grandfather and Grandmother. One travelled either by ship or car, or went on horseback. When my father went on trips or to meetings in Strandir he was usually away for a week.

When people from Strandir came to town, the home was always open to them. It was taken for granted that they be offered food and coffee, and lodging if need be. That has vanished. It is no longer known for people to come uninvited on such visits. Some were frequent guests, and my parents considered that a matter of course. My father felt he was repaying favours. He stayed with them up north, as I also did when I stood for election. I can hardly remember ever staying at a hotel in Strandir or the Westfjords while I was in politics, unless I had the whole family along.

From my childhood years, Dr. Bjarni Sæmundsson the fisheries scientist is among the more memorable guests of the household. He lived in Þingholt and was an old and gentle man, lean, grey-haired and bearded. I was often allowed to come down to his basement, where he had his laboratory. That was a great world of wonders. Bjarni sought out the company of my mother and grandmother a great deal. He and Grandmother Margrét were first cousins. Bjarni's father Sæmundur and my great-grandfather Þorlákur were brothers.

After we moved into the Ráðherrabústaður he often brought with him all kinds of fish, which he asked my mother to cook. He had a high opinion of her cooking. I remember that he once came with redfish and got Mamma to cook it. Redfish was generally thrown away or rendered down. We did not think much of it. Bjarni, however, said that redfish would prove to be one of our chief commercial fish, though it would be later. He also brought lobster and shellfish. I tasted crab too and thought it good, ugly though it was. All this my mother cooked according to the rules of the art. This delicious raw material was otherwise all thrown overboard. In the utilization of seafood and the resources of the ocean, Bjarni was far ahead of his time.

Various people also accepted a lump of sugar dipped in coffee from my mother in the kitchen. Many of my father's acquaintances had to get used to the fact that the prime minister was not always in or could not receive them. It often happened that these men came first and foremost for my mother's coffee and a chat over the refreshments. Among them, Benedikt Benjamínsson was memorable — or Bensi the Strandir postman, as he was usually called. He had been a staunch Tryggvi man when my father stood for election in Strandir. Nevertheless my father got his company on the first journeys and borrowed horses. Benedikt carried letters to farms from Hólmavík northwards and always had with him a flask of moonshine which he offered his travelling companions a sip of, especially when the weather was cold. It was often with the words: "Aren't you cold, my dear?" On one of their first journeys my father answered with a verse:
I am not cold, my dear, though a gust blows about me, now that I drink your precious wines, you incomparable postman.
There are other versions of this verse, but that is how I first heard it.

It so happened that the Strandir postman soon transferred his devotion to Tryggvi over to my father and became one of his staunchest supporters. Nor did he hold back in his descriptions of my father's feats of prowess. At the kitchen table in the Ráðherrabústaður I got to hear no small number of splendid stories of their journeys around Strandir; of manliness, clever sayings, or verse-making. Benedikt had by then given up carrying the post and moved to Reykjavík.

The government's banquets were all hosted by the prime minister in those days, and it fell to my mother to see to them. There were often many guests. We children were kept on the upper floor or in the kitchen. To assist my mother there were serving or parlour maids who always lived with us. Anna Erlendsdóttir is especially memorable to me, but they were all delightful. Anna was married to Daníel Ágústínusson of Akranes.

No less was put into these banquets then than now. After I became prime minister I always kept the custom I grew used to in those years of inviting guests home whenever it could be managed, instead of dining at a restaurant. Personal interaction is often more useful than formal meetings, not least where foreign politicians are concerned.

Once, when I was eight years old, it occurred to me that it would be fun to taste those beautiful, popular drinks that were served to the guests. It ended with me being put to bed. After that experience I did not taste alcohol until I was past twenty.

It went no better when I took it into my head to try smoking. I was probably ten years old when it happened. The way of it was that Stella, who was then living with us in the Ráðherrabústaður, was courting with Leifur Þorleifsson, who later became her husband. Once she asked me to go for them to Uppsalakjallari and buy half a pack of cigarettes. I did so, but stole one cigarette and took it out onto the balcony, where I lit it and inhaled vigorously. At once I became sick and threw up. When I recovered I vowed never to smoke again, and I have kept to that.
Gunpowder-making and gun antics

I actually had three rooms at my disposal in the Ráðherrabústaður. One was up in the rafters, though really one could say that we boys took over the whole attic. Then there was the room I slept in on the second floor, and finally we boys claimed a little-used room in the cellar, where I was allowed to tinker at various pursuits.

In the cellar, Björn Þorláksson and I manufactured, for example, firecrackers for New Year's Eve. We went down to the pharmacy, bought ourselves saltpetre and other ingredients for gunpowder, and mixed it all together underneath the prime minister's office. At first my father knew nothing of this. Of course it was necessary to test the powder. We would take a tiny portion, set it aside, and perform the experiment on it. Gunpowder burns with a great flash, and this was accompanied by a great stench as well. Bjössi says he often waited with his heart in his throat for someone to come upon us. He also maintains, in fact, that it was I who absolutely wanted to test the explosive power of the firecrackers. To that end we lit one of them there in the cellar. To muffle the sound we put it under a washtub, which in those days were all made of metal. This of course doubled the explosive force, and the noise was in proportion. We did not repeat that experiment indoors, though it never came to light, because we had the sense to bide our time until no one was home. Things went rather worse with the powder tests.

On one occasion, when my mother had guests in the parlour, we were at our work in the cellar and, as usual, wanted to test the powder. We probably had not moved the test portion far enough from the big pile; at any rate a spark leapt across. Then came this terrific flash that reached right up to the ceiling, and everything filled with smoke and fumes. Before we knew it we were grabbed and dragged out of the smoke. It was Anna the parlour maid. By then a great vapour had billowed up into the parlour. Our faces were coal-black. In the aftermath my father imposed a total ban on this manufacturing. The Ráðherrabústaður has probably never been so close to burning to ashes. After this we had to go elsewhere to mix powder for firecrackers. I often had trouble submitting to orders and prohibitions when it came to gunpowder, guns, and cars.

My parents went on a month-long trip to Denmark every spring while my father was prime minister and the Icelanders were under the Danish crown. There he presented the bills that had been passed by parliament to the king for signature. This was a great journey. I remember that my mother always looked forward to it. They stayed at the D'Angleterre, the famous hotel a short way

from the harbour in Copenhagen. This came with a colourful social life which she enjoyed. This period was often full of pranks in the Ráðherrabústaður, where we boys reigned almost unsupervised — as I believed, though of course it was not really so. Grandmother Margrét and Stella naturally lived in the house, and the parlour maids were there as well.

My father kept his shotguns in a special cabinet, which in fact I came to own later. Once I took a shotgun, went down to the cellar and to the cellar steps behind the house. There is a stone retaining wall opposite, which holds up the earth. At it I fired the shotgun. The gun, however, kicked me terribly, and I was badly bruised on the left half of my face and got a black eye. I did not know to hold it firmly against me. That was my first shot from a gun, and they have now become a great many. No one ever found out about this.

I must have been very young when this happened, because I was only twelve years old when my father gave me my first rifle some time after this. I often went with it after ptarmigan, among other places to the Vífilsstaðir hillside where Heiðmörk is now. Once I was hunting with my father and Björn Konráðsson, who was then farm manager at Vífilsstaðir. He was a close kinsman of ours from Skagafjörður and my father's playmate in childhood. They walked in along the hillside, but I stayed behind. Then a flock of ptarmigan came and settled a short distance from me. I rolled onto my stomach, and they did not notice me even though I fired. The rifle was loaded with the smallest cartridge type and was therefore very quiet. Before it was over I had managed to shoot ten or eleven birds. Such a thing has never happened to me, neither before nor since. When my hunting companions came back with two ptarmigan each, I had a whole bundle.

My father was very strict about the handling of the weapon. Of course I was never allowed to carry the gun loaded, and never to carry it other than with the barrel pointing either straight up or straight down. On one occasion he came upon me when the barrel was pointing forward, and he then took the gun from me. I was not allowed to have it for a month. That seemed to me a harsh punishment. He also always kept my gun at home and had it in a locked cabinet. I knew of course where he kept the key, but in this I did not disobey.
Swimming trips, skis, and the outdoor life

After the Sundhöll swimming hall was opened, it was very popular. My father was not much of a swimmer. He had learned to swim in some brook or pool. Once he decided to test his skill in a pond when he was haymaking at Syðri-Brekkur. I heard him say that he had come close to

drowning. He got water in his lungs because he could not keep himself afloat with his swimming strokes. To get his breath he had to let himself sink to the bottom and push off from there up above the surface. Nor was his ordeal made any easier by the fact that he had to go all the way across to the opposite bank, because he did not know how to turn around in the water. He later recounted this incident in the journal of the district's Youth Association (Ungmennafélagið).

It was a matter of great importance to my father that I learn to swim. I did so with Jón Pálsson at the Austurbær primary school. There was a small swimming pool there. He had a long pole with a loop of wide rubber band hanging from the end. The pupils lay in the loop and were held afloat. Then the Sundhöll swimming hall was inaugurated. I suppose I was seven years old then. It was a great palace of adventure. I went to the Sundhöll a great deal. I often went there alone, so my father asked the attendants to keep an eye on me. He also placed particular emphasis on my drying myself well between the toes. The attendants were asked to watch over this too. My father believed one was more likely to catch a cold if one's feet were wet. No doubt he was right about that. I quickly came to believe that swimming was a wholesome and good sport. I find swimming clears the mind well, and it may well be that I composed my best speeches while swimming. I have swum regularly in Laugardalur ever since I moved home from the United States — for more than 30 years.

I was not old when I began going to the mountains with my father. He enjoyed climbing mountains and cross-country skiing. He usually wore a peaked cap on these trips, and on top he wore a windbreaker over a light sweater. He would also typically wear knickerbockers and knee socks, ski boots or mountain boots. More often than not I was dressed the same and did not want to be otherwise. I took great pleasure in these trips. It could often be hard to keep up with my father, for he was a strong walker. He found it fun to slide down steep scree slopes and would often sail down them at breakneck speed. My father taught me about the wonders of nature and instilled in me respect for clean air and our wonderful country. At his best he would toss off a verse or recite a poem.

I was eight years old when my mother took us children to a skiing course up at Skíðaskáli. We stayed there for one week. The snow crust was so hard that the slope had to be dug open with shovels. When that work was done, the instruction began.

I quickly got a good command of holding my footing down steep slopes. Rough terrain and jumps have always fascinated me. Gunnar Flóvens, chairman of the Herring Industry Board (Síldarútvegsnefnd), told me long afterwards that his gaze had been caught by a young red-haired lad in knickerbockers with his socks fallen down, in a snow-soaked jacket, who strove to jump off a platform by the Skíðaskáli in

Hveradalir but always fell on the landing. Each time, though, the boy got up after the fall and said half aloud to himself: "Once more, next time I'll land it, once more," and then jumped again until at last he remained standing after the landing. The boy was me, and that is how I learned to jump. It was said that this bore witness to my determined will and competitive spirit. Others might perhaps call it stubbornness.

In the winters we sometimes went skiing on the Vífilsstaðir hillside. Once, after my father had become prime minister, he fell badly and had trouble with one leg. He was always more for cross-country skiing than slopes. Still, he let little show and drove into town. When the leg was examined it turned out that it had broken. He had to stay in bed for several days. During my own time as prime minister, a press photographer once lay in wait for me all day long to get pictures of me in a similar plaster cast. It would not have occurred to anyone to trouble a prime minister with such a thing in my father's working days.
"There's a five-eyrir coin missing"

In my diary I have recorded that I first went to Ísaksskóli, which was named after Ísak Jónsson. It was at Grænuborg, a short distance from us on Laufásvegur, where a preschool of the same name has since been. I went there at five years old and enjoyed it. I always took pleasure in learning. At Ísaksskóli I learned to read. I early developed a great interest in arithmetic and the sciences. Numbers suited me better than languages, spelling, and composition. My marks bore witness to that as well.

I remember terribly little from Ísaksskóli. I was taken southwards, and the place was full of children. We were either playing outside or learning inside, and Ísak taught us. Yet I feel I can see Ísak before me. He was a rather short but tidy man, with an unusually fine head of hair, in a suit and waistcoat. He had a very good way with the children.

When I entered primary school at the Miðbæjarskóli I was excellently prepared. From my primary school years I do not remember much more than from Laufásvegur. At the Miðbæjarskóli I was originally placed in the F class at random. After the first exams, where I did well, I was moved to the B class. That was a great stroke of luck, because Árni Þórðarson taught there. He became a good friend of mine. Part of the class went on together to the Menntaskóli grammar school, and we then invited this old teacher of ours, among other things, on a week-long trip to Tindafjallajökull. There he celebrated his fortieth birthday, so he was probably around thirty when he first taught me.
Árni was a man of medium height, slender and cheerful. He had
smooth hair. Árni later became headmaster of Hagaskóli. From him I learned to apply myself well to my studies and that learning was a good thing. He taught us good morals.

At the Miðbæjarskóli, pupils were sorted into classes by ability. In the A, B, and C classes were those who did best, and then came the others who did less well. From my primary school years I actually remember little other than fights. One boy from the lower classes is especially memorable. He was quite strong and was probably the biggest in the group. I sensed a certain envy or jealousy in him because I was in the B class. That is the only time I remember such a thing. There were several clashes between us. I do not know whether this was a consequence of the sorting into classes or whether it was something else. On the other hand, I have never been keen on mixing everything together into one hodgepodge. Outstanding pupils should be allowed to come into their own to some extent, and those who have more difficulty with their studies need to get more instruction in the fundamentals before going further. I am not sure that pupils who struggle with book learning are done a favour by being placed in a class with pupils who learn easily from books. We must acknowledge that the human creature is variable. Things come more or less easily to people, and people have their strong sides in different fields. This is, however, a delicate matter to handle.

In Árni Þórðarson's class I remember nothing but unity. Árni managed the class well. He took us on hikes and trips out of town. He was a superb educator. I remember one incident in particular. I was the class treasurer and no longer remember what we were collecting for. When I settled the accounts it turned out that a five-eyrir coin was missing from the fund. I had lost it somewhere or miscalculated. I was extremely worried about this. I went to Árni half in tears and told him this grave news. Árni went carefully through my bookkeeping. At last he said: "This all seems properly entered by you and correctly added up. We shall simply have to put it right." And he took a five-eyrir coin out of his pocket and added it to the fund. Árni won a place in my heart for life for that.
Ice-floe hopping on the Tjörnin

The Landakot field was our main play area in the summers, but the Tjörnin pond was added in the winters. I was young when I glided on skates for the first time. The old fire station stood at one corner of the Tjörnin, and the firemen would often spray water on the ice when it froze, which made for a smooth and beautiful sheet of ice. I had hockey skates and skated a great deal, since it was a short way to go. I could walk on them across the street and out onto the ice. Most fun of all, though, was skating with Pabbi.

My father had been quite a skater in his younger years. In those days he and his brothers skated on Héraðsvötn and were famous, among other things, for jumping over fences. He got himself skates when I got the good hockey skates. These were so-called long-distance runners, which were large skates. Pabbi often came out onto the ice after meetings in parliament. He sometimes wore a long, handsome scarf around his neck that streamed behind him as he sped across the ice. It happened that the children in the neighbourhood were allowed to hold on to it, and few things were thought more fun than getting such a joyride across the ice.

Tjörnin was also much used to shorten the way over to Lækjargata, or home, or wherever one had to go when it lay in between. We often skated on the thinnest of ice, quite literally, when it was untrustworthy. Björn Þorláksson tells the story that on one occasion we were walking across the ice toward the old KR house, where Reykjavík City Hall now stands. Halfway across, the ice broke beneath us. There was little danger, for Tjörnin is shallow and the bottom is in fact mostly mud. Bjössi says he looked at me as we stood there submerged, but that I let little show and simply looked straight ahead and kept on walking. He says I then waded through that muck all the way to the bank without hesitating, and he followed. I must have been determined that this mishap should not turn me from my path. Bjössi remembers this because he got a merciless scolding at home, being covered in mud from head to toe. The incident was also recalled there for years afterward, because the stench that came off him proved unforgettable to the household. I do not particularly remember the reception at my own home. My mother was used to a great deal.

Ice floes and drift ice were more common in Tjörnin then than now. The ice house Ísbjörninn was then at the southwest corner of Tjörnin. In those days fish was chilled with ice from Tjörnin. The ice was cut and fetched from that corner of the lake. There was therefore always an opening in the ice there, where we cut floes and sailed about on the open water. Floe-sailing and floe-jumping were a great sport. We also did a lot of "bobbing." Men would stand on untrustworthy ice, hold hands, and walk or run slowly in rhythm so that the ice moved in waves. Sometimes it broke and everyone fell into Tjörnin. This was considered exciting. Undeniably these games carried the risk of getting wet. One day I fell into Tjörnin three times. When I came home soaking wet for the third time, I was not let out again.

When Tjörnin was half free of ice, conditions for floe-sailing were often at their best. Once, two of us companions drifted on an ice floe east across Tjörnin. When we reached land, a police car was waiting there. Lárus Salomonsson, whom I have described before, seized us each under one arm and declaimed: "Two pups have I taken." We were taken down to the police station, where we were left to sit for a long time. Every now and then a policeman came out, looked at us gravely and said: "This is very serious; you will probably be put in the jailhouse." At last
we were released with a warning. Long afterward I found out that my father had telephoned the police and gotten Lárus and his colleagues to stage the arrest. We learned our lesson.

I once built a kayak in the workshop room in the attic, which I intended to use on Tjörnin once all the ice floes were gone. I devoted long hours to this labour, especially in dreary weather. I was tremendously proud of this piece of craftsmanship. The hull was built according to a drawing of a Greenlandic kayak. I assembled a lightweight frame and bent thin slats as crossribs. Canvas was then stretched over it and oiled. It was thus quite a vessel. It was probably between four and five metres long. At last it was ready for its maiden voyage on Tjörnin. I got my friends to help me carry it down. From the attic there is a very steep staircase, as described earlier. When we had made it nearly all the way down, Grandmother Margrét stopped us. Then something happened that I greatly regretted. I flew into a rage when she stood in the way. In my fury I kicked out, and it went so badly that my foot landed in her face. She got a nasty black eye from the blow.

I was very sorrowful about that black eye for a long time. But the old woman had her way. I never made another attempt. The kayak sat up in the attic for a long time after that without ever being launched. No doubt that was the only sensible thing. It probably leaked anyway.
Secret Passages and Spying

With the office of prime minister came a summer house at Þingvellir, the so-called King's House (Konungshús). It stood just south of Valhöll and was a delightful timber house, old and cosy. My mother liked to stay there in the summers together with my sister. I stayed there too, before I was considered old enough to be sent to the countryside, and after that I often stayed at Þingvellir in the spring before I went north, and in the autumn after I came back. My father regularly drove east in the evenings, and usually at weekends when time allowed.

Þingvellir was an enjoyable place to be, for there were many boys my age in the neighbouring cabins. I often went on walks with my parents, and we boys found it especially exciting to clamber in the rifts. We played a great deal in Hestagjá and Almannagjá. My father was apt to join the group, and he held nothing back in the climbing. To the boys this naturally seemed like something out of an adventure. In Hestagjá I had a secret place. If you walk up a scree slope there, you can find a cave that reaches nearly all the way up to the rim of the rift. It cannot be seen well either from above or from below. It is thus a kind of secret passage. The mouth
is very narrow, and the cave is dangerous to traverse because there is a deep fissure in the middle of the floor.

Among the boys was Kristján, son of Steindór Einarsson the motorman, who ran the vehicle station of the same name. He was called Kiddi. The story of his father Steindór is remarkable. He began his business by operating a ferryboat in Reykjavík harbour. He switched to a taxi in 1915, one of the first of its kind. He founded his delivery-van station a few years later in a closet under the stairs at Hotel Ísland. By the time I got to know his son, Steindór owned many vehicles, among them buses. Once Kiddi "borrowed" a full-sized bus, which we drove into Bolabás. We cannot have been very tall, for I still remember that he had to stand up in order to reach the pedals and see out at the same time.

We boys also found it exciting to spy on the grown-ups at gatherings in Valhöll. There was often hearty drinking there. The police used a method on severely drunken men that I have never seen anywhere else, before or since. They simply put a burlap sack over their heads, tied it shut, and laid them out on the slope, where they slept it off. It was an ingenious method. Once we watched two blind-drunk men labouring to empty the water out of Peningagjá. They filled bucket after bucket and poured it into Flosagjá. This had never occurred to us and seemed the strangest of undertakings, for we knew that the rifts are interconnected. As might be expected, their work progressed slowly.

I remember Jóhannes Kjarval well from my stays at Þingvellir. He was often out east there painting. Few things gave me more pleasure than watching him at his work. Kjarval was both peculiar and often very flamboyantly dressed. Nor did he talk about ordinary things, and he was apt to ask odd questions. "Has a wasp ever stung you in the backside?" he asked once. I pondered with utmost gravity before I answered. "No, that has never happened to me. Does it hurt?" Then Kjarval laughed but made no reply.

When it rained he spread a large tarpaulin over himself and the easel and carried on working undeterred. I, of course, was well outfitted by my mother. I particularly remember a sou'wester I was very proud of. Kjarval then took up the habit of making a stroke on the sou'wester with his brush while he was painting. Before long it had become the most colourful hat in the country. What I regret most is that the hat was thrown away. I would gladly have kept it.

Kjarval was a good acquaintance of my father's. On one occasion, after I had gotten my driver's licence, he suddenly appeared on the front steps at home on Tjarnargata. He was dressed in a sheepskin parka that he had turned inside out so that the fleece

faced outward. The trousers looked to me like pyjama bottoms. His errand was to get my father to come skiing with him. That was readily granted. It fell to me to drive them up to Sandskeið, where they then walked about. It is safe to say that they attracted the undivided attention of those travelling along the road.

In the first years at the King's House we got milk from Brúsastaðir. In the autumn, berries were picked to put on porridge and to boil into jam. I also remember that my mother clipped a good deal of wild thyme for a tea that she drank and had great faith in. She was very avant-garde in much that concerned cooking. Among other things she prepared gravlax in those years, when such arts were practically unknown. I have still not tasted better cured salmon, except perhaps from my wife Edda, though I have sat through many an expensive banquet. Much of this my mother had learned in Denmark or developed herself. She was a magnificent host, whether at the Prime Minister's Residence or the King's House. I have often been told so by the many who experienced it, then and later.

The King's House burned in 1970, and in it perished suddenly Bjarni Benediktsson, who was then prime minister, and his wife Sigríður Björnsdóttir, together with Benedikt Vilmundarson, their infant grandson.
Six Summers in Sheepskin Shoes

We siblings were first sent to the countryside in the summer of 1937, to our father's parents and siblings at Syðri-Brekkur in Skagafjörður. I was there every summer for six years. I went north in mid-June and came back at the end of August. It was quite a change from life in the Prime Minister's Residence. Whether I was in the countryside or in town, however, I was always outdoors most of the time, and in the spring I always looked forward to going to the countryside. Country life did not suit my sister Dolly as well. She stayed at home when I went north the following summer, and from then on. The journey north took two days. The first year our father got Viggó Eyjólfsson, who was a driver at the Vehicle Inspectorate (Bifreiðaeftirlitið), to take us along. That journey had barely begun when we got stuck in a river below Hafnarfjall, probably Tunguá. Viggó waded ashore and walked to the nearest farm, where he fetched men and horses that pulled the car out.

One spring I was sent north with Björn Blöndal Jónsson, who was called a "sniffer" (þefari). He earned the name from his office, which consisted of hunting down moonshine, which was very common in the countryside during the prohibition years. The sniffers came into being when Jónas of Hrifla declared war on the liquor question. New alcohol legislation was enacted providing for inspectors and search warrants without court orders, and those who were given this job were called sniffers. Many of them became known throughout the country, and Björn became one of the most famous. My father got him to

take me along to the countryside when he was heading north on one of his journeys. I always remember a dog that came running after the car, as happens in the countryside. Then Björn said: "Open the window and tell him to eat horsemeat. That will silence him at once, for horse is the worst thing they can get." I believed this and shouted "horsemeat, horsemeat" out the window; "eat horsemeat!" It did not seem to me to have much effect, though.

In an instant the news spread through whole districts when Björn the sniffer was expected. At every farm where he stopped, the call was passed on along the rural party line, reporting his movements so that the distilling equipment could be put aside. When we arrived at farms, people had even dressed themselves in their better clothes. Björn was, after all, a dignified official in uniform. Nor did we find anything on that journey, though Björn was renowned for having a keen nose for moonshine.

At Syðri-Brekkur I was given a warm welcome. Every year new sheepskin shoes awaited me there. Grandmother Pálína made them. She knew I found them comfortable footwear. Of course my feet were often wet for days on end, and later that came to trouble me. At the time, however, it did not matter at all. I found it worse when there were dry spells, for then the shoes became hard and stiff. They were best when damp. In my diary I speak well of Syðri-Brekkur in the overview of my life that has been mentioned before. It was written three years after I last spent a whole summer there. The diary says:

I was in the countryside for 6 summers, from 1937 to 1942, both years included. I was at Syðri-Brekkur in Skagafjörður, where Pabbi was brought up. Two of Pabbi's brothers now live there, Björn and Sigurður, and his brother-in-law Guðvarður Guðmundsson. His wife is named Margrét, Pabbi's sister. Björn and Sigurður are unmarried. Pabbi's sister Sigríður is there as well. She is housekeeper for Bjössi. Grandmother is there too, and Grandfather was there. Guðvarður has 3 daughters: Pálína, Ingunn and Kristín; Pálína is the oldest and Stína the youngest. They are all great fun. I took a particular liking to Stína. The first summer Guðvarður gave me a foal, and Siggi gave me a lamb as a birthday present. The horse was given the name Léttir and the lamb Bletta, because of a spot on one hind leg. I liked being in the countryside very much. I was always on horseback. I enjoyed myself most splashing about down by the Waters (Héraðsvötnin). I always looked forward to being allowed to come along when the sheep were driven to the mountain pastures. The only thing I found tiresome was how the girls, especially Grandmother, were always afraid for me, though I admit I was a bit of a daredevil. Grandmother always stood in the doorway with the binoculars if I went beyond the homefield wall. She never wanted to let me go down to the Waters, though she could not prevent me from going. Naturally

she meant only well by this, but it led to my being bored to death sometimes\ and becoming exceedingly unruly and boisterous. I wanted to be freer. The last summer my cousin Frímann Þorsteinsson from Akureyri, then 7 years old, was there too. I thought that was better than nothing, since there were few boys around there. I often went over to Ytri-Brekkur, where I have relatives. I began making hay for my animals at age 8. In the winter of 1942 I owned 3 sheep, but they had to be put down because of paratuberculosis.
Syðri-Brekkur in Skagafjörður

Grandmother Pálína lived at Syðri-Brekkur all her life. I doubt she ever came to Reykjavík. By the time I stayed at the farm, one may say that Grandmother had already divided the land among her children, for there were then several households on it, as was often the custom on country farms.

Syðri-Brekkur stands in Blönduhlíð, in a part sometimes said to be called Út-Blönduhlíð. There the Héraðsvötn rivers flow past, split by Hegranes into an eastern and a western branch. Grandmother received the farm from her father, Björn Pétursson of Hofstaðir in Viðvíkursveit, my great-grandfather. Grandmother's mother was Margrét Pálsdóttir, and her father Páll was district officer at Syðri-Brekkur. These forebears of mine I never met, but I have a very delightful photograph of my great-grandfather Björn and his brother Sigurður standing against a turf wall.

My father was very fond of his grandfather Björn and looked up to him greatly. Among other things, he hired on with him as a farmhand as a young man. In good moments and on festive occasions he liked to tell stories about his grandfather. Bishop Jón Helgason was on a visitation around North Iceland and called, among other places, at Hofstaðir, for there was an old farmers' church there. The bishop discussed life in Skagafjörður with Björn and said: "Too much is drunk here in Skagafjörður, my dear Björn." Björn is said to have replied: "I do not know how it is west of the Waters, my dear bishop, but here east of the Waters it could not well be any less."

Below the farm at Syðri-Brekkur there was also a good deal of land along the Héraðsvötn, or the Waters as they are often called, that belonged to the property. It is flatland there, marshes, fens and pools that one could easily sink into. Yet hay was made there, for on the banks were meadows, stretches of sedge and channels overgrown with mare's-tail. That was considered the finest fodder. On a bright, fine day the view there is very beautiful. Tindastóll rises majestic above Sauðárkrókur in the west
\ Here I have crossed out the word "often" and put "sometimes" instead.
and further inland to the south, Mælifellshnjúkur towers over the church site Mælifell and the whole district. It is the highest mountain in Skagafjörður.

Grandmother generally judged the weather outlook by how the clouds lay over these two mountains. Her sons always trusted that forecast more than the one read on the radio. If Grandmother came out and said, "Well, boys, today is the day to bring in the hay," they did so even if the Meteorological Office's forecast promised good weather. The old woman's forecast rarely failed. She had a very keen eye for weather.

In Skagafjörður one spoke of going "out" to Krókur but "up" to Silfrastaðir. When the sheep were driven to the mountain pasture, I was allowed to go along up to Silfrastaðir, which stands at the mouth of Norðurárdalur. That is on the way up to Öxnadalsheiði, which was the mountain pasture for Akrahreppur. The drive up along Blönduhlíð was half a pleasure trip, with stops at many places for coffee or a sip of milk. After the six summers I had thus visited most of the farms in the district. In those days housing was very poor in much of Skagafjörður, turf farmhouses almost everywhere. So it was also at Brekkur, where there were two houses. Half of the old farmhouse had burned in 1917, but the old sitting room where Grandmother lived was a hundred years old and made entirely of turf apart from the wooden panelling. The farmhouse next to it was slightly more modern but also built of turf. Both have now been torn down. I had to stoop when I walked into the house, and there was a long, dark passage, as there was everywhere. At the end of the passage on the left was the kitchen, which had a well-trodden earthen floor. Beyond the kitchen was Grandmother's old sitting room, where Sigríður slept beside her. Opposite the kitchen, on the other side of the passage, was the new farmhouse with three rooms. The baðstofa was in the middle, and there were quite a few bunks there. The better parlour was at the far end. It was very small, and the telephone was there. The third room was a bedroom where I slept. Upstairs in the new farmhouse was a sleeping loft. The other children slept there. There were three sheep sheds, one for each portion of the land, but the hay barn was shared. These buildings have now all collapsed except Björn's sheep shed.

I had many kinsfolk on the neighbouring farms. To the north lived Vilhjálmur Konráðsson of Ytri-Brekkur. We had extensive and good dealings with the people of Ytri-Brekkur. Vilhjálmur was the brother of Björn of Vífilsstaðir, who was a great friend of my father's, as mentioned before. Their father was Konráð Arngrímsson, who was a scholar and an antiquarian alongside farming. He prepared my father for study at the Möðruvellir School (Möðruvallaskóli). Pabbi was forever grateful to him for that. Vilhjálmur of Ytri-Brekkur was not much of a farmer. As I recall, he was mostly occupied with some kind of machinery work. He was as ardent a Progressive as one can be. When I later came to visit with some of my companions
from the Grammar School, he cursed those conservative boys roundly, and all their kind, who deserved nothing good.
Elves and Hidden People, Wights and Men

At Syðri-Brekkur I came to know my paternal grandfather and grandmother, Jónas Jónsson and Pálína Björnsdóttir. Grandfather Jónas was a farmer at Syðri-Brekkur but had sailed to Copenhagen and studied carpentry. He worked at carpentry alongside farming for as long as his strength lasted. He was considered among the best craftsmen of his day, meticulous and of fine taste. From him my father had his springy movements, his fine intellect and his ear for verse, as well as the gentleness of manner for which Grandfather was renowned.

Grandfather Jónas was often away because of carpentry work and house-building far and wide around Skagafjörður and Húnavatnssýsla, for he was a sought-after craftsman. He was never much of a husbandman; in fact he kept only a few ewes. I sometimes went with him to tend them, but in my last summers at Syðri-Brekkur he was mostly bedridden, and I then had less to do with him. He was of much slighter build than his sons. He seemed to me rather frail in comparison with them. Because of his absences, the farming rested heavily on the shoulders of Grandmother and the sons. Grandfather was very well liked. When he died, a huge tent was raised over the crowd that attended the funeral.

Of Grandmother Pálína I had more to tell. From her my father drew his firmness of character and his high spirit, his vitality, joy of life and warmth of heart. Grandmother had unusual mental stamina and was the equal of anyone in physical hardiness.

On ordinary days Grandmother was dressed in an ankle-length dress or apron. She was fair of face and wore her hair in braids. Work never left her hands idle. She always gave guests coffee and asked for the common news, as was the custom in the countryside. She was a woman of great force and among the most remarkable women I have known in my life. She was beloved by the whole district, for hardly a child had been born in half a century that she had not delivered. She delivered her first babies at nineteen years of age, after three months' training in Akureyri. A singular good fortune is said to have attended her more than half a century of midwifery, for none of the women she attended in all that time is said to have died in childbirth, though such a thing was then by no means unknown. Nothing could keep her from a woman in labour, neither weather nor rivers in flood. The men of the district knew countless stories of her perilous journeys and liked to tell them to me at pleasant moments. She herself never spoke of her feats of hardiness. Grandmother Pálína was both sensible
and determined and especially wise. Some said she possessed special powers. I do not intend to dispute that.

I myself witnessed that Grandma had second sight. When I was about ten years old I came in one time to see Grandma in the old sitting room. The old woman then rose from the bed and said: "I had better go and heat up some coffee. Villi is coming." I asked her how she knew that. She gave me no answer. The telephone had of course arrived by then, but I knew he had not called. I ran out into the yard where my uncle Siggi was. I asked him: "Grandma says Villi is coming — how does she know that?" Then Siggi said: "You can count on Villi coming if your grandma says so. How she knows it, I don't know. You'll have to ask her about that." I went back inside and repeated the question. She then said to me, as if it were the most obvious thing in the world: "Why, Snati was out there." "Snati?" I gasped, and ran out again but saw no dog. So I said to Siggi: "Grandma says Snati was out here and even jumped up at the window." Then Siggi laughed. "Snati was the dog at Ytri-Brekkur that was put down some ten years ago." Ten minutes later Villi arrived, and by then the coffee was hot. I found this quite remarkable and pondered it for a long time.

To Grandma, the elves in the rocks and stones were all good folk. She was a great lover of nature. She was also apt to say something along these lines: "Oh, I remember how she used to tease me . . ." and then she would name some ghost-girl, ". . . when I delivered this one," and then the name. Then she would slap her thigh.

Skafti Jónsson from Siglufjörður, father of Jón, the former member of parliament, told a story a few years ago about Grandma Pálína in an interview on the State Broadcasting Service (Ríkisútvarpið). One spring, he said, he had taken on the job of selling books. On that errand he went from farm to farm and came, among other places, to Syðri-Brekkur. After he had finished his business and accepted refreshments, he said his goodbyes and intended to walk over to Hegranes, across the Vötn, which were frozen over. The day was getting late. When he had come down past the home field he heard a shout and saw a young boy come running down the field — probably Hermann, Skafti said. When the boy had caught his breath he said: "Mamma asks you not to cross the Vötn tonight, because they will break up before you know it. She wants you to stay the night."

Skafti said he had laughed at this and replied that there was no likelihood of that, as the weather was good. Then the boy said, stressing his words: "In these matters we obey Mamma." The upshot was that Skafti stayed the night. The next morning when Skafti looked out he saw that the Vötn had broken up.
My grandmother's spirit has always brought me good fortune. When a government was formed under my premiership in 1988, the margin was very narrow. The Alþingi was divided

at that time into two chambers, and the government had a majority in the upper chamber, but the lower chamber was evenly split. Lots therefore had to be drawn to determine whether government supporters or the opposition would get the deciding member on the committees of the lower chamber. There had been much talk of a hidden man whom Stefán Valgeirsson, member of parliament, claimed to have access to and who would ensure that matters got through there. Stefán said, however, that he had not discussed the elections of speakers and committees with the hidden man. When votes fell even, lots were drawn. So incredibly it turned out that the government supporters won every single drawing of lots, nine in all, and thereby a majority on every single committee. When this was settled, Matthías Bjarnason, member of parliament for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in the Westfjords, walked into the chamber. He was in the opposition. He said rather loudly, and in a heavy mood: "Damn it! There's no hope of winning anything, because Steingrímur's old grandmother is in the ballot box." He had heard from someone that she had been versed in magic. The parliament would probably have gone sour for us if the drawings of lots had been lost.

More happened in the countryside. Opposite Varmahlíð, where there was a bridge over Héraðsvötn, a special guard was posted for the prevention of sheep disease. His name was Jónas, and he watched the gate so that livestock would not be moved between areas. Jónas was said to have second sight, so remarkable were the stories told of him. Once I travelled together with my uncle Sigurður on the way home from Silfrastaðir. We stopped in at Jónas's hut. His eyes were very sharp. I remember feeling as though he looked right through me. He looked at me for a little while and then said: "Hermann is coming to Brekkur tonight." We were taken aback, but he gave no answer. When we got home, however, it was not long before my father came driving up. I shall never forget it. He had been at a meeting in Húnavatnssýsla and said he had suddenly decided to pop over to Brekkur.
The Siblings from Syðri-Brekkur

As said before, four of my father's siblings lived at Syðri-Brekkur. That leaves only Pétur, who was the eldest of the six siblings. He moved to Sauðárkrókur and was district administrative officer there for a long time. Pétur married María Magnúsdóttir and they had one daughter, Pálína. Mother and daughter both live in Hafnarfjörður.

Pétur was the only one of the brothers who was an Independence Party man. When my father ran for office in 1934, famous meetings were held in Skagafjörður where Magnús Guðmundsson, the Minister of Justice, and my father faced off. Their main subject was my father's sentencing of Magnús, and no less the eider-duck killing affair. At that time two members of parliament were elected in Skagafjörður, and the Independence Party men had always held both seats. After a hard fight and well-attended meetings, the ballot boxes were counted, and the result was a tie between Jón Sigurðsson, one of the candidates

of the Independence Party, and the Reverend Sigfús Jónsson, cooperative society manager, who was a Progressive Party man. Lots were drawn, which the Reverend Sigfús won, and it was said that he had got in on God's vote. What fewer people knew was that my uncle Pétur had been so appalled by the treatment of his brother that he stayed home from the election for the first and only time. Pétur probably thereby decided the outcome that made my father Prime Minister, for not a single seat could be spared in the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) number of members of parliament if a majority was to be formed with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). The government enjoyed the support of 25 members of parliament out of 49.

Of those who lived at Syðri-Brekkur, only Margrét ever married; my three other paternal aunts and uncles never settled down. This clings to Syðri-Brekkur, for Frímann Þorsteinsson, who lives there now, is also unmarried. It is strange that things should turn out this way for my father's siblings, for they were remarkably handsome people, as was widely noted.

Björn was an exceptionally powerful man, and tales of his feats spread across the whole country. It is told of Björn, among other things, that when bridges were to be built over the Héraðsvötn, cement was transported on sledges over the ice during the winter. The material came in enormous barrels weighing about 200 kilos. The barrels were therefore rolled out of the cement store and lifted onto the sledge, and men usually worked two by two. Björn considered that he needed no partner. He is said to have run in, gripped the chimes of the barrel, set it up on his knee, carried it alone and finally thrown it up onto the wagon. He was always done loading before the others, who worked in pairs.

I had great respect for Björn. Once I was struggling to lift hay bales onto a pack saddle, and it was going badly. Pack saddles were laid on horses, and short pegs stuck out of them where the bale cords could be fastened. I was having some trouble getting this up when that giant of a man Björn came along with bales. He took the two bales, one in each hand, walked up behind the horse and set both onto the saddle in a single motion. That done, he remarked: "You still haven't grown into much of a man, Denni my boy." Björn's remark stayed with me for a long time. I did not let up until I had mastered the art of getting a bale up onto a pack saddle.

At some point I asked my uncle Pétur which of them had been stronger, my father or Björn. He answered very amusingly: "Your Pabbi sometimes threw his brother Björn twice, but never three times." Björn was slow to anger and not as hot-tempered as my father, who was by nature much more of a fighter. But if Björn's temper did rise, no one could withstand his iron grip.
In the stone wall of his sheep shed, which still stands, there is a boulder that Björn is said to have put in place. No one has been able to budge it since. Björn failed

nor when great strength was needed. The old farmhouse at Syðri-Brekkur burned in the 18th week of summer in 1917. It is said that Björn was then transformed and displayed superhuman strength. He kicked the sitting-room panelling loose in one piece and in that way rescued two enormously heavy tool chests belonging to his father. He pushed himself very close to his limits that night and hardly ever regained his former strength. One may assume that he overexerted himself. He later developed rheumatoid arthritis and died before reaching old age.

Sigurður was said to be the best scholar of the brothers, but as recounted earlier, the family finances only allowed the youngest son, my father, to embark on a long course of studies. When that was decided, all the siblings contributed their share. Björn rode with my father up onto Öxnadalsheiði, and from there he walked north to Akureyri to school. Yet I never sensed any bitterness or envy toward my father among those siblings. On the contrary, they were all very proud of his success. For many years he visited Brekkur every year and carefully maintained his ties to his home district. Sigurður's gifts, moreover, were proverbial. After I entered secondary school I fancied myself a great genius at arithmetic. I would then set all kinds of problems for Sigurður. He solved them all in his head, and quickly too.

The sisters, Margrét and Sigríður, were less conspicuous than the brothers. Yet all were branches of the same tree — sturdy, good common folk. Margrét in particular was reserved, and her appearance and bearing were exceptionally refined. She raised her three daughters with loving care. Margrét was an outstanding farm wife and a good housekeeper. Sigríður was of larger build, and there was a gale of energy about her. Her legs went bad early and she had difficulty walking. You could recognize her from far off by the way she carried herself. Sigríður made few demands on life and was content with her lot, no less than her siblings. She was closest to my father in age, the youngest of the siblings, and she held his banner high with me. She knew countless stories from their childhood years and rarely called him anything but "brother Manni" when she told them. They were probably the closest of the siblings. When my father worked from dawn to dusk in his teenage years to earn his travel money for school, it was Sigríður who carried the hay for him on her shoulders across the fens and home to the farm. I spent many an evening listening to Sigríður's tales, and I especially remember how she would slap her thigh heartily to emphasize her words when her descriptions of the feats of strength reached their climax.

Guðvarður, Margrét's husband, was an observant and handy man. In temperament he was very likeable, sensible and calm. It hardly ever happened that he lost his temper or got worked up. Before I met Guðvarður I thought the Bull of Þorgeir (Þorgeirsboli) was a folk tale. Guðvarður, however, convinced me otherwise. He said that in his younger years he had been travelling between farms, somewhere up in

Skagafjörður. He came upon some monstrous creature standing on a rise, not far from a certain farm. He was astonished at this, since no animal was supposed to be by the home-field wall. As he came nearer he saw that it must be a bull, and he was terrified when he saw that it was dragging its hide behind it. He then felt certain that this was the Bull of Þorgeir (Þorgeirsboli). So he took to his heels and ran home to the farm and told the news. He was then escorted home, but by then nothing could be seen. A man of the family that the Bull of Þorgeir follows arrived at that farm shortly afterwards.

There is no way to pass judgement on stories of this kind. Guðvarður was a truthful man. In those days, however, there were no electric lights. People lived in pitch darkness for a large part of the year. Now, by contrast, everyone is bathed in electric light as soon as dusk begins to fall. The closeness to the unknown and the inexplicable is no longer felt. It seems difficult to me to assert that all this was mere fantasy. Like when Villi came. How on earth could the old woman have known that? Was Snati there?

I myself have never seen a single thing of this kind. I would, however, have gladly met some beings from another world. I regret never having experienced such a thing. That is why, whenever belief in elves has come up in conversation, I have never been able to answer otherwise than that I cannot deny that elves exist, because my grandmother lived with them, saw them, and she never told an untruth.
"Only fools do that"

The diary relates that in my secondary-school years I was assigned to write an essay. I could choose between three topics. They were: 1. Describe a place or a poem. 2. Spring. 3. Hrafnkell Freysgoði. "I chose the first and wrote about Skagafjörður," the diary says. That choice was no coincidence. I often thought of the countryside and made an effort to go there on visits. From the countryside I had many precious memories. That essay of mine is unfortunately lost, and my description now is certainly different from what it was then. Farming was primitive at Syðri-Brekkur and the buildings old-fashioned. It would never have occurred to me to say so at the time. In all, nine people lived in the farmhouse besides me, and quarters were very cramped. But the life of the household was good and beautiful; alcohol was never seen and smoking was unknown. The food was good, and it was extremely rare for anyone to fall ill. I myself was never sick. A great deal of work was done on this farm as on others, but it was no drudgery. I always had plenty to do, and work often continued into the evening. Nor do I ever remember a day off being taken. Such a thing was simply unknown. On Sundays, though, we sometimes went to church or took short rides around the district.
At Syðri-Brekkur we rose around eight o'clock and ate a good

breakfast. I was assigned regular chores soon after I came to the countryside. Above all I was to look after the horses. I fetched them from the paddock and took care of them. I rode bareback from morning to night. After I acquired animals of my own, I made hay for them. During the haymaking season I would often go down to the meadows and lead the horses under their hay loads home to the barn. The springs revolved more around the sheep.
