Lambing was mostly over by the time I came north, but the ewes and lambs had to be watched. Not far from the farm there were peat pits and bog holes that could be dangerous. Then the sheep were driven to the mountain pastures, and once in a while I was allowed to go on a trip to town with the milk lorry.

One of my evening chores was to take the horses out to the paddock. That meant passing a barn, which was a great torment to me after dark, for I was afraid of the dark. On the way back I would therefore make a wide arc around the barn and then run home to the door. Grandma found out about this. She said there was nothing to fear. There were only good spirits there. In the end I therefore decided to summon my courage and went into the barn. Still, my nerve was no greater than that I turned around and ran home in one sprint. The next day, however, I walked through the whole of it and out through the sheep sheds. In that way I bred the fear out of myself and have never felt afraid of the dark since. I was nine years old then.

The food was ordinary country fare, and much meat was eaten from animals slaughtered at home. Slátur was made, and blood pudding was eaten in quantity, and liver sausage. Often this was soured food. There was a cellar under the new house, and there the sour whey stood in barrels. Naturally there was no cold storage; vegetables were hardly ever seen and fruit was unknown. Potatoes, however, were grown in a plot by the farmhouse which my father was said to have dug and prepared when he was young. A great deal of dairy food was eaten, and skyr was often on the table. We always drank fresh milk. I found milk warm from the udder very good, and still do.

One summer, water was piped into the farmhouse from a brook that ran just above it, and then a tap arrived. This was considered great progress. On one occasion I was having a sip of water. Grandma came upon me and said: "What a dreadful sight. Is there really nothing but water to give the blessed boy?" She thought it a scandal and hurried to fetch milk for me. Water and dry bread were paupers' fare in the countryside. The bread at Brekkur was baked at home. It was dark and coarse and probably baked in pots. I remember that my uncles spread each slice with so much butter that one could hardly tell which was thicker, the slice of bread or the layer of butter.

Semi-dried fish was eaten, and a good deal of fish from the Vötn, trout and some salmon. I learned to eat everything that was put before me in those years. I myself caught quite a lot in nets that I set down by Stórihólmi. I found it fun to splash about in the Vötn, but that was not particularly popular,

especially not with Grandma. Yet she was probably the most daring of all at swimming her horse across the Vötn when she needed to get to a woman in childbed. Then there was never any hesitation; she plunged into the Vötn no matter what state they were in. It was said that the boldest of men had not dared to follow her. My father and his brothers got their hardiness from her.

Grandma often watched me through binoculars when I was down by the Vötn. Once I took it into my head to wade all the way across. I did in fact have a small craft of the kind called a pram, and I kept it at my side. That was more sensible than having just a stick. But my grandmother knew the Vötn from her own experience and took to her bed at this sight. When I came home I was not given a particularly warm welcome. The scolding stayed in my memory, for this was the only time Guðvarður raised his voice. He said, and no doubt rightly: "Only fools do that." Guðvarður was otherwise a very calm and moderate man. The Vötn were not deep, but the quicksands hidden in them could be extremely dangerous. Travellers had got caught in them together with their mounts, and then the outcome was never in doubt. Neither man nor horse was ever seen again.

The clothes the household wore were homewoven and homesewn. Grandma kept the spinning wheel going almost without pause and was always knitting or sewing some garments. The women usually wore a long dress and apron, but the traditional peysuföt costume when guests came to the farm. The men wore homespun wadmal clothes, homemade. I do remember, though, that Guðvarður once bought blue overalls at the Cooperative (Kaupfélagið).

The heat in the house came from the cooking stove. It was of a world-famous Swedish make called Aga and was common in country districts. It was fuelled with dung that was cut out of the sheep sheds in the spring. I often assisted with that work and helped to stand the dung slabs up to dry. Two slabs or flakes of dung were leaned against each other so that the wind could blow between them and the dung could dry. There was no other source of heat in the house except the people themselves. This was ordinary country life of that time — not destitution or poverty, but by no means wealth either. The people deposited everything they had with the Cooperative and always had something there to fall back on.

Probably little had changed in farming practices at Brekkur since my father grew up there around the turn of the century. His brother Björn, however, was considered progressive in farming. In the years I stayed at Syðri-Brekkur he acquired a mowing machine drawn by horses, and later a raking machine, and these were considered tremendous steps forward. Apart from these machines the haymaking was traditional: mown with scythe and blade, raked and turned, and then the hay was gathered up into haycocks. These were often dragged home whole, or the hay was bound and put on a pack saddle, and we children were made to lead the horses under their loads home to the barn. Below the farm

there was extensive meadow haymaking. It was hard work. It was difficult both to get down there and then to bring the hay home. The banks along the Vötn, on the other hand, were very bountiful; the growth there was heavy, with considerable grassland, lush and good.

When the road ran above Brekkur and most travel was on horseback, those passing through often stopped and accepted coffee from Grandma. After a motor road was laid below the home field, where it still runs, people began to travel by automobile. Grandma considered this a great step backwards. I remember once she stood in the doorway, her grey braids lying in a beautiful curve around her head, underscoring the dignity she possessed. A car went by and I heard the old woman say rather loudly: "What a terrible hurry people are in these days — nobody stops any more for a cup of coffee." Then she turned and shuffled back into the house. The countryside was changing.

I only earned my keep those summers of mine in the countryside, though I did acquire a few sheep. Soon after I first came north I was also given the horse Léttir. He had a star on his forehead. After I stopped spending summers at Syðri-Brekkur I brought him south with me. He was kept, together with a horse Pabbi owned, south at Bessastaðir. One Christmas he got caught in a railed gate there and broke his leg so badly that he had to be put down. Later a man told me that the leg had hung on by a single sinew, for it had snapped clean through. The news of his death was withheld from me until the holidays had passed. I never got myself a horse after that.

The richest reward for my stay in Skagafjörður, however, was the memories and the experience. It was invaluable to come to know a healthy and good country life. That has been of enormous worth to me throughout my life. I learned what wholesome people farming families are. This is how Icelanders have lived in this country generation after generation. The people lived off the land, cherished it and tried to treat it well. It was a small community where people had their best friends on the neighbouring farms. I believe and hope that this remains so in the countryside.

When I come to Syðri-Brekkur now, many old memories awaken, though much has changed from what once was. The old farmhouse is gone, as is the bridge over the marshes, and the meadows are no longer used for hay. The only thing left standing of the old buildings is Björn's sheep shed. I cannot escape the thought that Syðri-Brekkur has declined. Frímann Þorsteinsson is a most excellent man, but he lives alone on the farm, and the farming is altogether different and smaller than it was. This is unfortunately the reality in many rural areas, though elsewhere people have managed to maintain and build up impressive farms. Even in the most flourishing districts, farming is in retreat, sadly. When production quotas are cut as much as they in fact have been, the outcome is not in doubt.
Chapter Three
"STURDY BOYS", THE WAR YEARS AND GIRL TROUBLE

I was eleven years old when war broke out in Europe. At first it was called the northern-continent conflict. After the theatre of conflict stretched its tentacles to most parts of the world, however, "world war" became the fitting name. In Iceland, "the later world war" thus became the name for these horrors, to distinguish them from the earlier one. "The later world war" is a name that testifies to the endemic optimism of us Icelanders. In other languages it is usually called World War 2.

I never remember being afraid of the war. The news was not enough to bring the fighting closer, only to arouse in me indignation at the folly of mankind. Of course I was aware of the war. After the army came to the country, it was an undeniable reminder of the conflict. Soldiers were everywhere, especially while the British were here. They were very conspicuous and commandeered not only the Grammar School building (Menntaskólahúsið) but also the National Theatre (Þjóðleikhúsið) and other important buildings. The Americans moved further out of town after they took over. We boys, however, never hung around the soldiers much.

The war did not have much effect on daily life in Reykjavík, though it came up in conversation at home and in the news. Sirens went off if German aircraft were sighted, and then we were all driven down into cellars. In the town, dozens of public air-raid shelters were set up in various cellars. They were marked with red arrows. Some said that as soon as the air-raid sirens sounded, they immediately filled up with British soldiers so that there was no room for those they were meant to shelter. Children sometimes stood out in the open and waved to German airmen, and they are said to have waved back. I

think that there was never more than one plane at a time. Nor was the fear any stronger than that I was most excited about trying to catch sight of the plane. Once I believed I had seen a German aircraft and proudly told everyone about it.

Air-raid drills were generally treated like any other joke. The army high command and the air-raid defence committee felt that Icelanders were slow to learn that air raids were dangerous. In Iceland, young men did not come home maimed from the battlefields, no houses were blown up, and in the first years nothing was reminiscent of war except the radio news and work for the occupation force for everyone who wanted it. The horror of the war was far away until attacks began on Icelandic ships. Icelanders made their sacrifices on the seas. I did not try to understand the war or the conflicts. It seemed to me that these were mostly damned fools out in Europe running each other through and killing one another. I think the general feeling was that we stood outside the conflict.
"Well, so they have come then"

The British landed in Reykjavík on 10 May 1940. I was eleven years old at the time. Fate arranged it so that I was with my father the day before the British came. He was then Prime Minister and the country's highest official. Perhaps one may say that an invasion was in the air. A question had been raised in the British Parliament a few days earlier about whether troops should be sent to Iceland. It was withdrawn without the minister giving an answer. On Thursday 9 May we were at Laugarvatn, where my father was observing the training of the police, a matter close to his heart.

That evening I had gone to bed when Pabbi nudged me and said we had to go into town. I was very disappointed at not being able to stay longer in the east, as we had planned. I was told nothing about the reasons for this change. It seems likely to me, though, in hindsight, that he had received some message that serious events were imminent. In my father's biography, Indriði G. Þorsteinsson tells of a mysterious telephone call that is said to have led to this sudden journey home. On the other hand, it is conceivable that my father saw for himself where things were heading, as Þór Whitehead argues in his book Milli vonar og ótta (Between Hope and Fear).

Historians are naturally curious to know whether my father received a message and whether the invasion was clear to him when the warships sailed into the harbour. A definitive answer will probably never be found. What is certain is that we set off from Laugarvatn and drove at speed towards Reykjavík. That I remember clearly. Somehow I feel that a third man was with us in the car, probably a policeman who drove. The spring light still lingered
as the car rattled along the potholed roads of the South. I remember distinctly that I spotted a flock of geese when we were below Ingólfsfjall.

I was extremely preoccupied with my own marksmanship that day, because shortly before we had watched the policemen's shooting practice on Lyngdalsheiði. My father, police chief Agnar Kofoed-Hansen and chief superintendent Erlingur Pálsson then held a shooting contest. They shot at bottles from a range of 70–80 metres. When the contest was over I was allowed to try my hand, and I hit three bottles with three shots. I was of course exceedingly proud of this. In recognition, I was allowed to carry a rifle over my shoulder while the policemen's practice went on. So I marched solemnly about in rubber shoes and a winter parka, with a cap on my head and a far too large, unloaded rifle over my shoulder — an eleven-year-old whippersnapper.

The flock of geese resting in the twilight kindled in me an unquenchable desire to prove my marksmanship anew. My father indulged me, stopped the car and allowed me to fire one shot. I hit one goose, which was wounded and fluttered out onto the Sog river. I never retrieved that catch. My father was also in a hurry to get on to Reykjavík. We hastened our journey and arrived at the Prime Minister's Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn) when night had fallen.

While our journey was under way, the British naval squadron sailed past Reykjanes. A reconnaissance plane was sent up in search of German submarines. It also circled over Reykjavík and made a great deal of noise. The townspeople were fast asleep, but some stirred at the noise. It was getting on for four in the morning. A little later, Einar Arnalds knocked on the door of the Prime Minister's Residence. He was serving as police chief in Agnar's absence, who was still at Laugarvatn. He announced that the British had landed. My father merely remarked: "Well, so they have come then."

The British landing in Reykjavík was much more peaceful than their celebrations at the end of the war, which I witnessed later. I do not remember much from the morning of 10 May. I do remember, though, that we boys ran down to the harbour to see the warships. At the corner of Tjarnargata and Kirkjustræti we came upon a group of soldiers whom we gawked at like a bull at a new gate. Blowing about the streets were the occupation force's badly worded and atrociously spelled leaflets, squads of soldiers could be seen here and there, and my father was unusually busy. The midday radio broadcast was cancelled and telephone calls were banned. In the evening I listened to the radio address of my father, Prime Minister of the national unity government, who protested against this violation of the country's neutrality but at the same time asked "that the Icelandic nation regard the British soldiers who have come to Iceland as guests and accordingly show them, like other guests, full courtesy in every respect." The radio played a special role in every home, and when something momentous

the household gathered around the radio set. In the half-dark of that spring evening I thought I could make out lines of worry in my mother's face as she sat silently listening, letting her needlework rest in her lap. The war had come to Iceland.

The effects of the occupation turned out, perhaps, differently from what most had imagined. With the soldiers came greatly increased work, war profits and nightlife. Strong currents collided — the national revival of Iceland and influences from abroad; the old times and the new, some would no doubt say today. Society has probably seldom undergone such rapid changes in Iceland as in the Reykjavík of the war years. I myself was only indirectly affected by this, since I had little or no personal contact with the army and did not see much of it.
Fighting in Hljómskálagarður Park

From the war years I recall that for a while a great many weapons were manufactured in the attic of the Prime Minister's Residence. In those days there were battles between the East Town (Austurbær) and the West Town (Vesturbær). The line was drawn at the Brook (Lækurinn), and fighting took place in Hljómskálagarður Park. The battlefield was mainly south of the Pond (Tjörnin), but that area has now changed considerably from what it was. There was a fair amount of mudslinging between the districts. I seem to remember that the actor Flosi Ólafsson once put it this way: in the eyes of us West Towners there was "nothing east of the brook except suburbs and rubbish heaps".

We in the West Town were KR supporters, while they in the East Town were Valur supporters. The Mid-Towners were Fram supporters, but they mostly kept the peace. If a West Towner made his way into the East Town, various insults were shouted after him, and the same story could be told in the West Town. All my friends were West Towners or Mid-Towners except Árni of Laufásvegur. We remained acquainted after I moved across the front line. In the battles of the factions, enormous crowds from each half of town clashed. I could well believe that a hundred fought on each side. We friends who had our base in the Prime Minister's Residence were only a small group in the army, but we manufactured an astonishing quantity of swords and shields. They were perhaps not fine swords, but they did have hilts, and the shields had handles. Many took hard blows, though I do not recall being wounded. We were also just youngsters, among the youngest who fought. The oldest boys were often five or six years older, up to 16–18, and all with wooden swords or clubs. Still, they thought it fine to have us and our weapons along until heavy fighting broke out. Then we were pushed aside. We were not always pleased about that.

The police often had to break up the fighting and even took some of the oldest boys into custody. Yet morals were better then than now. I do not recall any dirty tricks or brutality being employed. I never remember two attacking one, let alone more, and it would not have occurred to anyone to kick a boy who was down. The parents were no doubt not all pleased with the disturbances. Pabbi, however, placed the greatest emphasis on fair play. He often said: "It's all right for you to fight, but only one against one." He valued sportsmanship in a fight extremely highly. I have also tried to live by that.
First crushes on girls
After I had entered the Grammar School (Menntaskólinn), I wrote in my diary about my primary school years:

After I came to the Miðbæjarskóli school, Pétur Guðmundsson and later Björn Þorláksson were my best friends. With Bjössi I went up to Hávallagata, where he lived. There was a big group of kids there, whom I soon got to know. Some I had known before, e.g. Runólfur Þórðarson (Nunni), Þorbjörn Karlsson (Bötti), Friðrik and Robert Miller (Freddie and Bobbí), Jósef Björnsson (Ebbi), Matthías Jóhannesen (Matti), Haukur and Örn Clausen, Sverrir Scheving (later) and Guðjón Lárusson (later) and then Herdís (Heddý) and Rannveig (Ranna) Tryggvadóttir (awfully pretty girls), Theódóra Björnsdóttir (Dídó) (also pretty), Margrét Thors (Mabba) and Þorbjörg (Obba) Pétursdóttir. This was around 1938–39.

These were my first crushes on girls. I seem to remember that most often we boys were all smitten with the same girl, though it varied somewhat which of them it was each time. They were beautiful girls, but it was all very innocent. To one of them I sent a love letter, which I left under a stone where she was supposed to collect it. I do not remember which of them it was. It was not until later that I fell seriously in love.

Just like the boys, the girls were mostly from staunchly conservative families. Heddý and Ranna are the daughters of Tryggvi Ófeigsson, a trawler owner, and lived on Hávallagata. Obba is the daughter of Pétur Magnússon, government minister and director of the National Bank of Iceland (Landsbankinn). Erna Gunnarsdóttir also belonged to the group and is mentioned elsewhere in the diary. She is the daughter of Gunnar Einarsson, manager of the Ísafold printing works (Ísafoldarprentsmiðja). She lived on Garðastræti. There also lived

Mabba too. She is the daughter of Ólafur Thors, who was locked in great battles with my father in those years and long afterwards. Mabba lived in the house where the Confederation of Employers (Vinnuveitendasambandið) is now housed. Dídó, Theodóra Björnsdóttir, for a long time ran a women's clothing shop on Hverfisgata and later in the Kringlan shopping centre.

Our games often took place around Landakot Church (Landakotskirkja). There are plenty of nooks there that were good for hiding in. In those days there was a church warden there called Ferdinand. He was apt to chase us away. The Landakot field was our playground. It was much bigger then than it is now. Where the school garden of the Landakot School is now, there was a cowshed where the Catholics kept two cows. They probably supplied milk for the priests. They made hay on the fields, which then stretched to where there now stand houses built by bank director Vilhjálmur Þór, and Hamragarðar, which the Federation of Cooperatives (Sambandið) built for Jónas from Hrifla. On the green, football was played and various sports pursued. For timing the races, a splendid alarm clock was used, which probably was not all too accurate. Then there were distance runs along Hávallagata and Túngata, and throwing contests were held. Those were my events, especially the shot put. I was reasonably big for my age and was considered strong.

The girls took little part in the sports with us boys, but all the more in the games. We all got to know each other well and invited one another to visit. At one such visit I danced my first dance. Judging by the diary, these were glory days not only in memory but in reality:

There were games there every evening. We usually gathered at the corner of Hólavallagata and Hávallagata and played games, or chatted together. For a long time I had a crush on Heddý. Later Bötti's sister, Kristrún, also came. We kept coming there off and on until the latter part of the winter when Bjössi, Guðjón and I started at the Grammar School in 1942. Especially memorable are the confirmation parties. Most of us were confirmed around the same time, in the autumn of 1942. Then there were constant parties. That was when I danced for the first time, at Heddý's. It was either with her or Obba and then with Erna. Just about the biggest party was the one at my place. There were over 20 kids. Then this gradually died down. I am quite certain that these were by far the most enjoyable years of my life, at least up to now.
Sturdy Boys

On Hávallagata there lived a group of boys who formed a club among themselves called Röskir drengir (Sturdy Boys). Björn Þorláksson, my friend from the Miðbæjarskóli school, introduced me to this fellowship. The Sturdy Boys were founded on 6 March 1940. I was offered membership a little over a year later. Most of the boys were then aged 10–14. The club was mainly a sports and outdoor club, but it also held entertainment evenings at which plays were performed and stories told. The members were chiefly boys from Hávallagata, along with me and the Clausen brothers, Örn and Haukur. The Sturdy Boys published a paper that was read aloud at meetings. In it, the brothers were dubbed Haukur "Rheumatism" Klofson and Örn the Strutting. Sports were their strong suit, as later on the international stage. They were mainstays of Iceland's championship teams that drew attention around the world in the years after the war. Haukur won the Sturdy Boys' gold badge for victory in an intra-club competition. However, both brothers recall that in the Sturdy Boys the cousins Þorbjörn Karlsson and Runólfur Þórðarson were the fastest runners of all. Many from this group have been my closest companions and friends all my life, and this remarkable fellowship will therefore be described in some detail, as it deserves.

As mentioned earlier, the Sturdy Boys published a paper. Runólfur Þórðarson was its editor for most of the time and the main author of its content. This may be considered remarkable, because the group included, among others, Matthías Johannessen, who later became editor of Morgunblaðið, as is famous throughout the country. In the club's papers and minutes he is most often called Mattias Johansen, once Mattías Johassen and another time M. Johaenessen. There are no writings by Matti in the Sturdy Boys' paper, and Runólfur, who was among the paper's most energetic editors, has sometimes rubbed his nose in this when the group has met in later years. Matti has, however, in his defence that he is somewhat younger than most of the others. Three or four years was a great age difference in those years. Various humorous stories and jokes were written in the Sturdy Boys' paper. There are also photographs and drawings of the members, as well as caricatures of Hitler and Mussolini. There are also character descriptions in the style of the Icelandic sagas:

It was not so very long ago that I learned that the assembly which is called the "Sturdy Boys" had brought out a certain great paper. This seemed to me a matter of much import, and the wholesome counsel came into my mind that I should write about those men who are in this assembly. They are very many, some large and others small, and very motley is that folk. There the first man to be named is

he who is named Steingrímr and called the Red, very strong and stout and the most accomplished. He is also the chieftain of this folk and its lawspeaker. Then there is also that chieftain who is named Þorbjörn and called the Keflavíkian, a big man and very strong and stout and the most unscrupulous, and indeed many fear him when he is in a fighting mood. He is also the treasurer of the assembly. Then the third man is Jóseprr, called the Far-Travelled. He is thought a good tailor of clothes and he is well known especially among women. He is also much travelled and rides that beast which is called a bicycle. He is also very fortunate in some dealings, for his lucky stars are named Venus and Jupiter, and he is well known among their daughters. He is also the scribe of the assembly.

This was the board that sat longest. Þorbjörn Karlsson later became professor of engineering at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands). We went through our studies together for a long time, including engineering in the United States. Jósep must have been a skilled writer in those years and often wrote priceless minutes. Jósep was later the right-hand man of Magnús Víglundsson in his extensive business operations, but died before his time.

In this group were also Friðrik, who was never called anything but Freddie, and his brother Bobbý. His name was Robert. They were grandsons of Friðrik Hallgrímsson, cathedral pastor, but their father was Canadian and they had grown up there. The brothers later moved back to Canada but have kept up some contact with home here. Freddie, among other things, visited Iceland a few years ago, but he now lives in Australia.

Runólfur Þórðarson was among my best friends in those years, and that friendship of ours has continued unbroken all our lives. We went together to the United States to study engineering and shared a room there.

As a rule there were fourteen members, but fifteen when we were most numerous. Besides those already mentioned, there were the brothers Ólafur Valur and Ágúst Sigurðsson. Ólafur, among other things, had a motion passed that "if more than half the members have gone to the countryside, then those who are in town may not take any sum of money for travel or the like." We all went to the countryside at some point, so the motion was passed unanimously. Ólafur Valur later became a captain with the Coast Guard (Landhelgisgæslan). Ágúst Sigurðsson was elected a member shortly after me. He was a modest lad but cheerful and sometimes given to pranks. Thus writes Jósep Björnsson, secretary, of the meeting at which I was elected chairman of the club:

After this, open discussions began, and much that was good was said, or at least a very great deal, for sometimes everyone spoke at once, so that Ágúst had to stand waiting for five minutes for silence, but everyone was so busy getting out what they wanted to say that no one noticed him until he had got hold of a foghorn.

Ágúst took up glider training a few years later. In those days gliders were towed aloft at Reykjavík Airport. During one practice session, which took place on the runway in Skerjafjörður, the glider went out of control and swerved to the right. It ended its flight on the roof of a house, with the tragic consequence that Ágúst was killed. Bergur Jónsson was also a member. He was one of those who was expelled for some breach of discipline but readmitted. Þórður Þorvarðarson was in the club as well, and Gunnlaugur Björnsson for a short time.
My First Election Victory

From the sixteenth meeting of the club onward, which was held on 2 June 1940, the minutes were recorded in books made for the purpose, which I still have in my keeping. The first two motions recorded there were put forward by Björn. The first stipulates that "anyone who quarrels and fights with the others shall be liable to expulsion from the club". The second motion is that "the inspection of each man's membership card at meetings shall be discontinued." Both were approved. Runólfur Þórðarson was the first chairman, but Jósep Björnsson had taken over by the time I attended my first meeting in the autumn of 1940. I was admitted right away, though it was no trivial matter and required a special vote among the members. The margins were often narrow when new members were approved. At one meeting it is recorded that Daði Hjörvar, son of Helgi Hjörvar, was granted admission to the club for one month on probation, but candidates were rejected without hesitation in such elections.

Röskir drengir adopted a set of laws in twelve articles. There it says that the purpose of the club is to work for cooperation and sports among boys. General meetings were to be held twice a year, and the board was to consist of a chairman, a secretary, and a treasurer. At my second general meeting in the club I was elected secretary, and chairman at the next one, on 11 January 1942. I was thirteen years old then. The laws state that members shall pay one króna quarterly, on 1 January, 1 April, 1 August, and 1 October, and that arrears mean expulsion until the debt is paid. The article on conduct is the most detailed:

If a member is caught making a disturbance or unnecessary noise at a meeting, a) the chairman or meeting chair may order him to leave the meeting, b) he may be expelled from the club with the approval of a majority of those present.

From the minutes one can see that conduct at meetings was much discussed. We observed rules of procedure and strict regulations even though we were no more than twelve, thirteen, fourteen years old. Still, it happened that the open discussions got out of hand. When things went too far, however, no kid gloves were used. At the 30th meeting Jósep writes:

The open discussions went badly. The Clausen brothers had to leave the meeting, owing to other engagements. There was great restlessness among the members, and Róbert and Runólfur must be named first in that regard. Róbert was to be ordered out of the meeting, but this [was] abandoned. Runólfur was ordered out, but he then claimed a great numbness in his legs, so that he had to be carried out. [...] It is certain that if more meetings are held like this one, it will become impossible for anyone to hold meetings because of the rowdiness.

During my time as chairman, the meetings of Röskir drengir were always held at the Prime Minister's Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn). That was, of course, not a bad arrangement. We were allowed to take over the large dining room. There we divided ourselves between two tables, one large and the other smaller. At the smaller one the family ate its meals, and there the board of Röskir drengir sat during meetings. The rest of the group then sat at the larger table. This was considered a most dignified setting, and the boys knew how to appreciate it.

As the next general meeting approached, thoughts turned to a change of chairman. It had been the rule to change the chairman and the board every six months. My fellow members remember it this way: that I took it well that I was to step down from the office. Soon afterward, however, I let word go out that in that case the meetings could, of course, no longer be held at the Prime Minister's Residence. All plans for a change of chairman were then forgotten, and so it came about that I continued to hold the office — and still do.
Tarzan Games, Joyrides, and Provisional Laws

My father thought well of Röskir drengir and considered it a good and wholesome fellowship. We were therefore allowed to gather at the Prime Minister's Residence. In later years these old friends of mine have often remarked on how much forbearance my parents, and especially my mother, showed us boys despite the busy household. My mother always received this noisy crowd warmly, and although they all knew that the country's prime minister lived there, no ceremony or special airs went with it — rather the opposite. Many of them recall that in my childhood home there was more freedom than in most other homes of that time.
Games of hide-and-seek ranged through the whole house, and boys could be found up in the attic rafters,

down in the cellar or under my parents' double bed. It was not until my mother came upon some of us among her evening gowns in the wardrobe in the bedroom that a place was found where we were unwelcome. Into the better sitting rooms we were, admittedly, not allowed to go, and we obeyed that.

The Tarzan game was popular. In it we all hid except one, who was Tarzan. He then ran about the house and shouted "Tarzan" loudly and smartly whenever he detected someone. Matthías Johannessen recalls that on one occasion it was his turn, and he yanked open the door to the prime minister's office. He then yelled "Tarzan" triumphantly when he noticed signs of movement. It turned out to be my father, who sat there writing. He is said to have uttered nothing more than: "Shut the door, man."

Otherwise my father managed to earn the title of Tarzan in the eyes of these friends of mine. At the end of meetings we were in the habit of jumping off the south balcony of the Prime Minister's Residence. It is a rather high drop, so that only about half of us dared. My mother worried about this and asked my father to intervene. At some point, when a jumping contest was at its height, he appeared unexpectedly on the balcony. The group hesitated. Instead of giving us a lecture, however, the prime minister swung himself over the railing and sailed down into the garden. I was below and can still picture him stepping out onto the balcony and then floating down in grey trousers and a waistcoat. When he had landed he simply said: "It's quite all right, I'll have a word with your mother."

When we boys grew up a little, our interest shifted from Tarzan games and model aeroplanes to real automobiles. The streets of Reykjavík were gravel roads in my growing-up years, and at first there were few cars. Around 1930 there were about 400 of them in Reykjavík, and ten years later 677. Pabbi acquired a car rather early. Some said he was car-crazy. I remember many cars that he owned — first an old Ford, a Chevrolet, then a Mercury, and at some point he owned a Packard. He always had good cars. All along he had the registration number R-25.

I particularly remember when my father owned a splendid Mercury which we boys found too magnificent to be able to leave in peace. It usually stood on the slope in front of the Prime Minister's Residence. We were in the habit of commandeering it and driving out onto Hringbraut along the little Tjörn. We were probably about 13–14 years old then. On one occasion I had got up to a fair speed. Runólfur Þórðarson says, in fact, that I had meant to reach a hundred. The road, however, was full of potholes and by no means intended for fast driving. I lost control of the car for a good stretch, so that it swerved about on the road. It all ended well, though, but seldom have we been as frigh-
-tened in our lives. Nunni maintains, in fact, that I was ice-cool the whole time, but the truth is that I drove home half-trembling. We did not, however, let this teach us a lesson.

Once, when my father had walked down to town, I got hold of the keys. There by the street was a concrete curb with a railing on top, but because of the slope the curb was very low near the top of the hill. I backed the car up and then meant to drive down along it, but the bumper rode up onto the curb. There the car hung, stuck on its bumper, and my father found out that I had been sneaking off with it. I got a scolding for that.

Debates at the meetings of Röskir drengir were often vigorously fought, no less than on the sports field. Following the first re-election of a chairman in the history of Röskir drengir, Björn Þorláksson put forward a motion "that the board be authorized to issue provisional laws without the consent of all members and outside meetings (i.e. at board meetings). Provisional laws are necessary and people must accept them." The club had never before taken up motions on contentious issues that were simultaneously under discussion in politics. We were presumably coming of age and had probably begun to follow politics and public debate more closely. Previously, motions had mainly been put forward about sports tournaments or the awarding of the club's badges. On the provisional laws, Jósep, the minute-taker, was blunt as before:

Long discussions took place about such a self-evident matter, and some did not want to vote until the board had promised that no dictatorship would take place. The motion was approved by 6 votes against 1; one was invalid.

We naturally considered it necessary, in such perilous times as the war years, to be able to issue provisional laws. I do not remember whether we ever used the authorization. At least it is nowhere mentioned in the books. I seem to recall that it was specified that the provision could only be invoked in cases of absolute emergency. No doubt we had learned that from politics as well.

The board of Röskir drengir was granted the authority to issue provisional laws on 13 September 1942. Provisional laws on arbitration in wage and price matters had been issued by the national unity government earlier that same year under the leadership of my father, with the support of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) but against the opposition of the ministers of the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). Provisional laws had also been issued postponing the municipal elections in Reykjavík because of a printers' strike at the beginning of that same year.
This authorization to issue provisional laws is recorded in the last preserved

minutes of Röskir drengir from those years. The club did not, however, split over dictatorship or politics, but over smoking. Haukur Clausen proposed that those who smoked should be expelled from the club. It was approved by a margin of one vote. I was among the supporters of the motion, being very much opposed to smoking. Those who had begun to dabble in cigarettes therefore departed, and regular activities ceased shortly afterward.

The group from Hávallagata scattered after some of us began studies at the Grammar School while others did not. We still met from time to time after that, though. Our games died out around the same time as Röskir drengir stopped gathering. Our interests were changing.
In the diary, my account of this period of my life ends with words tinged with melancholy:

We boys had a club among ourselves, a sports club, called "Röskir drengir". I was for a long time (the longest) its chairman, and its last. It has folded [...]. Now one hardly knows the girls any more, barely greets them in the street. They have become "ladies".

Röskir drengir still lives on, however. There are now ten of us in the country. Meetings are not as frequent as they used to be. Three meetings have been held since the fellowship's heyday, two of them at the Prime Minister's Residence, during my time as a minister. These are joyful reunions, though our gatherings now have a different and more restrained tone since wives joined the group.
Setting Course for the Matriculation Examination

For a long time I intended to become a carpenter. My father said he had no objection to that; both my grandfathers had been good craftsmen and it was a good trade. We agreed, however, that I should first go to the Grammar School, since it would do no harm to have a matriculation examination. For that to be possible one had to do well in the entrance examination, and I went, along with a great many of my friends, into the preparatory department run by Einar Magnússon. I did very well in the examination, placing third highest, and thus got into the first form of the Reykjavík Grammar School (Menntaskólinn í Reykjavík). For six years the school was my second home; the first two years one studied for the intermediate examination, but from the third form onward one studied for the matriculation examination. Around the time I graduated, the arrangement changed and the intermediate course was abolished at MR. Even now, however, people still speak of studies for the matriculation examination beginning in the third form.
I entered the 1st form of the Reykjavík Grammar School in the autumn of 1942 and graduated in the spring of 1948. In those days the school was seldom called anything but Menntaskólinn. In

in the third form we were joined by many who had fallen overboard after the entrance examination for the first form and had taken their intermediate examination at other schools. We who had been at the Grammar School from the beginning, however, had already grown close and stuck together at the school for all six years. My closest circle of friends nevertheless also included those with whom I had formed bonds of friendship in my childhood years. The intermediate years were in part the era of Röskir drengir, and then, one might say, the student years took over. In life, though, there are no sharp divisions between periods such as one sometimes tries to construct in history books.

Jóhannes Nordal, later Governor of the Central Bank, was inspector scholae when I began my studies at the school. He described the attitudes of us schoolboys toward the school and our studies in an article he wrote to spur the school's womenfolk to great deeds. The article appeared in Skólablaðið at Christmas 1942.

Most of your schoolfellows have come to the school to take the matriculation examination and then continue their studies, and they dream of becoming great men, of use to their country and nation. They feel that at the school they are preparing themselves for the life's work they intend to take on. Activity in the school's social life is the beginning of their struggle in life, and they feel that their studies at the school, and especially the education they try to acquire outside the school, have a purpose as preparation for the tasks they long to grapple with.

There were 86 girls and 207 boys the autumn I began my studies, but 145 to 300 boys in my last winter at the school. Proportionally, then, their numbers increased only slightly during those years. The women did not become very active in the school's social life until a year after I graduated from there. Then the girls founded their own society, the Debating Society of Grammar School Girls (Málfundafélag menntaskólastúlkna, MM). Its leading figures were Ragnhildur Helgadóttir, Vigdís Finnbogadóttir, Hrefna Sigvaldadóttir, and Ingibjörg Pálmadóttir.

Ingibjörg was the daughter of Pálmi, the headmaster, and became the first woman president of Framtíðin, the Grammar School's debating society, a year later, after a special women's list stood for election in the school. The board was made up entirely of women that winter, and the Debating Society of Grammar School Girls was then dissolved.

Ragnhildur was later to become a minister for the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in my first government, and Vigdís upheld the honor of these progressive grammar-school girls and became the first popularly elected woman president in the world. Yet neither these excellent women nor Jóhannes Nordal can be counted among my most memorable schoolmates.
My first winter at the Grammar School was unusual because the school

had just returned from two years of exile. The British had seized the school building by force of arms shortly after their landing. Teaching took place in the newly built premises of the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands) on Melarnir while this lasted. The British did not hand the Grammar School back until 13 June 1942, despite repeated appeals. The exile had weighed heavily on the students and also on various teachers of the school. According to what appears in the school's history, Bogi Ólafsson is said to have taken leave of his students in the first year of the occupation with the words: "I would most earnestly beg you not to go rubbing shoulders with those lice-ridden wretches." Thus spoke the English teacher. The German teacher's words were not put on record, since he was arrested on the very day of the occupation and sent to detention in Britain.

In 1940 there were for a time sandbag shelters in the vicinity of the Grammar School and a military guard at the school building. The British initially used the building as an infirmary for the land forces, and many stories about it circulated in the following years. In the first issue of Skólablaðið to appear that autumn, the obituary ran thus:
Right after the occupation the Grammar School was used as a lunatic asylum, and unconfirmed reports state that the most utterly mad were kept in the teachers' room.

It was not possible to begin teaching in all the classrooms that first autumn, in 1942. The state in which the British had left the building in mid-June was so bad that nearly the whole house needed repairs. The opening of the school year was therefore not traditional; instead, the forms started up gradually as the repairs to the classrooms were completed. Teaching began first in the 2nd and 6th forms on 16 October, but for us first-formers somewhat later. The gymnasium was in the worst state and was not used for teaching until the autumn of 1944. The ceremonial hall had been used as a bar by the British and painted pink. It was brought back into use at the Christmas festivities.

The students strove to revive the school's old traditions that first winter after the exile. These years, however, were marked above all by the arrival of new customs that forced their way in with the soldiers and the war. The Christmas festivities bore the marks of both currents — strong traditions and "world culture", in that order. In the time-honored ceremonial hall the Christmas festivities began with a dignified ceremonial procession led by the headmaster and the inspector and the Reykjavík poet Tómas Guðmundsson, who delivered a poem to the school, Skólaminni.

Once the traditions had been dispensed with, however, the students thronged onto the floor "with heaps of brilliantine in their hair and lady-killers around their necks", to quote the description in Skólablaðið. There were no folk dances or round-up waltzes

that were chosen when the dancing began. The girls had "freshly set hair and were fragrant with Christmas Coty". Bubble gum and Coca-Cola had made their entry into society, and the school did not go untouched by it. The older boys often wore hats instead of school caps. "Skalli" was opened, where one could buy ice cream and cola drinks during breaks.

Icelandic society was changing rapidly in those years. Two things had the greatest influence: the occupation and the war profits on the one hand, and the revival of the ideals of independence, with independence newly won, on the other. It has often seemed to me that too little has been made of this transformation and too much of the so-called '68 generation. It was in these years that modernity came to Iceland, whereas the hippies did nothing but smoke hashish and neglect to visit the barber. What was good in their ideas had existed before, and what they added has aged badly.

We young people let the worries and pessimistic grumbling about the demise of Icelandic culture pass us by like the wind. We tried to be "smart", used brilliantine in our hair and knotted ties around our necks, drank Coke, and said both "hi" and "bye", though neither was Icelandic. I was, in fact, an exception in that I drank neither Coke nor coffee. I did not consider those drinks healthy and sipped milk and malt ale instead.

We friends were probably quite finely dressed by today's standards, in dark suits of coarse fabrics. Later I began to wear tweed suits, which became very fashionable. Without exception we wore ties. Björn Þorláksson was tremendously diligent about buying himself new ties, and I was not far behind. When my hairstyle turned out well, a lock hung down over my forehead.

The music of the new age we also embraced with open arms. We cared little that some considered jazz evidence that "national culture was giving way to American low culture derived from Negroes," as it was put. We friends were very fond of good jazz and scoffed at the notion that it was "one of the clearest examples of bad foreign influences". After lessons ended at the Grammar School in the afternoon, we often went to someone's home to listen to the latest records.

One of my classmates, Guðjón Lárusson, owned a great many jazz records. He was the son of Lárus Jóhannesson and lived on Suðurgata. The Clausen brothers also had a considerable collection. We adored jazz musicians like Fats Waller and Art Tatum. They were played day in and day out. Duke Ellington and Benny Goodman were also frequently on the turntable. When I was in the United States I got the chance to see and hear some of these masters. One always flew through New York on the way to and from Iceland. We schoolmates from Chicago would then go to jazz joints on 42nd Street and in Greenwich Village,

where the atmosphere was relaxed. We also followed the jazz to Harlem and were never harassed. I understand, however, that hardly a white man goes there now. In Chicago we saw Art Tatum and Duke Ellington.
Movies, jazz and dance practice

During my secondary-school years I generally put my homework before everything else, and my mother shielded me from all disturbance in the meantime. Once it was done I liked to go to the movies or over to one of my friends' homes to listen to jazz. I mostly read books in the evenings after I had gotten into bed. It is no exaggeration to say that in those years we got to know the world through radio news, films, thrillers and jazz. We drew our dreams from the same sources.

I could always turn to my father with whatever was on my mind, and at the office we often talked about the future. But we also pondered life and existence, dreams and yearnings. If something was stirring inside me, I usually brought it to him. Once I mention such conversations in the diary. When this was written I was 17 years old.

Friday 23 November 1945. I have sometimes been thinking about what meaning there actually is in all this toil, in studying — why not just enjoy oneself? On the whole I have grown very tired of this studying. Most people's lives are so unvarying their whole life long: to the office and back. What I would most like is to go out, see the world and enjoy myself, land in exciting adventures and win fame and success that way. But unfortunately no one can do this except someone who is very wealthy. I would also most like to be my own master, to be able to work when I want and play when I want. Pabbi and I were debating this until 10 and agreed in many respects.

I agreed with my father that the most sensible thing would be to finish my examinations if other wishes were to come true. The dream of becoming rich and famous followed me to the United States, where I recorded ideas for getting rich in a special black notebook. Some of them I put into practice, as will be recounted later.

In my first years at the Gymnasium (Menntaskólinn) I was an enormously prolific reader, and books about explorers absorbed me completely, along with the usual adventure books. The stories of Stanley and Livingstone were great favorites, adventure books such as Tales of an Army Doctor (Sögur herlæknisins) and others in that vein. Most of these books I borrowed from the National Library (Landsbókasafnið). There reigned a librarian who went by the namename

"Red body". He was very stout and red-nosed. Up in a cupboard he kept a hip flask in a safe spot, from which he regularly refreshed himself. He was often as gentle as a child, though he was firm that books could not be lent out to take home. I got an exemption from this strict rule on the condition that my father stand surety for the books. And so I buried myself in the National Library's books.

At the Gymnasium, social life took up more time as the years went by. The adventure books gave way to the Sagas of Icelanders, which were read both out of interest and for examinations. Textbooks grew ever more substantial, and in addition to them I studied chess books with zeal.

I often went to the movies in those years. Television, of course, had not yet arrived, and the cinema was the best entertainment. Most weeks we went to the movies two or three times. I recorded the names of the films in my diary and passed judgment on them as well. Usually those verdicts were just one word: poor, fair, good or excellent. Only the occasional film received a fuller treatment. Gone with the Wind I declared in the diary to be one of the best films I had ever seen. I did add, though, that it was so long that all my limbs were numb after sitting through it. Most of the titles I have long since forgotten, but adventure films were the favorites. We picked up the cinema tickets in advance, preferably around noon on the day of the showing. When popular films were shown, long lines formed and there was a fight for every ticket. Some films we saw many times. Especially if Rita Hayworth was in the leading role. Bjössi Þorláks and I saw her surely three or four times in a film whose name I have long since forgotten. Rita, however, I will never forget; we were utterly enchanted by her. The main cinemas were Gamla bíó and Nýja bíó, but it happened that we went all the way to the Hafnarfjörður cinema. Later Tjarnarbíó came on the scene. During the war years a cinema was also set up in a Nissen hut on Melarnir. Concerts were held there from time to time as well.

Special review boards examined every film and decided whether they were fit for showing or not. They also cut out pieces of unnecessarily long kisses or violent scenes. The board members sat in the auditorium and passed their judgments. Garðar Þorsteinsson at Gamla bíó was an old schoolmate and friend of my father's. He, of course, held special review screenings like the other cinema owners. Garðar often invited us boys to attend these screenings. We were placed out in a corner under the overhanging balcony where the board sat. There we huddled and watched what we considered the very worst horror films.

Music was an integral part of life in those years. We boys worshipped jazz on our own, but dance music was the way to the girls' hearts. I never recall us inviting girls to the movies. We came into contact with them

mainly at dance practices and balls. I often recorded in the diary whom I danced with. If it had been a lively evening, the list could get long. In November 1945 the diary mentions two dance practices. Of the first it says:
I spun completely wild with Tóta for 2 dances and once with Gitta. Gitta dances about the best of all the girls I have danced with, and then Tóta.

This Gitta was not from the Gymnasium, and she is mentioned only in this one place. Tóta, on the other hand, was my classmate and a great friend. Her full name is Þórunn Guðnadóttir. She is married to Axel Kristjánsson, a lawyer, who was also in our class.
The time came when it mattered greatly whom I danced with. Then jealousy could even begin to stir.
I danced with: Rósa, Beta, Gunna, Ólöf, Hildur, Sigga Löve, Högna, Margrét Vilhj. (in 3b), Jagga, one more from 3b, and others, and last but not least Didda. She was with some "damn" boy.

Didda's full name is Kristrún Karlsdóttir, and she is the sister of Þorbjörn Karlsson from the Hardy Boys (Röskir drengir). I first got to know her in the group on Hávallagata. They were born in Keflavík. She was very beautiful, blonde and handsome from every point of view. I think all the boys were taken with her. Didda came to the Gymnasium and we were in the same class. We fell for each other.

Before we got together, Didda was in a relationship with Ásmundur Bjarnason, who later became Icelandic champion in the sprints. It was probably he whom I called "some 'damn' boy" in the diary. I was already taken with her then. She got engaged to Ásmundur and had a child with him. Ásmundur was at the Commercial College (Verslunarskólinn). Once, as so often, I was walking along Tjarnargata and Bogi Ólafsson, the English teacher, was striding along on the other side of the street. He called me over to him, as was his habit if he had something on his mind. "That's ugly news I heard," said Bogi. "What was that?" I replied. "This business with Kristrún, the most beautiful girl in the school," he says, adding: "That you boys there should be such wretches as to let a boy from outside the school snatch her away from under your noses."

Bogi had a special concern and ambition on behalf of the school's students. I, however, stared down at the street and kept my thoughts to myself. Didda and Ásmundur broke up some time later, and Didda and I then got together. We

were in the fifth form, and this was my first romance. We were both very smitten, I think I may say. Didda was a very entertaining companion and has always been light-hearted. We went to dance practices together, met in the evenings, and probably behaved no differently than young lovers have done through the ages.

Our relationship did not last, and the main reason was that I went to the United States after my matriculation examination. In the aftermath we mostly lost touch. She and Ásmundur got back together, which in itself was perfectly lovely. Didda and Ásmundur married and moved to Húsavík. They have lived there ever since. Didda was the first love of my life and holds a special place in my heart as such. I think everyone looks back with longing on their youthful love, and I am no exception.
Nearer death than life
The time came when I took on other summer work than farm labor. On Wednesday 23 June 1943 I set off for road work north at Vatnsskarð. About it I have written in my diary:

I got up at 5:30. The weather was the most ideal, sunshine and calm. I went at 6:30 down to the Laxfoss, with my bicycle, [. . .] but Mamma and Pabbi came with my things afterwards. The trip went splendidly. There were many boys there whom I know. Jóhann the foreman was waiting for us in Borgarnes.

Life was good at Vatnsskarð. I worked there for two summers, in 1943 and 1944. A camp of tents was pitched where we were quartered, and our camp was called Reykjavík. It stood on a grassy bank with Valahnjúkur towering above. There were numerous boys there from Reykjavík and further afield. Many of us were in our fifteenth and sixteenth years and worked from morning to night. This would probably be considered slave labor now and strictly forbidden by the European Union. Yet I am not aware that any of us suffered any harm from it.

Everyone shared tents with others. I was in a tent with Matthías Johannessen, whom I knew well from the Hardy Boys (Röskir drengir). The tent life with Matti is memorable not least because one night we were nearly dead. It is described thus in my diary:
On Saturday night [21 August 1943] Matti and I had gone to bed. I then ask him to turn off the oil stove. He blew on it. We then fall asleep. Around one o'clock I wake to Gendi bursting in. It was
everything inside had turned black. It was hard to wake Matti. He was so far gone. We aired the tent out. Matti fell asleep again at once, but I got out of bed. We owed Gendi (Guðm.) our lives.

I still remember the feeling of dread while Matthías was coming back to life that night. It took an eternity before he was breathing properly. Jóhann Hjörleifsson was the head foreman, and he was so shaken by the news that he took to his bed, distraught. The foreman did not get up for a whole day, and Matti and I coughed up soot for many days afterwards.

Matthías and I long believed that we owed our lives to our workmates. They had come home late from a dance at Varmahlíð. In the diary I say that our workmate Gendi was the first on the scene. That is wrong. The truth is that Þorkell Zakaríasson, a truck driver from Vestur-Húnavatnssýsla, saved our lives. He drove past the road-work camp that night with his companion and saw smoke pouring out of one of the tents. They were transporting herring from Sauðárkrókur to Vatnshlíð. The two of them dragged us out of the deadly smoke. Matthías therefore likes to put it this way: that it was herring that saved us, not merrymaking in Skagafjörður. I have never been able to thank Þorkell adequately for the gift of life, but Matthías has met him. Once, when Þorkell was in a gloomy mood over politics, he is said to have remarked that he probably should never have bothered to save us.

Our workmate Guðmundur, Gendi, we called our rescuer that summer. He was admired for his strength and physique. But the time came when I considered that I repaid him the gift of life. The whole group went out to Drangey one Sunday. The island is cleft in such a way that the headland is on one side and the island itself on the other. The headland overhangs on all sides, and when you have climbed up into the notch there is a sheer precipice below, probably a good 100 fathoms. There were rusty chains there with rotten wooden slats between them, forming steps up onto the headland. Three of us decided to go up: myself, Gendi and Bjarni Guðnason, who later became one of my best friends and my desk-mate at the Gymnasium. Among his claims to fame are becoming a national-team player in handball and football, a member of the Althing, and a professor of the kings' sagas at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands).

Bjarni was sturdy, though Gendi was by far the strongest of the three of us. We got up without any difficulty to speak of. At the cliff edge, the topmost steps of the ladder were missing, so that when standing on the highest crossbar we had to haul ourselves up onto the brink. That proved easy for us, but the way down was the harder trial. The height then seemed much greater down to the topmost step, and below that came the sheer drop to the sea, where the birds could be seen gliding like

tiny specks above the surface of the sea. When we looked over the edge, a terrifying sight met us, and before we knew it Gendi was seized by an indescribable fear of heights. This big man stiffened up and trembled. Bjarni and I were at our wits' end. It ended, though, with me going down the ladder first, receiving Gendi and guiding his feet. Bjarni waited up top, tried to calm him and directed his hands. We finally got him to go over the edge, since there was no other way down. I remember well how terribly those big feet shook. In the end I managed to wedge them onto the topmost step, and Bjarni managed to get Gendi to loosen his grip and inch his way downwards. I feared that Gendi would drag me with him into the deep if he fell. So I hurried down as fast as I could, and the other two made it down after me.

That done, we went up onto the main island. Matthías tells that where the island is highest, a competition was held over who dared stand closest to the edge. I am said to have won it by standing with only my heels on solid ground and my toes out over the edge. I remember it only vaguely. What I do remember is that for many nights afterwards I woke up from nightmares.
Driving carts, "knocking up" the edge and working the tip

Life in the road work was good, but we often got salt fish that was not considered particularly good. Then there was invariably fish hash (plokkfiskur) the next day. I make repeated comments on this in the diary: "Salt fish to eat, barely edible." (29/6) "We got salt fish to eat and it was bad." (30/6) "We got salt fish to eat. It was inedible." (1/7) I have not been able to eat fish hash since, and I am particular about salt fish. Soon after arriving I also felt I lacked various things, which I then brought with me the following year: "I had discovered that I was in need of many things, e.g. a mattress, a washbasin, more soap, (an oil stove) etc."

After the swimming pool came to Varmahlíð, we piled onto the bed of the truck when work was done and sped off for a swim. That was great bliss. At the farm Stóra-Vatnsskarð lived young men who were eager to play Lomber. I learned the game and sometimes played with them. I bought my first hat before I came north the second summer. It was a Battersby hat, with a large wide brim, and very fashionable. To one of these card players I sold the hat for 35 krónur. I considered I had made a very good deal, since I had bought it for 25 krónur.

The second summer a bulldozer arrived that graded up the road. One of the older men was named Jónatan and was tremendously hard-working. He was rather small and not much to look at. Jónatan always cut turf sods, as it was called. These were

soil wedges from which the road edges were built up. He never at any time paused in his work but cut sods practically without letup all day long. The arrival of the bulldozer was an insult to Jónatan and bordered on blasphemy in his eyes. He never called it anything but "the ugly contraption" or "the wretched calamity". Most of the older men joined in these curses. When the bulldozer finally got stuck in a bog, they positively perked up. "Didn't we say so? It may be that such machines can be used in America, but here in this country it makes no sense at all." It took a good three days to get the bulldozer out. Nothing worked, even though all the horses and trucks available were harnessed to the task. Finally, enormous quantities of rock were driven in under the bulldozer, which was made to trample them beneath itself.

When I started in the road work I was put to "cart-driving" (kúska), as it was called. It consisted of leading the horse carts onto which sods and gravel were loaded. Bjarni Guðnason and I, however, soon rose in rank. We were allowed to build up the edges, which was considered work of great distinction. The building was demanding, too. The foreman on this part of the road construction was named Brynjólfur, a nationally known road worker with great experience. He made regular rounds and checked whether everything was done correctly and free of bulges. If it was not, the scoldings rained down. On one occasion my skill had failed me and there was a bump on the edge. Then Brynjólfur said: "You are far too young to have started fathering children." It was called "knocking up" the edge (að barna kantinn) if a bulge appeared on it. He then took the shovel and began pounding the unevenness in. Another position of honor I attained was to be "on the tip" (á tipp), as it was called. There I received the gravel and spread it out on the road. It was damned drudgery, because the boys liked to load the gravel toward the front of the carts so that it would be hard to tip them out. So it was often a great struggle.
The second summer in the road work was for the most part like the first. I did not devote many lines to describing it in my diaries. The following passage covers 1 July to 3 September 1944:

I arrived at the pass at 5:30. There was no bed free, so I slept in the bed of a boy who was not at home. There were many there whom I knew from the year before, e.g. Bjarni Guðnason, Garðar Gíslason, Ragnar Gíslason, Bangsi (Björn B.), Jóndi (Jón Magn.), Matti (Matthías Jóhannesen), Árni Björns., old Stebbi (Stefán of Æsustaðir), Jónatan, Jói from Langidalur, and others. [. . .] Then time passed always the same, the weather was good, except for the next-to-last week. I cut sods and did a little building and so on. The last 3 weeks I was always "on the tip", that is to say spreading out the gravel.
A thirst for adventure and Iceland's wilderness

My love for Iceland and its nature is a blend of patriotism and a thirst for adventure that was kindled in my youth and still finds an outlet in travels around the country. I grew up with the outdoor life. The same was true of various of my friends, and in my teenage years a group quickly formed around traveling about the country. Our mountain trips became numerous. They lasted up to a week, and many mountains were climbed on each trip. We climbed Strútur and Okið, went down into Kaldidalur and to Brunnar, where Uxahryggir branch off from Kaldidalur. We went to Tindafjallajökull and climbed all its peaks. There was fierce competition over who could get across fastest, especially between Sverrir Scheving and me. On the Tindafjöll trip I outdid everyone because I walked on skins, as it was called. These were sealskins stretched under the skis: a pouch was slipped over the back end of the ski and the skin tied underneath. The hairs point backwards, so the skins give incredible grip. With skins under the skis you can walk straight up a precipitously steep slope. We climbed many other mountains: Kerlingafjöll, Hekla, Botnsúlur, Eyjafjallajökull, Snæfellsjökull, Vífilfell, and often Esja. The most difficult mountain I climbed, though, was Herðubreið.

This enthusiasm for the outdoors led us to form an association to erect a ski lodge out of an old Nissen hut on Hellisheiði. In that group were, among others, Guðjón Lárusson, who became a doctor, Haukur Jónasson, also a doctor, Daði Hjörvar and Ágúst Sigurðsson, who are both deceased, Björn Árnason, who became town engineer in Hafnarfjörður, and Sverrir Scheving. Sverrir is a man of many talents and achieved success in the fields he devoted himself to. Studying was not always one of them. When his parents expected him to be sitting over his books, he might be perfecting his skill in mirror writing, which he mastered completely. Sverrir later became a geologist and worked at the Building Research Institute (Rannsóknarstofnun byggingariðnaðarins). Sverrir's foster father was Þorsteinn Scheving Thorsteinsson, who owned the Reykjavík Pharmacy (Reykjavíkurapótek). Sverrir now lives in Höfn in Hornafjörður. This group that built the lodge went on many mountain trips together. In all there were about ten boys.

For the lodge we chose a beautiful spot east of Skarðsmýrarfjall on the way into Innstidalur. After dismantling the hut in town, we rented a ten-wheel truck with a trailer to haul it up there. Daði sat up front with the driver and was supposed to show the way. First he went past the turnoff. It was very difficult to turn the truck around on the narrow roads and it took a long time. When we came to the most impassable stretch of the route, Daði told the driver to go straight ahead instead of threading the path we had already chosen around a bog. The truck got stuck, and we did not get it out until we had

finished emptying everything off the platform. The hut never made it to the spot we had intended for it; instead we carried it about a hundred metres from the bog and erected it there in a small hollow. The work plans must have been somewhat inaccurate. We had intended to finish the hut in two weeks, but we did not manage it in two years. It therefore never came into full use before we scattered across the world. Scouts used the hut for a while, but by now it has fallen into a very poor state.

After I bought a jeep, it became our main means of transport. We drove it everywhere. One of our most famous trips was our journey to Arnarvatnsheiði in the spring of 1948. It was my first mountain trip by car. With me were Guðjón Lárusson and the late Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson. We intended to make use of fishing rights on Arnarvatnsheiði that came with the farm Klettur in Borgarfjörður, which my father had bought. The weather was raw, overcast, with drizzling rain now and then.

At Kalmanstunga we met the farmer Kristófer Ólafsson in the farmyard. We told him we were heading up to Arnarvatnsheiði to fish. He burst out laughing. "Do you really think you'll make it up to Arnarvatnsheiði?" he said with a grin, being a man of good humour. "You'll never even reach Norðlingafljót," he added. This spurred us on, and I pressed him and asked where it was best to cross Norðlingafljót. Kristófer then smiled and said that after passing Surtshellir and crossing Þorvaldsháls, the best place to cross was at the first bend. We believed this.

Once past Surtshellir came Þorvaldsháls, which was very hard going. We got the car stuck repeatedly. When things were at their worst we tried the jack that came with the car, but it broke. At the same time it emerged that we had forgotten a shovel. So I got under a corner of the car and managed to lift it enough that stones could be placed under the wheel. We finally made it over the ridge. When we reached the river we followed Kristófer's advice and tried to cross at the first bend. There the car plunged almost completely under in the river. We barely got out by backing it up. We then drove farther up along the river. At the next bend my companions waded out to check the ford. We then made another attempt, which succeeded except that the bank on the other side was far too high and impassable for the car. So we had to turn back a second time and drove still farther up along the river. We did not make a third attempt until I had myself waded across the river and inspected the bank carefully.

On the other bank a bog awaited us. We saw a lake nearby and decided to take the plunge and try to skim the jeep across the stretches of bog at high speed. Of course this was recklessness, and it is hard to see how we would have freed the car if it had sunk. We made it across and pitched tents for the night. However, not a single fish came out of the lake, and we decided
therefore to head back to inhabited areas rather than look for the next lake, since the petrol was beginning to run low. We made it back the same way without major mishap, incredible as it may seem.

When we arrived at Kalmanstunga everything was in an uproar. My father had telephoned and spoken to Kristófer, who said he had told us it was out of the question to cross Norðlingafljót. He was even certain that we had never reached it because of the impassable terrain on Þorvaldsháls. We phoned town at once and got the news that a search party was about to set out after us. Fortunately it was stopped in time. On this trip we showed an incredible lack of foresight, which I have tried to learn from.

Some years later I met Kristófer in Reykjavík. He said he had to apologise to me for not having believed that we had made it across Norðlingafljót. Our tracks in the bog had been found during the autumn sheep round-up. "On the other hand," he said, "you hit upon the only lake on Arnarvatnsheiði that has no fish." And then he chuckled.

Later that same spring, Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson and I drove east to Hekla and climbed it. We went around the north side to a place called Skjól and got the car stuck. We walked from there. The crater was smoking heavily. Those who have seen Hekla in that mood understand well why it was once believed that the volcano's crater was the antechamber of hell. In Halldór Laxness's Iceland's Bell (Íslandsklukkan), Jón Hreggviðsson says that this is probably true, since Danish can often be heard rising from the crater.

I inherited my love of the outdoors from my parents. My father believed in land and nation, and few things were closer to his heart than the motto of the youth movement: "Everything for Iceland." It was in his blood. The nation's autonomy and independence were his most precious jewels, and in equal measure he sought rest and enjoyment in Iceland's nature. In this my mother was truly of one mind with him. I have therefore pursued outdoor life from early childhood and am happiest in the mountains. A few peaks still remain for me to climb. Shortly after my seventieth birthday, however, their number dropped by one when I climbed Hvannadalshnjúkur together with my sons, Hermann and Guðmundur.
Chapter Four
STUDENT YEARS AND GREAT AMBITION

At the Reykjavík Grammar School (Menntaskólinn í Reykjavík), the spirit of headmaster Pálmi Hannesson hovered over the waters. Pálmi was of great stature, remarkably hale and exceptionally deep-voiced. His spirit was the spirit of the school. Pálmi was a very strict administrator and kept things under firm discipline. Many felt he went rather far in those matters, and I was no exception. Looking back, however, I am extremely grateful to him for the provisions he gave me for the road. He instilled self-discipline and good manners in his pupils. Among them was punctuality, which I myself value very highly. Pálmi wanted to push back against dissolution in society.

As mentioned earlier, Pálmi's appointment to the post met with great opposition both within the school and outside it, especially in Reykjavík, and people divided very much along political lines. Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) supporters backed Pálmi, while Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) supporters and other conservatives raged against him. Pálmi weathered all the opposition, and I am glad of it. Otherwise our paths would never have crossed.

Despite discipline and clear rules, Pálmi was liberal in many respects. He wanted to be in close contact with pupils and let us come nearer to him than had previously been known. He was also among the first teachers at the school to invite pupils to address him informally, abandoning the formal mode of address. In many matters he introduced new attitudes.
