The older teachers still almost all used the formal address. Pálmi Hannesson is one of the most memorable men I have ever known. He held the minds and hearts of most pupils during the years I was at the school. It made no difference where people stood politically. Everyone respected Pálmi.

School began at eight in the morning. On the minute, the headmaster himself locked the front doors and the pupils gathered in the venerable ceremonial hall on the second floor. There we sang a morning song every morning. These were mainly patriotic songs. In the Hall the headmaster also addressed the pupils and dis-

cussed the most varied of subjects: the school, studies, the country's history and nature, the Icelandic language, or outdoor life. These addresses are very memorable and left their mark on all who listened.

Classes always began at 8.15. At that moment the headmaster opened the front doors and wrote down the names of those standing outside. If this recurred, Pálmi contacted the parents. In this way the headmaster took a keen interest in the affairs of each and every one, and would even visit those who reported in sick to check on their condition. Some would call this meddling and mistrust, but I prefer the word caring. Only once in those six years did I arrive late. I was then in the second year and was very uneasy when the headmaster opened the front doors. Sure enough, Pálmi fixed his eyes sharply on me and said: "And you too, Steingrímur." "Yes," I muttered, "I fell into the Tjörnin." For a moment the headmaster seemed about to keep the same stern expression, but then he could hold back no longer and burst out laughing. The ice on the Tjörnin had proved rather weak that morning and had given way under me. I had therefore had to go home and change clothes.

One thing Pálmi could not change, however gladly he would have wished to. Dance practices, as the grammar school balls were called, were often held in the Hall, as it was known, much to the headmaster's annoyance. He demanded that a teacher always be present, and the dancing never ended later than half past eleven. As the evening wore on, the boys in the upper forms would start holding the girls close, and they would then often turn off the lights in the hall as the night progressed. Pálmi would always come in and turn them back on. The lights would be switched off again, and again Pálmi would appear, and so it went until he had become quite angry. On one occasion he finally threatened that the ball would be over if this happened one more time. Then we at last gave in, for Pálmi was a man who kept his threats. On the next school day we were treated to a forceful lecture on morality and the lack of good manners.

In his school speeches Pálmi was unequivocal and direct. We listened attentively, even if we perhaps did not always obey his commands. In my diary I have recorded a fragment of his New Year's speech in the Hall:

4 January 1947. The headmaster summoned everyone to the Hall and gave a New Year's speech. He settled the accounts for the past year, and it seemed to him that much had changed for the worse in the conduct of pupils, e.g. punctuality, eagerness to learn, behaviour, outdoor activity had declined, drinking had increased, and dance practices, etc. He said, among other things, that he believed the boys nowadays preferred to have a Coca-Cola in one hand, a cigarette in the other, and a girl pressed against their stomach at dance practices, plus dark corners where they could rub their sweaty cheeks together! He spoke very well. He said he had great experience from his "dog's life".

Headmaster Pálmi was very robust and always enjoyed good-natured scuffles. In those years, twelve corridor wardens were elected from the sixth form, whose job it was to clear the corridors during the long break. Pálmi had nothing against them throwing us younger pupils out. Nor did he see anything wrong with the younger ones fighting back. Pálmi would even join in the fray himself and let them feel his strength. That is how we first became acquainted. I was then in the first form, and my diary tells it thus:

18 January 1943. I got up at 8 because I had trouble waking. At school most things went their usual way, but one remarkable thing happened. It happened that 2 second-formers grabbed Daði [Hjörvar], and we tried to help him by storming into their classroom. Pálmi came in and seized me by the neck, because I was nearest to him, and drove me toward the window. I hit the back of my head on the windowsill and almost saw stars. But it was some small consolation to me that I had given him a few good jabs with my elbows when he grabbed at me, since I did not know who it was. In the next lesson Pálmi came in and said something to the effect that this had apparently been a misunderstanding on his part. It had apparently been second-formers who grabbed Daði, while we had meant to rescue him, and he had apparently been rather rough with me. Then he patted me on the cheek (though rather firmly) and said we should only make attacks on the "kastringar".[^]

I came away from this tussle satisfied, because I had managed to keep the rule my father taught me: "to land a blow on him". As often happens with those who fight on the first day of school, Pálmi and I were good friends from then on.

My deskmate Bjarni Guðnason and I once took up position at the front of a band of fourth-formers on the staircase between floors in the Grammar School. This was quite a large group, and we intended to block the sixth-form corridor wardens from coming down. The staircase was a good place to defend, and the sixth-formers could get nowhere. Pálmi, however, had banned fighting on the staircase, since this old staircase bore the strain poorly. At the height of the struggle, before I knew it, Bjarni was swept up into the air, over backwards and down the stairs. Shortly afterwards I went the same way. There stood Pálmi, furious, yelling: "Did I not forbid you to fight on the staircase."
[^]: This was the old traditional name for fourth-formers.
Friends for Life

This story describes not only headmaster Pálmi but also Bjarni Guðnason. He was a good companion to have in the scuffles of those years. He was both big and strong. Bjarni could always be relied on. He stood his ground. He was competitive, daring and always ready for a tussle. Bjarni was a fine chess player. I think our friendship endured not least because we were evenly matched in many fields. He was one of the few whom I could bear to have get the better of me. The description "a man of honour" was the highest term of praise my father had for his fellow travellers through life. Bjarni Guðnason is a true man of honour.

At the Grammar School I made my best friends. The friends who are close to me as the years advance are, moreover, mostly from this group. It is strange to think that bonds of friendship from youth and from those years have proved far more durable than all the friendships from my political career put together. These companions of mine became true friends for life. Among good acquaintances I could count nearly everyone who entered the first form in the autumn of 1942. As close friends, however, I would count only part of that group.

Many of my companions from Hávallagata stuck together at the Grammar School. Björn Þorláksson remained a good friend of mine even though he was in the languages stream. Runólfur Þórðarson, Nunni, was a good acquaintance from the Vigorous Boys (Röskir drengir). We later became even closer friends when we went together to the United States to study engineering. Nunni was a year ahead of me at the Grammar School. Also joining the trip to America was Þorbjörn Karlsson, who later became a professor of engineering. He was two years ahead at the Grammar School. My friendship with the Clausen brothers also continued after we came to the Grammar School. They were usually light-hearted and entertaining companions. Haukur had passed the entrance examination into the first form along with me, but Örn had to go to the lower secondary school. He therefore did not come in until the third form. The Clausen brothers made their mark on the Christmas festivities committee, being very artistic. They drew well, and their talents came into their own when everything was decorated in the old building. Örn also played the piano.

At the dance practices, bands were often engaged to play for the dancing. Örn was frequently ready to relieve the pianist. He often played the same tunes, and some people were making remarks about it when I was inspector. So I went up to Örn and said: "Now play the other tune." I probably said this rather too loudly, for laughter broke out around the hall, and I saw that Örn grew angry. It took him quite some time to forgive me, and indeed it was badly done and unfair. Örn is a fine pianist.
The Clausen brothers were men of strong temper. But they took it out chiefly

on each other. During the grammar school years it sometimes happened that I had to step in between them when they fought. Later it even happened that I was called in when nothing else seemed able to stop them. At some point after I had come home from the United States, Haukur had a dental practice on Öldugata and lived in the same house. Parties were sometimes held there. One evening I received a phone call asking me to come and break up a fight. The brothers had begun to brawl. It could be ferocious when they fought. So I drove west at once. They were in a wild fury when I arrived, and I saw no better course than to try to break up the fight; I stepped between them and grabbed hold of them. At that very moment Haukur swung at his brother. The fist, however, landed on my cheek, and it was quite a blow, for the brothers were strong men. Still, I withstood it. But then it was as if Haukur came to his senses, and they stopped fighting, embraced me, utterly crushed, and said: "Denni dear, forgive us — hitting you is the last thing we would ever want to do." The brothers are good lads, loyal and true friends on whom I have relied more than most other men through the years. I have always valued their friendship highly.

There was a pause in my dealings with the Clausen brothers when I went to study in the United States, and much changed in the meantime. I was with them the evening before I flew out of the country in 1948. I drove them home to Freyjugata where they lived. We sat talking for a good while. We argued about whether it was a crime to have a drink or to smoke. We all agreed that one should not smoke. I maintained, however, that it was all right to have a drink in moderation if one had reached the required age. With this they utterly disagreed. The next spring I came home, and one of the first things I asked about was the Clausen brothers. The answer was that they were surely down at the Borg. There I found them, surrounded by girls and with glasses in hand. The women doted on them to such a degree that it was a downright plague. They were great heroes and handsome men. So the women quite literally hung about their necks.

Örn studied law and is one of the country's best-known supreme court attorneys. He is married to Guðrún Erlendsdóttir, supreme court justice, that great and excellent woman. Haukur is a dentist, as mentioned before. That profession suited him particularly well, for he was both deft and meticulous. His wife is Elín Thorarensen, who is likewise a fine woman.

Haukur Jónasson lived on Sólvallagata. We became good friends in those years. He is one year younger than I. His father, Jónas Sveinsson, physician at Sólheimar, was a good friend of my father's. Jónas often dropped by in the mornings and would sit talking with my father. Before long, Haukur and I began going skiing together and on mountain trips. From those trips I have numerous

pictures and good memories. Haukur later became a physician and is one of my very best friends. I also gained various companions through the social life at the school. But it never developed into as close a friendship as with my childhood companions.
"What a Parrot You Are"

The teaching at the Grammar School was, I believe, not unlike what it still is. The school has been conservative in this respect. I wholeheartedly support that. Although the studies could no doubt be improved with new and better books and newer technology, I am convinced that in these formative years everyone needs substantial discipline. I at least consider myself to have benefited from it. Fifty years ago, however, the curriculum was far less varied than what was set before my three children who have attended the Grammar School. Now there are many different streams, but in my day there were only two, the languages stream and the mathematics stream. I was in the mathematics stream.

Studying came easily to me. I had a photographic memory, as it is called. I could read a page or a chapter of a book and recite it almost word for word, because I saw the text before me if I closed my eyes. I am not sure that is a particularly good thing. It could, however, come in handy. I especially remember the matriculation examination in French, where I came up and was supposed to translate. At first nothing happened. But when the teacher had reminded me of the first words, I suddenly saw the page before me and translated the text word for word. I received a high mark, 8.0, and outfoxed various people who nonetheless considered themselves special geniuses in French. In the lower secondary examination in history under Einar Magnússon, we were to write an essay on the World War of 1914–1918. I wrote more or less what was in the book. I felt, though, that a small section was missing, which I can almost still see before me. At any rate there was a picture on the left-hand page, and the text that had been omitted was beside it. I saw this vividly before me and inserted the missing section. With that done I left some time before the examination period was over. The next time I met Einar the history teacher, he stopped me and said: "What a parrot you are, Steingrímur. I couldn't even be bothered to read this. I've read it a hundred times in the book." He then gave me 9.8. I was thinking afterwards how unjust it was that I did not get 10, since it was word for word. He probably did not think the book good enough.
The diaries bear witness that I read steadily, something every day throughout the winter, and trained myself in organised working habits. In examinations I
I made special plans that took account of the exam timetable each time. I arranged my reading over the days leading up to the exams, and each subject got as much time as I considered I needed for it.

When the lower-secondary examination (gagnfræðapróf) approached, I resolved to study well. I decided to make myself a work schedule which I followed to the letter. I got up at five o'clock every morning, took my bicycle and cycled around town. No one was about. Around six I came home and took a shower. Then came systematic reading, non-stop until five in the afternoon. My parents saw to it that no one disturbed me. I did not even give myself time to keep my diary during those weeks. After the exams I therefore wrote a single entry for the whole period from 10 May to 16 June 1944:

The reading break began on the 10th or 12th [of May]. It was now arranged differently than before. The exams came gradually, with breaks in between. I studied well. I often got up at 5–6, had a bath and ate, and then read most of the day. I never went to the cinema. I went to Icelandic lessons with Sveinbjörn. I did splendidly in the exams. They ended on 5 June. Shortly afterwards we got to know the grades. I was at the top of the lower-secondary examination and received 9.19 as my main grade. Icelandic, prepared texts 9.4 — geography 9.5 — history 9.8 Icelandic, unseen texts 9.7 — physics 9.8 — Danish 8.6 mathematics 10.0 — natural science 9.2 — English 8.4 gymnastics 9.1 — drawing 8.6 — composition 8.2 With the year's grade included I was 2nd, with 8.67 as my final grade.

There, for the first time, I set myself goals and kept to them. I have believed in that method ever since. As a rule I have made it my practice to work systematically. To tell the truth, I am much more organized in my work than my father. For instance, I get up earlier. He worked quite differently and was more of a man for intense bursts. With me the work is more continuous. Still, there was often much that distracted my mind from school and study, and so my year's grades in my youth were always lower than my exam grades. Thus I was never at the top except in the examination itself. This was never as noticeable, though, as in the final winter, when I was inspector. Nothing of what otherwise governed my studies held up that year. My exam grades then fell from having been around 9 down to 8.63 in the matriculation examination (stúdentspróf). As usual, the year's grades were somewhat lower than the exam grades, which pulled the main grade down a little. It is the average of exam and year's grades and worked out at 8.28.
At least once during those years, ambition in my studies was overpowered by something else. In the diary it says on 19 November 1945: "I did only
passably in Latin, though I leaned a little on what I had scribbled on the desk." Such things are easy to forget, but diaries forget nothing.
"If I am a codhead, then you, sir, are a bullhead"

Rector Pálmi taught natural science and stood head and shoulders above the school's other teachers in my eyes. Bogi Ólafsson, the senior master, taught English. I quickly took a liking to him. As so often, a small incident served to seal this friendship. I was in the first form, and the sixth-formers came, as they so often did, to throw us out. We decided to put up resistance, and a considerable brawl ensued that lasted the whole of the break. Sveinn Torfi Sveinsson, who later became an engineer, was on the bouncers' team, and he and I grappled. I knew a tiny bit of Icelandic wrestling (glíma) and managed to catch him with a throw. He fell backwards and I fell on top of him. A glass door separated the corridor from the teachers' room, which at that time was on the ground floor at the south end of the building. Bogi Ólafsson and Jóhannes Áskelsson, the natural science teacher, were on their way to class, and Sveinn and I half landed on them, ending our journey against the door, where we broke one pane. Jóhannes turned rather grim and said: "You two shall pay for this." Bogi, however, immediately put his arm around my shoulders and said: "Damn well fought, boy. I'll take care of the pane." He was the senior master, and those words held.

Bogi was a colourful teacher, and I doubt he ever learned the art of whispering or keeping quiet. The school paper was brimming with stories about him. He would go over the English compositions in class with bloodcurdling scoldings, calling people donkeys and other choice names. Meanwhile the pupil in question stood by his chair. When he had finished going over the composition, he took the exercise book and hurled it at its owner. On one occasion Bjarni Guðnason came in for a heavy downpour. Bogi flung the book at him and added: "You, sir, are a prize codhead." Bjarni shot back: "If I am a codhead, then you, sir, are a bullhead." A shiver of suspense ran through the class, which looked from Bogi to Bjarni and back again. Bogi stared at him for a while but said nothing. He had an exceptionally large head, and his hair stood on end. After this, Bjarni's grades in English rose sharply, for Bogi respected people who could answer for themselves. Bjarni, however, refuses to acknowledge the story.

I myself got to know Bogi well. He lived in the house opposite ours on Skothúsvegur. As I have said before, Bogi offered me extra lessons at his home after I had lain ill in the second form. He made a habit of calling me over the street to join him on his way home. He always walked along Tjarnargata, swaying greatly, and made slow progress, having grown enormously fat.
I usually tried to slip past him, especially when I was in a hurry. Then I would even take a detour along Suðurgata to avoid the slow going.

Sigurkarl Stefánsson taught me mathematics. In his student years he had been very much to the fore: he was president of the debating society Framtíðin, a good glíma wrestler, and argued emphatically that compulsory instruction in Esperanto should be enshrined in law. Sigurkarl was a good mathematics teacher, but when the mood took him he would take the class out into the yard for shot put. He was also a fine chess player and often came to meetings of the school Chess Club. For Bjarni Guðnason and me, enthusiasm for chess sometimes overpowered mathematics in those years. We would often sneak games on pocket chess sets during lessons. On one occasion Bjarni and I were absorbed in a game during one of Sigurkarl's lessons. When I had made my move, I heard Sigurkarl say over my shoulder: "No, that was not a good move, Steingrímur." He then pointed out a better move to me. We stopped playing on the spot.

Magnús Finnbogason taught me Icelandic. When I was inspector scholae I was busy with all sorts of things and picked and chose which lessons I attended. That winter I skipped nearly all the Icelandic lessons. Of course that was a shame, for I could well have used the instruction. Once I was going down the stairs in the Grammar School building when I heard quick footsteps behind me. There was Magnús, who said politely: "I say, Steingrímur, don't you think it is about time you attended one of my lessons?" I turned around and went back up. Magnús was very kind.

Among the other teachers was Ólafur Hansson, who taught history and did it very well. He made us learn a great deal by heart. When we were tested, pupils were made to account for the material that had been assigned. If anyone was unprepared, he "excused" himself. Ólafur had Latin names for everything, and they could tie me up in knots. On the other hand, I greatly enjoyed history. Ólafur later became a professor at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands). Then there was Magnús "the French" Jónsson, who taught French, as his nickname undeniably suggests. He was an exceptionally gentle soul.
Atlas and sports

There was a lively social life at the school in those years. Sports flourished considerably. I myself practised with great zeal the exercises associated with the bodybuilder Charles Atlas. He was world-famous, and his books were, among other things, translated into Icelandic. I still own them. I also studied the Müller exercises and the way of life that Müller preached. I practised

cold baths with great vigour and always slept with the window wide open. My mother thought this was carried to extremes and said she shivered to the bone every time she came into my room. That habit, however, I keep to this day. The Müller exercises consisted of various stretches and the famous skin-rubbings that were supposed to stimulate the circulation. Probably the most famous of the Müller devotees is Þórbergur Þórðarson. He swam naked in the sea off Grótta and did the exercises for the good of his health.

I was fonder of the Atlas exercises. No equipment was used, only bodily movements. There were push-ups, various exertions with the hands, knee-bends, a variety of stretching exercises, and the abdominal exercises were especially good. Many of the gymnastic exercises most people know come from Atlas.

I did Atlas exercises for many years and grew much stronger from them. I conscientiously monitored the results by measuring the various body parts and muscles, as the book prescribed. I recorded all the measurements in my diaries, and there one can read that a flexed upper-arm muscle thickened by nearly an inch in two years. Thighs, chest, stomach and the other main training areas were measured in the same way, sometimes with the muscles relaxed and sometimes flexed.

A few years ago my friend Jón Hjartarson introduced me to the training system of the Canadian air force, the Canadian Royal Airforce Fitness Program. He did those exercises himself and sent me a photocopy. They too are performed without equipment. I do them regularly in the winter for the good of my health. In many ways they resemble Atlas, but they are based on only five exercises which are repeated. They have done me a great deal of good.

At the Grammar School, handball was played in the gymnasium, often with shots from goal to goal. There were good handball players in my class, and we became school champions in the 5th form. I was on that team. It is comical that the tiny sports hall of the Grammar School should be the cradle of handball in Iceland. We made do with it, though, and played with five men in defence and attack. The defence very nearly reached from wall to wall if we held hands. Swimming was practised at the Sundhöllin swimming hall, and ski trips were popular. Quite often special leave from school was granted for such trips. There were no lifts in the mountains, and one walked up on one's own two feet with the skis on one's shoulders. That would not be considered acceptable now.

When I was in the first form, the class was given ski leave, as happened from time to time. That trip, however, had repercussions. When the pupils were fully ready for the trip and on the point of setting off, the weather suddenly worsened. Then word came from the rector that the trip was cancelled. The pupils paid no heed and went anyway. When they came home, the bomb dropped. Everyone who went was

instantly expelled from school. That was nearly half the class. I was lucky enough to be laid up with the flu and escaped. Otherwise I would doubtless have gone. Little could stop me when it came to mountain trips.

Many of my best friends were expelled, and for a long time Rector Pálmi seemed unbending in his position. After a week or two, however, he agreed to take the group back on the condition that a formal apology be submitted and that the parents come to a meeting with him in the Assembly Hall (Salur). So it came to pass, and Pálmi thundered over the parents' heads and taught them how children ought to be brought up — though it was mainly the fathers who were present. The story goes that several of them had no idea what had hit them, and no one raised a voice in protest. There sat some of Reykjavík's leading citizens and the great orators of the Althing (Alþingi) like children at their school desks. The parliamentarian Ólafur Thors and the broadcaster Helgi Hjörvar were among them, sitting side by side, thunderstruck. After the dressing-down, Helgi was the first to collect himself and delivered a brief word of thanks to the rector for the speech, saying that those present would doubtless take his words under consideration. Then the whole troop shuffled out, and the children began attending school again. Pálmi was like no one else when he was in full fury.
Chess life and trips to Selið

The Chess Club flourished greatly in those years. I took part in reviving it and sat on its first committee. At the first meeting it was resolved that the club should adopt no rules, "since it was agreed that they would only do it harm," as the minutes put it. I was in the third form when this happened, and our class won an intramural tournament. On the winning team were Skarphéðinn Pálmason, later a mathematics teacher at the Grammar School, Bjarni Guðnason, Ólafur Ólafsson and Flosi H. Sigurðsson, besides myself.

Interest in chess was great, and most of us were relatively evenly matched in ability. The girls at the school did not play. In the winter of 1946–1947 there were 69 members, all boys. Yet the girls made up about a third of the pupils. At first, mainly intramural chess tournaments were held, along with simultaneous exhibitions against strong players from the ranks of the teachers. Magnús "the French" Jónsson and Guðmundur Arnlaugsson — a mathematics teacher and later rector of the Hamrahlíð Grammar School (Menntaskólinn við Hamrahlíð) — were both national-team chess players, and they played against pupils on 13–33 boards. Sigurkarl Stefánsson the mathematics teacher, Sveinn Bergsveinsson the German teacher, Jón Magnússon the English teacher, Finnbogi Guðmundsson the Latin teacher and Sigurður Þórarinsson the natural science teacher also played against pupils. We made every effort to pit ourselves against the country's foremost chess players, and other national-team players played against the group; Guðmundur Ágústsson, Baldur

Möller, permanent secretary of a ministry, Guðmundur S. Guðmundsson and the engineer Árni Snævarr. I won my games against both of them, Guðmundur and Árni. The game against Árni stuck especially in my memory because he wrote the comment "Well played" on the score sheet, and I was proud of that verdict.

Even more memorable was the visit of the grandmaster Daniel Abraham Yanofsky, who played a simultaneous exhibition against 30 of the school's pupils. He was received with ceremony. Árni Snævarr accompanied him, Magnús "the French" introduced him with a few words, and Rector Pálmi presented him to the school's chess players. Only one of us carried off a victory against the grandmaster: Guðmundur Pálmason, who was our best player. When he was in the fifth form he played, among other things, a simultaneous exhibition against other pupils on 27 boards; he won 18, drew five and lost only four games. In the chess club's records it says that Yanofsky remarked after the contest that the school had a strong chess team, especially considering how small it was. Yanofsky talked with me after the games and made a point of inviting me to a simultaneous exhibition that the Chess Federation (Skáksambandið) held shortly afterwards. There, as it turned out, I beat him. Exulting in victory, I wrote in my diary:

At 1 o'clock I went into the Dairy Station (Mjólkurstöð) to play in a simultaneous exhibition against Yanofsky. He greeted me and asked whether I intended to beat him today. I said I would try my best. And so it went — I won! He resigned after 39 moves. I talked with him afterwards, and he said I had played very well. He said he had played too much for a win, that he should have played more for a draw!!

I still have that game, and long afterwards it appeared in the journal of the Reykjavík Chess Club (Skákfélag Reykjavíkur) with annotations by grandmaster Friðrik Ólafsson. It is quite well played, and it can safely be said that this was the high point of my short chess career. Shortly afterwards another international chess player visited the school, Robert Wade from New Zealand. He was not as strong: he won 17 games, lost 6 and drew 7. I was nevertheless among those who lost.

I devoted considerable effort to chess in those years and had a whole shelf full of chess books. I read these books a great deal and practised openings. I was no genius, but I think I played fairly logical games. My best boast is that I have one of the most favourable winning percentages of all Icelandic chess players against grandmaster Friðrik Ólafsson. I played in a tournament of the Reykjavík Chess Club when I was in the 6th form, finished at the top together with another player, and thus worked my way up from the 2nd class into the first. Among those I faced was Friðrik
and I won. He was only twelve years old. I have taken great care never to give him a chance to play against me since.

The work around the chess club took both a great deal of time and energy, and the lack of rules by no means prevented the activity from flourishing. It did, however, mean that the committee held neither meetings nor annual general meetings for the first three years, and as time went on I was in effect condemned to the chairmanship of the club. In my last year at the school I was the only one left of the original three-man committee. Then at last an annual general meeting was held. A new committee was elected and rules drawn up for the club. I thus left it in the hands of Guðmundur Pálmason, who was elected chairman. Later Friðrik Ólafsson took over the club, but by then, it seems, the excitement went out of it. He was far too good compared with the school's other pupils.

Trips to Selið were popular. The Grammar School's mountain hut, Selið, stands in Reykjadalur, above Hveragerði, and is still used for class trips where games, evening gatherings, hikes and outdoor life hold pride of place. Its construction began in 1937, and the house was built through pupils' fund-raising and volunteer work. Rector Pálmi had early on begun thinking about a house for the school amid the delights of the countryside, for it accorded with his view that the countryside was a counterweight to the mob rule of the town. An unconfirmed story actually has it that the pupils got timber on credit from an unnamed building-supplies shop, but that by mistake the bill was always forgotten. What is certain is that the house stands and is enormous. Its assembly hall is said still to be one of the largest at the Grammar School's disposal.

Trips to Selið were made at weekends, and a teacher always came along. Sometimes the rector himself went. That was considered both good and bad. It was a pleasure to go hiking with him. He was extremely knowledgeable, not least about the country's natural history, and seemed to know about everything. On the other hand he was considered strict at the evening entertainments. On one occasion, as often before, the rector came east with us. I was then in the 6th form and was inspector scholae. After an excellent hike we sat down to cards and games. Among other things, three of us played bridge with Pálmi. Around midnight the rector stood up and said it was now time to retire. On behalf of the class I objected. The rector took this rather badly, marched out and said as he went: "At 8 o'clock tomorrow morning we set off for town." He himself stayed the night in a summer cottage he owned a short distance away.

We then enjoyed ourselves well and long into the night. When we went to bed we gathered up all the alarm clocks that had been brought along and placed them with me and my roommates. They all rang in a deafening chorus at seven the next morning. We hustled everyone to their feet and put everything in order, neatly and systematically. On the stroke of eight the rector arrived. When

he opened the front door, a sight met him that he obviously had not expected. He no doubt intended to catch us in our bunks, but we stood in an orderly row in the entrance hall, ready for the journey home. The rector turned on his heel without a word, and we tramped after him.
An election battle with the communists

When I leaf through my diaries from grammar school, I am surprised how often school politics crops up. It figures far more there than in my recollection. At any rate, I did not go in for political writings or social issues. That much I remember. Ideals and politics I discussed mostly with my father. More often, though, I was merely a listener when he discussed social issues with guests. I soon absorbed the ideal that I think is best described in my father's words: "Human worth must be set above the worth of wealth. Honour should govern men's deeds, and there shall be equality in society." That soon seeped into me. Very soon.

The independence question loomed largest among national issues at the Grammar School during the war years, especially as the founding of the republic drew near. Debating meetings were held on the matter, and people divided sharply along political lines at first, but eventually united, like all Icelanders. Political stirrings quickly found their way inside the school's walls. I myself did not take a prominent part in these discussions. Naturally I was at Þingvellir on 17 June 1944, and I note in the diary that the independence men did not all cast their votes for the first president of the republic.

The Republic of Iceland was proclaimed in pouring rain and gale at 2 o'clock. Sveinn Björnsson was elected 1st president of the new republic, but unfortunately the Althing did not show the same unity there as the nation. [. . .] Many people were at Þingvellir. It was estimated at some 20–30 thousand.

I wrote nothing in my diary that suggests love of country or sentimentality was uppermost in my mind on that rainy day. What I chiefly mention is that I could not find the car where we had parked it, but found my parents with other guests at Valhöll. My national consciousness in the grammar-school years in fact consisted mainly in slacking off in Danish. Some of us schoolmates saw it as part of the independence struggle to read as little of it as possible. I have often regretted that, not least when I speak my Scandinavian.
As time went on, the communists were the most prominent force within the school. I got

to feel it because I was the son of a politician. My father was not prime minister beyond these years, but he sat in Parliament and was a controversial politician. He and Ólafur Thors clashed forcefully in those years. I was probably not popular with hard-line Independence Party men because of this. Heimdallur courted young men and invited them to meetings. I did not think this was right. Yet I do not recall ever having borne anyone ill will over politics.

In the diary I mention, among others, Geir Hallgrímsson, later prime minister, after a school meeting. There I say that he "always dances along a straight line, namely the line that [. . .] the ringleaders of the conservatives draw up." I add that Geir never sees anything wrong in what they do. Geir was a few years ahead of me in the school, and I got to know him only slightly. The topic of the meeting I have long since forgotten.

It was mainly the radicals, however, who were opposed to me. My father had always been an anti-communist. After the formation of the Innovation Government (Nýsköpunarstjórnin), in which the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkur), the Socialist Party (Sósíalistaflokkur) and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkur) formed an alliance, his distrust did not diminish. His quarrels with the communist leaders were probably at their most intense, though, in the wake of the invasion of Stalín's armies into Finland in the winter of 1939–1940. My father was then prime minister, and Parliament voted to expel the communists from the Inter-Parliamentary Union of the Nordic Countries (þingmannasamband Norðurlanda). The air was electric that winter, and fisticuffs broke out in the Althing. Brynjólfur Bjarnason, member of Parliament for the Socialist Party, said from the parliamentary rostrum toward spring that in "one of the side rooms of Parliament" the "honorable prime minister" had gone at him and struck him in the face. My father was said to have become angry over an exchange of words that was "not so momentous as to be worth recounting." Then Brynjólfur said:

On account of this I wished to ask the honorable ministers who hold seats in government with the honorable prime minister whether they would not see to it that members of Parliament could walk about the premises of the Althing more or less safe from the fits of temper of the honorable prime minister.

Tíminn describes these events thus: several members of Parliament had been discussing the war between the Finns and the Russians in the ministers' room. Mention was also made of the execution of the leading men of the Russian revolution, and of whether Kuusinen would have been killed.\ Someone then said that such was often the end of traitors. My father interjected that really the Icelandic communist lead-
\ Kuusinen was prime minister of the "Finnish people's government," a puppet government of the Soviet Union in the Finnish territory under their control.

ers ought really to adopt the nickname Kuusinen. Brynjólfur was strutting about in the doorway and swung inside at this. He turned to my father, grabbed him by the shoulder and said there was no need for him to invent lying tales for the nation; his lies were not believed, for he was famous throughout the land for stupidity and lying. My father turned sharply on Brynjólfur, asked who had given him leave to paw at him and address him, and at the same moment struck him a slap with the flat of his hand. Brynjólfur said he would not strike back, and my father said that did not surprise him — Brynjólfur was not that foolish. In a debate outside the order of business he answered Brynjólfur thus:

It is an old and good Icelandic custom, which has been used for many hundreds of years on boys who are unscrupulous in their words, in order to discipline them and at the same time show them the deepest contempt a man can show — to give the so-called Icelandic slap. And when a prime minister is accosted in his private room and such words are used as I do not intend to repeat here, and hands are laid on him, as this honorable member of Parliament did, then I consider this a fitting answer, and I expect many will consider it so. As to my having been angry, I will say this: if I am angry, I do not strike with the flat of my hand.

My political clashes in secondary school were never of this kind. One fought tooth and nail against being thrown out by the corridor monitors, but grappled with the communists in elections. There they sometimes put up a hearty resistance. In between the times when Bjarni Guðnason, my seatmate, and I fought in the corridors, we contended over who should represent the class. I describe one such election in the third form in detail in my diary, and I am obviously rather worked up. This was probably my first defeat in an election, and clearly I took the communists' meddling to heart. I have always found it hard to lose. What stung me worst were the unscrupulous methods of my opponents, who offered soft drinks in exchange for votes:

They circulated a list around the class, but since they did not get half, they resorted to other methods. They now began taking the waverers down to a bar, to Skalli and to Freyja. Bjarni Guðna knew nothing about this at first. I did not mind at all not becoming class monitor, since Bjarni became it [. . .]. I find it sad that the class should blaze so with politics, as is plainly the case; such things ought not to happen in a school — rather, everyone should try to live in peace and harmony.

Bjarni Guðnason was never a communist, though he enjoyed their support on this occasion. I silently vowed to get even with them. I felt they owed me a slap. At the beginning of the year an opportunity came that I did not let pass me by. For the board of the debating society Framtíðin, candidate lists were put forward, and the elections were political. On one of the lists were mainly communists. I took a place on the other, the B-list, which I call the "list of the Anti-Communists" in the diary. There I took the fourth seat, and we won, 89:72. It was a proportional election, but when it came to the point the opponents declined their seats on the board. I do not explain the reasons for this in the diary but say only: "The commies did not want to take part in the board." The air was probably thick with menace, for only five days later the municipal elections were held in Reykjavík.

School politics in these years revolved not least around Bjarni Bragi Jónsson. He was a hard-line communist and the chief instigator of the radicals in the school. I got on very well with Bjarni Bragi, however, and among other things we sat together on the editorial board of the commemorative paper for the school's 100th anniversary in 1946. He was inspector scholae the year before me. He was one of the main ringleaders of the Aðalmannafélag society, which I describe with some suspicion in the diary:
In it are all the (leading) communists in the classes and many more, and it is in reality only a disguised "cell," which aims systematically at instilling the program of communism in its members.

Bjarni Bragi studied economics, which must be an excellent cure for communism, and has long since lost the faith, like most of the most radical ones from those years. Our paths crossed again when he sat for a time on the executive board of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). We later had offices on the same floor in the Central Bank (Seðlabankinn), where he has been assistant governor and special adviser to the board of governors. In good moments I cannot resist reminding him of the ardent ideals of his youth.
The End of the War in Europe

One of the most memorable events of the secondary-school years was the rejoicing at the end of the Second World War. Peace Day, as it was generally called in Europe, was one of the most unpeaceful days of the century in Iceland. Indeed, some say the greatest riots ever seen in Reykjavík, before or since, took place then. The first news of the peace agreements naturally found its way into my diary.
The irony of fate arranged it so that I was sitting at my German studies when I heard on the radio that the Germans had surrendered to the Allies.

This good news was the calm before the storm. Peace Day at first bore all the main marks of a festive day. I went with my friends to listen to the speeches of President Sveinn Björnsson and Prime Minister Ólafur Thors from the balcony of the Parliament House. I mention in the diary that we settled ourselves on the roof of the National Telephone Exchange (Landsímahúsið). We therefore had a good view despite the throng of people on Austurvöllur. We also went aboard the Esja, which lay at her moorings, and joined a procession to the Danish and Norwegian envoys. They were cheered on account of the liberation of their countries from the hands of the Germans.

The first thing that occurred to us students was to get a day off because of these great events. As so often, our teachers disagreed with us on this point. Rector Pálmi delivered a speech to the assembled students, as was his way. He proved prophetic about what followed on that Peace Day. Pálmi said it was not enough to obtain peace; it also had to be kept. "We have yet to win the peace," I have recorded from him in the diary. It takes strong bones to endure good days.

One did not have to wait long for that to be put to the test. Toward evening there erupted what Peace Day is most famous for in Reykjavík: riots, brawls and disturbances. The diary tells of the trip my friends and I made into town. The tumult began when British sailors decorated the statue of Ingólfur on Arnarhóll with the British flag. A group of Icelandic boys promptly tore it down. The diary says:

Then everything had ended in brawls and uproar. At 8 o'clock a group of sailors came up from the harbor with stones and threw them at the crowd on Arnarhóll. Now the greatest stone-throwing began, and the British even brought guns. But then troops came and intervened. We arrived exactly when all this was over. Nearly all the windowpanes in the Varðarhús building were broken. The British now marched through the town in ranks, and scuffles broke out in many places. They broke most of the windows in Hafnarstræti and overturned a car. Several waded out into the Tjörnin.

Soon the British military police began using tear gas, and before long the Icelandic police followed suit. As evening drew on, I found myself in a sizable group of Icelanders by Arnarhóll. The British arrived and wanted to disperse the group with tear gas. They succeeded. But what followed was no better, for Icelandic policemen came from the opposite direction, and suddenly everything was in a haze. The diary continues:

My eyes were absolutely killing me. [I] had a burning pain, likewise in my throat and mouth. I ran up Lindargata and then up to Skólavörðustígur. Now the crowd began to disperse, and around 12 most people had gone away. We strolled up to the Menntaskóli, and it was as if a haze lay over the town center. At 12:30 I went home. Pabbi spoke with the chief of police, and he said the British had been out on Skúlagata with guns and had shot at people and cars.

No one seems to have been hit by the British shots. One bullet, though, is said to have gone through the trouser leg of an Icelander. It is less often mentioned that the disturbances stretched into the next day, though the clashes were then on a much smaller scale:

Around 10 o'clock a bit of commotion began. The British broke windows in Lækjargata and in Freyja. Tear gas was thrown at them. [. . .] We were mostly by the Government House (Stjórnarráðið). There was a drunken boy there who impressed upon the crowd that we should sooner let ourselves all be killed than have the Government House taken. The English police charged up to the Government House building, and he rushed at them, but was knocked down. At 12 I went home.

There was some tension between British soldiers and Icelanders in the wake of these clashes. But no riots occurred beyond what was usual on weekends. On June 8 the Icelanders took their revenge and won a football match between a select Reykjavík team and the British garrison, 4:0. I say in my diary that I had never seen so many people at the ground. The tension found release in sports, as so often before and since. Shortly afterward the British were crushed in track and field, and full victory was thereby won.
Herring at Siglufjörður

In the summer of 1945 I took a job in herring work at the factories at Siglufjörður. It was an enjoyable summer. Admittedly, very little herring came ashore, so we spent nearly the whole summer "rust-banging," as it was called — beating rust off the pit beams, the unloading cranes and whatever needed it. My job otherwise was to operate an unloading crane. I thus took part in landing the little herring that was caught. I have sometimes said that I became strong at arm-wrestling after rust-banging for a whole summer. Very few could beat me at arm-wrestling.
At Siglufjörður I was placed in a very good home, with Jóhann Þorvaldsson, a teacher. He later became headmaster at Siglufjörður and was a well-known

figure in the town. He lived with his wife on the hillside above the town. An eye was kept on me, though there was no question of orders or prohibitions. I was never forbidden to go into town, though things often got quite lively there. In fact there was no need for strict supervision, for I abstained from both tobacco and alcohol. I was extremely comfortable with that couple — fine people indeed. The atmosphere in their home was also good. They were of the turn-of-the-century generation that grew up in the spirit of the youth societies (ungmennafélög). That generation wanted to do its part to make the dream come true of building an independent welfare society in Iceland.

I met Jóhann later on my trips to Siglufjörður after I had entered politics. He still gave speeches and urged people to support the cooperative movement and the welfare ideal at every single political meeting. He has always been a staunch Progressive Party man and is still alive at a great age.

Soon after I came north I met Garðar Gíslason, or Gaji. He had been with me in the road work the summer before but was now on the herring boat Austri. I knew other boys too, but most of them were on boats. Bjarni Guðnason was on the Skógafoss. We spent a fair amount of time together that summer, and in addition I got to know a great many boys who worked on the same herring dock as I did. There were fifteen of us together, and meal was produced there. I acquainted myself thoroughly with the production process and wrote it down.

From the measuring devices the herring travels along chutes up into the holding pits and from there into the rendering ovens, from them into the presses and then into the tanks. The bones go from the presses into the dryers and from there along conveyors into the mills, and then as meal into the sacks. By then 20 minutes have passed since they came out of the pits.

Other things also aroused our admiration, though. A short distance away was a herring-salting dock, and there were the girls. It was magnificent to watch them work; often it was as if ten hands were in the air instead of two, such was the speed. It did not hurt that many of them were pretty.

Life at Siglufjörður was a great adventure for young boys. Because of the lack of herring the boats often lay idle in port, and then the seamen came ashore. Many of them were Norwegian, but there were of course also Icelanders, Danes and Swedes. There were often great brawls then, and they are among the most memorable things from that summer. We boys often went to Hotel Hvanneyri, sat up on the steps there and watched the spectacle, or took ourselves off to a dance at Siglunes.
Above the town is the Hvanneyrarskál hollow, and young lovers walked up there in the evenings. We had not yet reached that stage in romance, however, if I remember

correctly, but we strolled up there now and then out of curiosity. Siglunes I call "one of the worst dives in the country" in my diary, in one description of a brawl. The police could do nothing about all this. They were in fact constantly in retreat, for it was beyond the power of five or six policemen to keep control of hundreds of seamen in fighting spirit. It was an unequal contest. I remember that once the seamen took it upon themselves to overturn the police car when they thought the guardians of the law were making unnecessary trouble. Only one man could handle the Norwegians when they were in a frenzy. He came from Skagafjörður and was called Fúsi. His full name was Sigfús Guðbrandsson, a great strapping fellow who was often sent for if the hotel needed to be cleared of troublemakers. At Siglufjörður there were two cinemas, and we went there now and again. I enjoyed this bustling life.
The herring work itself could be lively even though herring was scarce. The following description was recorded in mid-August 1945.

We were sent to do sacking. We worked like berserkers right up to 10:30. During the coffee break there was great commotion. Men splashed water on one another. It is thus often very lively, especially on the night and evening shifts. Various pranks are played then. On Wednesday, for example, Steini was hosing down (cleaning) the crane and I stood nearby. The first I knew, the jet of water was trained on me, and I was soaked to the skin. In the evening Indriði had a hose while we four others had herring, and we fought that way for a long time. The hose is extremely powerful.

We also traded verses within the group, and I have recorded in the diary more than one verse of my own. It is, however, neither remarkable nor elaborate poetry. Most of it takes as its theme the companions' luck with women and their wits.
I did not think much of the organization of the herring factories, though. In the diary I have written:

It had been announced that the factories would begin receiving on the 8th, but they did not start up until the 14th, so that if a run of herring had come, everything would have been in jeopardy. That is how I am told most things are, and it seems to me the worst mismanagement in everything. Instead of doing the main things over the winter, everything is left to the last minute.

I had already begun thinking a good deal about efficiency, utilization, engineering and other such matters. Work at the herring factories took place in the summers, but in winter operations lay dormant. We were mainly attending to maintenance, but in the summers when the herring did show itself, little attention was paid to that. I wondered whether the winters

might not be put to better use, or whether the herring factories could be used for something else during those months. Perhaps I made more of this than was justified. Naturally I did not have access to the feasibility studies that no doubt existed. It may well be that it paid to close down entirely and then call out a full crew shortly before the herring season. In those days there was also no fishing for capelin or other species that could be processed alongside the herring.

In these musings of my teenage years it nevertheless emerges that I have always wanted to look for ways to make improvements if I thought something was lacking. It may be that politics is never far off for those who are made that way.
On Ocean Voyages

The last summer before my final examinations I got a berth on the Hvassafell, the flagship of the Icelandic merchant fleet. Guðjón Lárusson, my classmate, and I both tried to get taken on, but he was turned down. I went north to Akureyri, where the ship lay at her moorings, and two of my friends, Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson and Guðjón, came along for the trip. They drove the car, which I had recently bought, back south. It was my first car, a splendid Willys soft-top jeep. I bought it with the herring money from the summer before.

My father was rather opposed to the car purchase, but I had my way. The car was bought in the name of a farmer in Borgarfjörður, Einar Sigmundsson at Klettur. Farmers received exemption from duties and charges on such vehicles. They were classed as agricultural machinery. My father did not care for this arrangement but did not prevent the purchase. In the end he put up half the purchase price to match my share. When I went to study in the United States he bought my share as well. He became very pleased with the car and often traveled around the country in the jeep on election trips. By then he had had a hard top built onto it.
I received unexpected news when I got north. In the diary I tell it thus:

It came to light that I was to be a mess boy. I disliked that intensely. I telephoned south to Mamma. The next day I worked as a mess boy on board and intensely disliked having to do the washing-up and scrubbing. Around 5 o'clock I was called to Kristinn [Guðmundsson, tax director and later foreign minister]. He told me that Pabbi had telephoned and spoken with Jakob Frímannsson, the cooperative society manager, and with himself, and that he had been very angry. At 9 I spoke with Pabbi. He wanted me not to go as a mess boy, and I agreed to that.

My father got his way and no one was more relieved than I. I thus became an assistant in the engine room on this largest ship of the Icelandic fleet. The Hvassafell was 230 tons, and I described it thus in my diary:

The superstructure is aft but the holds, of which there are four, are all forward. It has a very large carrying capacity. The ship was built in Genoa in Italy and was completed last summer. It makes 12–13 miles per hour. It is a very good seagoing ship, though it rolls considerably, but it withstands heavy seas.

That would prove useful in the wild weather and rolling on the way home. I was one of the few who did not get seasick in that mayhem. While the others writhed in their bunks I recorded in my diary that I had "great fun standing up on the bridge and watching the commotion in nature. I watched the tumult for quite a while after my watch was over." I witnessed Iceland rising from the sea, and it was an unforgettable sight: "It was a magnificent landfall to see the sheer, rocky mountains of the East rising up out of the storm." The captain of the Hvassafell was Sverrir Þór Jónsson. He was from Eyjafjörður and a nephew of Vilhjálmur Þór, director of the Federation of Icelandic Cooperatives (Sambandið).

My main job on board was stoking and lubricating. On a run, the fire was stoked every hour and at the same time water was pumped into a boiler for the part that was steam-powered. The ship's engine was a diesel, but the winches and the motor ran on steam. The steering engine had to be lubricated once each watch. We left port shortly after I came aboard. The voyage was bound for Russia to fetch timber, with stops in the East Fjords and in Norway.

On Sunday, July 20, 1947, we arrived in Bergen. The passage in through the skerries took nearly two hours, my diary says, and the sun shone in a clear sky. Never had I seen such a beautiful approach. This was the first time I laid eyes on foreign lands. That sight was not unpleasant: "There is much settlement on the islands. There were many boats and sailing vessels in the sounds. People lay sunbathing among the trees and on the rocks." On all the skerries lay girls, either half-naked or completely naked, and we thought this fun to watch. Gissur, the second engineer, sent me up into the funnel to shut off the water to the water tanks, but there was also a valve there for the steam to the steam steering gear. I ran up and shut off one of the valves. Just as I had finished turning it off, the entire alarm system went off and the engines went into reverse. The rudder had suddenly jammed and the ship was heading for a skerry. I had shut off the wrong valve. Gissur realized this and reacted angrily. I had often been sent up before on the same errand and should have known better, but it had always been out on the open sea. In the end
it was Gissur who got the blame for having sent me, the greenhorn, up to shut off an unmarked valve in a dangerous area.
Russia of the Revolution

The superpower summit in Reykjavík was among the greatest moments of my political career. In its wake I felt the world's increased recognition of Iceland, and the goodwill of these guests of ours toward me. Among other things, I was invited on an official visit to Russia. At the farewell dinner, which I hosted at our embassy in Moscow, I gave a speech of thanks. I said there that I had probably come to Russia one more time than the KGB knew. The Russians were somewhat taken aback by this remark, but then there was laughter. After the speech, many asked how I could have come without it being entered in the records. I then told them of my voyage on the Hvassafell to the small town of Kovda on the Arctic Ocean. They found this very amusing. The propaganda department would probably not have been quite so amused if they had known my diaries. There, this first experience of mine with Russian communism was recorded.

I did not know what to expect in Russia. My expectations were not high. We were of course not headed to a world metropolis but to a far-flung corner of the universe which, on top of everything else, had come through the war particularly badly. On the way across the Atlantic I wrote in my diary:

I dread having to lie so long in this Russian hamlet. [. . .] On the day watch I cleaned the fuel-oil separator. Then I washed myself and changed into other clothes to show the Russians that there are no savages here, and we are expected to arrive around 9 this evening.

The surveillance of us foreigners was both extensive and close, especially at first. The Russians distrusted us and we distrusted them. I was not grateful for the reception, especially the fact that our cameras were confiscated. I had always taken a lot of photographs, ever since my childhood years, and I have my whole life on film. That is to say all of it, except these days in Russia. In my diary I recorded: "Something needed hiding."

We soon went ashore after customs inspection and formalities. I explored the place, which I later learned was called Kovda, and made a sketch of it in my diary. There I describe a shabby environment. The dock was "piled with timber refuse" and "in many places badly worn, sagging and rotten." The roads looked no less dilapidated:

All the "roads" are such that planks are laid parallel, crosswise to the road. It is extremely dangerous to step on the end, because then it can tip up. The houses are all log houses, most with thin boards on the outside. Most of them were very poor. All of them are unpainted. Many of the windowpanes are broken and in general the buildings seemed to me shoddy. The roofs are also of wood. The chimneys are built of brick. Most of the houses are single-story with a gable running their whole length.

To one house I then gave the assessment that it seemed "quite well-built." "It seemed newly finished or varnished. There were many flowers in the windows and the panes were all intact. There we heard a radio one evening. Probably upper-class people live there." The house next door, however, I gave a different assessment, and it seemed to have been placed there to emphasize the contrasts.

It was a two-story house, large. I have never seen a more decrepit human dwelling. Most of the windowpanes were broken and stuffed with rags. The house was crooked and unfinished. Garbage heaps and privies were by the doors. There were a great many children there. They were barefoot and dressed in rags. Often the clothes were far too big. Likewise the adults were poorly dressed. Could these be Russian workers' housing?

When the Russians had grown accustomed to our presence, they invited us to a dance in the local community hall. Most of the men had perished in the war, so the girls would have danced with one another had we not been available. We therefore got to dance with the girls without any trouble. Their figures seemed to us rather on the generous side, but that was no obstacle on our part. More memorable is how terribly bad we thought they smelled. They apparently wore something that was supposed to be fragrant, and we learned that it was considered extremely fine. Nothing further came of our acquaintance with the women. If the girls thought we were getting too forward, they pointed to their hair. They would apparently have been shorn if they were seen in the company of Germans during the war years.

I describe the people's diet by saying that they probably eat a lot of berries; many were berry-stained blue and drank juice with every meal. The bread seemed to me very coarse, and the teeth of some of the children were badly decayed. The clothes were shabby.

It rained heavily for several days. Then there was no loading. Our stay thus became longer than had been planned. By the ship there was a military guard in a little shelter. The cook felt sorry for him and wanted to bring him food. In the first attempt

he was driven back at rifle-point. But the cook stubbornly persisted. Next, the soldier grabbed the plate, wolfed down the food, and hurled the empty plate into the cook's arms. After that, the gifts of food went more smoothly.
At last the loading began. It was handled exclusively by women, but a man was the foreman. The women were loud and seemed to start quarrels about everything.

Some of the crew sympathized with the cause of Russia and the revolution. I never called them anything but communists in my diaries. I was never a communist and did not become one upon arriving in Russia — far from it. On the contrary, my aversion to this ideology hardened on encountering the actual conditions of the common people. I soon realized, though, that life in this hamlet did not give a true picture of the Soviet Union as a whole. It mattered greatly that I got to know a German-speaking forestry scientist with whom I talked a great deal. He enthusiastically instructed me on everything from the successful five-year plans and the country's incredibly rapid industrialization to the delights of cultural life in Moscow. About my stay, however, I reached this conclusion in my diary:

I must say that I was greatly disappointed. I thought that conditions in a modern state like Russia could not be so hard. Admittedly the people seem quite content, and no doubt are not accustomed to better. I had hoped that the many good doctrines of socialism were better implemented.
Serving as Inspector

When we got home, it looked for a time as though there would be a voyage to Italy. I very much wanted to go on that trip, but it would have meant losing a whole month of school, and in the end that weighed heavily. It came about that I stayed home and worked a little in my father's nursery in Fossvogur. About seafaring, however, I wrote in my diary:

This time that I was at sea I enjoyed very much, and I was determined to go to sea again next year. Naturally I had only come to know the best side of a seaman's life — been on a good ship, with good companions, and in summertime — but that side seemed to me exceptionally good.

I was of course unaware that one of the most instructive years of my life was on the horizon. That was the winter of 1947–48, when I held the office of inspector scholae. At the same time, it was one of the busiest years of my youth. I think I did not even fully realize until later how rewarding it

had been in my dealings with schoolmates and teachers, maturing in leadership and work, and no less educational than the studies themselves. It was a unique school for the trials of later years, a well of experience that I drew on greatly afterward. Of the election I write thus in my diary:

The Gymnasium began on October 1. [. . .] Now I was a sixth-former. It was the custom (this changed after that winter) that the mathematics division and the languages division each choose their own candidate for the inspector scholae election. I had intended not to stand, because I meant to study. Nevertheless it turned out that I became the candidate for the mathematics division. [. . .] I do not know why I gave in; perhaps it was ambition. Later I half regretted it. The majority of the languages division wanted to unite behind me and put forward no one. Still, the upshot was that Daði Hjörvar ran for a minority of the languages division (ca. 10 people). The result was that I was elected with ca. 250 votes while Daði received ca. 50. Thus began this sixth school year of mine, and it proved extremely eventful.

Daði Hjörvar was for a time in the Vigorous Boys (Röskir drengir). I myself put forward the proposal that he be granted temporary admission, on probation. He was the son of Helgi Hjörvar. Daði was always somewhat peculiar, considered eccentric, and had an unlucky life.

Daði was for a time with Iceland's permanent mission to the United Nations. His wife left him and took up with a man from the Base (Völlurinn). Shortly afterward we classmates met at Hótel Borg. Daði was there, and the wife as well, but with the new man. Daði wanted to get us to join him and mob the man or beat him up. This we of course refused. The next morning I met our classmate, Kata Thors. She said: "Do you know, Daði is dead." I began to laugh and answered: "He wasn't that drunk last night." Kata was as serious as before and said: "No, no. He died this morning."

Daði had taken his own life, swallowed a very large quantity of sleeping pills, and finally fallen asleep over a Bible he had laid in front of himself on the table. This was a shock to us all and caused great grief to his parents and family.
The school paper reported the results of the inspector election thus:

Suffice it to say that Steingrímur was elected with a more tremendous majority than any other inspector to date, and indeed he is well equal to the task and known for his unselfishness and diligence on behalf of the school's social life.
I would not have agreed wholeheartedly with this writing. At first I felt I sorely lacked sufficient experience:

When I took up the office I was completely unaccustomed to appearing in public. So I was not free of a certain nervousness when I chaired my first school assembly. But everything went off without mishap, and such things soon became routine. Quite a few school assemblies were held. The first assembly was devoted to electing the school's officers. Ólafur Haukur Ólafsson was elected scriba scholae. Then there was an assembly about a birthday gift for the rector. Since it would not do to request an assembly for that purpose, I requested an assembly to discuss reviving the temperance society of the Reykjavík Gymnasium (Menntaskólinn í Reykjavík). At that assembly a remarkable thing happened: it was approved, by about as many votes as the founding of the temperance society, to declare support for the beer bill then before the Althing. This caused considerable controversy and made it into the newspapers, among other places, because a fanatical temperance man [. . .] wrote a long article about drunkenness at the Gymnasium. Naturally there is some drinking at the school, but even so a drunken man is hardly ever seen at school gatherings. The article therefore angered many, and the rector replied to it. More assemblies were held, but I do not remember their business.
Before that I had hardly given a speech worthy of the name. In the inspector's job, however, organizational ability was tested more than eloquence.
The Office Staked on a Dance
I did not give myself time to keep a diary that winter, which shows better than most things how besieged every minute seemed to me. As before, I put down an overview in the diary at winter's end:

I regret now not having given myself time to write a diary this winter. These lines will never be more than loose reminiscences. Where to begin? Inspector scholae. That position has always been considered one of very great honor. It carries, however, the fault that little time is left to keep up with classes. So it went for me. Frequently I attended only two classes out of six. I was then attending to various duties. The inspector scholae is first and foremost

the representative of the students in every public arena; he chairs school assemblies and entertainments; he confers with the rector about matters of interest to the students; he is chairman of the dance committee, the Sel-trip committee, the Christmas festivities committee, and the brothers' fund committee. As often happens, the work of these committees fell mainly on the chairman. There were also a great many other duties to speak of.

The rector turned fifty that winter, and there was considerable busyness on that account. The students celebrated the birthday in grand style with a varied program, and I wrote a birthday article about Pálmi in the school paper.

My dealings with Pálmi were not without friction that winter. On presentation evenings an educational film was usually shown or some other instructive material introduced. Then there was dancing. One such evening followed a trip to the Sel. The rector intended to show a film of the 1947 Hekla eruption. Owing to some misunderstanding the film arrived late and the screening was delayed by an hour. It did not begin until around nine. Little time was therefore left for the dance once the screening was over. I then went to see the rector and asked for a one-hour extension, since the delay was not our fault. I got a firm no. The rector said we sixth-formers could use the sleep after having amused ourselves most of the night before at the Sel. I immediately called a meeting of the dance committee. I decided to resign as inspector scholae, along with the entire dance committee, if no extension was granted. Again I knocked on the rector's door. I informed him of my decision and the dance committee's, since one could not serve under such unfairness. The rector took off his glasses with a great sweep as he said: "Do you think, Steingrímur, that I am a doormat for you students?" As he uttered the word, he dropped his glasses on the floor. I bent down for them, handed them to him, and answered: "No, but we expect fairness." Soon the rector came out, walked into the Assembly Hall (Salurinn), and announced that we would get 45 minutes. This was greeted with great rejoicing. We considered ourselves to have won a complete victory.

It was just as well that dancing mattered to me that year, so much of my time did I devote to organizing entertainments and dances of various kinds. As said before, my studies suffered for the extracurricular work, and my year-end grades bore the mark of it. I am, however, in no doubt that I chose rightly.
Great Ambitions at War's End

By the end of my gymnasium years the Cold War had already broken out, and many feared a new world war between the new superpowers. In practice, however, that fear gave way to the ideal of building up the society of an independent nation. Anxiety

gave way to the great ambition and optimism of the postwar years in Iceland. The war and the high aspirations of newly won independence were the two things that left the deepest marks on the mental world of the generation that was with me at the gymnasium. Of that there is no doubt.

In general, young people looked to the future with bright eyes at war's end. The wartime profits made themselves felt in society, and prosperity grew. Contact with the outside world increased in these years, and it is certain that young people looked at the wide world with hopeful eyes. I was no exception. At the Gymnasium I gave the farewell speech on behalf of the graduating class, as it is traditional for the inspector to do. Every year the riddle of life is solved, and there is no shortage of prophetic postures or speculations. I still have the speech, and it is most solemn throughout. I probably have no document that better describes my attitudes toward society at this time and the role of us young people whom the school was sending forth. The closing words went like this:

But the future is also in many ways bright. We are of a nation that has been independent only a few years, a nation that has so much left undone, but owns a land of inexhaustible possibilities. We live in times when nothing seems impossible for technology. All these tasks await us, the young people, and we look forward to tackling them. It is our resolve to accomplish these tasks. We want to strengthen and protect the nation's independence and secure it a place among the foremost civilized nations. We believe that in this way we can best increase the nation's prosperity. Only experience can reveal how this will succeed.

Indeed, the faith in progress and technology was so strong that when news arrived that the first atomic bomb had been dropped on Japan, it was taken above all as a sign of progress and an endless source of energy for the benefit of mankind. The news reached me at the herring work in Siglufjörður, and I recorded my thoughts thus in my diary:

Monday, August 6, 1945. The news reported a new atomic bomb. But now the atom has finally been split, and scientists believe that with this the power of nature has been harnessed and electricity and coal will be eliminated. One bomb was dropped on a city in Japan. In the test, the explosion threw up a measured 13 km into the air and hurled men about at a distance of 10 km.

This event did not have a strong effect on me. Few, moreover, seemed to foresee the harm to the world and the menace that nuclear power would bring with it. I believe most people regarded it as an unequivocal and incredible technological advance. Nuclear power was to be an inexhaustible source of energy. I was certainly in that camp. It was not until the world realized what had happened that people began to have second thoughts.

Faith in progress and optimism permeated everything, not least in Iceland. The nation was of a mind to rise from the ashes and become something. Independence was a resource in our eyes, and from it we wanted to draw strength for new ideas. I myself wanted to do my part and learn something practical.

In the aforementioned farewell speech at the dimission ceremony, I said I did not intend to judge how we had used our years at school or what "material would prove to be in us as the men of the future." I myself was determined to go to the United States for study and to seek there an education that would benefit the nation.

We know nothing about the future, and wise men say that we understand the past moderately well and the present often little better. But it is certain that we are all children of our time, with its virtues and its flaws. We graduating students have, even though we are youngsters, already lived through a great time of change.
