For the greater part of the years that we have been here at the school, the most terrible war the world has ever had to endure has raged, and now there is talk of a coming war. History tells us that there is often great restlessness in the youth who grow up in wars and in the upheavals that follow them. There is much talk and writing about young people these days, and grown-ups consider them to have various of those bad traits of dissipation which characterize young people who grow up in wartime. It may be that this is to some extent true, but it is a comfort to us that from the earliest times youth has usually refuted such judgments.
Chapter Five
THE PROMISED LAND

After I had come to the conclusion that I wanted to study engineering, I soon set my course for the United States. The reasons were in themselves simple. I wanted to go abroad to study, and Europe was in ruins. In those years there were considerable currency restrictions and rationing in most areas in Iceland. Partly for that reason, limits were placed on what studies one could pursue abroad. In engineering, one was not permitted to study abroad what was taught at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands). There, a two-year preparatory program was offered in civil engineering, mechanical engineering, and electrical engineering.

Electrical engineering had fascinated me from the very beginning, and I intended to study it. Most avenues for going abroad to study therefore seemed closed for the time being. Runólfur Þórðarson heard that two Icelanders had gone to the United States for engineering studies and enrolled in chemical engineering. After one semester they had then switched over to their chosen fields without difficulty. These were Sveinn Björnsson, who was for a long time director of the Industrial Technology Institute (Iðntæknistofnun) and later director of the Reykjavík City Bus Company (SVR), and Björn Sveinbjörnsson, who later came to be associated with the Vefarinn company. My father got in touch with Árni Helgason, the consul in Chicago, to see whether Nunni and I could get into this same school, the Illinois Institute of Technology. Árni had gotten Sveinn and Björn in there, and a few years earlier Bragi Freymóðsson, engineer, and others. Chemical engineering was not taught at the University of Iceland, and so it came about that we both enrolled in it. Þorbjörn Karlsson — Bötti, Nunni's cousin and "a capable lad" — also went to study at the school. Runólfur had completed one year at home, but Þorbjörn had two years behind him. He therefore went straight into mechanical engineering over there. Together with Sveinn and Björn, we in fact became a five-student "Icelandic colony."
Árni Helgason was an acquaintance of my father's. He was from Hafnarfjörður and

one of those who founded Rafha in his day. Árni moved to Chicago when he was about twenty and became a great helping hand to Icelanders. He founded an electrical appliance factory and became wealthy. Among other things, he had supported Illinois Tech with substantial financial contributions. He was therefore in a good position to get Icelanders admitted. We five companions had him to thank for our places at the school.

After the first semester I switched from chemical engineering over to electrical engineering, but Nunni stayed faithful to chemical engineering. He was the only one of us Icelanders who graduated as a chemical engineer.
The journey to the promised land

Runólfur and I traveled together across the ocean on August 25, 1948. Considerable excitement accompanied setting out on this journey. We were far from being seasoned travelers, and neither of us had flown before. We had so much with us that our excess baggage was beyond all measure. Among the things we could not fit into any suitcase were enormous winter parkas. We decided to carry them. That proved fateful.

My family accompanied me to the airport, and in addition quite a few friends came to say goodbye. We were tired of the rationing society we were leaving, if the diary is to be believed, where it said: "The customs inspection was very lenient, since nothing can be taken along from here anyway."

The flight itself was a great adventure. This was the first regular scheduled flight to the United States. Those who take their first flight as adults know what a strange feeling it is to soar through the skies for the first time. The young generation, who fly before they are out of childhood, must surely find it hard to put themselves in these shoes. I wrote a rather detailed description of the journey in my diary:

The airplane was from Loftleiðir and is called "Geysir." There were seats for 46 passengers, and 45 were aboard. Nunni and I sat in the seats just in front of the entrance. From there the view was good. The weather was fine, somewhat cloudy toward the sea. We set course southwest. When we were over Keflavík we climbed up into the clouds and our country vanished from our sight. This was the first time I had flown. I immediately liked the smooth gliding of the airplane very much. It took small dips while it was in the clouds, but as soon as we were above them the flight became smooth. It seemed strange to me to see the clouds spreading out in snow-white billows as far as the eye could see. Now and then, to be sure, one could see down to the blue sea. Because of the weather, we flew over the southern tip

of Greenland. We flew over it at 1 o'clock. It was dark, to be sure, but the ice sheet and the fjords, all full of icebergs, could still be made out well. The lights had been turned off, and soon most people fell asleep.

A stopover was needed at Goose Bay in Labrador. There was a two-hour stop there. Soon after we took off again I fell asleep and did not wake until a vast and fertile land lay below. In the diary I recorded that concrete roads ran the length and breadth of the country, and that alongside them were large farms. In between, the land was all covered with forest. Finally New York appeared in the distance. A haze lay over the city and the traffic was very heavy. At last we landed at the new Idlewild airport, "the biggest in the world," I said in the diary.

Everything was "the biggest in the world" in those first days in the United States. The first thing that struck us, though, was the heat. It was overwhelming and met us like a wall when we stepped out with the sheepskin parkas in our arms. We sat near the exit and were therefore the first out of the plane. The diary says: "The temperature was 100.5 F! (about 39 C.) What made the heat even more unbearable was the great humidity. It was 90 degrees." The reception was no less unexpected, as the diary testifies:

Photographers were there to receive us, because this was the first Icelandic scheduled flight to the United States. We were all made to go into a single hall. Then our medical certificates were collected. We had to wait there a long time. The traffic at the airport was very heavy. Airplanes were constantly coming and going.

Unexpectedly, we became photographic subjects in The New York Times on our first arrival in the United States. Three things accounted for that. There was a heat wave in the city, this was the first regular scheduled flight from Iceland, and thirdly, the leading dignitaries of Loftleiðir were on board. In the picture, however, were not only the reception committee, Kristján Jóhann Kristjánsson, chairman of the board of Loftleiðir, captain Alfreð Elíasson, who later became the company's managing director, and others from the plane's crew, but also two young men looking in opposite directions and carrying enormous winter parkas over their arms. That was Runólfur and I.

The paper's headline was: "Record heat in New York! – dozens of people dying from the heat," and beneath the picture it said: "Icelanders land in New York in record heat, dressed for winter." Later we heard that the picture had been put up in the window of the magazine Fálkinn in Bankastræti and remained there all winter.
After a wait of many hours in the halls of the immigration service, we finally lugged this heavy baggage of ours onto a "bus," or motor coach. We must havedoubtless

been a sight to see, with gigantic travel suitcases and the sheepskins on top of it all. We were also more dead than alive from the heat and on the verge of giving up. We would probably have gone straight back home if we had been able to afford it. But the travel story grew longer, because strange incidents kept happening to us on the way to the hotel. This is how I tell of it in the diary:

In the bus a curious incident occurred. A man came into the bus and said: "Damned hot, this." I addressed him at once and said: "Yes, it is hot." A conversation immediately sprang up between us, for Icelanders outside Iceland are always acquaintances.

This was one Bjarni Þórðarson, who had been staying four months in New York. He proved very helpful to us in those first days in the city and gave us various pointers. He began by getting us to the hotel by means of great wonder-machines, the underground trams. I tell of them with admiration in the diary. "Some of the stations [are] many 'stories' down, with escalators in between. It costs 10 cents by subway, but for 10 cents one can travel 210 miles, so it is said, because one can always change trains." Runólfur probably gazed a bit too intently at the underground wonders. On our third day in the city, he failed to get into the car before the automatic door closed. I arrived at the hotel about half an hour ahead of him that day.
Bjarni Þórðarson met us several more times while we stayed in New York. He was known in Iceland, among other things, as an excellent pianist and the accompanist for the MA Quartet (MA-kvartettinn).

New York seemed incredible to us. The subway system was not the only marvel. Not least, we stared at the skyscrapers. We were in a metropolis, there was no mistaking that. Here everything was the biggest, the fanciest, and the best. On the first evening we did not stay long at the hotel but went to Radio City: "The fanciest cinema and theater in the world." The largest hall seated 6,300 people. We could hardly find words to describe our enthusiasm. This was certainly something other than Gamla bíó.

We used our time in New York well and saw the city's chief landmarks, among others the Empire State Building and the Statue of Liberty. I noted down the height of both structures with engineering precision. To understand our astonishment in those days, it may be mentioned that the tallest building we had seen before was probably the main building of the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands).

On the very first evening we went out walking and bathed in the lights of the advertising signs for which New York was famous. Illuminated signs were unknown in Iceland and probably in most of war-ravaged Europe. Sigurður Jónsson,
one of the Icelanders in New York, introduced us to these splendors. He was studying for a doctorate in chemistry. This is how the diary tells of it:

We strolled up 5th Ave. to 42nd Street and from there up Broadway. It was bright as day, because everything was covered with illuminated advertisements. Some were magnificent, for example at Bond's. Very many people were out and about. All without jackets. Everywhere one can get something to drink, both out on the street and indoors. We went into the Jack Dempsey bar, which is very fancy. At 1:30 we came home.

A great many Icelanders lived in the city, and a group of them stayed on 104th Street. We went there in search of companionship and guidance. Sightseeing tours of the city's entertainment districts were most welcome. They showed us places we would never have imagined existed, let alone that we would have gone there on our own initiative. Among these places was Greenwich Village, or "Green Village," as I call the neighborhood in the diary. There it was not the buildings but the people that most caught the eye:

Strangest of all, I found, was to see the homosexuals ("kynvillingar") who were there, for the neighborhood is famous for them. Many of the women were dressed and had their hair cut like men, and vice versa. They were dancing and embracing. The neighborhood is quite shady. At first I found it strange to see men and women embracing in public. There was one such couple at the Eddie London bar who kissed too long and too ardently.

At this bar there were only homosexual people. Runólfur and I were not at all accustomed to such things. In Iceland, sex education had hardly begun to be mentioned in schools; homosexuality was never called by name except as perversion (öfuguggaháttur) or sexual deviance (kynvilla), and it was taken for granted that one looked down on those afflicted by it. This was, however, an entertaining place, and we dropped in at this bar more than once when we came to the neighborhood to enjoy ourselves.

I did not think much about these matters, but I felt for the people and still have full sympathy for them. On the other hand, homosexuality does not seem natural to me. Nevertheless, I believe that gay men and lesbians should be allowed to live their lives undisturbed and should be given whatever assistance possible, because homosexual people face an uphill struggle in society.
The city of gangsters

After a week's stay in New York we took a train to our destination, Chicago. We did not fully know what to expect. Shortly before I went abroad to study, I drove north to Skagafjörður together with some of my friends from the Gymnasium. I wanted to say goodbye to my relatives at Syðri-Brekkur, not least Grandmother Pálína, who had grown old. We were, of course, received with open arms. My grandmother did not at all like the look of things when she heard that I was on my way to Chicago. The first thing she said was: "I don't like the sound of that, Denni dear. Isn't he there, that Al Capone?"

Though the fame of this gangster had traveled all the way to Skagafjörður, news of his death had been slow in coming. Al Capone was six feet under by the time of this story. I did not notice much crime in the city while I lived there. I understand, though, that the Mafia largely controlled its western part. We never went there. Almost none of our schoolmates ever set foot in the black neighborhood surrounding the school. We Icelanders, on the other hand, went there undaunted and had a beer at a bar in the school's vicinity. We never got into any trouble.

That trip to Syðri-Brekkur was our farewell, Grandmother's and mine. I did not see her after that, for she died that same winter. The old woman's words of warning perhaps still lingered in me during my first days in the city. At least, Chicago did not seem to me to have the same luster that New York had appeared to have. Downtown Chicago is called The Loop. I say of it in the diary that the Loop did not seem to us nearly as splendid and clean as the shopping district of N.Y. On arriving in Chicago, September 2, 1948, I also recorded that I did not much like the look of the place at first sight. "The neighborhoods we passed through were dirty and run-down." Later I discovered that there are very beautiful neighborhoods in Chicago. Around the school, however, the surroundings were not attractive.
The city has a rather unlovely history of relations between the races. The neighborhood around the university bore witness to it. I recorded the following in my diary on arrival:

We looked at the school and the neighborhood. We liked the school, but not the neighborhood. The school is between Michigan Ave and the New York Central tracks and between 31st Str. and 35th Str. It is completely surrounded by Negro neighborhoods. At one time these were rich men's neighborhoods. Then Chicago was "small." But Chicago grew, and the rich moved out to the new suburbs. Jews bought these neighborhoods and sold them to Negroes. It is very squalid almost everywhere around here. There are now plans to clear
away all the Negro houses from the site and build a splendid campus district. Something has already been done in that direction.

Later I read that this complete separation of whites, Jews, and blacks had been a characteristic of the city for some time. We became acquainted with this little by little. The diary fragment above was written long before I had ever heard that the word "negri" had a derogatory meaning. The shock of coming from the homogeneous Icelandic society into the diversity of America was of course enormous, and it took time to get one's bearings in the new environment. Society was almost completely sorted and divided by race, far more than it is now. There were only a very few black students at the school. They were certainly no more than five and kept very much to themselves. I got to know only one of them. We Icelanders also soon became aware that people were divided into Jews and those who were not Jews. I had never imagined this, and in my mind it put a stain on the United States. I found this racial division extreme.
The community of Icelanders

Nunni and I were roommates in the student dormitory, Farr Hall, for the first two winters. Most of our neighbors there were Americans. The bonds of friendship between Runólfur and me strengthened in those years and have neither broken nor frayed since. We have, one might say, traveled through life together, as appears in many places in this account. Runólfur is a quiet man, highly intelligent, and has the soul of an artist. He plays the piano very well, owns one of the largest collections of classical piano music in this country, and is one of the leading figures in the musical life of Kópavogur. Immediately after finishing his studies he joined the Fertilizer Plant (Áburðarverksmiðjan) and worked there as plant manager until he retired a few years ago. Runólfur is married to Hildur Halldórsdóttir, my classmate, a most excellent woman.
We often found the Americans amusing, but at the same time some were strange fellows, as the diary describes:

A few Americans may also be mentioned, e.g. Joe Lorden, who lived here in the "dormitory": He is an odd bird, with a half-shaved head, and talked a great deal about himself and his "girlfriend." A strange "gal" she must have been. He was a fine example of many Americans. Here on this floor lived Fred and others whose names I do not remember. They are fine fellows.

Otherwise we Icelanders kept very much to ourselves. Of all the Americans I got to know, it can probably be said that we quickly became acquaintances but a lasting friendship never formed. This seemed to me a national characteristic. After having been in the country for half a year, I gave the Americans this assessment:

It is said that the three factors that govern the life of the general public here [. . .] are “money, sex and action.” And this indeed comes across very clearly in the films, which faithfully follow these paths. On the whole, the horizon of the ordinary people I have come to know here seems to me rather narrow. Those who are not hard-line Republicans or Democrats are Communists, in the view of the masses. Generally they are not well acquainted with Europe, or with what is happening there. It seems to be the opinion of many that something is amiss over there, and that the United States is helping the poor wretches.

Runólfur and I had arrived some time before classes began because we wanted to get a better grip on our English. We certainly needed it. It was probably comical to listen to us just after our arrival in New York, since we sometimes had a rough time making ourselves understood. We once sat for a good long while at a bar where I tried to convey that I wanted to buy milk: “Milk please.” Somehow this must have come out of me backwards, because I got just about every other liquid in the place but no milk. We were served orange juice, soft drinks and beer. Nunni drank the beer for me.

Þorbjörn Karlsson arrived in Chicago a good week after us. By then Runólfur and I considered ourselves quite the accomplished men, having learned our way around the cafeteria, where we picked out dishes ourselves on a tray and then paid. Among the things we had discovered were corncobs, which we had gotten the knack of gnawing clean. We recommended this food to Þorbjörn. He took the plunge and launched an assault on the specimen. He had the greatest difficulty cutting it into slices, as everyone knows who has attempted such feats with rock-hard corncobs. We held in our laughter for a good while until we burst out laughing and taught Þorbjörn the trick. We considered ourselves great cosmopolitans for knowing how to gnaw corn.

Þorbjörn's path and mine did not intertwine as much as Runólfur's and mine. Still, we spent one year together in graduate study in California and have kept in good contact since coming home. Þorbjörn was a very good student, even-tempered and reflective. He became a professor at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands). Þorbjörn

married a girl in the United States named Celeste. It was a difficult marriage and they divorced. His second wife is Svala Sigurðardóttir. Their marriage has been a happy one, Svala being a fine woman.

In Chicago there was quite a sizeable community of Icelanders. We were regularly invited to the home of Consul Árni and his family. Árni lived in Villmette, a district north of the city. There we were often treated with great hospitality. Árni leaned to the right and was a staunch supporter of the Republicans. We often sparred vigorously over politics and policies. Shortly after our arrival, Guðni Ívar Oddsson, an engineering technician, visited us at the suggestion of Consul Árni. They were kinsmen. Guðni worked as a technician at Motorola. He was a delightful man but recently divorced from his wife and rather lonely, it seemed to me. Guðni was rather small of stature, brisk and usually cheerful. He greatly enjoyed it when new Icelanders arrived and busied himself around them. He showed us the city during our first days in his splendid car, a 1937 Lincoln.

Guðni taught us to use the “elevated,” which were streetcars on raised tracks. They became our main means of transport in the city. I make no mention anywhere in my diary of the fact that Guðni took us to “burlesque” shows, which we had never seen before but which he was very fond of. That is the striptease dancing for which Calumet City, the district south of Chicago, was famous. We no doubt found this exciting at first sight, but we soon grew tired of the dancing. To me these seemed rather mechanical performances and not very artistic.

Guðni Ívar proved a good friend to us and was a fine companion. He was, however, unhappy deep down. I heard back in Iceland long afterwards that Guðni had been found dead in the vicinity of the city. He is said to have lost his job shortly before.

Also living in Chicago were Valur Egilsson, who was studying dentistry at Northwestern University, the son of Egill Benediktsson, restaurateur at the Oddfellow House, and his wife Ólöf, always called Lulla. She was studying dental care, Dental Hygiene. The couple were cheerful and entertaining companions and were regularly part of our circle.

We also soon got to know Gissur Brynjólfsson, a physician working in Chicago. There he had met Sigrid, a woman of Swedish descent, and he married her while we were in Chicago. They lived on the “Southside,” in the southern part of the city, and treated us as if we were part of the family. We were often invited to their home on Thanksgiving Day, which is a great feast day of food and drink in the United States. This honorable couple are still good friends of mine and I visit them whenever I pass through. The same good story

can be told of Gissur's parents-in-law, Svea and Axel Söderlund, who also lived on the “Southside.” Through their mediation we companions got a house to rent for the winter of 1950–51. It was owned by friends of the parents-in-law and stood on Euclid Avenue.

The house was on one floor and six of us rented it together: I, Sveinn, Nunni and his wife Hildur, and Björn along with his wife Bíbí. Þorbjörn had gone off to graduate study in California. Sveinn and I were unmarried when we moved in. Hildur worked in one of the university bookstores while Bíbí, Björn's wife, looked after the household.

Sveinn and I had become slightly acquainted in secondary school, particularly through chess. In Chicago we became good friends and have been ever since. Sveinn later sat for a long time on the executive board of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) when I was its executive director, and he served as its chairman for several years. Sveinn was executive director of the Industrial Technology Institute (Iðntæknistofnun) and later head of the Reykjavík Bus Company (Strætisvagnar Reykjavíkur). He is married to Helga Gröndal. She is an energetic, handsome woman.

Björn's path and mine ran together for a shorter time, as he died before his time. He was a good fellow, like all these companions of mine, and wanted to smooth everyone's way. After coming home he took over Vefarinn, one of the companies of his father, Sveinbjörn Jónsson of Ofnasmiðjan. Björn and Jakobína Finnbogadóttir, Bíbí, who was with us in Chicago for one winter, later divorced. Björn's second wife was Guðlaug Björnsdóttir.

In the first years after coming home, the Chicago group kept together as card-playing companions. At first we were too many for bridge and played poker. This card-playing gradually died out. Three of us, however, have kept up the habit and now play bridge: Runólfur, Sveinn Björnsson and I. The fourth man has come from outside, first Pétur Pálsson and now Bragi Guðmundsson, both engineers. Occasionally my brother-in-law Böðvar Guðmundsson steps into the breach. We play once a week during the winter, starting at eight o'clock and stopping at twelve. Most things are made to yield to these card evenings. I made every effort to protect these evenings during my ministerial career, and mostly succeeded despite the pressures. Politics is not discussed over the cards. These evenings were therefore a welcome respite for me from the political grind.
Loneliness and homesickness

The first years far from family and homeland can be lonely and difficult despite good companions. Sometimes gloom descended on me and existence felt empty. I turned to my diary with these thoughts and corresponded with a large

group of my friends in Iceland. I have all the letters I received in a thick folder: Bjarni Guðnason wrote poetic letters about life, existence and the “damned conservatives”; the Clausen brothers boasted of various conquests, and there was plenty to draw on at that farm; Guðjón Lárusson wrote long letters about medicine, the “blessed conservatives” and even about love; Haukur Jónasson wrote warm, friendly letters about life in Reykjavík and asked me to buy shoes and a coat and other things he lacked from America; my sister Dolly wrote regularly, and Sveinbjörn Dagfinnsson, my future brother-in-law, sent various news; Sverrir Scheving wrote briskly of outdoor excursions and the barracks-life struggle. Everyone wrote to me about the riots at the Alþingi over Iceland's entry into NATO, and everyone sent news of who was going with whom, when and where; I heard of engagements, marriages, affairs, divorces, dances and births.

I also corresponded with my female friends: Tóta, Þórunn Guðnadóttir, wrote long and lively letters about scandals and entertainments. We were always excellent friends. I also wrote to my old girlfriends, Kristrún Karlsdóttir and Halla Guðmundsdóttir, as well as to Nína Kampmann, until I met my future wife, as will be related later. Then I had other fish to fry.

I answered all my friends with thick and detailed letters, such as only a lonely perfectionist can produce. No one, however, received more or thicker letters than my parents. Letters passed between us on virtually every flight to and from Iceland.

The first Christmas was the hardest for me. There was a break then from the rigorous studies, and time to turn one's thoughts to life and existence. Not much seems to have remained of the new graduate's optimism half a year after the matriculation examination. In my diary I have written:

I know more or less exactly my future now. From here I will graduate, God willing, as an engineer, get a job at home, and that's that. I miss something I can live for, something that seizes hold of my mind, something I am prepared to risk everything for. It seems to me that this something cannot be created from scratch by a man himself. It has to come to him. Ah, yes, sometimes I wish I were a pirate in the 17th century, or a gold prospector in America's pioneer days. But did they have any goal then? Did they not also miss something? Probably. But I feel that physical danger and feats suit me better. There, it seems to me, I would most likely find this “something.” Perhaps it would be a beautiful girl, perhaps . . . yes, something else, something I would want to attain or else not live at all.

In the winter break a year later my spirits were still heavy. Þorbjörn, Sveinn and Björn had gone on a trip around Canada while Runólfur and I stayed home. “We did not have grants like them,” I say in the diary. “It was thoroughly dull. There was little else we could do but go to the cinema, look at museums and sleep.” I was again seized by the same feeling of emptiness as the year before.
Whether an “empty” life is better or one too “full,” I do not know. Mine is empty.

No doubt similar thoughts have come to most of those who have lived abroad for an extended time. I was like a missionary without a calling. It may be said that I did not find this “something” I was searching for until I found a channel for my ambition in reforms in Iceland.

Yet it evidently seemed to me most within reach to find a beautiful girl when this was written, for I had hardly written these lines at the beginning of 1949 before I met an American girl. It was at the wedding of Valur and Lulla. Lulla had a friend from Iowa whom she was tremendously eager to introduce to me. Her name was Mary Lou and she was very beautiful. I describe her thus in the diary:

She is jet-black-haired, with beautiful brown eyes. She dances exceptionally well and sings splendidly. She called me two days after the wedding and asked me to come to Lulla's. We went there. We enjoyed ourselves well. Naturally I bade her farewell with a few kisses. Bade her farewell, yes, because she lives 200 miles from here, in Iowa. I then received a letter from her every 3rd day. Sometimes pink or blue, or bright red. Lastly she absolutely insisted that I come to Iowa between “semesters.”

I thought very well of the girl, but she was very ardent and it was just as if she wanted to get married on the spot. I therefore saw it as my best option to push her away from me. The trip was something I could not imagine making:

I both wanted to be rid of [the trip] and my finances were nothing to boast of, so I cobbled together excuses. They do not, however, seem to have worked well, because now I have not received a letter for several days, and indeed she signed her last one “Love, Mary Lou.” Well, the poor girl, the very best of girls. But that is how these American ones are “said” to be.
If I thought I was free and clear, I was mistaken. Somewhat later another attempt was made to get me to Iowa. This clearly affected me somewhat, judging by the diary:

I am in very great difficulty now. Lulla called and said I was invited to Iowa along with them next weekend. I do not know what I am to do. She seems to be quite in love. I received one letter after another signed “Love.” I, on the other hand, am not at all smitten, so I think I will only make bad things worse if I go. But I do not know how to get free. I am thinking of writing Mary Lou and telling her straight out that I do not consider it good that I come.
While I racked my brains, Mary Lou did not sit idle. The very next day she called me, having by then arrived in Chicago. I postponed all our meetings and recorded this in the diary:
Mary Lou called. I said I could not meet her today. I do not know what I am to do with her.

I wrote to my friends at home and put it to them whether it could be considered normal for a woman to ask a man out. I did not have to wait for an answer: An entire dance practice was held at the Grammar School (Menntaskólinn) where only the girls were allowed to ask for a dance. “No boys were allowed to ask anyone to dance except during the gentlemen's break, and this is said to have been one of the most entertaining dance practices ever held at the school.” The debating society of the grammar-school girls had made its entrance.
I pulled myself together and told Mary Lou frankly that I was not out courting. I was in no mood for love my first winter in Chicago.
Electrical engineering and giant computers

Life for us Icelanders revolved first and foremost around our studies. We all placed great emphasis on them and read with great vigor. The studies were entirely different and much more rigorous than we were accustomed to. One examination followed on the heels of another and the pressure was considerable. It was especially palpable the first winter, but one got used to it as time went on. The Icelanders all did well and passed their examinations with excellent results.

I have always inclined toward the logical and want clean lines. Mathematics and the sciences were my favorites all along, and so engineering suited me well. My supervising teacher, Dr. Menger, was a famous mathematician in the field of infinite dimensions. He was one of the stars of the school and had come there from Germany just before the war. He was a Jew, and I describe him as “exceptionally enthusiastic and constantly in motion.” This memorable German is one of the best teachers I have ever known.
Dr. Menger believed I could skip over the first part of the mathematics course.

He decided to have me take a placement test out in the corridor while he was examining a class. The test went well, and he therefore recommended that my grammar-school mathematics from home be credited toward my degree. The head of student registration, however, refused this. I told Dr. Menger about it and he became furious. He dragged me along behind him out to the offices and shouted there at the cowed staff: “You do not accept Dr. Menger's recommendations! This man is to have his mathematical knowledge credited. I know about these matters, not you.” There was some muttering of objections, but this diminutive man did not wait around; he stormed out with the words: “Then I am leaving!” People were startled. The next day I was informed that the mathematics from home would be recognized. The same thing happened with my grammar-school German. It was credited to me after I passed a placement test. I thus managed to complete the four-year engineering program in three years. That done, I was determined to go on to graduate study.

Sveinn and Björn graduated at the same time as Runólfur and I, and went home. Runólfur received a good grant for graduate study at the university in Madison, a very good school in the state of Wisconsin. Þorbjörn Karlsson finished the first part of his mechanical engineering studies a year ahead of us and went on to further study at the California Institute of Technology.
“Big Red” in wrestling and track and field

I soon began taking part in sports at the school and competed both in wrestling and in track and field. The wrestling was under the direction of a young coach. I told him that I would probably have difficulty taking part in the training sessions because a muscle by my right shoulder blade was ruined. In the sixth form of the Grammar School (Menntaskólinn) I had attempted a somersault in gym class but slipped on a wet patch and landed on the back of my neck. Around the same time I had enrolled in KR and begun track and field. I trained in the throwing events, and it was always the same story: after three or four throws I had to stop because of this injury. I therefore had to give up throwing practice.

I expected that wrestling would be beyond me, since it involves difficult bridge positions on the neck and hard grappling. The coach had me put on a warm-up suit and told me to skip rope nonstop for about 15 minutes. I was exhausted when he laid me on a bench and massaged my back. This went on for two weeks. After that I was allowed to start wrestling. If I began to feel pain in my back, the same treatment was repeated. Nor were the results long in coming. I have never felt pain there since. Not only could I take part in wrestling after this, but I could also throw the discus and shot put, and I consider myself to owe this young coach a great deal.

I did well in wrestling, competed in the light heavyweight class and was among the best. This wrestling is very unlike the clownish sport that can be seen on television and is called “fjölbragðaglíma” here in Iceland. This was Olympic wrestling, which is very fast. No foul holds were allowed. Neck holds, for example, could only be taken with one hand. I benefited greatly from what I knew of Icelandic glíma wrestling, for I often managed to catch my opponents with a heel-hook or a leg-trip. They did not realize what was happening until they were down.

I took sports very seriously, like everything else in those years. The training sessions were hard, two hours at a time. They began with a rigorous warm-up before we set to wrestling: rope-skipping, push-ups and stomach exercises. I progressed quickly and grew much stronger and lighter. In my diary I drew a graph showing how my weight changed. I lost two kilos in two months, which is hardly worth mentioning, so muscle probably replaced the fat I shed.

The coach finally decided to form a special select squad to prepare for competition. The condition was that we train four times a week, two hours at a time. I was in my final year at the school and told him truthfully that I did not feel able to do it. To gain admission to a good school for graduate study I would have to graduate with high marks. The coach was quite downcast over this, and I felt I was letting this excellent man down.

In track and field, the throwing events remained my best events, as they had been at home. At engineering schools, sports were generally an amateur affair, and we were therefore naturally far behind the big schools that bought up the track-and-field stars. With us, sports were a sideline and never pursued as a course of study. We competed mainly against smaller schools in the vicinity. I quite often managed to win the discus throw in such meets, and sometimes the shot put. My best marks were just over 42 meters in the discus and about 13 meters in the shot. The school paper took to making much of this. I still have the clippings. In a team presentation before one meet I was called the godsend from Iceland and reckoned capable of carrying off victory in any throwing event whatsoever:

Throwing the weights is Iceland's gift to the Middle West, Steingrímur “Big Red” Hermannsson. One of Tech's most consistent performers, he is capable of winning his favorite event, the discus, as well as the shotput and javelin in any meet.

From track and field, then, comes the nickname “Big Red” — or “stóri rauður” — which has sometimes been heard since. My schoolmates considered me a track star, which of course I was not at all, though I took great pleasure in

throwing for the school. Despite this nickname I was generally called Denni in the United States, and that suited me fine, since I was used to the name. Nobody could manage to say Steingrímur properly. Runólfur, on the other hand, was never called anything but Ronny. It was equally hopeless for Americans to say Runólfur and Steingrímur.

Through sports I made many fine acquaintances, and the training sessions led to my getting to know people other than the Icelanders. Of the acquaintances I made in Chicago, and later in graduate school, there is nevertheless only one from whom I have received greetings now and then.

The fellows from the wrestling team were in the habit of going out to a bar for a beer after practice or a meet. One of these teammates was small and wiry and competed in the lightweight class. Once we went together to one of the strip clubs in Kalumet City. Scantily clad girls flocked around, obviously wanting to strike up business with us. We had no interest and said we only intended to make a short stop. They then complained about us to one of the bouncers. He came over to us, a stout and powerful fellow, and asked whether we had been rude to the ladies. We denied it, but he nonetheless prepared to throw us out. He was standing in just the right position: I set my toe behind his heel and kicked with my other foot into the knee of that same leg. With that, the big brute crashed full-length onto the floor. We did not wait around but fled at a run and made it around the next corner before the bouncer and his none-too-inviting companions rushed out to seek revenge. We would have stood no chance against those muscle-bundles. I have seldom run as fast in my life.
The Worst and the Best

Life far from home became familiar, and in the end I was quite content. If I could have imagined living anywhere other than Iceland, it would have been in the United States. My stay there had a profound effect on me. It strengthened me in the belief that a good and prosperous society could be built in Iceland. My acquaintance with the United States likewise strengthened my opposition to the excesses of the profit-seeking mentality that characterizes the modern age.

It was incredible to see how some people lived in utter abundance. In other neighborhoods of cities like Los Angeles or Chicago, the poverty was heartrending. Driving through the Southern states, the wretched conditions of Black people were plain to see. They were crammed into miserable hovels that sometimes stood on swampland. It was sad to see beggars sitting out in the streets, and incredible that the richest nation in the world should tolerate such a disgrace. It has no need to.

I was captivated by many of the ideals and undertakings of the Americans and thought Icelanders could learn much from them. Some of that I still hold in esteem, but in other respects my views have changed. It is every man's good fortune to be able to learn and mature. The United States is a democracy with free elections. When I began to study American history I was captivated by Franklin Delano Roosevelt, not least by his vision of a welfare system in the United States and the so-called shake-up, the "New Deal." I read a good deal about his work and, among other things, wrote an essay about him for which I received an excellent grade.

Later I found the social-democratic Democrat Adlai Stevenson a most interesting politician. He lost to Eisenhower in the 1956 presidential election. Many of his speeches in that campaign seemed to me to bear witness that he was a remarkable thinker. Eisenhower was no doubt a decent fellow, but in my view he did not hold a candle to Stevenson. There, nothing ran much deeper than "I like Ike." It later emerged, in fact, that Stevenson seldom wrote his own speeches; rather it was an economist by the name of John Kenneth Galbraith, who was, among other things, a professor at Harvard University. I had seen my father sit far into the night composing his speeches, and it never occurred to me that politicians had others write their speeches for them. I have since read various books by Galbraith and find his ideas very interesting.

In those years the Cold War was in full swing, and a congressional committee chaired by McCarthy conducted a kind of show trials, or witch hunts, against alleged communists. The hearings were beyond belief and were televised across the length and breadth of the United States. Scrupulous individuals were all but excommunicated for having an acquaintance who had studied the theories of the communists. Most educated people held these methods in contempt, and I felt the fanaticism went far beyond the bounds of decency. Anti-communism was endemic, and few spoke up for people on the left. I was no exception.

Right-wing politics dominated American public life. It is important, however, to distinguish between that and the right-wing extremism now running rampant, which preaches that state power is another word for evil and that no government involvement is to be tolerated. To my mind, the doctrine that individuals should enjoy absolute freedom of action without government interference is akin to saying there should be no rules for driving on the highways — that everyone may drive there as he pleases. Fortunately, no one entertains such a notion.

With the "New Deal" there arose in the United States the beginnings of a welfare system, which was built up substantially in the 1950s and 1960s. Yet the social safety net there has never seemed to me sufficiently sound. It does not reach everyone. The states are

quite different in this respect, though, as in many other things. In Wisconsin, for example, there is a solid welfare system that in many ways resembles what is found in the Nordic countries. The state capital, Madison, has time and again been chosen as the best city in America to live in. About the United States as a whole one can hardly generalize on any matter, so different are the individual states from one another. Those who have only been to New York have seen little of the United States. In 1956 I traveled through a great many states in the central and northwestern parts of the country to study rural electrification. Small towns in Oregon are as unlike New York as the Reykjavík of my youth was unlike the New York I first came to know. Though the same language is spoken in the village and the metropolis, the life of the people is different.

I have been to every state in the Union except one, Alaska. The more I saw of the United States and the better I got to know it, the more I began to distinguish what I found exemplary from the rest. I believe, though, that developments over there have in many respects taken a turn for the worse since then, for example in environmental matters. I fear this is a consequence of that excessive emphasis on libertarianism — or profit-worship, as I prefer to call it. I was captivated by much in that great country, and it saddens me when its policy toward the outside world and toward nature seems to me to fail in certain areas. The United States has some of the best but at the same time much of the worst. The United States is the land of the well-to-do. For them, there are few better places to live.
"That Is My Beer"

The Icelanders stuck closely together. On one occasion, as so often, we went out for an evening's entertainment. This time it was at a very large nightclub called the Aragon. We got a table up on the balcony. I had not yet begun to taste alcohol at that time and had therefore been recruited to drive. In the Icelandic fashion, my companions wanted to save on liquor purchases and brought along a flask of whiskey, which Þorbjörn Karlsson kept. At one point, while the others were dancing, Þorbjörn took out the flask and loosened the cap. He filled a rather large glass from the flask and was about to pour from it into the others' glasses. Just then a waiter of the establishment came by. He thought there was something unusual in the glass and asked what it was. I answered on the spot: "That is my beer," and drained the glass in one gulp. Thus I tasted alcohol knowingly for the first time, and at the same moment saved us from being thrown out of the place. It did me no harm; I remember nothing of feeling any effects, and I drove the whole group home that night.
One day Þorbjörn and I came across a poster on a telephone pole by a street near the school. Duke Ellington was coming and was giving a concert at

a nightclub at the southern end of the Black district. Guðni Ívar drove Þorbjörn and me to the place. When it came to it, we were the only white men in the house apart from two older men and a girl who seemed to be there on her own. I described the circumstances thus in my diary:

We came into a large dance hall. We had thought this would be a "concert." There were only benches along the walls, much like at Iðnó. Soon the whole place filled up with Negroes. We did not much like the look of things. There were no more than about 5–6 white men there, but the place was packed with Negroes. After a long wait some small band began to play; no Duke. We enjoyed listening to them. They played with enthusiasm. It was also very entertaining to watch the Negroes dance. When the evening was well advanced and we were half thinking of going home, Duke arrived. We listened to him for 1 hour and enjoyed it.

Because of the lack of chairs there was nothing for it but to sit on the edge of the stage. The adventure was in fact all the greater for it. One might say we sat at the feet of the master. The atmosphere was tremendous; the guests sang and danced with incredible feeling and artistry.

It was late when we headed home, and the streetcars had stopped running. We could not bring ourselves to spend money on a taxi and so had to go on foot. It was a long way, some 30 blocks, as they said, through the Black district. We walked past a grocery store where all the food had been removed from the shelves and locked away in cabinets. Enormous rats were helping themselves to the crumbs on the floors. Houses in many places were on the verge of collapse, in glaring contrast to the big Cadillacs parked outside. It was an incredible sight. We probably forgot to be afraid. The people we met seemed not to believe their own eyes, as though they had never seen a white man before, and our schoolmates' astonishment the next morning was no less. The Americans simply did not believe us when we told them we had walked that whole way unmolested. It could not be done, they said.

In Chicago I also saw Art Tatum in concert. He was blind and was therefore led onto the stage. The concert proved unforgettable. In those years Runólfur also gradually introduced me to classical music. Among other things, we saw Horowitz, one of the greatest piano virtuosos of all time, in concert. At the time I was struggling with some homework problems in mathematics. At the start of the concert the solution suddenly dawned on me, and I worked out the problem on the program. I have seldom seen Runólfur so scandalized — but that is how good an effect Horowitz had on me. He enchanted everyone present, and the atmosphere

was tremendous. He was called back for six encores. Gradually classical music gained the upper hand with me, and I am fondest of Wagner. He strikes me as very deep and contemplative. Usually I settle myself comfortably in the basement at home, turn the volume up high and get to enjoy him undisturbed. That is a good time for thinking. The one exception was when the children were studying for exams. Then they would often shout down: "Oh, turn that Wagner down." They have, however, come to appreciate him better in later years.

I found American food good, and the portions did nothing to spoil it. The steaks were large and the desserts divine. Banana splits were a favorite, and I devoured them whenever I had the chance. Usually this was a split banana, three scoops of ice cream, strawberries and whipped cream. It was a great deal of food.

In my second winter in the United States, a daughter was born to Björn back in Iceland. We friends went out to dinner and had steak at Alexander's, a good restaurant in Chicago. After the meal Björn offered everyone a cigar. I did not smoke, so instead I was treated to a banana split at a place a short distance away. There they were made with twelve scoops of ice cream, three bananas, accompanied by three cups of strawberries with whipped cream on top of it all. If anyone finished it, he got a second serving free. I finished my serving but declined the second. I had just eaten a large steak.

In those years an idea took root in me of running an ice cream parlor and ice cream factory, which later became reality with Ísborg on Austurstræti and ice cream production in Eskihlíð, as will be told later.
Sara Jane Donovan

In the fall of 1949 I acquired an Oldsmobile, model year 1946. This was a true luxury cruiser, as they said, four-door and with a dollar grille. Cars like this are nowadays seen nowhere except at vintage car shows and in mafia films. As mentioned before, I financed the car purchase by selling my splendid stamp collection and with a remittance from my mother out of her savings.

Sveinn Björnsson and I went skiing a good deal during our student years. The ski trips did not become fewer with the arrival of the car. Among other places, we went to Boine City in Lower Michigan and Porcupine Mountain in Upper Michigan. Most memorable of all, however, is the trip to the state of Colorado in December 1949. It was also the most fateful, for there I met my first wife, Sara Jane, who was called Dolly.

The ski trip was organized by the University of Chicago, which was not our school. Sveinn and Björn lived near it in the so-called International House. They therefore got to know various people from the University of Chicago, and several of them joined

joined us in the Oldsmobile, which was easily arranged since we were glad to share the cost of gasoline. A whole bus, on the other hand, went from the university itself. Dolly came with it. I was probably among the better skiers in the group, along with a Swiss fellow I skied with a great deal. The area was undergoing extensive development, and the slopes were exceptionally long and good.

I met Dolly on the slopes. She said she had noticed that I was a good skier. She herself did very well and moved beautifully. In the evenings there were festivities in the dormitory lodge where we stayed — a merry crowd, as one can well imagine. I found Dolly both attractive and fun. She was also spirited and determined. At the end of the trip she traveled with us back to Chicago.

Our acquaintance continued once we reached Chicago, and it grew closer the more often we met. She showed me her favorite places in the city; we went to good restaurants, saw films and lost track of time in heartfelt conversation. Dolly lived on her own, and in her apartment we had our own little haven. I quickly became very taken with her.

Dolly was a great athlete. Among other things she was good on skates, and we often went together to a skating rink in the city. Dolly devoted most of her free time to synchronized swimming, both training and competition. She pursued her sports and interests with an intensity that was almost excessive. I admired her drive.

Dolly had a fine figure, an elegant bearing and a lovely face. Her eyes were brown, and her dark hair usually hung loose to her shoulders. Her full name is Sara Jane Donovan, and she was the daughter of a dentist in Chicago. Her apartment was near the University of Chicago. Her father was Irish and her mother of Scottish and German-Jewish descent. Their marriage was not a happy one. The mother is said to have taken control of the household and the finances early on. They once separated from bed and board but got back together. The father had suffered two strokes and was a broken man, often heavy of spirit, and kept to himself.

Dolly is four years older than I. She was born in 1924 and was an only child for six years. Then a second daughter was born, Barbara, and later a third, Corky. Dolly felt she had been neglected and left out after their births. She soon fell out with her mother, and the two were constantly at odds.

Dolly began earning her own living at a young age. Among other things she performed water ballet, being a very good swimmer. For this reason she was constantly traveling the length and breadth of the United States. She said she had looked forward every winter to getting away from home, but looked forward just as much, as the summer wore on, to coming home again. Then she would hope that all would be well between her
and her mother. It never lasted long, though. That did not change as long as they both lived.

Dolly had to accomplish most things by her own strength and diligence. She paid for her education largely herself. She studied music at the university, despite being forbidden to play the piano at home. Her parents showed no interest in her studies or achievements. She blamed her mother for this and traced it to flaws in her character, which she tried to remedy by various means. Among other things, she tried to get her to see a psychologist.

Dolly is said to have taken her father's side early on, and for that she earned her mother's ill will. I naturally supported Dolly's cause myself. I believe this trouble between mother and daughter left deep marks on her personality. All of this was in fact quite clear to me soon after our acquaintance began, but it did not put me off. On the contrary, I felt great sympathy for Dolly, and still do, and I often dreamed that I might make up to her what she had missed in her childhood.

In the summer of 1949 Halla Guðmundsdóttir, who later became Halla Linker, and I were together. That summer I came home and worked at the sports grounds in Reykjavík. Halla and I had met while I was in secondary school. After Dolly and I became acquainted the following winter, I broke off that relationship. Shortly afterwards Halla met Hal Linker and married him. I was very fond of Halla, for she is a most excellent woman. I was, however, in love with Dolly and could not imagine marrying another woman. Halla and I have nevertheless become good friends, especially in later years.
Doctor or Not Doctor?

After I graduated from Illinois Tech, my excellent adviser and mentor pointed me toward four schools that would be promising for graduate study. They were MIT, Harvard, the University of Texas and Cal. Tech. I applied to these schools and was admitted to all four, since I had excellent grades in most subjects. MIT offered me an assistantship that would pay 1,400 dollars over the school year. Harvard and Texas offered me a 600-dollar scholarship, but Cal. Tech offered me a so-called "fellowship," which entailed no work obligation but a grant of 1,500 dollars. Offers as good as that were rarely seen. Not only was this a great deal of money, but the school, along with MIT, boasted probably the best engineering faculty in the United States — and indeed still does. Cal. Tech is considerably smaller, though. That school was my choice, and I never regretted it. This grant would not be considered large today, but the amount was equal to the tuition fees at
that time. For comparison, the tuition fees at Cal. Tech are now probably about 25,000 dollars a year.

Cal. Tech, or the California Institute of Technology, is in Pasadena, near Los Angeles. The school is in California, as the name suggests. I found it a good place to live. There was, however, one great drawback. The school lies in a mountain hollow. Occasionally cold air would settle over the hollow, and pollution would then accumulate because it could not rise. This produced a heavy haze of pollution, which the locals called "smog," consisting mainly of exhaust from cars. My parents once visited me in California, and I showed them the school on that occasion. My father was then with the United Nations in New York. We had no sooner arrived at the school than he begged me to get him away. His eyes had begun to water and his throat had become sore. Fortunately, pollution in that area has diminished since then.

Cal. Tech is a great scientific and research institution. There were about 4,000 professors, researchers and staff but only 1,500 students. It was a very wealthy school and still is. They had enormously large computers and well-equipped laboratories for every purpose. The computers of that era were so-called "analog" computers. They worked by simulating whatever was to be examined, for example the stresses on an airplane. First the electrical system was calculated and drawn up to imitate what was to be studied, and then the electrical network was connected with resistors, capacitors and so on down the line. By varying the electric current, one could read off the effects of stress on various parts of the machine. This was considered a tremendous advance, and these computers were no small pieces of work. One of the most powerful computers in the world was housed in one of the school's buildings. It filled a room the size of a detached house, with cabinets from floor to ceiling. That giant computer would be no match for a modern home computer.

At Cal. Tech an enormous amount of work was done for the aircraft industry in California. A special research institute was operated in this field, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Jet engines were developed there. It later became one of the principal research institutions for American space exploration and is often heard mentioned in connection with such missions.

A completely different spirit prevailed at Cal. Tech than at Illinois Tech. In graduate study, two students shared each office, and the professors had their offices on the same floor, so there was a great deal of interaction. The academic community was a community of equals. Students and teachers went out of the city together with packed lunches and had good times together. The studies were also utterly different and all the working methods more independent. It was taken for granted that we made use of all the facilities, handbooks
and reference materials to solve the problems we were given on exams. I liked this environment and could well have imagined staying there longer than I actually did.

I completed the master's degree from Cal. Tech in one year. Following that, I was offered the chance to begin doctoral studies on excellent scholarships. Doctoral studies did not appeal to me, since I considered them first and foremost preparation for teaching engineering at the university level. I intended to work as an engineer. If I had continued, I would in all likelihood have specialized in computers.

I was in fact awarded the equivalent of an honorary doctorate at Cal. Tech in 1986. Strictly speaking, they do not grant honorary doctorates. There was a special ceremony on the so-called Alumni Day, which is dedicated to former students of the school. The award was presented in a new, splendid assembly hall which the school had received as a gift from a wealthy old alumnus. The ceremony concluded with a dignified banquet. The award is called the California Institute of Technology Alumni Distinguished Service Award.

On this occasion the president of the school gave a speech and praised Iceland and Icelanders to the skies. Among other things, he made much of the fact that illiteracy among the nation's people was only 0.3 percent, whereas in fact it was up to 30 percent in the United States. I expressed my thanks with a few words about the school and the honor being shown to me. I added that it was doubtless correct that 0.3 percent of Icelanders were illiterate. I had to admit, however, that I had never met anyone from that group. This drew quite a bit of laughter.

In 1991 I received the so-called Professional Achievement award from Illinois Tech. I still cannot boast of a doctoral title, however. At one point I did seriously consider beginning doctoral studies, when I was offered the opportunity to earn a doctorate alongside exciting work at a computer company in the United States. But I could not imagine anything other than living in Iceland and therefore declined the offer. The reasons were as natural to me as existence itself. My upbringing and my familiarity with the country meant that nowhere did I feel better. I loved Iceland. My father had paid for my education because I was meant to acquire knowledge and bring it home to help build a better society. In Iceland a role awaited me.

I had also come up with many ideas that I wanted to put into practice. I had a great interest in harnessing waterfalls and in heavy industry, and I wanted to work for many kinds of industry, increased mechanization in the fishing industry, and new methods in construction technology, to name a few. I saw great possibilities in Iceland and wanted to take part in building a model society. This early on became an integral part of who I was.
It also seemed to me that most of the Icelanders I got to know in the United

States and had settled there were rootless men. I had hardly sat down during my visits with Árni Helgason, that delightful and excellent man, before he began talking about Iceland and Icelandic politics. His mind was very much bound to his home region.

I found the same rootlessness in Guðni Ívars. Gissur was perhaps the only exception. He married into a good family and got a good job. He became a pathologist at a very large hospital and was well regarded. Yet he too often had his mind on home. My stay in America changed nothing about the love of my native land in my heart. Iceland was where I belonged.
Words of Warning from My Father's House

Marriage first came up in conversation when I had known Dolly for half a winter, in the spring of 1950. I was then heading to Iceland for the summer, while Dolly intended to take part in a swimming exhibition tour of Europe lasting several months. She placed great emphasis on knowing my mind before we parted, and said she could not be sure of my love unless I proposed and led her to the altar that very summer. I was hesitant and suggested that she come to Iceland, since it would be good for her to become acquainted with conditions there and with my relatives. She then reacted angrily and rebuked me harshly for needing to seek my parents' approval of the match. In her eyes, such a thing was the greatest disgrace. We made no firm commitment to marry.

I went home that summer and corresponded with Dolly during her travels. I received numerous letters from her, sent variously from Zürich, Paris, or Rome. My thoughts dwelt very much on her during this time, and I was considered absent-minded and unlike myself. My friends wrote to me the following autumn and said they had seen that summer that I was very much in love. My parents also sensed how I felt inside. I discussed my feelings with my father, who later said in a letter that he understood fully, after our conversations that summer, that I was completely serious about marrying Dolly. He added: "I told you then and I say it still that I will not set myself against it. I have only one objection, that the girl is foreign, from a hot country, and I therefore fear that she will not be content here."

At the end of August I finally met Dolly in London. I still have the bill from the hotel confirming payment for two, Mr. and Mrs. Hermannsson. When we met, we felt as if we had grasped heaven in our hands. Before long, however, the friendship soured and Dolly broke off our relationship. She gave me no explanation for her change of heart. In old papers I have written that I consider it likely that the reason was chiefly that she thought I was dependent on

my parents' consent for our marriage. Later I came to the view that the break-up was connected to the fact that in London I told Dolly frankly that I could not imagine spending my life anywhere but in Iceland, and that a precondition of my entering into marriage was that she agree to move there with me.

When I leaf through old letters from my student years in the United States and the period when my acquaintance with Dolly began, I am surprised at how thoroughly my father and I discussed my prospective marriage. Much would probably have turned out differently if I had followed his advice. I cannot say that I regret how I arranged my life, but I certainly become pensive when I read these old letters.

The letters from my parents fill many folders. It was usually my father who held the pen, and his letters are sincere and warm. Naturally, many of them deal with my finances and how I am doing, my studies and my results. When I read these letters, my father appears to me as an unusually warm man with almost boundless care for his son. He sent me advice on whatever was on his mind; everything from a numbered list and instructions on the value of good sleep, a healthy diet, and a suitable amount of outdoor exercise, to reflections on the effect of academic performance on the future. When Dolly entered the picture, love became a subject dear to him.

My acquaintance with Dolly in the spring of 1950 gave my father occasion for considerable reflections on the value of marriage and the qualities of a good wife. My parents were unassuming people in emotional matters, rarely spoke of such things, and did not parade their feelings in public. I myself am not unlike them in this respect. My father says in a 20-page letter at the beginning of 1951:

We two, father and son, you and I, are perhaps somewhat reserved and not much given to speaking our whole mind. That is why your mamma says, laughing: – "You two, father and son, are fondest of each other when you are each in a different country."
My parents' first written remarks about my relationship with Dolly illustrate this well. The letter is from Pabbi:

Your mamma has (though she has not spoken of it) read between the lines that you were acquainted with a young girl called Dolly. – I wonder whether that has some influence on her wanting you to come home [this summer]. You have been your own master, my son; I
have trusted you. In these matters, however, each person must be his own master.
I do not doubt that my father meant every word about my having autonomy in these matters. Yet in the very next sentence of the letter his concern breaks through:

What your acquaintance is I do not know, and need not know until it well suits you. But watch your step carefully – what sort of people this girl comes from, etc. One sees the woman as she will become, if one sees her mamma and relatives, – usually. – No more about that.

These thoughts did not leave my father despite these words. He was never sparing with good advice and suggestions about my future. Yet he repeatedly stressed that in "matters of love" I would have to decide alone. Distance can be helpful for putting difficult thoughts into words. I was contemplating marriage and my father understood how serious I was. He sent me long letters about his views on love, marriage, the qualities of women, and the roles of the sexes.

I include these letters in this book not only to give a picture of my parents' attitude toward my prospective marriage. They also show my relationship with my father in a special light, besides revealing his opinions on matters that are seldom mentioned in memorials to departed political leaders. This side of my father has never appeared anywhere else:

I now see nothing that you lack, except perhaps to be free of puzzling over what you should do regarding this woman. Naturally these girls press on, wanting to secure a husband whom they believe to be promising material, – and to have it without delay, which no one knows where it leads. In this matter it is hard to decide and nearly as difficult to advise. One thing is certain, that you can of course pick from the girls here at home – when you come here. But perhaps this girl is the one who would suit you and whom you would hold dear in the long run. The relationship between man and woman is at a young age most often based on what they call love – and perhaps it is. But most of the content of this "eternal" love is sexual. Naturally that element (the sexuality) must be satisfied in healthy people, even though excess in it is worse than drunkenness and enervating both mentally and physically. But when all is said and done, when the kernel is separated from the chaff in

the experience and toil of life, then the person in one's traveling companion (the spouse) is put to the test, and then new bonds form which grow stronger with the years, – while the earlier ones fade into the shadows. – Or else the other outcome, that when the "young love" breaks, no new bonds form, and then aversion arises and the whole relationship breaks apart.

So numerous were my father's words about love. He by no means believed, however, that the message would reach me, for there the heart held sway. "The truth is, my son, that however sensible the advice given to you and any other young man or woman in this matter, – it is meaningless. Here – I know it – feelings rule, not deliberation."
The continuation of the letter was nevertheless devoted to describing the ideal wife.

One does not think about it in young love: whether the woman is clean, good-tempered, upright, cooks good food and is domestic, not prone to nagging, presents herself well and intelligently, is persevering, thrifty, does not think all too much about herself, etc. etc. As the years pass, one fault, let alone several, can smother the passionate bond of the first years. For you this is much more worth pondering than you imagine. You are used to everything being in order at home, whatever name it may go by, without there being any need to speak of it. That is why you take it for granted.

The letter then describes how this is by no means the state of affairs in all homes, and that one can best see how the woman will turn out in these respects by looking to her parents and relatives, though nothing is certain in those matters. The discourse concludes with sound advice that if I married Dolly I should not give her false hopes of wealth and prosperity, "and let her know that the door there is closed if she cannot live in Iceland."
It is as if his closing words on these matters were a prophecy:
Naturally she agrees to it cheerfully at home and means it, because she feels it, that she will gladly live here, – but then life comes with sunshine and showers, and then it can change.
And change it did, with a vengeance.
My father hesitated to send me these writings of his, so unlike were they to his other letters and thoughts. He says himself that he was astonished when

he read it over two days after it was put on paper. "But it is not so foolish and I will let it go," he adds. He says he had just come from my mother's birthday coffee gathering, had looked over the crowd of women, and seen how varied the wifely qualities of her guests had been.
The Athletic Feats of the Century

After the break-up between Dolly and me, I went from London to Brussels, where I was a reporter for Tíminn at the famous European Championships in track and field. There the Icelandic competitors performed better than at any time before or since in the nation's sporting history. Gunnar Huseby became European champion in the shot put and Torfi Bryngeirsson won the long jump. Örn Clausen came second in the decathlon and Haukur fifth in the 100-meter dash. In fact, Haukur was not allowed to compete in his best event, the 200-meter dash, because of some incomprehensible cronyism in the Icelandic sports movement. It can be considered certain that he would have reached the medal podium if he had been allowed to compete.

A similar story can be told of the results in the decathlon. Before the meet, the French demanded that the newly approved scoring table not be used to assess the competitors' performances, but rather an older and obsolete version. They got their way. As a result, Örn was judged second behind the French competitor. The absurdity was most evident in the fact that both of them set national records at the meet, but Örn's performance was reckoned the better one, since where records were concerned the rules in force were naturally followed. Power struggles and rivalry thus cast a shadow over the true champions in more places than the Icelandic sports movement, and perhaps still do. Iceland's other competitors also did well, and it was fun to be an Icelander in those days.

The entire national team counted among my acquaintances, since I had stayed with the group during training at Laugarvatn earlier that summer. Throughout my secondary school years I had also followed the Clausen brothers to their athletic meets and taken pictures. I have many hundreds of photographs of them and other track-and-field athletes from those years. Many of them are, in fact, very good.

Discipline in sports was not as strict as it is now. After the competition in Brussels we explored the city's nightlife and enjoyed ourselves thoroughly. On the last evening, however, we took it easy, since a train journey to Copenhagen was planned for the morning, and from there the route continued on to Oslo. When it was time to turn in, it so happened that Gunnar Huseby was nowhere to be found. We therefore searched for him and combed nearly every dive in the city without success. But when the train had begun inching along the rails the next morning, Gunnar came running and made it aboard with
by the narrowest of margins. He would not say where he had been, and we had to content ourselves with guessing. He received a rather frosty reception from Benedikt Jakobsson, the coach.

In Copenhagen I parted from the group for two days. I wanted to see the city. Getting a hotel proved difficult. I therefore went into an airline office on the Town Hall Square and deployed my best secondary-school Danish to get a girl at the counter to find me a hotel. She picked up the telephone, called many hotels, and asked for a room for a young Icelander. Everywhere the answer was that they were fully booked. Then I walked straight across the hall and asked another girl for the same thing, but now in English with an American accent. She called one of the hotels that had refused and asked for a room for a young American. That was readily granted. When I left the hotel two days later, doormen and porters stood in a row in the lobby, obviously expecting a large tip from the rich American. They were disappointed, for he marched straight past. For many years afterward I regularly spoke English in Copenhagen.

The English came back to haunt me, however, when I got to the railway station. There I wanted to buy a ticket to Oslo, but the girl at the counter insisted that I pay for it in dollars. When I said I was an Icelander, she wanted me to show a receipt proving that I had bought the currency at a bank. That I could not do, and I missed the train. Since I could not afford a plane ticket, I went to the embassy and took out a loan there for the airfare.

In Oslo I met the track-and-field team again. The group had by then competed at the Bislett stadium and repeated their splendid results. The Icelandic team was received like heroes in Norway. In the evening we went out on the town as usual. When we arrived at the nightspot Regnbuen there was a great crush outside. I managed to push my way to the doors and told the doormen that some Icelandic track-and-field athletes had arrived. The doors opened instantly and we were let straight in. There we enjoyed ourselves amid noise and merriment. Around midnight, Ásmundur Bjarnason and I offered to escort two ladies home. The offer was accepted. When we had walked some distance, we began to have second thoughts. They lived far away, and we could not bring ourselves to spring for a taxi. In the park by the royal palace we said we needed to slip behind a tree, and then we ran off from there as fast as our legs could carry us.

When we got back to the hotel, everything was in an uproar. Huseby had been arrested. He had made his way to one of the worst taverns in Oslo and got no peace there from Norwegians who wanted to take him on
