their strength. In the end it all descended into a brawl, and reportedly few chairs remained intact after that commotion. It was said that Huseby had thrown all the other guests out the door before it was over. When the police arrived he was still in fighting spirits, and four burly police officers had their hands full restraining him. Benedikt Jakobsson and I went to the police station and got Gunnar released. We had to promise that he would not be let out again. If that happened, he would be our responsibility.

I flew home from Oslo, but the Clausen brothers continued on a competition tour of Sweden. On it, Haukur Clausen demonstrated, among other things, his strength in the 200-meter dash, set a Nordic record that stood for seven years, and achieved the best time of the year in Europe. He ran it in 21.3 seconds, and that performance would of course have secured him the European championship title a week earlier.
Marriage and Heartbreak

I went to Chicago in the autumn as had been planned. I did not see Dolly for the next two months. I did not do as well as I was accustomed to in my exams despite careful preparation, and in letters to my father I attributed it to bad luck. He continued to write about my prospective marriage, and I answered something or other. I refrained from telling him everything about how matters stood between us. That could wait.

My schoolmates and I had moved into the house on Euclid Street. I lived in a decent room in the basement, and I had nearly given up hope of seeing Dolly again. The odds seemed to me to shrink with every passing day. One evening, as I was about to turn in for the night in my room, I found her there. She had crawled in through the window. I never learned what caused this turnabout. Nor did I ask.

Everything seemed to me to fall into place after I regained my love. I understood the reason why I had not been myself that autumn and had done poorly in the exams. I also feared that my hesitation about marriage had sown doubts in Dolly's mind. All hesitation vanished from my mind at our reunion, and the romance blossomed. We lived together as man and wife.

We decided to marry on December 16. She was Catholic and wanted to have the ceremony according to her tradition. I agreed to that. The preparations were considerable, since her parents wanted the celebration to be lavish. I got Runólfur to be my best man. With a week to go, everything was ready. I felt as probably most bridegrooms have before and since, alternating between anticipation and anxiety. It seemed to me that the greatest moment of happiness of my life was

in the offing. Then the world collapsed. Dolly announced without preamble that she had changed her mind, she did not want to marry me, and broke off our engagement. I sent word home that the wedding was cancelled.

I saw little or nothing of Dolly that Christmas. At first it was as if I did not fully grasp what had happened. I said little and felt exposed and utterly defenseless. I waited to wake up from this nightmare. Then the blow descended on me with full force. I was stuck in pitch-black quicksand and felt that all my attempts to struggle free only sank me deeper. When two weeks had passed I could no longer bear my grief in silence. I wrote to my parents with the whole story and everything about my feelings. I felt I was alone in a deep darkness from which there was no way out. I had been rejected before everyone's eyes.

I do not know how I would have fared had I not had the support and encouragement of my father. He sat at his desk up in Iceland late into the night, until three and four o'clock, evening after evening for two weeks, instilling courage and comfort in me; he wrote long and loving letters, searched for words of consolation, drew from the well of his own life experience and my mother's. He told me of his youthful love in Akureyri who left him for another man. He described his despair and loneliness in a dark little room on Lækjargata in Reykjavík, without an overcoat in the great frost winter, when he took to his bed from grief and sorrow. This strong man told of his weeping and his despair. He told me more about himself than he ever thought he would; he "dug up what had been buried." I knew that I did not stand alone. My father's feelings are best conveyed by an excerpt from a letter of his own:

I dreamt of you on Christmas night, and we were out in a snowstorm up in the mountains; we were in grave danger but somehow we scraped through. It will now prove true that when the wind blows and the snow drives, we will stand together — and not least then.

Dolly's parents showed me great sympathy while this was going on. Her father was ordinarily a man of few words. But this time he was not merely saddened by his daughter's behavior. He became furious. It was the only time I saw him lose his temper. Dolly's mother and sisters were dumbfounded. This was a tremendous disappointment to everyone. On one occasion during this period I was a guest in their home. Dolly's father broke the silence and remarked out of the blue that in all likelihood I need not mourn the end of the relationship. He said he had never understood his daughter. She frequently made decisions that noelse
would ever think of, without the slightest regard for others. I took this as conventional words of comfort.

Dolly and I got back together shortly after the new year. A little later we decided once again to marry. The new date was March 24, 1951. My father said he was happy if I was happy. Dolly's parents threw us a big party. The ceremony was in the Catholic manner, attended by a sizable gathering. These were chiefly friends and acquaintances of Dolly and her family. The Icelanders in Chicago attended, of course, but my parents and other friends in Iceland could not get away from home. On our wedding night we stayed in the bridal suite of Chicago's finest hotel, the Palmer House.

We moved into my basement room, as final examinations were close at hand. Dolly continued working at an office. My father said he was delighted with the photographs from the wedding; Dolly and her family seemed to be the finest people. "Dolly has an exceptionally kind smile," he said, and it was true. I wrote that we were doing well. The honeymoon was short-lived, however. Only a week passed before Dolly informed me that she was determined to divorce. I was naturally shaken, though I had begun to learn that she was capable of anything. She was hardly willing to discuss her decision. I have noted on some old papers that her chief criticism was that I came to bed too late. My examinations were then close at hand and I was studying with great intensity. The divorce did not happen. Dolly was expecting a child.

Living together with the other Icelanders proved difficult for Dolly. She was very critical of our housekeeping, found the food bad and different from what she was used to. She therefore often ate by herself. She showed her displeasure through silence. I often had to steer between rock and wave in dealings with the other residents of the house and try to make peace when things boiled over.

Dolly got to know the Icelanders quite well as time went on. In particular, she and Lulla, Valur's wife, became good friends. I believe they kept up their friendship for a long time. Dolly, however, learned no Icelandic and never tried.
Home Life and the Journey Home

In June we moved to Pittsburgh, and that trip may be said to have been a kind of honeymoon. Over the summer I worked at the great Westinghouse corporation, where I studied the company's production systems and its investment policy. It manufactured generators and transformers and in general everything relating to electricity. Westinghouse was the second-largest electric power company in the United-
States and consequently of the world, and it manufactured a considerable share of the electrical goods purchased for Iceland.

This was a romantic time, and I became convinced that the sorrows were behind us. We lived on the upper floor of an old woman's small house. The house stood beautifully on a hill. The surroundings were delightful, and we enjoyed ourselves especially when it rained. Lightning would then strike all around the house, and candles were our only light. The louder the weather grew, the more tightly we wrapped ourselves around each other. From that summer stay I have many of my best memories of the marriage.

In the autumn we went to Pasadena, California, where I enrolled at Cal. Tech. The journey was delightful and love blossomed. We drove through Iowa and the Badlands of Dakota, where one can see the portraits of past American presidents carved into Mount Rushmore. We drove through Yellowstone National Park, Salt Lake City, and the Yosemite Valley, which is one of the most beautiful national parks in the world. From there we drove straight on to Pasadena. This was my first trip across the United States. The autumn weather was beautiful, and the colors of the landscape took on a fiery red hue. Dolly was far along with our first child. We were blissfully happy with life and existence.

A boy was born to us on October 23 that autumn, 1951. He was christened John Bryan, and I often called him Jón or Nonni. As the birth approached, Dolly threatened divorce three or four times and said she wanted to give the expected child away. She began criticizing Iceland and most things Icelandic. Few things wounded me more. I tried nonetheless to keep the peace and answered only with reserve and silence.

Dolly was mostly with the child while I attended to my studies as best I could. I was determined that the marriage and the child should not harm my studies, as my father had warned could happen. These months became very difficult. It irritated Dolly that I had to study a great deal, and she found fault with me in almost everything. She soon wanted to set about remedying these defects and obtained a great number of books on the relationship between man and wife, which I was to read and learn. She also consulted various specialists on personal matters and counseling. It seemed to me that she was raising a wall between us that I was expected to climb in order to show and prove my love and my worth.

At Christmas there was a break from studying. I then went skiing near Salt Lake City with two of my schoolmates. We took our car, the good Oldsmobile, against Dolly's wishes. On the way we hit ice and had a violent collision. The car was destroyed, and one of my companions was badly cut in the face. This affected me deeply. From Dolly, however, there was no comfort to be had. Instead she reminded me that I had gone against her wishes, and for the next
two years she brought up this example to anyone who would listen, as proof that she was generally right and I was not, and as an example of my shortcomings.

I finished my exams at the end of May 1952. The graduation ceremony, however, was not until June 8. In the meantime we went on a three-day ski and fishing trip in the Sierra Nevada. After the diplomas had been handed out, we drove from Pasadena in a Buick automobile we had recently bought. The insurance on the wrecked car paid for it. We drove north along the entire west coast of the United States. The coastal road is very beautiful, one of the most beautiful roads I have ever driven. It runs to San Francisco and through the enormously vast redwood forests. From the coastal road we then drove along the Canadian border to Chicago.

The trip took ten days. We often slept outdoors, but little Jón slept in the car. He was seven months old at the time. It was both a peaceful and a romantic journey. Once I awoke to the sense that something was snuffling around me. I was startled, because this was in an area where there were black bears. I was lucky — it was a deer. Another night I was greatly tormented by swarms of midges. I hit upon the plan of trying to cover myself completely with the sleeping bag and stuck straws in my nose to breathe through. That went rather badly.

In Chicago we visited my parents-in-law and stayed with them for about a week. They received us wonderfully, overjoyed at the new descendant. Dolly and her mother soon clashed, because her mother criticized her handling of the child. I did not get involved in those disputes. We drove to New York in two days, arriving there at the end of June. We had passage booked to Iceland by ship on July 3.

Then the thunderbolt struck. I can still see every circumstance before me. We were coming out of a grocery store the day before our planned departure. It was as if Dolly made her decision right there on the sidewalk where she stood. She suddenly announced to me that she was not going to Iceland. She said that I should go and take the child with me. I was utterly stunned. I canceled the ship passage, and for two days I begged Dolly in tears to come. She would not be moved. I gave up and bought tickets on the next flight.

When the airplane lifted off, I sat alone with our boy in my arms. I declined the meal and closed my eyes. Jón had settled down before long, but I had trouble falling asleep. The time I had had with Dolly ran like a film through my mind. Again and again a trivial incident from the early days of our relationship kept coming back to me. When Dolly and I met, she had been half-engaged to a man who was studying psychology at the University of Chicago. They had known each other a long time. Once I ran into this man, and he

took me aside for a talk. He informed me that I should not even dream that a marriage to Dolly would be a happy one. He said Dolly was a very unusual girl, unbalanced and given to extremes. She would never stop until she got her way unless she was handled with special skill and know-how. It seemed to me he was implying that only he was capable of such a thing, and so I paid little heed to his words. I have often thought back on them since.
Dolly took the first plane back to Chicago. We left the car with Daði Hjörvar, my old friend, who was then at the United Nations in New York as a correspondent.

This was the first serious crack in our marriage. In the months that followed, my faith in the relationship began to fail and my trust in Dolly waned. I doubted her willingness and ability to live in Iceland. Nothing had ever been discussed other than that Iceland would be our home. For the first time I contemplated that the marriage might have been a mistake. Nevertheless, I pleaded persistently with her to come with me to Iceland, not only for the sake of the marriage and the boy but no less for my own sake. I loved this woman.

Three or four years later I found among Dolly's things a written explanation of the decision in New York on that memorable day. No doubt it had been put down on paper for one of the counselors or the psychologist she was constantly seeing. She wrote that immediately after my examination we had been forced to hurry to Chicago. The trip had taken four days. There we had stayed with her parents for only three or four days and then rushed off to New York. I had been in such a hurry to get to Iceland that it was obvious she was a complete afterthought in my eyes. Iceland was what mattered most to me, and it was my parents' fault, because they were constantly trying to draw me home by writing to me far too often. The dates of my examinations, the graduation, and our scheduled ship passage show that her story was self-deception, but it did me no good to point that out. Dolly was satisfied with her explanation and stuck to it firmly.
Chapter Six
YEARS OF ENTERPRISE IN ICELAND

The homecoming to Iceland in July 1952 was a dreary one. I moved right away, together with my son Jón, in with my parents on Tjarnargata. I soon got a job with the Reykjavík Electric Utility (Rafmagnsveitur Reykjavíkur), while my mother took on the care of the child. Jón thrived under her loving care. She was like a mother to him, and they grew very attached to each other.

I met with genuine sympathy from my family. However, I decided not to tell the whole story. It did not seem timely to me while I still held on to hope. In my heart I hoped that Dolly would change her mind, and I kept that idea alive among my friends and acquaintances. Deep down, however, reason told me that the marriage was over. At first I found it hard to come to terms with that thought. Had I made the wrong decision in defiance of my father's words of warning? I did not feel that had been fully put to the test. As time passed, though, the hope gradually died out within me. I kept the disappointment to myself. In hindsight I believe my parents knew all along how matters stood, even though few words were spoken about it.

A few letters passed between Dolly and me that autumn. She said she missed the child and me and said she was grateful to my mother for her care. My mother-in-law also wrote to me and described the shock the family had suffered at the daughter's homecoming. Nothing in these letters hinted that she was changing her mind. I was therefore surprised and glad when Dolly announced without preamble that she was on her way. She wrote that she had bought passage on a ship and wanted to live with us in Iceland. This was in October. By then we had been separated for nearly four months.
The time Dolly had spent alone in Chicago proved harder for her than she had expected. That was always the case. Her parents had received her badly
and she was not allowed to live with them. So she rented a room in a boardinghouse and worked in an office.

Dolly came to Iceland on the Tröllafoss on November 17, 1952. I had hastily obtained Grandmother Margrét's apartment in my parents' house. My friends were called out to paint everything from top to bottom. I intended to reward them for the favor with a bottle of vodka. It was, however, opened too soon. We did not realize how badly alcohol mixes with lacquer paint, and some got sick. The next day the unpainted areas were almost larger than the painted ones, and lines that were supposed to be straight were without exception crooked. The whole crew was called out again — and without alcohol this time.

At first Dolly seemed to like it quite well. That lasted a week. Then discontent began to show. Few people spoke English to her satisfaction, she found the weather impossible, and there was nothing to do. To my friends she seemed cold and indifferent toward them, and that was probably true. She said her greatest dream was to have a daughter. In Iceland, though, that could not happen, because everything here was primitive. Her discontent grew day by day, and she became ever more determined that we should move to the United States.
Reykjavík, electricity, and fertilizer

Reykjavík was a small town. It had one good hotel and restaurant, Hótel Borg. The National Theatre (Þjóðleikhúsið) was still under repair after the occupation, and Iðnó was in effect the only theater. The cinemas were the main pastime. There were three of them, and each showed one film per evening. There were no community centers, and discussions of national affairs took place at the kitchen tables of homes and on street corners, while the old swimming pools were also a popular gathering place. Swimmers also frequented the Sundhöll indoor pool, and Melavöllur field was the center of football and track and field, which were flourishing.

In the evenings, young and unattached people could be seen walking the rúntur — the town circuit — round after round, whenever the weather gods granted a respite from rain and wind. Young men strutted about proudly with romance on their minds, and beautiful girls floated by in the bloom of youth. More often than not one could see badly drunken men, who regularly ended their evening's entertainment in the basement cells of the police. Little in this social scene was likely to charm a woman of the world.

After I came to Iceland in the summer of 1952, I soon began working for the Reykjavík Electric Utility (Rafmagnsveitur Reykjavíkur) and worked at the Elliðaár power station under the direction of the late Ingólfur Ágústsson, engineer and station manager. He was a very fine man. I was engaged in various calculations and studies. Among other things, I examined the feasibility of transmitting electricity by submarine cable from Iceland to

Scotland. When my son Hermann, who is also an electrical engineer, was studying some 30 years later, he worked for the National Power Company (Landsvirkjun) in the summers. One of his projects then was to make comparable calculations on the feasibility of selling electricity via submarine cable. I quickly came to the conclusion in 1952 that far too much energy would be lost along the way and the operation would be too expensive. Technology has advanced by leaps and bounds since then, and I understand that, given certain assumptions, such energy exports can now be considered.

I was with the Electric Utility only a short time. In the spring of 1953 I was offered the position of electrical engineer at the Fertilizer Plant (Áburðarverksmiðjan). My friend Runólfur Þórðarson had come home from the United States ahead of me and had become the plant's chemical engineer. My father and Runólfur's father had become good friends on account of their sons' stays in the United States. They were in constant contact with each other and consulted about our affairs. My father kept his eyes open for job opportunities for Runólfur, and the Fertilizer Plant project had some influence on Runólfur's specialization in his graduate studies. It was tailor-made for the plant's needs. I decided to join the team and did not regret it. The plant was under construction and there was tremendous enthusiasm in the group.

Under my direction worked some 16 electricians and assistants. This was a hand-picked crew, and many of them became my friends for life. Everything was done in group cooperation, where each treated the other as an equal. Among these men were Ragnar Stefánsson, who later became the plant's chief electrician, Auðunn Bergsveinsson, Haraldur Steingrímsson, Kjartan Guðmundsson, Óskar Hallgrímsson, Páll J. Pálsson, Sigurður Leifsson, and many more. We installed all the electrical wiring in the plant and built the entire electrical system. I myself enjoyed this greatly. In this project my dream of combining engineering with working with my hands came true.

As so often happens, we worked in a race against time. Often we did not know in the morning how late into the evening we would be working, but the final deadline had long been set. It worked out that we finished our part of the job at eleven o'clock on the appointed evening. We switched on the current to the system and threw a great party. To split water in the plant, alternating current has to be converted to direct current. For this there were special rectifiers from the Oerlikon company in Switzerland. The instructions said they should be cleaned with pure ethyl alcohol, otherwise known as spirits. So I went to the State Alcohol and Tobacco Monopoly (ÁTVR) with these papers and bought enough cleaning fluid for the rectifiers — several liters. I locked the alcohol in a cabinet so there would be no shrinkage of the supply.
The Oerlikon inspector arrived shortly afterward. He declared this long obsolete. Generally other cleaning agents were used. So people rushed off and new agents

bought, but the other part — returning it — was forgotten. When the current was switched on, however, our stock of alcohol came back to mind. It naturally followed that Runólfur was entrusted with mixing the drinks, being a chemical engineer by training. He mixed the party punch diligently. When the celebration ended around three o'clock, most people were reeling. Yet only a fraction of the spirits had been used up. It was presumably brought out later when there was a big occasion.

The work at the Fertilizer Plant (Áburðarverksmiðjan) was very rewarding, and there prevailed one of the most enjoyable working spirits I have ever known. The plant manager was American, named Van Ness. He was the superior of Runólfur and me. He was a capable man and a good manager. The organization was exemplary; meetings and plans were first-class. This period proved most valuable to me. I learned a great deal about good working methods and supervision that has served me well ever since.

The Fertilizer Plant was built with part of the Marshall aid that Icelanders received. The Marshall aid was unquestionably one of the most sensible policies the Americans have ever pursued in foreign affairs. Through economic assistance to Europe, the continent's economy was set moving in a big way after the destruction of the war. It is debatable, however, whether we should have been among the recipients, for financially we had profited enormously from the war. Perhaps one could say that we slipped in through the back door. We squandered the war profits in two years and ended up just as broke as before. There is no doubt that the Marshall aid helped us greatly in making up for those mistakes and in putting the country's economy on a firmer footing.

At some point I heard it said that Vilhjálmur Þór, director of the Federation of Icelandic Cooperatives (Sambandið), had come up with the idea that the Marshall money should go toward building the Fertilizer Plant. It is certain that he worked hard to secure funding for the project. He was chairman of the building committee and later of the plant's board for quite a long time. Progressives (Framsóknarmenn) and farmers had long dreamed of building a fertilizer plant, and my father had entrusted his friend Sigurður Jónasson with investigating the matter as early as 1934. A year later he introduced a bill on the matter in the Althing (Alþingi). Many more became involved in the matter over the next 15 years, among them Vilhjálmur Þór when he was Minister of Industry 1942–44. It is safe to say that things would have been very difficult if the Marshall money had not been obtained.
Working for Vilhjálmur Þór and SÍS

I was full of ideas and considered myself equal to almost anything in those years. I soon found in Vilhjálmur Þór a man who listened to much of what interested me with greater attention than most other men. Among these ideas were great dreams of harnessing the rivers and of heavy industry.

Vilhjálmur Þór was exceptionally inventive and one of the greatest men of action I have ever known. A more far-sighted man was hard to find. Under his leadership the Federation (Sambandið) grew and extended its operations into far more fields than before. Most of the enterprises that created its empire were founded during his tenure as director.

Vilhjálmur Þór was tall and always impeccably dressed, often with a hat on his head and a coat over his arm. He was decisive and commanding, quick to answer, and went about his work methodically. Vilhjálmur was quick to reach a conclusion in every matter. That quality I greatly appreciated.

When Vilhjálmur walked through the halls of the Federation, it was remarked that he seldom greeted anyone. He made little effort to be a man of the people. He summoned employees to meetings through the Federation's internal intercom system and habitually addressed them in the imperative. Without exception, the employee in question arrived panting and out of breath at his office a very short time later. Vilhjálmur was not kept waiting. At the Federation he was a legend in his own lifetime. At twenty-three he had worked his way up from the job of errand boy and become director of KEA, which he raised up out of great difficulties. KEA has been one of the most powerful cooperative societies in the country ever since.

Vilhjálmur Þór had good connections abroad. I made several trips overseas at his initiative. In April 1953 he sent me to Germany to explore the possibilities of establishing new industries in Iceland. I recorded my findings in a special travel journal. The survey was divided into several categories. First, I looked into the production of electrical sockets, switches, wood-chip boards, and other things that could be manufactured from waste materials by using plastic binders. I also investigated the production of salt, glass wool, and rock wool, in addition to establishing trade connections. I visited dozens of companies all over Germany, and one agreement I concluded during the trip itself. I made a deal with two East Germans to move to Iceland and manufacture there electric motors for hay-drying ventilation, which at that time were very hard to obtain. This was the first special assignment entrusted to me and the first agreements I made with foreign parties.
On the trip I traveled through the Ruhr districts. The marks of the war's enormous destruction could still be seen there. Eight years after the end of the war, whole neighborhoods

still in ruins, and smoke rose here and there from dwellings where people huddled by open fires in cellars. In my travel journal I mention Düsseldorf especially in this connection. On the other hand, it seemed to me that the shops had a good selection of goods: "The Germans seem to have everything," I noted down. The impressions that stayed with me most strongly came from going from West Berlin to the eastern sector. On the western side there was hustle and bustle, but in the eastern part little could be heard except my own footsteps on the paving stones. I ate lunch at a restaurant, and even there an oppressive silence reigned. Yet this was nearly ten years before the building of the Berlin Wall.

I met the two East Germans at their run-down workshop. I managed to convince them of the advantages of moving to Iceland with their families and starting production under the auspices of the Federation (Sambandið). And so it came about. On the same trip I also went to Oerlikon, a large company in Switzerland which, among other things, had sold the rectifiers for the Fertilizer Plant, as mentioned earlier. Through that company, Swiss Aluminium became interested in Iceland. Dolly was with me on this trip. At the end of it we went skiing in Austria for a few days. As ill luck would have it, she broke her leg on one of the first days, and so I skied the slopes alone from morning to evening for the rest of the trip.
Politics in a Cold War

After the construction of the Fertilizer Plant I stayed on there for a few months, but when the works were completed there was no need for a full-time electrical engineer. I therefore continued only as a consulting engineer and took up a position with the defense division of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs (utanríkisráðuneytið).

Dr. Kristinn Guðmundsson, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, appointed me his engineering adviser on construction at Keflavík Airport at the beginning of 1954. I also took a seat on the Defense Affairs Committee (varnarmálanefnd), which in fact received a new name the very day I was appointed: the Foreign Ministry's Liaison Committee with the Defense Force. The old name was soon taken up again, however. Six months earlier, my father had appointed me to take part in electric-power negotiations with the Defense Force together with the Defense Affairs Committee on behalf of the Ministry of Industry. I therefore had fairly good insight into the tasks that awaited me.

Kristinn was a Progressive but did not hold a seat in Parliament. He became a minister when the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) renewed their three-year-old coalition in 1953. Ólafur Thors then took over the premiership from Steingrímur Steinþórsson, but my father remained outside the government despite being chairman of the Progressive Party. Ólafur had in fact strongly urged that my father become Minister for Foreign Affairs, but my father is said to have remarked at a meeting in

the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) that he "considered it an insult to himself personally and to the party to expect" him to take "over half of Bjarni Benediktsson's ministerial office." Bjarni had been both Minister for Foreign Affairs and Minister of Justice in the outgoing government. The Independence Party men relinquished the foreign affairs portfolio but not the justice portfolio, because Bjarni had been harshly criticized for his handling of it. They felt they would be conceding the validity of that criticism if they handed the justice portfolio over to others. My father therefore chose to seek a man from outside the ranks of the members of parliament, and the choice fell on Kristinn, who at the time held the office of tax director in Akureyri. They had been close friends ever since the days when they confided their heartaches to each other and studied together for the matriculation examination in Reykjavík. Kristinn had in fact also been a schoolmate of my father's in Akureyri.

Kristinn held a doctorate from Germany and taught in the north. He was a man of large build and early on turned handsomely gray-haired. He was quiet, deeply thoughtful, and a formidable linguist, but some thought he went about things rather too slowly. I very much enjoyed working under his direction.

At the ministry, difficult tasks awaited Kristinn. Relations with the United States and coexistence with the military were not free of setbacks in those years. The Defense Force pressed hard for permission to expand its activities in the country, among other things by building an airfield at Rangárvellir. On the other hand, support for the military presence was waning, and the Progressive Party's following shrank because little difference could be discerned between its policy and that of the Independence Party. The Progressives therefore turned their attention ever more to the problems of coexistence between Icelanders and the military, about which many party members had serious concerns. They held that the base needed to be isolated, that American workers should be sent home, and that Icelanders ought to take over their jobs. A negotiating committee was established in February 1954, on which my father sat among others, together with Kristinn, the Minister for Foreign Affairs. After a three-month round of negotiations, the Americans agreed to fence off certain areas of the Keflavík base, to have Icelandic contractors take over from the American ones, and to build a new air terminal at Keflavík. In connection with these talks it fell to me to carry out an assessment of the possibilities of selling electric power to the military, and together with four other staff members I also prepared a report on "An Examination of the Possibilities of Icelanders Taking Over All Construction Work for the Defense Force." Both were done at the start of the talks at the beginning of 1954. I also attended several meetings of the negotiating committees as an adviser.

As spring wore on, it became clear that there seemed to be difficulties in getting the Americans to give clear answers about carrying out works on the basis of the agreement from March. They did not give way until representatives of the government, among them my father, had hinted that the defense agreement would be terminated otherwise.

The Minister for Foreign Affairs announced the conclusion of the negotiations at the end of May. The truth, however, was that numerous meetings were held over the summer to untie various knots and finalize the agreement once and for all. Among other things, I still have minutes of meetings at which Tómas Árnason, Hörður Bjarnason, Thor Thors, and I sat in negotiating sessions with sixteen representatives of the United States government, military officers, and special negotiators.

There was little peace in which to discuss the affairs of the Defense Force calmly in those years. While the negotiations were under way, the newspapers hammered away at the issue, each in its own fashion. People's worries about coexistence with the military could doubtless be traced in part to these writings. Drunken American workers in the city's taverns fed people's prejudices in this regard. In 1952, tall tales of the soldiers' fornication and moral corruption had reached previously unknown heights. At that time, the papers that had been most assiduous in keeping the nation informed about the debauchery and swinishness of the Defense Force reported that soldiers had given Icelandic girls aphrodisiacs, with the result that the girls tore off every stitch of clothing in public. Mánudagsblaðið, Þjóðviljinn, and Tíminn carried reports of similar striptease incidents in Vestmannaeyjar, and Þjóðviljinn did not spare the ink on its front-page headline that day. A special investigation is said to have been carried out into the incident. Morgunblaðið reported that the stockings of the girl in question had torn as she climbed up a hill with a soldier to get a view of a football match. Þjóðviljinn, however, stuck stubbornly to its assertions about the notorious "sex poison," while Morgunblaðið called this "the lust-pill affair." In a cold war, every trick is employed.
Engineering for the Defense Force

At the defense division I was the liaison between the military's engineering department and the Icelandic authorities. At that time it was first and foremost American contractors who worked for the Defense Force. Various things had to be worked out, and the construction had to be monitored. I went to Keflavík twice a week and sat in meetings with the engineering department. In between, I worked at the defense division in Reykjavík. This was in many ways an instructive job. I got to know the Americans quite well, both soldiers and contractors.

The presence of the American contractors in the country sat differently with different people. They were not under military discipline and were apt to enjoy themselves rather boisterously in the city's restaurants, even though the soldiers' behavior had been brought under control. Some said the workers were brawlers from the worst neighborhoods of the big American cities. I do not know whether that was true, but there was a certain amount of brawling

at Hótel Borg and elsewhere. The government considered it necessary to deal with this matter. My work was directed not least at that part of the agreements with the Defense Force which concerned Icelanders taking over construction work for the military. In the wake of these agreements, Icelandic Prime Contractors (Íslenskir aðalverktakar) was founded — or the Association of Icelandic Contractors (Samband íslenskra verktaka), as the company was called at first. I made quite a few trips to the United States as an adviser in these negotiations.

It has often been criticized that a single company was established with an exclusive right to construction work for the military. Two considerations are said to have guided the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) in that matter. Both appear in the memoirs of Eysteinn Jónsson. There he says the aim was to "prevent an unnatural and tiresome internal competition among Icelanders for the contracts, which would give the Americans increased influence, a strong position to dispense sunshine and rain, which could bring many hazards in its train." The other point was to safeguard the interests of the Cooperative Movement (Samvinnuhreyfingin), since "it would be unnatural for the organizations of private capital to have this project in their hands alone." In this whole story, however, it is well to bear in mind that no domestic contracting firm was anywhere near able to handle this giant project alone and unaided when Íslenskir aðalverktakar was founded.

There was some struggle over the ownership of the new contracting company. I have in my possession a memorandum marked strictly confidential, in which the state's share in the new company is envisaged as 40 percent; Samvinnuverktakar (the cooperative contractors), Sameinaðir verktakar (United Contractors), and ABF, which were independent "Independence-Party contractors," were then each to receive 20 percent, and it was assumed that they would withdraw from Sameinaðir verktakar. The document has, however, been altered with a blue pen to provide for equal shares for these four parties. In the end, the state and SÍS each acquired a quarter share. A half share was held by Sameinaðir verktakar, which was owned by many companies and individuals generally considered devoted to the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn). ABF remained part of Sameinaðir verktakar and never received a separate ownership share in Íslenskir aðalverktakar.

The composition of the company may be cited as an example of the so-called fifty-fifty division rule of the Progressive Party and the Independence Party. I know that my father disliked SÍS's participation in the "army profiteering," as he called this business when speaking to me. Vilhjálmur Þór and the leaders of the Federation, on the other hand, pressed the matter very hard. Many meetings were held before my father agreed to the arrangement, and it probably mattered a great deal for the outcome that Eysteinn strongly supported the Federation in the matter. My father set great store by his judgment.
My part concerned first and foremost the construction side. I negotiated,

among other things, the terms of Aðalverktakar's first project for the military: the laying of the road to Keflavík above Hafnarfjörður. That project was intended to train Icelanders in operating large earthmoving machinery.

I also worked on ideas for the sale of electric power to the military, the establishment of a district heating service at the base, and harbor works in Njarðvík. While I was at the Defense Division (Varnarmáladeildin) I traveled a good deal to the United States and Canada, where I visited numerous heavy-industry companies. In this way I gathered ever more detailed information about Icelanders' opportunities in heavy industry and employment matters.

In 1954 an increasing thaw began to be felt in international affairs, which may be said to have reached its high point with the Geneva meeting of the leaders of the great powers in 1955. Many pinned their hopes on the end of the Cold War coming into view. The reasons were not least that a certain turning point was thought to have come with the death of Stalin in 1953. I was on my trip to Germany when news of his death got about, and I remember well that most people seemed anxious over his passing. The most pessimistic predicted a new revolution in Russia or even a world war. People knew what they were losing but not what they would get. In this respect there was no difference between the eastern and western parts of Germany. Everyone fears uncertainty and instability. A year later it had become clear to most peace-minded people that Stalin's death had been for the good. The Soviets seemed to show an increased willingness to negotiate.

My father was among those who believed that the improving state of international affairs called for a new policy toward the military presence. He declared this view of his, among other occasions, in debates in the Althing (Alþingi) at the end of 1954. One may say that little by little the foundation was laid for the left-wing government, as will be related later.

The Cold War sprang from mistrust between the great powers that emerged as victors from the Second World War. I will not assert that it could have been prevented. It has always been my view, however, that most things can be resolved if people sit down and talk them through. Stalin, of course, long stood in the way of that and provoked strong reactions on the other side of the Atlantic. Perhaps more hard-liners are elected in democratic elections when the atmosphere is poisoned in this way. It is hard to understand why Stalin was granted a large part of Europe as a fief after the Second World War. Much would probably have turned out differently had that not been so. Perhaps, though, it reflects the fact that the Russians had a larger share in the Allies' victory over the Germans than has commonly been proclaimed. They made great sacrifices.

The subjugation of Eastern Europe after the war was shameful for all those who took part in the partitioning of Europe, but probably no one foresaw it before 1945. It must not be forgotten that the chief adversaries of the Cold War were former allies, and their combined armies went under the name of the Allied armies of liberation. In keeping with that, it was said that the Red Army had liberated Eastern

Europe from the hands of the Germans. The Americans likewise sent vast quantities of war matériel to the Russians while the German invasion of that country was under way. Both parties preferred to forget that fact in the postwar years.

We Icelanders were bound to place ourselves in the ranks of the Western nations under these circumstances. That is where we belong. I therefore considered it right that we should join NATO. It seemed to me a far better option to have the British come here when a German invasion loomed during the war years, and in the same way I considered the Americans a far better option than the Russians after the war. On the other hand, I agreed with my father, and still do, that there should be no military force here in peacetime. It is humiliating for us Icelanders how in recent years we have gone begging at the doors of the Americans and NATO, imploring them for all we are worth to keep their forces here when they themselves consider it most sensible to leave. It is a disgrace.

Foreign minister after foreign minister goes down on bended knee in Washington and asks the Americans to stay. To me it seems more than self-evident that the military should be allowed to leave if it wishes. That is how I would have handled matters as foreign minister. Foreign ministers do not, of course, decide defense matters alone. But who is the enemy? Does anyone imagine that the Russians will attack the Western powers? Why are military exercises still held in this country? It is like children playing at guns. The army units are like the rowdy games of plucky boys, or Vesturbær and Austurbær having a street fight. The Norwegians seize the Sog! It is like a bad joke. Why is this money not used to help the Russians and the countries of Eastern Europe get on their feet economically? We are in a military alliance and have had a military presence here out of dire necessity. Now such a thing is no longer necessary.
Land-Seller

As my political career went on and opposition to joining the European Union became a stronger element in my public arguments, it probably occurred to few people to call me a land-seller or an agent of foreign trusts. At the end of 1954, however, there was a great commotion and much newspaper writing in which I was accused of just that. On November 26, 1954, in bold type right across the front page of Þjóðviljinn, stood:
Has the government handed foreign trusts control over the country's largest rivers? The son of Hermann Jónasson proclaims that this will soon become "aktúelt" [topical].

I had landed in the first political skirmish of my life. The occasion was a lecture I gave at a well-attended meeting of the Engineering Society of Iceland (Verkfræðingafélag Íslands) on heavy industry in Iceland. There I reported on the interest of three foreign companies in heavy industry in this country. I traced the history of such interest all the way back to the investigations of the poet Einar Benediktsson and the Norwegian Titan company at the beginning of the century. I described the country's opportunities for heavy industry, the need for greatly expanded power plants to supply such companies with electricity, and I argued that Icelanders ought to attract foreign capital to the country. I recounted the experience of the Norwegians and Canadians in that regard, both nations having begun large-scale development of heavy industry and energy with the help of foreign investors. I asserted that the development of such industry in Iceland would be slow if we waited for Icelanders themselves to have the strength to harness power and build energy-intensive industrial enterprises. The Icelandic state should build and own the power plants, but the heavy industry could be foreign-owned. I proposed that aluminum production should be at the top of the wish list. I warned, however, against unwarranted optimism.

We should not think that we need only stretch out our hand and a host of foreign companies will come running and accept whatever terms we see fit. Finding an interested and good company with the ability and willingness to undertake such a venture will, I believe, prove to be one of the most difficult tasks.

In the Þjóðviljinn article my words were twisted and my lecture interpreted as government policy. The paper quoted me as saying that "it was urgent to hand over the hydropower" and said that everything indicated that what the socialists had repeatedly warned of in recent years had now come to pass: that the government had already decided, or intended in the near future, to hand over to foreign trusts control of the country's largest rivers, Þjórsá or Jökulsá á Fjöllum. I was angered by Þjóðviljinn's reporting and wanted to bring a libel suit against the paper. My father, however, strongly advised me against it. Litigation would yield nothing but a well-hidden apology in the middle of the paper — and, moreover, the misstatements would be repeated regularly for two years instead of two days. He was probably right. At the very least, Bjarni Benediktsson and the Morgunblaðið men reaped little but the laughter of their opponents for their incessant lawsuits against Þjóðviljinn and its editors in those years. I followed my father's advice and have in fact followed it ever since. I have never sued newspapers or journalists for libel, though I have often felt there was ample reason to.
Power plants and heavy industry

Heavy-industry matters took up much of my time in 1954. In my lecture I reported on the visits of representatives of three aluminum producers to Iceland; earlier, I had been assigned to receive them. My friend Runólfur Þórðarson assisted me in these matters. One of the companies, British Aluminium, had ever since 1942 been interested in exploring aluminum production here in Iceland if electricity could be obtained for it at a favorable price. A board member of the company, George Boex, had come to Iceland during the war years. He came back to Iceland in September 1954. The other companies that showed interest in Iceland were Aluminium Industrie de Lausanne in Switzerland (Alusuisse) and Aluminium Limited in Canada (Alcan).

First came the representatives of Alusuisse, managing director Rudolf Hardmeyer and plant manager Hans Dinner, who stayed here for two weeks. They spoke with Kristinn Guðmundsson, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Jakob Gíslason, the Director of the State Electricity Authority, and our Icelandic experts about possible hydropower options. The Swiss also inspected power-plant sites on the Þjórsá and the Jökulsá á Fjöllum rivers. They considered our research into promising power-plant options to be at an early stage.

In August came F. L. Lawton, chief engineer at Alcan. He stayed in Iceland for three weeks. I was with him the whole time as well. He examined the same hydropower options very carefully, the Þjórsá area and Jökulsá á Fjöllum. For the trip through the Þjórsá area he hired the driver Guðmundur Jónasson. It was an adventurous journey and took many days. We drove over rough terrain and swift rivers — across the Tungná at Hófsvað ford, across the Köldukvísl, and across the Þjórsá at Norðlingaalda. I greatly admired Guðmundur's resourcefulness. That lesson served me well later on my own travels in the wilderness. It was also very instructive to be with Lawton. His conclusions seemed drawn from good sense and knowledge. He wrote off various ideas about power-plant options and pointed to others in their place. We inspected the Jökulsá from the air, and the pilot Björn Pálsson was hired for that trip. Lawton's conclusion was the same as the others': that our hydropower options were little explored.

In fact, these visits had a considerable prelude; more companies had shown interest, and my involvement in heavy-industry matters had been more extensive than came out in the lecture. The interest from abroad could partly be traced to the technical director of the research institution Battelle Memorial Institute in the United States, Bruce W. Gonser. In 1953 he had compiled a report on the utilization of Iceland's natural resources and the development of industry in this country. He came here quite often and was in good contact with Baldur Líndal and Jakob Gíslason, the Director of the State Electricity Authority. The Battelle Institute had

an office in Switzerland and had drawn the attention of the Swiss to Iceland. Gonser did not stop there; he also spoke with Reynolds Metals, the Aluminum Company of America (Alcoa), Olin Industries in the United States, Alcan, and various other companies in America. I met Gonser on one of his trips here in the autumn of 1953.

By the time the lecture was given, I had thus spoken in all with representatives of six companies. Besides receiving representatives of three of them here at home, I had gone to the United States in April 1954 for talks with the aforementioned companies at the request of the Minister for Foreign Affairs. I compiled a report on hydropower options in Iceland in preparation for the trip. I then flew between New York, Pittsburgh, Montreal, Richmond, and Chicago for meetings with the companies. The trip took just under three weeks, and I delivered a detailed report when it was over. I felt it had gone well, even though the meeting with Louis Reynolds in Richmond, head of the company of the same name, fell through owing to a misunderstanding. I sent him a rather sharp letter with comments on this conduct and received an apology by return mail. The ties with the company were not severed by this, however. For a while I corresponded with both Louis Reynolds, one of the principal owners, and Walter Rice, vice-chairman of the board, and this led among other things to my being offered a job with the company. I declined that offer.

The meeting with I.W. Wilson, president and chairman of Alcoa, was among the most memorable of that trip because of how unexpected its ending was. I was invited to the president's magnificent office on the top floor of a high-rise in Pittsburgh, tens of meters above the heads of ordinary people. After an excellent conversation, Wilson informed me that it was out of the question for Alcoa to build factories in Iceland, since the communists here were far too numerous!

My involvement in heavy-industry matters by no means ended with Þjóðviljinn's scaremongering. As mentioned before, I investigated various things in this field after I moved back to the United States in 1955. Among other things, I went with Vilhjálmur Jónsson, the head of Esso, on behalf of the government for talks with Reynolds Metals. They expressed interest but wanted us to hire a recognized engineering firm to assess the hydropower options. They pointed to Harza Engineering in Chicago in that connection. I went to Chicago together with Eiríkur Briem, director of the State Electric Power Works, for talks with Harza. Subsequently a contract was made with the firm, and it provided consulting for the Búrfell hydropower project. In fact, it seemed to me that Louis Reynolds was every bit as interested in raising beef cattle. He said he owned thousands of cattle that he grazed on the company's raw-material mining lands in Jamaica and wanted to know whether taking up such farming in Iceland might be considered. He offered me a partnership with him if I procured the necessary permits.
Later I was once again involved in heavy-industry matters in Iceland. From 1964 and for more than

a decade I sat on heavy-industry committees under the chairmanship of Jóhannes Nordal. We negotiated, among other things, the aluminum smelter at Straumsvík and the ferrosilicon plant at Grundartangi. I will describe that in more detail later, but it may be said that I was involved in heavy-industry matters in Iceland from idea to execution and had the opportunity to learn this field from the ground up. Over the course of my life I have swung from being one of the leading advocates of heavy industry in Iceland to joining the ranks of the skeptics. These changes in my conviction stem first and foremost from environmental and pollution considerations. In my younger years I had no idea, any more than others at that time, of the damage heavy industry does to the environment. There was a race to build factories all over the world, and I felt we Icelanders should not be left behind. The enthusiasm could be traced to a belief in progress and ambition on behalf of the nation, as was natural.

At the beginning of the 1960s, scientists began to realize the damage man inflicts on the environment. In my opinion, this problem has become the greatest that mankind faces. Gradually, it has also weighed more heavily in my mind that working in heavy industry is not attractive. It is mechanical. I would rather wish Icelanders work in high-tech industry and software production. To that end, emphasis should be placed on education rather than investments in concrete and steel. Around the middle of the century, however, we were struggling out of poverty toward decent living standards. Then heavy industry was a natural step.
"The Grímsá Power Plant Scandal"

I was not always in the role of a wage earner in those years. When I look back, I am amazed at how many of my ideas became businesses. Few, admittedly, proved profitable, but the undertakings were often interesting. Large sums of money were in circulation in the first half of the 1950s because of the Marshall aid and the military's major construction projects at Keflavík Airport. During the left-wing government of 1956–1958 there were in addition foreign borrowings and assistance from the World Bank, along with the incredible zeal for construction among Icelanders that followed in the wake of the upswing.

In business life, most things were still tied to strict licenses. Special permits were required to import or export. Purchases of foreign currency were subject to official approval. Fish exporters were actually half-exempt from this because of the rules on the so-called boat currency (bátagjaldeyrir). They were allowed to sell half of their export earnings in foreign currency on the free market. State participation in business expanded greatly during this period. This was due, among other things, to the fact that in Iceland,

here as elsewhere, the Marshall Aid and the assistance of the World Bank, as well as all loans, fell into the lap of the public sector. No doubt these state activities had a positive effect on the economy. Enterprising individuals did not hold back either. In those years, businessmen were guided, no less than now, by the principle of seizing the opportunities that presented themselves and creating the conditions where they were lacking. I unquestionably counted myself among that group.

At the end of 1954 I took part in founding the company Verklegar framkvæmdir hf. together with Ólafur Jensson, Helgi Bergs, Guðmundur Björnsson and Rögnvaldur Þorláksson. We were all engineers and all Progressive Party men. The intention was to undertake "all kinds of engineering work, construction projects and related operations," to quote the minutes of the company's founding meeting. We looked above all to the power-plant projects that were planned, as well as the laying of transmission lines connected with such projects. The company's first job, however, was a joint venture on maintenance work at Keflavík Airport. The company Byggir hf., which was managed by Birgir Frímannsson, had been awarded the job, and we entered into its contract.

The next major job that Verklegar framkvæmdir took on was the construction of the Grímsá power station in the East Fjords. The company submitted a bid together with a Danish firm, E. Phil & Søn, and won the contract. This Danish firm has long been active in Iceland and holds, among other things, the largest share in the contracting company Ístak hf. Some newspaper articles followed in the wake of the Grímsá power-station contract, in which Steingrímur Steinþórsson, the Minister of Electric Power, was criticized for awarding us the job. The papers claimed that other bids had been more favorable. I took no part in that debate, as I was abroad at the time.

In the letters that passed between me and my co-owners, however, one can read an interesting story about the relationship between politics and business in Iceland in the 1950s. Helgi Bergs recounted it in his letters in 1955:
When the bids were opened there were three of them, and they looked like this: Snæfell h/f (the Eastfjords men) — 8.5 million kr. Almenna — 10.6 million kr. Vefra and Langvad\ — 10.88 million kr.

Helgi said that the Eastfjords men had not been considered qualified for the job, and it had come to light that sales tax had been included in our bid but not in the bid of Almenna (ABF), which was regarded as a conservative company. After Sig-
\ Vefra was an abbreviation of Verklegar framkvæmdir, and Langvad was used for the Danish firm.

urður Thoroddsen, who was the minister's advisor, had taken various reservations into account, he finally reached the conclusion that our bid was slightly higher than Almenna's — by 9 thousand krónur. Steingrímur Steinþórsson, the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) minister, thereupon decided to disregard his advisor's assessment and award us the job. The matter was much discussed in the newspapers afterwards. Helgi describes it thus:

Then Þjóðviljinn carries the news with a big headline on the front page. This was said to be one of the greatest government scandals of recent years, since named in that connection were such wicked men as the son of Hermann Jónasson and the chairman of Aðalverktakar. Shortly afterwards Frjáls þjóð, Vísir, Mbl. and Alþbl. joined the pack. Vísir was about the nastiest of them . . .
Around the same time, scattered reports of the affair reached me in the United States, and I wrote to Helgi to obtain further news:

I have heard a little about the "Grímsá scandal" . . . To tell the truth, it seems to me that these attacks have done us no harm at all. We got a great deal of publicity. How does it strike you? For my own part I have little objection to it, except that what I find worst is that my father must always be attacked for everything I come near. It actually matters little to him, he is used to such things, but it is rather pitiful for me never to be able to stand on my own feet.

Throughout Helgi's letters it is evident that he and the other people behind our company had no involvement in the decision in the matter or its preparation. There is in fact an account there of how things happened behind the scenes in the final stages:

One fine day Ólafur [managing director of Verklegar framkvæmdir] was summoned to a meeting with Minister Steingr. Stgr. informed him that our bid had turned out to be 9 thousand kr. higher than ABF's. He said furthermore that Eysteinn [Jónsson, minister] was pressing hard to accept the bid of the Eastfjords men, and at the very least absolutely refused to consider ABF. Stgr. himself said he did not want the Eastfjords men, because the experts considered them unqualified for the job, and so the conclusion he and Eysteinn had more or less reached was to offer it to us. Ólafur warned against accepting the bid if ABF's was really lower, and thought it would be badly received [. . .] The conversation of Ólafur and

and Steingrímur's conversation ended with Stgr. asking: "Does this mean, then, that you are declining the job on behalf of your company?" Ólafur answered no, and said he needed to confer with his partners. We then discussed the matter thoroughly and came to the conclusion that it would be absurd to decline the job. We had seen no comparison and did not know whether ABF was really lower. The next morning Sigtryggur Klemensson telephones Ólafur and says: "Do you mean to sulk like a dog if the Grímsá is handed to you on a silver platter?" Ólafur said no, and that same day the matter was decided.

Political decisions and processes of this kind were the rule rather than the exception in those years of the fifty-fifty coalition governments of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) and the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), and for much longer. In fact, it may be said in Minister Steingrímur Steinþórsson's defense that he arranged a tender, did not engage an unqualified company despite pressure, and the difference between the two bids was less than 0.1 percent. He must therefore have regarded it as practically a matter of taste which company was chosen, and then there was nothing more to be said. For my part, I found it instructive to become acquainted with the country's business life from this angle, even though it came down on my father. Helgi Bergs put it aptly on that subject in a letter to me:

I well understand that you find it hard, as you say, not to be able to come near anything without your father being attacked. On the other hand, you must learn to stop taking it to heart. With the lack of morals that prevails in Icelandic politics, hardly anything else is to be expected.

Nor did my co-owners involve themselves in these political disputes. It is recorded in the company's minutes "to leave these discussions alone, since the company had not had the opportunity to examine the other bids." Shortly afterwards we bid on the construction of the Mjólká power station, but we did not get that job.

Things went better when bids were invited for the Upper Sog power station. Our old partner E. Phil & Søn did, it is true, turn out to have a lower bid, but the board that had been placed over the project, the so-called Sog Board (Sogsstjórn), was keen that Icelandic parties should work on the project. The upshot was that we once again entered into cooperation with the Danes and undertook the job jointly. All these works went well. In their wake, the company took on numerous projects, large and small. More will be said of that later.
An Ice-Cream Adventure in Austurstræti

Verklegar framkvæmdir never made a fortune, but a different story is to be told of Ísborg, a company which may be said to have sprung from my love of ice-cream dishes and banana splits in the United States. When I came home from my studies in 1952, I had various ideas about how I could get on my feet. I had written them down in a little black notebook which unfortunately is now lost. On its first pages were ideas about ice-cream production and ice-cream sales. Pálmi Jónsson, a lawyer who was later associated with Hagkaup, approached me sometime in 1954. Pálmi's father had grown wealthy from the sale of land at Hofsós, and Pálmi had considerable money from his father at his disposal. He wanted to put that money into a profitable business. He said he had heard of my ideas and wanted to form a partnership to run an ice-cream parlor. I liked the idea.

At first Pálmi said he saw no reason for there to be more than the two of us in the company. At most, one share could be sacrificed if someone could contribute a good location for the operation. I was quite happy to work with Pálmi but had no ready money. Pálmi therefore lent me the money for my share until things improved. After the preparations were well under way at the end of 1955, Pálmi proposed that his brother-in-law, Ásberg Sigurðsson, a lawyer and managing director of the Ísafjörður trawler company, should hold a one-third share alongside us, and that a limited company should be formed for the business. So it came about, although the founding was not formally completed until August 1956. Earlier that year we had agreed on a certain amount of share capital. Capital that Pálmi contributed beyond that was regarded as a loan to the company and would be repaid to him with interest. It may be said that Pálmi handled the financial side entirely in the early part of the company's life.

The preparations began in earnest in 1955, shortly after I had left for a two-year stay in the United States. My role at first was to gather information about ice cream and the ice-cream business: machines, ice-cream mixes, flavorings, cones and packaging. We also became subscribers to magazines about ice cream and ice-cream production. I sent numerous letters and inquiries from California and went to business meetings with sellers of ice-cream machines. Pálmi, for his part, looked for premises on the main circuit in Reykjavík and began working on obtaining a license for importing ice-cream machines. I finally found excellent "Sani-Serv" ice-cream machines from the General Equipment Company, a solid firm with a branch in California. Pálmi had good luck with premises. He got a very good location in Austurstræti, where the sales offices of Samvinnuferðir-Landsýn are now housed.
The import license, on the other hand, was a long time in coming. That process is a good example of how the rationing system worked. The licenses were regarded almost as

a favor, and for a favor another had to be given in return. At the same time, it could be decisive to have someone within the system speak on one's behalf. Pálmi had to go from man to man for several months in search of such support. Finally a promise was obtained from the Minister of Agriculture. It was not yet time to celebrate victory, however. Three months passed before the license was issued, despite the minister's word. The consent of two men was required: Jón Ívarsson, who was director of the Import Office (innflutningsskrifstofan), and Sverrir Júlíusson, who was deputy director of the same office. In their duumvirate was crystallized the so-called fifty-fifty system, in which the Federation of Cooperatives (Sambandið) and the private merchants divided the market between themselves. Jón supported granting the license, but Sverrir stood in the way — according to Pálmi, "unless Jón also signed the same kind of license for a protégé of Minister Ingólfur Jónsson." Jón Ívarsson, however, flatly refused to grant a license to Ingólfur's protégé. For a long time it seemed we had run aground. Before it was over, Pálmi had enlisted my father's help. He praised him for his conduct in the matter. The license was finally obtained on 22 November, a good two months after the promise was given on 17 September 1955. With the license in hand, all that remained was to find a name, fit out the premises and open.

Pálmi at first wanted us to look for a good American name for our company, and among other things proposed that we call the company Dairy King. Other English names I found among American ice-cream chains were Dairy Delight and Snow White. I was more in favor of "a beautiful Icelandic name" and suggested Frosti. My first idea for an advertisement was:
Buy Frosti ice cream; Icelandic ice cream produced by an Icelandic company, or . . . produced by an Icelandic company after the best American model.

Pálmi liked the name but pointed out that a bad-tasting and unpopular ice-pop was produced under the same name in Iceland. He suggested the name Mjallhvít (Snow White) instead, but I thought it declined rather awkwardly. I proposed that the ice-cream parlor be given one of the names: Ísborg, Ísborgir, Íssalir, Fönn or Ísbúðin Fönn. Pálmi declared himself in favor of the name Ísborg and proposed that we call the ice cream itself Borgar-ís.

I wanted the counter to be long and for hamburgers, waffles and other things of that kind to be sold there as well. At first Pálmi did not like the hamburger idea and thought too much "smoke and stench would come from that kind of frying." We agreed, however, on investing considerably in the fittings and appearance. We exchanged ideas and drawings of the place. I purchased what was needed from the United States, bar stools and furnishings. I also sent

numerous recipes for ice-cream dishes and gourmet waffles from the United States. When the place was opened on 13 May 1956, the result was everything one could have wished for. Pálmi said the ice-cream sales were "enormous" and described the opening days thus:

The place is celebrated for how tasteful it is, and this exceeds the hopes I had formed for it, which were nevertheless considerable. The main sales are of course in the ice cream, but there are also enormous hot-dog sales.

The business developed, and Ísborg soon began selling large hamburgers alongside the ice cream. The place was one of the country's first fast-food establishments. I procured a "juke-box" — or glymskratti, as they were later called — the ice-cream dishes multiplied, and the ice cream improved in taste and quality.
Competition from All Sides

From the beginning we had a formidable competitor, Dairy Queen, which had opened the first ice-cream parlors in Iceland shortly before. That company was owned by the brothers Þorvaldur and Tómas Árnason, who were staunch Progressive Party men. I later sat in parliament with Tómas; we were fellow ministers in the government of Ólafur Jóhannesson and that of Gunnar Thoroddsen, and we became good friends. He later became Governor of the Central Bank (Seðlabankinn). Pálmi and I took our cue from what the Dairy Queen brothers' ice-cream parlors offered, in quality, appearance, packaging and even price. About prices and competition, Pálmi wrote in a letter:

We are going to sell at very high prices. The prices will naturally be modeled largely on Dairy Queen, because I have no wish to get into any quarrels with them; besides, all underbidding is dangerous and can set off general price reductions among competing firms — it is better to let such reductions take the form of some perks or outright increased service.

Pálmi was prepared for anything in the competition and usually got early word if others had expansion plans in the works on the ice-cream market. When Tómas and Þorvaldur intended to open a new place in Austurstræti, he turned to me and wanted my father to use his influence to stop their plans. Pálmi said in a letter in March 1956, shortly before the opening of Ísborg:

They must know, especially Tommi, that competition on their part against us will be viewed seriously. Tommi is dead set on running in the elections now, and he of course depends very much on your father for whatever political advancement he gets.
I wrote to Tómas and gathered from his replies that no expansion on their part would take place. That changed, however, and early in 1957 Dairy Queen opened an ice-cream bar in Lækjargata.

Competition loomed from all sides. Shortly before Ísborg was opened, word reached Pálmi that SÍS (the Federation of Icelandic Cooperatives) was importing 10–20 ice-cream machines into the country. They were said to have been registered as refrigerators in order to get them through customs without objection! Pálmi was for a time seriously worried by this news and said about the importation in a letter:

It is hard to have gone through as much for the license as I did, and then this is imported entirely without hindrance — and this business morality of the Federation (Sambandið), doing such things, just like the scum among the wholesalers.
I myself could not hold my tongue, and wrote my father a letter in which I recounted the news of this illegal importation. I go on to say:

It is understandable that many small businessmen hate SÍS, if such things happen often. SÍS is like a guillotine hanging over their necks. Now it so happens that both Dairy Queen and Ísborg are mostly owned by Progressive Party men. I really do think this ought to be looked into more closely. Is SÍS not supposed to be above all corruption and exceptionally honest?

Our worries about the Federation's importation proved largely groundless. The machines were Swedish and inferior to ours, and moreover far fewer than Pálmi at first believed. His competitive spirit in business did, in fact, more than once lead us to react sharply to every rumor of competition. It was equally certain that the business moguls of SÍS were no lambs to play with where competition was concerned. Perhaps this experience of dealing with the Federation marked me to some extent, though it did not cut deep. I was, however, never a fiery Federation man like many of my comrades in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) — no more than my father was, compared with Eysteinn or most other Progressives of his generation.
We soon hired Leó Árnason to manage Ísborg in

Austurstræti. He took over the position of managing director and the power of procuration from Pálmi. Leó was married to Pálmi's paternal aunt and was called "the lion." He was slender, and his gray hair grew thick and abundant in a veritable mane. Leó was light-hearted and cheerful, and in his eyes dwelt a flashing spark that spread humor wherever he went. He had an artistic disposition and a philosophical turn of mind. He painted in his spare time but attended to the running of Ísborg with great conscientiousness, even though he never owned a share in the company. After Leó left Ísborg he moved to Selfoss, where he was quite active in business. Among other things he ran a fish-processing operation, besides pursuing his art with great energy.

Once I co-signed a small promissory note for Leó. When it came due, he had difficulty with the payments. I therefore covered them, and Leó promised me a painting in return. He reminded me of this many years later, but unfortunately I never got around to coming and collecting the painting. I deeply regret it.

Pálmi's and my ice-cream sales went well, and we soon began thinking about enlarging and expanding the business. From the beginning I had been interested in opening in Akureyri and Selfoss. Soon, however, bigger ideas took priority: ice-cream production in Eskihlíð.
A Dreary Existence for Dolly

Dolly was unhappy in Iceland and in the small town of Reykjavík. It seemed to me she did little to change that and make her life more cheerful. She found fault with most things. We lived in very close quarters with my parents. Dolly found that oppressive and said they had too much influence on me. I often talked with my father, as I had always done. In that respect Dolly perhaps had something of a point. I have always thought it natural to listen to good advice and have always been ready to reconsider my position if I hear sensible arguments. I probably listened to my father more than to most others.

Dolly's and my life together on Tjarnargata was not without friction. My parents probably felt it no less than I did. They never mentioned it, however, but tried to make the best of the situation. My mother and Dolly got along well, though, and I often admired my mother's deftness in steering between rock and wave. It therefore never came to serious clashes between them, and Mamma got to see a good deal of Jón. Dolly, on the other hand, bore a grudge against my father and expressed it freely to me and to our acquaintances. She believed he was pulling every oar to make me settle in Iceland. I thought that unfair, because nothing else was ever an option as far as I was concerned. Dolly should have known that.

I worked long days during these years, often into the evening, and I can understand that Dolly resented it. She did not have much to occupy her and had few acquaintances. Many of my friends were not to her liking either. She did, however, keep in touch with our friends from Chicago.
