In particular she made acquaintances in the KR swimming club, where she took on coaching synchronized swimming and did very well at it.

The tug-of-war in our life together probably strained the nerves of us both. As time went on I perhaps felt more at ease at work than at home, and was therefore all the less inclined to shirk from working my fingers to the bone. It would take too long to recount the turmoil that raged in my marriage during these two years, 1953 and 1954. In hindsight it is plain that there was an incurable flaw in the marriage. Dolly could not imagine living in Iceland, and I would not settle anywhere else. In her eyes everything in Iceland was impossible: the people, the weather, the roads, whatever met her eye at any given moment — and she never tried to learn Icelandic. It seemed to me that with every word she was attacking what was dearest to me: my parents, my native land, and the family's future home. At first I met most of it with silence, but as time went on I answered back at full pitch more and more often, which of course did nothing to improve the situation. Dolly sent vases flying into walls and broke plates on the floor. The marriage had reached the breaking point.

We seldom went out among people or to parties. Dolly strongly disapproved of Icelanders' drinking and did not want to take part in merrymaking past midnight. She abstained entirely from alcohol and tobacco. I myself have never smoked and have always been moderate with wine. Nevertheless, it was a foregone conclusion that if we were invited out, there would almost without exception be unpleasantness for several days afterward. Our discord extended over everything.

While Dolly's aversion to Iceland intensified, I tried to awaken her interest in building a home of our own. That was probably about the last thing she wanted. I got nothing but scolding for my suggestions. I stuck to my guns and tried to resolve matters by proposing that we rent an apartment far from my parents. Dolly refused to move anywhere but to the United States. We stood on opposite sides of an unbridgeable chasm.

If I had been asked at the time whether I loved my wife, I would probably have had to think it over before answering. I loved Dolly nonetheless, and in the end I gave in to her determined will. I agreed that we would go to the United States for two years. She had by then already applied for immigration and work permits for me without my knowledge. We agreed that our attempt to live in Iceland had failed, and arranged to use the next two years to prepare our homecoming to Iceland better. She agreed that we would build our own home in Iceland. This was also meant
to give Dolly time to adjust to the idea of spending her life in Iceland.

My acquaintances considered this ill-advised. Of my parents' feelings I knew nothing. They said they were content if I was. I decided to take Dolly at her word despite what had gone before, and wanted to try to save our marriage. I refused to believe that it could not be done.
Back in America

We left Iceland on January 2, 1955. For the first three months we were in Chicago while I looked for work. Shortly after our arrival there, Dolly brought up having another child. I was reluctant. I wanted us to postpone it until we had settled in and bought insurance. Dolly repeated these wishes of hers over the following days, but then it seemed to me that she accepted my proposal. Two weeks later I discovered that this had not been the case at all. Dolly had, as usual, taken matters into her own hands. She was with child.

I was deeply shaken. I had grown used to a great deal, but not to being deceived behind my back in this way in my marriage. I spoke my mind and discussed this at length with Dolly. She said she repented, but that she had considered a second child necessary for our marriage. She vowed never to resort to such tricks again, and we reconciled. A wonderful little daughter was born to us on November 6, 1955. She was christened Ellen Herdís — Herdís after my sister, who died shortly after birth. Two or three months after the birth, however, I discovered that Dolly was trying to repeat the trick and lied to me. It has always been in my nature to trust people. It is a healthy rule not to believe tales of deceit until confirmation has been obtained. I learned to believe in the good in every person from my mother's example. One betrayal, on the other hand, is enough to destroy trust between people. That I have experienced many times over. The closer the person in question stands to one's heart, the harder it is to come to terms with such a thing. From then on I found it ever more difficult to trust my wife's word.

After I came to the United States I was at first traveling a great deal and continued my investigations into Icelanders' opportunities for heavy industry. So that I would be given the necessary assistance, I carried a special letter signed by my father, who was chairman of the State Committee on Industrial Affairs (Atvinnumálanefnd ríkisins). This committee had been established pursuant to a parliamentary resolution proposed by him and others. Its role was to "make proposals for new industries for production and increased employment, and for the utilization of the country's resources in that connection." From the Foreign

Ministry I received a diplomatic passport, and these two things opened various doors for me abroad. I gathered all my main findings together in a detailed report with 75 appendices of various kinds. I also studied the advantages of foreign investment for the Icelandic economy and the electrification of the countryside, both matters that I would go on to devote much attention to during the two years in the United States.

In addition to the heavy-industry matters, I worked on various other ideas that had arisen in connection with the defense affairs committee. One of the first things I did was to negotiate with men from the American army's map-making service for Icelanders' use of their data, and for more precise land surveys to be undertaken here in Iceland. This proved quite valuable for road construction and scientific work in Iceland. I also met with the Americans about an Icelandic electric utility for the military — which later became the Suðurnes power utility — and a comparable district heating utility. The electricity negotiations were in fact difficult, because the military had newly built a power station for its own use. At the special request of the foreign minister, I also held discussions about the construction of a harbor at Ytri-Njarðvík and about funding for work on separating the military's operations areas at Keflavík from other parts of the airfield.

My job search in the United States was directed chiefly at California, since Dolly was fond of that state. Before I left Iceland I had written to the head of the electrical engineering department at Cal. Tech, Dr. McCann, and told him of my plans to move back to the United States. He owned a company called Analog Computers Associates. He telephoned Iceland straight away, which was very unusual in those days, and offered me a job at his company at a good salary. I was to receive 1,000 dollars a month and at the same time complete a doctorate at the school during working hours and at the company's expense. I was allowed to coordinate the work on my studies and for the company without any reduction in salary. This was a very tempting offer, and probably the best job offer I have ever received.

If I had accepted it, I would have had to commit myself for three years because of the studies. Naturally, Dr. McCann also expected that I would continue working for the company after the doctorate and put my knowledge to use there. Dolly was extremely taken with this offer and wanted me to accept it without further deliberation.

After we arrived in the United States I soon paid Dr. McCann a visit. I told him that I had thought a great deal about his offer but had decided to decline it. He was astonished and said that no one received better offers. I said the reason was that I was determined to return to Iceland after two years and did not want to conceal that from him. He was grateful to me and said that many would probably have taken the offer and then run off. He
added that he had certainly hoped I would stay with the company for the long term.

Two or three of my classmates from Cal. Tech received comparable offers, and they all accepted them. They were very content with their lot. The company was a pioneer in the field of computer technology. Digital computers were just coming onto the scene.

I was also offered a job with the World Bank (Alþjóðabankinn) as an engineer on electrification in Persia, in what is now called Iran. The Bank paid for my flight to Washington for discussions, and I was offered a good salary and generous benefits. I was greatly interested in the job, and it would no doubt have been very instructive. There I would have come to know an entirely different culture and a foreign way of thinking, which would without question have broadened my horizons. Probably nothing could have stopped me except my wife, who could not be persuaded to go. She would not hear of such a thing. Perhaps I would be an immensely rich shareholder in some oil company if this had come to pass.

In the end I took a job with the Southern Californian Edison Company, the electric utility of Southern California, and was there for just under two years. The salary was 600 dollars a month, and without a doctorate. The job was nonetheless instructive, and I am convinced that my choice was the right one. I intended to go home.
Chapter Seven
BROKEN HOPES AND THE LATER AMERICAN YEARS

My new workplace, the Southern Californian Edison Company, the electric utility, had its headquarters in Los Angeles, and that is where we moved. Soon I raised with Dolly the matter of seeing to the building of our house in Iceland and the other preparations for the journey home, as had been agreed. At first Dolly kept pushing this ahead of her. Time and again she said she was not in the mood to discuss the return home. Finally she came out with it and announced to me that she had no intention whatsoever of moving back to Iceland. She said it would be tantamount to divorce if I moved back there, or even if I built us a house there. She was not going anywhere.

The situation worsened steadily from then on. Most evenings Dolly delivered tirades against Iceland, my parents, and my friends. I myself found it harder to restrain myself and quarreled with her more often than I had done before. That, of course, only made bad things worse. I became very tense, my appetite diminished, and I grew pale and withdrawn. Severe stomach pains began to cause me great discomfort. I saw a doctor and was diagnosed with colitis. It did not improve with treatment and was to stay with me for many years. Naturally I could not conceal the illness from my parents, and it worried them greatly.

We rented a small single-family house in a quiet neighborhood in Westchester, a suburb of Los Angeles, near the shore and the city's international airport. It was not a bad place to live. On the other hand, it was about an hour's drive to work and back on densely packed freeways. That could be very tiring. A few years ago I was in Los Angeles. I intended to have a look at the old neighborhood but could not find it anywhere. It had vanished. In place of a quiet residential district there was now a mass of high-rises and the big-city bustle that goes with it.

Dolly went constantly to counselors and psychologists. She had in fact done so ever since I first met her. She professed to find in them the solution to most problems. She pressed me hard to attend their sessions and even threatened all manner of trouble if I did not comply with these wishes of hers. I therefore visited several of them and had perfectly good conversations with them. Without exception, Dolly stopped seeing the specialist in question shortly after my visits. It gradually became clear that she was concealing from them various things that I disclosed. This indulgence of psychologists often became a matter of dispute between us, as it was very costly. It seemed to me that her blind faith in their advice took the place of all self-criticism and self-examination.

The marriage held together only because of the children. My relationship with Dolly was stripped of nearly all trust. I also had growing worries that the children, whom we imagined we were protecting, were getting nothing but harm from our life together. We often quarreled in their presence, and Dolly frequently called me all sorts of names and leveled accusations at me within little Jón's hearing. It did not help matters when I became aware that she was poisoning his mind with slander in my absence. She told him that I did not want to live in California because I did not love them and wanted nothing to do with them, and other things to that effect. Jón often came to me and said in his toddler's English: "Mamma says you are [...] but I don't think so."
Ponderings on the Marriage

It can probably be said that I was at my wits' end as the second year of the American stay wore on. Work gave my life little fulfillment, and the home was the scene of constant tension and quarrels. My friends and parents were far away, and my heart was heavy. In April 1956 I had begun to turn my mind to the dismal thought that perhaps the only way out was for Dolly and me to part for good. By then we had lived in the United States for nearly a year and a half. In these deliberations I sought advice and understanding from my parents. In California I had no one I felt I could trust. My first letter on this subject was quite long and began with these words:

There is one matter which has lately weighed rather heavily on my mind. On the whole I have spoken little to you about Dolly and our relationship. There is no need to burden you with worry over it, though of course you have realized it without that. I would now like to discuss it somewhat.

I recounted the agreement Dolly and I had made in Iceland about the return home, and expressed my disappointment that she had been unwilling to entertain any talk of building a house back home, or of the agreement at all, and that it appeared she did not intend to keep her word, or what "she promised me." "It is obvious that she wants to settle here and nowhere else." I, on the other hand, was determined to go to Iceland:
At home I want to live and work. That is why I came here to study, so that I might become a more useful man there. There lie my mind, my ambition, and my longing.

I said that I had wanted to learn from the troubles we had run into when we first lived in Iceland, and that I had believed the key to a successful way forward was good preparation for the homecoming, among other things by making the family a good home in a house of our own. Dolly, on the other hand, had done nothing but object to the building plans and refused to engage with them in any way, even though I had offered to let her have the last word on most things. There, for the first time, I put the thought of divorce into words:

This has weighed on me greatly in spirit and caused me physical distress. It often crosses my mind that she will not go home at all when it comes to the point. In view of what has happened before — in New York at the departure for home in 1952, all the commotion back home in Iceland, and so forth — it seems almost right to let her go her own way. But Nonni and my Herdís, the little darlings, deserve all the best. If Dolly refused to go home, she would no doubt see to it that I could not take them home, but that is what I would dearly want to do, in order to provide for them as well as possible.

Reading these old letters, however, it cannot be concealed that I was still fond of my wife despite all our difficulties. I offered explanations for Dolly's behavior and traced most of what was bad to her childhood and upbringing. It may seem strange that I did not discuss my marital troubles with my parents until a year and a half after we moved to the United States. Perhaps in this respect I took after my family. The fact is that I discussed such matters in letters rather than face to face, and not until it seemed to me that things had reached an impasse. At my father's office I certainly put my decisions before him when I was in Iceland, but I rarely discussed my feelings. That is how I am made.
In his letter of reply, my father said that he had not wanted to bring up my marriage of his own accord but was glad of the chance to give his opinion. From what he wrote
his words that these matters had churned strongly within him despite the silence. He said he was not surprised to hear that Dolly did not want to move back to Iceland:

To tell the truth, all your friends felt enough was enough when she turned back in New York, after everything that had gone before. – When you told me here at the office (Tjarnargata 42) that you were thinking of going to the United States with Dolly and staying there for two years, – you asked me my opinion. – Half a month before, I had already heard through Dolly that the two of you were going west, and she said then that she had no intention at all of coming back. – I said nothing about this to you; I did not want to be telling tales. However, I told you that she would not come back and did not intend to. – You said you could get this in writing from her. But you have not, my dear son, considered that Dolly respects no promises or agreements – stops at nothing when she needs to carry through what suits her.

My father laid out his reasons for this and said: "Just a few months after she came here, she had begun preparing to get you to move west – cf. her letters in which she applied for a job for you, etc." He also wrote to me that Dolly had written him a letter asking him not to encourage me to build a house at home. "I have never answered that letter with a single word [and] this I have likewise not wanted to discuss with you." My father was evidently relieved to be able to speak his whole mind, and he did.

I pondered deeply whether my marriage was worth still trying to save. Little by little I was coming to the view that it was not. I was torn in two by this question. Perhaps realism and stubbornness were pulling against each other. The experience of recent years all pointed toward divorce, but a strong part of me wanted to keep trying, not to give up. Divorce is not a simple matter. It touches one's innermost feelings, and Dolly still stood close to my heart. At the very least, it was far from true that I was indifferent to my father's opinion of her. I therefore objected to his view that Dolly's faults could be seen in her mother's character. I responded with a numbered account of my wife's virtues:

1. She is as good and conscientious a housewife as could be wished. Her mother never was. She hardly bothered to do anything for the home herself but traveled often to Florida and other resorts. Such is very far from Dolly.

2. She is an excellent mother and takes great care to give both children equal love and affection. That was entirely lacking with her mother, who no doubt bears the greatest blame for Dolly's troubles. 3. She is extremely caring toward me, yet with the flaw that she practically has to agree with whatever is under discussion. Her mother has tormented everything imaginable out of Leo [Dolly's father]. Many more differences could be named.

At the same time, it seemed to me that my wife's faults or difficulties could be traced to her mother and her upbringing, rather than being something mother and daughter had in common. The things in her character that I felt were spoiling the marriage I considered to be chiefly four:

1. She can never commit herself to anything unless her inner voice is in complete agreement from the very start. She says she consents, but when it comes to the test the unrest beneath the surface gains the upper hand, and she does not have the willpower to suppress it — compare New York, 1952. 2. Deep down she trusts no one but herself; though she tries and wants to, she usually fails involuntarily when it comes to the test. 3. She almost never sees or acknowledges her own fault, but always puts the blame on others. [. . .] She sometimes realizes this and sometimes regrets it, but she rarely admits it. 4. When something wounds her emotionally, she tends not to complain until things have come to a head. All of this I believe can without hesitation be traced to her childhood, her upbringing, and her parents. She was the eldest and bore the brunt of her parents' quarreling. She understood that all was not as it should be. Love and affection were largely or entirely lacking. This naturally wounded her deeply. Her parents did not heal the wounds but aggravated them. She therefore learned quickly that it was least painful to bottle up her worries. Most of what she wished [for herself] was denied. The parents had no time to attend to the children's wishes. Dolly quickly learned that the only way was to do things herself. [. . .] Naturally she could never admit her faults. She had to have self-confidence.

From these passages in my letters one may conclude that I considered Dolly to bear the greatest blame for the state the marriage was in. I did, however, place some emphasis, with my parents, on the fact that I could not be considered entirely blameless:

I feel sorry for Dolly and would so gladly like to help her. Unfortunately, my patience and good sense fail me all too often in that. I am ambitious and often stubborn, as such men usually are. I have firm opinions. This does not always blend well.
My mother's reaction was in some ways different from my father's writings. She did not have many words for things, but said:
It somehow seems to me that everything has not gone as well as circumstances allowed, and some things could have gone better. But there is no use dwelling on it.

This was written in Reykjavík, but in California life together at home had become unbearable. I felt caught in a net where all fulfillment in life was lacking. I found the workplace unrewarding and the work monotonous. In a letter to my father I put it this way:
I am doing this for her, but the results seem to be nil. I am therefore very keen to quit here, and would then want to begin this study of rural electrification and farmers' use of electricity.

I made this dream come true and applied for a travel grant from the "State Department" in the United States in midsummer 1956 to acquaint myself with rural electrification in the United States. The grant was approved. An extensive program was put together, intended to last six weeks in the autumn of 1956. Before setting off I decided to go to Iceland and try to get my bearings.
"The Alliance of Fear" (Hræðslubandalagið)

In Iceland, momentous events were unfolding on the political scene in 1956. My father had been out of government since 1953. As various historians have argued, my father's mind inclined toward cooperation with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). That vision of his was built on an old foundation and can probably be traced all the way back to the successful coalition of the Government of the Working Classes (stjórn hinna vinnandi stétta) and the origins of both parties. Before the cooperation with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) was ended in the spring of 1956, great clashes took place on the political stage. Alþingi passed a resolution on the departure of the American military from the country in order to "secure the independence and security of the country" and "in view of declarations that there shall be no foreign army in Iceland in peacetime."

Behind the scenes there were no less dramatic maneuvers. Historians have found sources showing that secret talks took place between the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) about an electoral alliance late in the spring of 1955. They probably began earlier, however, for as early as January of that year my father said in a letter:

There is much talk here of a left-wing government, but it is all up in the air, as usual. It will certainly take 1–2 years to put together such a government – if it succeeds at all. – Before that could happen, elections would have to be held in which the left-wing parties (other than the Moscow communists) stood together. – I will not say more about this for now.

This plan held in its essentials. A little over a year later the parties came together and formed the "alliance of the reform parties," as they called it, though others called the cooperation the "alliance of fear" (hræðslubandalagið). In its wake the government resigned and elections were called. The alliance consisted in the parties not running against each other: Progressives voted for the Social Democratic Party's candidates in the towns, and Social Democrats voted for Progressives in the countryside.

It may perhaps strike some modern readers as odd that the Progressive Party is unhesitatingly counted among the left-wing parties in all these old letters. The fact is, however, that no one would have thought otherwise in those years, even though it played the role of a centre party when the views furthest to the right and to the left had to be reconciled, as my father had sometimes emphasized. The Progressive Party has for most of its history been the party that has most identified itself with social solidarity (félagshyggja), and I find it strange that in recent years the party's leaders have avoided mentioning that word.
I was only moderately taken with the joint venture with the Social Democratic Party, although I supported a united front on the left. I wrote to my father in a letter:

I understand that the Progressives and the Social Democratic Party have largely joined together in an alliance. I hope it turns out well, though I somewhat fear that the Social Democratic Party will be a burden. It is certainly necessary to get a united, strong left-wing party in the country, but I am convinced that such a thing will never become a secure reality until single-member constituencies are introduced. It seems to me that the Progressives ought to fight for that.

A policy of neutrality in defense matters was uppermost in my father's mind in this cooperation. Icelanders had followed it before they were drawn into the conflicts of the world war. My father was of the opinion that the military should

leave as soon as peace was in prospect in the world. There is, however, no reason to focus too narrowly on the military-base issue in connection with his interest in cooperation and alliance with the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn). I believe one must not underestimate the common ground my father shared with the ideals of the social democrats. General views on equality in society and the role of the labor movement played, I believe, perhaps the largest part in his attitude toward cooperation to the left. He described those ideals of his in a letter he wrote to me in 1955, a year and a half before the Alliance of Fear (hræðslubandalagið) was formed:

Where government is best in the world and stability is greatest is where a democratically minded working class is strong: Denmark, Norway, Sweden, England, Belgium, Luxembourg, Holland, etc. This is because in all these countries the working class has held power from time to time. That has given it the opportunity to bear responsibility, to see and understand the nature of society, and to fully control how the national income is distributed.

This is sensibly said and with great foresight. It is sad but true that the labor movement in this country did not truly live up to these expectations of my father's in full until the National Reconciliation Agreements (þjóðarsáttarsamningarnir) of 1990. In 1956 I was far from being as optimistic as he was. Not only did I find the labor movement suspect, it even seemed to me there might be reason to split it. I distrusted the new People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið), which was founded by a resolution of the Federation of Labour (Alþýðusambandið) and through the merger of the Socialist Party (Sósíalistaflokkurinn) and the Social Democratic Debating Society (Málfundafélag jafnaðarmanna). Hannibal Valdimarsson, president of the ASÍ, was chairman of the new party, and Einar Olgeirsson was vice-chairman. I considered the People's Alliance communists in disguise. In a letter to my father before the 1956 elections these views of mine come through:

Hopefully these elections will go well. What I fear most is that the Conservatives (Íhaldið) will win a majority, but no doubt that would not be so bad. Then they get all the responsibility for the time being. Perhaps it would teach the left-wing parties the necessity of standing together. I also take a dim view of getting communists in disguise under the banner of the Federation of Labour. Is not the only remedy to found a new Federation of Labour at once and brand this one communist? Can you not get those Social Democrats you have to do it?
Nothing came of a split in the Federation of Labour. A few trade unions protested the leadership's actions and the founding of the People's Alliance, but with little force.
The Left-Wing Government

The elections took place on June 24, 1956, and proved a disappointment for the Alliance of Fear. The parties fell two members short of a majority in Alþingi. It was therefore necessary either to seek the favor of additional parties for a coalition, leave the government to others, or shatter the newly founded alliance. Extensive soundings began, and my father described the situation as follows five days after election day:

The elections went tolerably – though not as well as could have been wished. – Hannibal split off a considerable part of the Social Democratic Party's following – and very much so in many places. You now see all this in Tíminn. What will come of government-formation talks is entirely uncertain. It may be taken as certain that the Progressive and Social Democratic parties will not work with the Independence Party. – But the Independence Party is eager to get into a coalition, even with the "communists," and not least with them – the communists are now called, as you know, a people's front – or alliance. In the coming days or weeks all this will be decided.

The reform alliance had ruled out coalition with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) before the elections, since the two reform parties were aiming for a majority in parliament. Now, however, a new situation had arisen. With the change of policy on the military question an important foundation for such cooperation had been laid, and mistrust had lessened correspondingly. I doubted that the departure of the military was timely, and I therefore dreaded that my father would choose a coalition with the People's Alliance rather than remain out of government.

I had seen news of the election results the same day on television and in the newspapers out west, where foreign news agencies and television stations showed great interest in Icelandic politics for the first time and sent reporters to the scene. The results of parliamentary elections in Iceland have probably never attracted as much attention from the outside world as in 1956. The defense issue was of course the reason. In a letter I wrote to my father two days after the elections, I described my views on the coming formation of a government:

I earnestly hope that you do not form an alliance with the communists. That would completely shut us out of Western cooperation. It would be much better to hold another election in the autumn. Could one not try to form a minority government with a definite platform.

In fact, the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) at first tried to obtain the support of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) for forming a minority government. The People's Alliance, however, held the balance of power and immediately dashed such hopes. The "communists" exploited the situation to the utmost. My father greatly feared that they would form a government with the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn), which he called "the army" („herliðið“). When the government-formation talks had gone on for about ten days, he wrote:

I do not yet know what will come of forming a government. The army is courting the "communists" – the People's Alliance men – heavily. Negotiations are now under way between the Progressives, the Social Democratic Party, and the People's Alliance, but everything is still uncertain. – These matters must of course be resolved in such a way that the settlement will be acceptable to the United States, and indeed I have a suspicion – more than a strong likelihood – that this can be done, if only they can be brought to believe that we are sincere about having the base ready should the need arise. – And we are of course determined that it shall be so. The People's Alliance, even if it were in the government, will have no influence on that.

Later in the same letter my father puts the odds of the parties coming together at "one against two." The left-wing government was formally formed under his premiership barely two weeks later, on July 24. His fellow minister from the Progressive Party was Eysteinn Jónsson, minister of finance. The Social Democratic Party then appointed Guðmundur Í. Guðmundsson, who became foreign minister, and Gylfi Þ. Gíslason, who became minister of education and industry. The cooperation between Gylfi and my father was probably decisive for the founding of the Alliance of Fear. They became good friends and colleagues. Gylfi has often said that he bore great respect for my father and cared for him as a good friend. I know that my father also held Gylfi in high esteem and spoke well of him. He was hurt, however, when Gylfi entered into cooperation with the Independence Party in the Reconstruction Government (viðreisnarstjórnin).

Hannibal Valdimarsson took a seat in the government on behalf of the People's Alliance and was minister of health and social affairs. Lúðvík Jósepsson became minister of fisheries and commerce. My father's ministries were agriculture and justice, in addition to the prime minister's office. With the formation of the government one may say that his dreams of left-wing cooperation had come true. I am not sure that my mother entirely shared his joy. The three years, 1953–56, when my father had been out of government, had been to her liking.
Three months before the elections, four months before the formation of the government, she expressed her mind thus:

The Progressive ministers resigned from the cooperation with the Conservatives (Íhaldið) today, but it is expected that this government will nevertheless stay on until after the elections. Though of course one hopes that the Progressives win the elections, I truly do not want your father to go into government again.
Half a month before the government was formally formed, however, she stood firmly at my father's side, as was always to be expected of her, and gave this verdict on the government-formation talks:
We are all doing fine here at home. Your father is of course hard pressed now, but he is doing well, and one can safely trust that he will do what is right.
The words were meant for me. She probably felt that my letters were not sufficiently supportive of my father around this time.
Out with the Army!

The departure of the military was unquestionably the issue of issues in the opening months of the left-wing government, whether one looks to the public debate of that time or to the government's legacy. The matter of the Defense Force (varnarliðið) was also the point in Icelandic politics on which I differed most with my father in these years. I had had occasion to think a good deal about relations with the Americans because of my seat on the Defense Affairs Committee (varnarmálanefnd) and my work for the foreign minister at Keflavík Airport, as recounted earlier. I had also been involved as an adviser in various of the agreements that were made in the years 1954–1955. When Alþingi had passed the parliamentary resolution on the withdrawal of the military, I wrote:

I have often thought about how our attitude [toward the military] has been much marked by naivety. It was certainly a good deed to get rid of the contractors. But these passport matters and the fence have always seemed to me half nonsense, and at the very least played up far too much. [. . .] I think we should have put more emphasis on economic assistance to remedy the inflation. For example, a loan for the cement factory could easily have been obtained sooner.

In my heart I was of the opinion that the military should leave if it was not needed. However, I did not think its withdrawal was timely, and as long as soldiers were here I felt it right to treat them like men and not like apes in a cage.
A good deal was written in American newspapers about Icelandic affairs and the policy of Alþingi at this time:

Here I have seen in the papers that Alþingi has asked the United States to call the military home. The reception has been mixed. [. . .] I myself am half afraid of this. Certainly I agree that it is good to get the military out of the country, but it must be done with great caution. I also find it regrettable that we should be about to become the first dupe of the new Russian policy. Who are we to decide that the state of the world is now such that no defense is needed? This is of course a great blow to NATO. No chain is stronger than its weakest link, and I understand the Russians gloated greatly at the news.

My father had more faith in a thaw in international affairs. He answered my letter the same day and placed great emphasis on the military having a secure haven and facilities should events take a turn in the world or things look ominous:

It was always stipulated [. . .] that the military would leave – if the outlook improved. The stations would be kept ready here, should the need arise – if the outlook became dangerous. – To maintain the installations and keep up policing naturally requires a large Icelandic workforce – though hardly as many as the number of Icelanders now working on these matters.
In my estimation, my father remained at all times true to this view of his after the left-wing government was formed.

These views met with limited understanding in the atmosphere of the Cold War, and there are still people who seem to be of the opinion that the only Icelanders who were consistent in their stance on the military were those who were either supporters of the United States or supporters of the Soviet Union, come what may. To these people it seems impossible to suppose that Iceland's interests could have lain in maintaining neutrality in dealings with the superpowers.
In the United States there was no holding back in the unflattering descriptions of the opponents

of the military presence. Even the most reputable papers showed this to a considerable degree. I was a loyal reader of The New York Times and considered it among the most reliable media. On the national holiday of the United States, July 4, 1956, things went over the top when the paper called my father the originator of an "anti-American" policy of the Icelanders, and the leaders of the Progressives were called "adversaries of the United States." I sprang to the defense and wrote an article in the paper in which I criticized its reporting and traced the sources to Morgunblaðið and Vísir, the mouthpieces of the conservatives. I then tried to give an accurate picture of the policy of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and of my father.

I sent the article to my father but then received the news that he had already read it in an Icelandic translation in Tíminn, which had also written an editorial about it "and shoved it down Morgunbl.'s throat." In its wake followed exchanges of telegrams between the two papers. He said he had put off writing to me about this so that I would not get mixed up in the game, because "if one is engaged in bitter disputes then one must be on the spot in order to be able to stand one's ground in them [and] always – answer right back." He then added:
You will probably land in such disputes soon enough, but until then it is best and most practical to let others answer after one has stated one's own opinion.

All of it was to no avail, however, where the New York Times was concerned. The great paper continued to lap up all kinds of distortions from Morgunblaðið, and Morgunblaðið then published quotations from the New York Times in the aftermath and considered them confirmation of its own reports. I again sent in comments, but they were nowhere published despite my repeated efforts. That article was in fact considerably more sharply worded than the earlier one. I declared that Morgunblaðið's rhetoric was excellently illustrated by the paper's recent "news item" that the government intended to introduce the death penalty and "that the prime minister himself intended to carry it out." Perhaps this harsh writing by daily newspapers in the United States was one of the surest signs that no thaw was to be expected in international affairs.
Loans and defense matters

Despite what I said in my article in the New York Times, I was worried about the participation of the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) in the left-wing government, as mentioned before. I feared the increased influence of the Soviets in Iceland and urged my father rather toward agreements with the United States. I wrote to my father:

Yesterday I received the telegram about the formation of the government. I thank you for it. Hopefully this will go well. It gives me some apprehension to have the communists in there. It is a fact that in recent years the country has drifted further and further into the economic sphere of influence of the Russians and other communist states. That is bad, for we do not belong there at all. Our culture is entirely Western. No doubt this was the least bad option, but now the cards must be played well, not least in negotiations with the United States.

It is safe to say that major negotiations with the United States characterized the first months of the left-wing government. Over the supporters of Western cooperation hung the Soviets' generous promises of loans. In recent years much has been written about the relationship between the negotiations on the departure of the military on the one hand and the agreements on American loans to the Icelanders on the other. Some of the most remarkable documents on this subject are to be found in the book by the historian Valur Ingimundarson, Í eldlínu kalda stríðsins (In the Line of Fire of the Cold War). Judging by that work, it seems clear that various parties to the matter were prepared to mix together the economic interests and the security affairs of the nation. The United States government appears to have wanted to arrange the negotiations in that way, although there was some dispute about it among government agencies there. Likewise, Vilhjálmur Þór, my father's chief confidant and Iceland's principal negotiator vis-à-vis the American government, seems to have discussed these two things in connection with each other without much hesitation. As to my father's awareness of such a linkage, I consider there to be more doubt. Valur Ingimundarson notes in particular that at the end of October 1956, at a meeting with the American government, Vilhjálmur Þór spoke frankly about economic matters in one breath and defense matters in the other. He did not mention this to my father; on the contrary, he sent him a telegram in which he said, "for a given reason," that the Americans had agreed that negotiations on loans to the Icelanders would proceed "in parallel with" but not "in connection with" the defense matters.

The defense matters may nevertheless have been something other and more than a negotiating ploy on Vilhjálmur's part. It is not inconceivable that he intended the loans to delay the expulsion of the military from Iceland. At the party congress of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) earlier that same year, Vilhjálmur Þór had been one of the few Progressives who wanted to soften the party's policy on the departure of the military. My father was very displeased with Vilhjálmur's proposal to that effect. He therefore worked strongly against him in the matter, and the outcome was that the proposal received the support of only six of the 400 congress delegates. Vilhjálmur stormed out at the result and refused to attend the closing reception. He felt the Icelanders lacked goodwill toward the Americans and believed economic assistance could help in that regard.

Another explanation for why Vilhjálmur discussed economic matters and defense at the same meetings could simply be that he was very anxious for the loans to be obtained. Vilhjálmur's innate ambition on Iceland's behalf was enough on its own to make him a tough negotiator for these necessary loans. The government stood or fell on whether money was obtained for important undertakings.

My father took the view that the presence of a foreign military in Iceland should be determined by security in international affairs, as the defense agreement of 1951 in fact provided. He held unequivocally that there should be no military here in peacetime. That view can be found unchanged in all his letters, before and after the formation of the left-wing government. I therefore think it is safe to assert that whatever the situation with the loan matters, it is beyond all doubt that the invasion of Hungary at the turn of October–November 1956 converted him to the view that it would be premature for the defense force to leave as things stood. The loans thus changed nothing, at least, in my father's belief that negotiations on the departure of the military should be taken up again when peace was once more in prospect. At the end of November 1956 he wrote me the following:

The negotiations on the defense matters will probably be that we come to an agreement to postpone negotiations because of the serious outlook in world affairs. – We long for the time to come – so peaceful that the military may leave – but we are, as we have said many times before and after the elections, equally resolute in standing by agreements made and with the Western nations if there is a state of danger, among other things by allowing them to have a defense force here. This has been our declared policy and we stand by it. According to it, the moment is not now to begin negotiations on departure. Consideration for the communists does not enter into it one way or the other – that is gossip. I have told them, [among other things] before the formation of the government, that this policy would be followed and to that they must bow.
Nothing in these words was new to me. This is what my father had always said.
"No communists here!"

Shortly after the formation of the left-wing government I made my dream of a trip home come true. I stayed in Iceland for about three weeks. Dolly's last words before my trip were that it would mean divorce if I settled in Iceland
or undertook house-building there. After only a few days in Iceland, however, I knew that I would not be budged from those plans of mine. I drew up plans for building a house on Laugarásvegur.

I returned to the United States in September 1956 and went to meet Dolly, who was with her parents in Chicago. I announced my decision to her. She was true to her word and threw the wedding ring at me. I went to the state of Wisconsin the next day and stayed there for a few days. When I came back to Chicago, Dolly had changed her mind and said she now wanted to stand by our agreement and move with the two children to Iceland. I do not recall feeling relieved. Still, I soon resolved to give it another try. I could not see what would become of our children in the United States if they were left there with their mother, as insecure as straws in the wind.

I did not go untouched by my father's formation of a government even though I was on another continent. I flew to Washington in September to collect the travel grant I had been awarded to study the electrification of rural areas. I presented myself at the appointed place as a foreign grant recipient. There, however, everything was in an uproar. I was politely informed that the Americans could not honor the grant to me because my father had formed a government with communists!

This was a major blow to me. I had quit my job to make the trip and had arrived on the spot. This showed me better than almost anything else what big children the Americans can be in foreign affairs. Their first reaction after the formation of the government was to try to isolate the left-wing government within the forum of the Western powers. That was obviously to be done in matters large and small.

I called home and told my father how things stood. He was furious. It shows how ill-advised it was of the Americans to withdraw the grant. Admittedly, this had no lasting effect on my father's attitude toward the United States or the military, but it could have.

The matter was, however, of a different nature than I could have suspected. More than one government agency in the United States had been alerted when I submitted my grant application, and great effort was made to procure the funds before the elections and the formation of the government because of the delicate situation in Icelandic politics. This is revealed in secret documents from archives in the United States, which Valur Ingimundarson has provided to the compiler of this book. Among them is a letter from the American State Department dated May 24, 1956, dealing with the grant applications of three Icelanders, including mine, and informing the embassy in Iceland that no grant money would be available until the following year, and then from funds intended to support cooperation in the field of education. The letter is signed

on behalf of Dulles, the Secretary of State of the United States. A few days later, on the other hand, there is a record of a telegram that Muccio, the American ambassador to Iceland, sent to the Secretary of State on June 5, 1956. It is thoroughly marked as a secret document front and back. In it the ambassador says it is very urgent that the requested grant for me be approved and that it should take effect after July 1. I was, moreover, to be notified of the grant award as quickly as possible. He adds that he considers the matter so pressing that it justifies drawing on the so-called OCB funds if it proves necessary. These were semi-official funds that came directly under the National Security Council and were used in the "fight against communism around the world," as it was probably phrased. Perhaps the generosity of these parties diminished after my father formed his government. I, however, had no idea where the grant promise or the funds came from and thought it absurd that the formation of a government with the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið) in Iceland could affect an engineering study tour of rural America.

I stayed in Washington for two weeks without knowing the fate of the matter. I used the time to educate myself about foreign investment. To that end I regularly sat in the Library of Congress, which was one of the finest libraries in the world and no doubt still is. There one could find an enormous amount of information about investment around the world. I looked particularly at Norway and India. I then wrote a report and sent it home. I believed we should follow in the footsteps of the Norwegians and attract foreign capital to the country so that power could be harnessed and heavy industry begun in Iceland. I sent my reports on these subjects to my father. Some of these writings also appeared as articles in Tíminn. It is comical that this work of mine seems to have been transformed in the retellings and speculations of American embassy officials in Iceland. In Valur Ingimundarson's excellent book, Í eldlínu kalda stríðsins, it emerges that late that same autumn the American ambassador sent out a confidential letter which said:

Hermann Jónasson is said to have examined the attempts of the Egyptians, Indonesians, and Indians to obtain American financial assistance and to have reached the conclusion that the way to get hold of our money is to conceal one's intentions from us.

The outcome of the electrification matter was that the Americans stuck to their position. The State Electricity Works (Rafmagnsveitur ríkisins), however, were interested in getting a report on this subject and paid for the trip. I followed the same itinerary as had been planned. The trip proved very informative.

I traveled mainly through the midwestern states, Michigan, and the Rocky Mountain states. All these areas had recently been electrified, and these observations were therefore very useful for the same kind of project in Iceland. On this trip I also became acquainted with much more than electrification. I became convinced that the United States is as diverse, and its states as different from one another, as the nation-states of Europe. Little recalled the blaze of Broadway lights in the sandblasted small towns, and at times it seemed to me that it would be hard to get further from world civilization than precisely in the heart of the United States, the rural areas of the Rockies. I wrote home that much could be learned from the Americans besides electrification. I thought especially of many things relating to construction, among them social solutions in housing matters. Both the electrification of the countryside and development in housing ended up high on the agenda in the left-wing government's program.

While my journey lasted I received many beautiful letters from Dolly. After she changed her mind about the move to Iceland, it was as if peace settled over everything. Her letters warmed me on my travels:

We miss you very much. The last weekend we had together was so wonderful, and it is so good to be able to think of it when I lie down to sleep in the evenings. [. . .] Even M&M's are no use. I need you.

She also became more positive about the house-building and sent me praise for the drawings, saying she had nothing to add to them. She said nevertheless that she would prefer to buy fixtures and furniture in the United States, if at all possible, and to import vegetables and clothes from there when the time came. Dolly described the children's games and said they missed me and needed my support and guidance.

I told my parents about this change of heart with delight and said Dolly was now quite determined to go home. "Her state of mind in that regard seems to have changed greatly and suddenly for some reason," I remarked in a letter. This was a complete reversal from the preceding winter. What raised hopes most of all was that Dolly's interest in the house-building was kindled. In a letter to my parents is this sentence:
This is certainly good, especially because of the kids, and hopefully it will last.
Ice cream production in Eskihlíð

After the informative trip through rural America I went to Los Angeles and stayed there with the family for what remained of the autumn, until the end of the year. During this time I worked, among other things, on investigations relating to the plans that Pálmi Jónsson and I had for ice cream production in Iceland. The ice cream shop Ísborg had by then been in operation for about half a year. When its setup was well under way, Pálmi came across an article in the magazine "Ice Cream Review" about a new method for producing and distributing ice cream. "At first glance this seemed to me very promising, even to the point that we should be able to capture the bulk of the ice cream trade here," he wrote to me in a letter. He proposed that I immediately look into the possibility of buying equipment for ice cream production by this method.

After some searching I found excellent used machines for ice cream production. Pálmi obtained premises for us in Eskihlíð, in the old cowshed of the farmer Geir Kristjánsson, who was a relative of his. The town had by then encroached completely on the farming operation near Miklatorg and Geir had to move. He in fact bought land from my father in Fossvogur where he had been growing forest. When it came to obtaining an import license, however, we got a flat refusal. As the end of the year drew near, Pálmi then found out that the Milk Distribution Center (Mjólkursamsalan) intended to begin ice cream production and had received an import license even though we had been refused. It seemed to him then that "the bottom had fallen out of our plans for first-class ice cream production." Pálmi said that competing with Mjólkursamsalan was "too risky first and foremost because they would be likely to resort to underselling." He said the distribution center "operates, like other monopoly enterprises, as a kind of state within the state and always gets on its high horse." I did not want to give up at that point; instead I stiffened Pálmi's resolve and sent my father an overview of the matter. The letter is interesting in that it well illustrates my attitudes toward monopoly and the value of competition at this time. Those attitudes seem to have been somewhat at odds with the policy of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn), as appeared at the founding of Íslenskir aðalverktakar, as cited earlier:

December 20, 1956 Dear Pabbi In addition to my letter today, I would like to discuss a certain matter which I have just heard from Pálmi Jónsson. He tells me that the bottom has fallen out of our plans for first-class ice cream production. That is apparently because the Distribution Center (Samsalan) has decided to go into such production. Now it is not that I necessarily mourn missing out on the ice cream trade, for there are many other things to pursue. On the other hand

I find this a serious enough matter for other reasons that I am loath to give it up. Here the total monopoly of the Milk Distribution Center (Mjólkursamsalan) is revealed. Private individuals have had the initiative to blaze a trail for ice cream production at home. Mjólkursamsalan itself has never done anything about it and doubtless never would have, but now its managers are filled with envy at our success and intend to pull the rug out from under us. This is the reward for our having been the Distribution Center's biggest customers in the past year, and it has probably made over 500,000 kr. on Ísborg alone. A good example of the utter lack of enterprise of Mjólkursamsalan can be found here [in the United States] in every grocery store. Here everything is full of dozens of different kinds of cheese, American, Swiss, Danish, Norwegian, and more. They are the greatest delicacies and all of it in appetizing packaging. It has often been mentioned at home that the Distribution Center ought to make more kinds of cheese than the two which have been made since the age of settlement, and which can hardly be said to be packaged at all. All to no avail; the Distribution Center shows no interest, since there is no competition to speak of and these cheeses sell. Here is a field in which the sale of agricultural products could be greatly increased.

The conclusion was that Pálmi and I met force with force. We did not let ourselves be deterred even by the refusal of a license for importing the factory equipment. The machines were brought through customs as ship spare parts. The customs officers had never seen such curiosities but made no objections.
At the United Nations

At the turn of the year 1956–57 something new began. I went to New York, where I took the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) seat at the General Assembly of the United Nations. With that stay I also finished fulfilling the agreement that Dolly and I would spend two years in the United States. Dolly refused at the last moment to accompany me from California and therefore did not come to New York with the children until a month after me. It soon became clear that the thaw that had prevailed in our relations in the autumn was over. She soon began to speak of various conditions she wanted to set for the return home to Iceland. Among other things, she was absolutely opposed to our living at all with my parents while our house was being finished. Despite her consent, it evidently became
increasingly reluctant for Dolly to move to Iceland. This period became difficult for our relationship.

My stay at the United Nations (Sameinuðu þjóðirnar) was arranged, among other purposes, so that I could familiarize myself with housing matters, which were in the spotlight because of the housing shortage in Iceland. For that work, the facilities at the organization were exemplary. The company from Iceland did not hurt either. The governing parties had their representatives at the assembly, and Finnbogi Rútur Valdimarsson sat for the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). He was no less interested in housing matters than I was, and our acquaintance became most enjoyable. Other representatives at the General Assembly were Haraldur Guðmundsson for the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkurinn) and Þórarinn Þórarinsson, who was the representative of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) along with me. I had the most dealings with Finnbogi.

Finnbogi Rútur was calm and moderate, with greying, unruly hair. He smoked incessantly, sat conspicuously low in his seat and speculated, as it was said. I thought Finnbogi was a man of integrity and ideals, and it was instructive to talk with him. My father valued Finnbogi more highly than his brother Hannibal. I came to the same opinion. Hannibal was a warrior in politics, but politicians must not be mere swordsmen. I find it a great flaw in men if they choose war rather than peace when they have both options. The brothers had both taken part in informal discussions with my father in the years before 1950. There, new directions in national affairs and changes to the party system were discussed. Finnbogi Rútur, however, was above all reflective. I agreed with him on many things, and together we drafted a bill on housing legislation in which, among other things, the foundation was laid for the so-called housing loan fund. It was established in the aftermath by law from the Althing (Alþingi).

All that winter at the United Nations I was in a good position to follow the progress of national affairs in Iceland and the fortunes of the left-wing government. In my letters a certain impatience can be detected. I especially commented on economic matters and progress in housing, which I felt was moving slowly. Perhaps I was too rash in these dispatches. In response, my mother sent me sharply worded writings and showed there a side of herself which I have perhaps not done adequate justice to earlier in these pages. She could be hard, resolute and even unsparing. I think few came to know her from this side. I could not say a word against my father.
I cannot refrain from mentioning that I do not much like these constant criticisms of him regarding the government's inaction, as you express in your letters. For even though some young men are

grumbling about this to you and claiming to know best what should be done and what should not be done, it is because they do not realize what difficulties are being contended with and what chaos this government took over from the hands of the previous government. We know, my Denni, that you mean only well by this, but many men here at home, who are fair-minded, say that it is a miracle to have been able to keep the industries running and avert strikes, as has been managed so far. For a great deal of agitation is now being stirred up by opponents.
I cannot resist including my mother's psychological explanation along with these writings. She unhesitatingly traced my criticism of the left-wing government to the troubles in my marriage:

I know that this dissatisfaction of yours, my Denni, stems largely from the fact that you are not in good health and not least from the fact that you are dealing with various difficulties. You need to be able to come home as soon as possible in order to look after your own affairs yourself, not least the building. [. . .] Your Pabbi has done a great deal for you, my dear Denni, and I hope that you always show him full trust and fairness and warmth. He fully deserves it.

My marital difficulties, however, changed little about the matters I found worthy of criticism. Perhaps her presentation nonetheless bore the mark of her knowing that this was in many ways a difficult time in my life together with Dolly. The colitis continued to trouble me and affected all my energy.
In conflict with Thor Thors

Thor Thors was Iceland's ambassador to the United Nations (Sameinuðu þjóðirnar). Thor was an imposing man, commanding in all his bearing. He enjoyed respect and was in many ways an outstanding representative of Iceland. Thor had been at the United Nations since its founding and by 1957 was already among the most experienced ambassadors. Before he ended his long career he had become the "doyen," that is, the ambassador who had served longest at the United Nations and indeed also in the United States. This brought various honors but also duties, for instance that of hosting receptions for new ambassadors. Thor's dignified position had thus become costly for Iceland. In my opinion it is not good for anyone to remain very long in the same ambassadorial post. Ólafur, Thor's brother, however, held a protective hand over him, and others did not dare to disturb him.

I had become fairly well acquainted with Thor on my trips to Washington for the defense affairs department and the Ministry for Foreign Affairs (utanríkisráðuneytið). I had also enjoyed his help in my difficulties over my planned journey through rural America, as described earlier, and he had always treated me well. At the United Nations (Sameinuðu þjóðirnar), however, we soon clashed. Our disputes arose chiefly because I felt Thor neglected to smooth my path and introduce me to the staff of the organization's housing office and to others who might be of use. He did not hand over to me documents that were sent to us at my request, and he failed to send me confirmations of the agreements I made. I complained about this in letters to my father and asked that my role be reaffirmed by the relevant ministers in the government. The ambassador received very firm instructions from Guðmundur Í. Guðmundsson, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, following the first complaint. It stated that I had been entrusted with studying housing matters for the government and that it was his duty to assist me to the best of his ability. Thor reacted furiously, and this gave rise to an exchange of letters between us even though we both worked in the same building. He had, however, to comply with the instructions. History repeated itself three months later when my inquiries turned to technical assistance rather than housing matters. Then a telegram arrived from Gylfi Þ. Gíslason, the Minister of Education, in which Thor was instructed to assist me in examining the United Nations' technical assistance.

While this struggle was going on, I considered the most likely explanation for Thor's conduct to be that he had become too long entrenched in his position. It seemed to me that hardly anyone was allowed to get a chance because of him. It also stung me that Thor belittled the fact that I was studying housing matters. He said he could just as well have done it on his own. It may be that Thor's resentment could be traced to other matters. He was kept out of Vilhjálmur Þór's loan negotiations for the government in the United States, which took place that winter. It has later come to light that the brothers, Ólafur and Thor, were greatly vexed by the left-wing government's success in these borrowings. During my stay, Ólafur Thor wrote his brother, among other things, a letter, as appears in Ólafur's biography, in which he says that with the Americans "the fist and not the palm" had achieved results, since the left-wing government received large loans while the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) government got nothing. That letter was written on Easter Sunday 1957. It is likely that our disputes, Thor's and mine, were at their height around that time. Thor was not a man who appreciated agreements being made without his involvement, least of all with high-ranking representatives of the United States government.
After my time at the United Nations I wrote an article in Tíminn in which I gave an account of the conclusions and resolutions of that session of the General Assembly

session. There I emphasized the positive aspects of the organization. It seemed to me that many good things could be said about the United Nations (Sameinuðu þjóðirnar). I considered the assembly, however, first and foremost a crowded gathering where the representatives of the nations got to voice their opinions. In reality the General Assembly was a gigantic talking shop. I sat on a committee on economic and social affairs. A number of instructive matters were dealt with there, as in the General Assembly itself. It soon became clear to me, however, that everyone had to speak. It seemed to be a point of pride for every nation that its representative put in a word. Much of it was worthless.

There are more sides to the work of the United Nations than endless debates. During my stay I also became acquainted with the organization's offices and staff. There I found that in many places sensible work was being done toward useful and noble goals. I therefore made a distinction between the debates and the work of the United Nations in my view of the organization. I believed that Icelanders could benefit greatly from much of the information that the organization's staff and offices possessed, and that we were missing out on a great deal in that respect through inattention.

I am of the opinion that the United Nations is an important institution and that it is necessary for smaller nations to have a forum in which to express themselves. The current arrangement, however, causes the organization's inefficiency and lack of influence. All kinds of resolutions are passed after long debates without any expectation that they will be enforced. The Security Council, where the great powers have a veto, is the only institution of the United Nations that has power. In 1958 the veto was perhaps natural, since relatively little time had passed since the end of the war. Now, however, the time has come to abolish it. The veto regularly stands in the way of sensible majority decisions. The influence of the great powers in this respect must gradually be reduced. In recent years, moreover, various information has come to light that has eroded trust in the United Nations. It has been asserted that horse-trading and cliques rule supreme in the governance of the organization. It would never have occurred to us, for example, that the Norwegian Trygve Lie, who was the organization's first Secretary-General, was a captive of the United States, as has later come to light.

I have long been firmly of the opinion that it is urgent to reorganize the United Nations. During my time as prime minister I declared this, among other things, at the meetings of the Nordic prime ministers. The Nordic countries were united in that position and pressed for reforms. Hopefully those matters are inching forward, though progress is slow.
I attended the United Nations assembly again in 1992. If anything, the situation seemed to me to have worsened. In addition, the organization's lack of funds was crippling.

Neither the Americans nor the Russians had paid their contributions for many years. The organization has therefore had to scrape by from day to day. Hopefully the new Secretary-General will manage to change this state of affairs and make the United Nations (Sameinuðu þjóðirnar) the institution the world so badly needs.

It should perhaps be added that I was offered the post of Iceland's ambassador to the United Nations when I stepped down as prime minister in 1991. Both Prime Minister Davíð Oddsson and Foreign Minister Jón Baldvin Hannibalsson offered me the job. I had no interest in the office. It must be extremely tiresome to sit out in New York and listen to endless debates falling on the deaf ears of the great powers who in reality control everything. I therefore declined the offer without much deliberation.
The house rises but the trust wanes

I was at the United Nations until the spring of 1957. The family was to go home by ship in June. Two weeks before departure Dolly informed me that she would not go home until she had stayed at least a month with her parents in Chicago. I was not unprepared for such a thing. I agreed to the Chicago trip and cancelled the sea passage. Three days later she called. As usual, the friendship with her mother had broken down, and now she wanted to get away from the city as soon as possible. She nevertheless had to stay there for a few days. We flew home in June after a journey up the east coast of the United States, during which we visited, among others, Dolly's sister in Boston. Shortly before the departure for Iceland, Dolly informed me that she was pregnant. It was not done by mutual decision, no more than before.

In a marriage, small incidents can undermine trust. Dolly constantly surprised me in this respect. In California I was due a refund of over 300 dollars for overpaid income tax. This was a considerable sum that made a difference in the household finances. I had begun to wonder why the payment had not arrived, and to worry, because we had purchased furniture at Dolly's urging without having the money at hand. I then came across the check in Dolly's drawer by chance. It had lain there for some time. She considered this both natural and praiseworthy. I was of an entirely different opinion and told her so. The story repeated itself in New York. That time she forged my name on the back of a check sent from home and deposited the proceeds in a bank. In that case, however, we had agreed to buy a dishwasher with the money. Incidents of this kind poisoned the marriage. I will never understand what drove Dolly to do such things.
When we got home we rented an apartment, which we kept until the latter

part of September. By then the house on Laugarásvegur was to be ready. I worked there most evenings. The work, however, was not finished on schedule, and we then had to move in with my parents. That was difficult, as it was cramped. Every evening my mother made up a bed for me on a sofa in my father's study, while Dolly and the children slept on the floor above during the three months we lived in the house until our own home was ready. Dolly long held this arrangement against my mother and believed she had wanted to keep us apart. I did not find that fair, since lack of space was surely the main reason for my mother's decision.

Our house at Laugarásvegur 15 was largely built while we were in the United States. My companion and friend, Runólfur Þórðarson, bore the brunt of the construction work during the time I was abroad. He went daily to supervise the tradesmen and managed the whole project admirably, as was to be expected of him. He carefully entered every expense in a ledger which I still have. My father also kept an eye on the work and helped with procuring financing.
The end of Ísborg and Pálmi of Hagkaup

Immediately after coming home I set to work building up the ice cream business that Pálmi Jónsson and I owned. Among other things, it fell to me to install the machines and start them up. We soon began producing excellent dairy ice cream. The only trouble was with the fat homogenizer, but before it was over I had become an expert at repairing it.

The ice cream production went quite well, and we bought a car to distribute the ice cream quickly and efficiently. The Milk Distribution Cooperative (Mjólkursamsalan) begrudged us this. In reality it had us in the palm of its hand, since it sold us all our raw materials. We were forced to buy the milk from the Cooperative because farmers were not allowed to sell it directly. We had to pay cash for every króna. Soon MS imported its own production line for dairy ice cream. After the Milk Distribution Cooperative's product came on the market, it controlled the price and kept it down. We saw that there was no future in competing under these conditions. In my opinion this was an ugly example of the abuse of power under the shelter of monopoly. Although I am in favor of a milk distribution cooperative, such things should not happen.

I finally went to Stefán Ólafsson, director of the Milk Distribution Cooperative, and sold him our ice cream factory. We received a considerable sum for it. The Cooperative bought from us the machines, packaging and raw materials, as well as the company's goodwill, which was about a third of the total purchase price. We agreed

at the same time that the Ísborg name would be included in the sale. Pálmi thought the purchase offer too low. We nevertheless accepted it, since the sale price was forty times the company's initial capital.

The Milk Distribution Cooperative (Mjólkursamsalan) apparently threw away all our machines, and the price of ice cream rose by 20% a few days later. The contract stipulated that we could not resume ice cream production, which we considered a great imposition. I raised this with Benedikt Sigurjónsson, supreme court attorney, now deceased. He laughed and said we should have no worries about it. The clause was meaningless, would not hold up in court, and there were a hundred ways around it if we were interested in producing ice cream again.
The Ísborg adventure is the only business venture I have profited from. With that money I was able to pay for a considerable part of the house on Laugarásvegur.

Pálmi Jónsson was an even-tempered, unhurried man. He was a farmer's son and joined the Young Progressives' Association (Félag ungra framsóknarmanna) at an early age. When asked, he indeed said he was a Progressive in those years. He was, however, never seriously political. Pálmi was constantly contemplating business and forever looking for a prospect of profit. I liked Pálmi very well, with the sole exception that his bookkeeping never seemed transparent to me. Really it deserved the name back-pocket bookkeeping, because it was difficult to get information about the finances. Sometimes many months passed before reasonably clear answers could be had about the company's position.

Pálmi founded, among other things, the import company Tungufell hf. with a group of other young Progressives. I had a small share in it. Tungufell mainly imported building materials and whatever else import licenses could be obtained for. Pálmi's enterprising nature, however, took the most varied forms. On one occasion Ísborg's storeroom had become full of shirts. He had then bought up the stock of someone who had gone bankrupt. I never knew whether it was Ísborg's money or other money of Pálmi's that he used for the purchases. In the end, though, I believe everyone got out of Ísborg what was owed them. While the ice cream business lasted, however, we seldom knew how the company stood.

Pálmi and I exchanged many ideas about ventures and businesses during my later years in the United States, 1955–57.
