I was in a key position to investigate whether the ideas could be made reality, and in fact it was nearly a full-time job to follow up on everything. Pálmi wanted to look into building a motor hotel, a "motel": "on the tongue of land where the South and North Iceland roads meet inside the Elliðaár rivers." His idea was that my father would be a participant in the enterprise. Soon the idea came to be called "the hotel affair" in our letters, and I tried to get a meeting with the director of the Hilton chain in New York with cooperation in mind.

We intended to build a hotel of up to 200 rooms. However, we heard of plans by the tradesmen's association and Loftleiðir to build a large hotel, which later became Hótel Loftleiðir. That put an end to our plans.

I looked into more ideas. Ásberg Sigurðsson had an idea for operating a cargo ship in international shipping. I investigated the purchase of such ships and whether an exclusive right could be obtained to transport for the military at Keflavík airport. In that inquiry it emerged that the navy turned out to have ocean-going tugboats for sale. Ásberg said he thought such a boat could be used for whaling, for salvaging ships run aground, or for towing disabled boats.

Among other such matters may be mentioned the purchase of diesel engines that could be installed in the Icelandic "new development" trawlers (nýsköpunartogarar) in place of the obsolete steam engines they had. This could have become a most profitable enterprise. Both Ásberg, who was himself the managing director of a fishing company in Ísafjörður, and Tryggvi Ófeigsson, a trawler owner in Reykjavík, were interested in the purchase of diesel engines.

At one of the last board meetings of Ísborg, Pálmi reported that he was favorably disposed to investing Ísborg's funds in salmon and trout farming at Ísafjarðardjúp. Fortunately, that never came about. He also offered me the chance to found a store in partnership with him and Ásberg, which later received the name Hagkaup. I declined. I had had enough of business and had grown tired of chasing after the bookkeeping from Pálmi. I had also secured the good position of director of the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins) and had developed a greater interest in national affairs. No doubt this was a fateful decision. My whole life would probably have turned out differently had I continued in business with Pálmi and Ásberg. Who knows but that I would be a rich businessman in Reykjavík if I had carried on, and would be called Denni of Hagkaup among people. I chose another path and have never regretted that decision.
Rationing and restrictions

It was not possible to take part in business life in Iceland in those years without feeling the constraints that were placed on freedom of enterprise. Licenses were required for most imports, and everything had to go before sluggish committees and councils. The system was unpopular with the public, and even today it is easy to make it appear to have been entirely unreasonable and based on no rational grounds. It seems to me, however, that historical understanding and realism are often lacking when harsh judgments are passed on the rationing system, as has often been done in recent years. It was no coincidence that rationing was introduced at the proposal of all

the nation's leading economists and with the support of all the political parties in Alþingi. The country lacked most means of production, and capital was wanting in all sorts of basic infrastructure, such as roads, bridges, and electric and hot-water utilities, despite several years of prosperity. The wartime profits had for the most part gone into consumption and into the purchase of trawlers, which could hardly sustain themselves when the markets for fish and other products failed at the end of the war. Fish prices fell enormously and the herring failed, but the fervor at home was as though the golden age would last forever. The Innovation Government (Nýsköpunarstjórnin) of 1944–47 invested first and foremost in fish. Zeal far outran foresight. Of course, the rationing office and the import committee were established out of dire necessity. That must not be forgotten.

I am convinced that giving everything free rein was out of the question. Icelanders simply did not have enough foreign currency for that. Many people no doubt find it hard to understand now how such a situation could arise. Foreign currency is obtained through exports or foreign borrowing, but in those years exports were only a fraction of what they are now, and loans were very hard to obtain abroad. Other nations were no less cautious, with import restrictions and rationing of their own. In Iceland there was also strong opposition to devaluing the currency because of the cut in living standards that undeniably follows. The shortage of foreign currency was therefore a fact. On the other hand, the rationing could perhaps have been lifted somewhat faster than it was.

The import committee could be difficult to deal with, and sometimes impossible, as in the Ísborg affair. It sometimes ended with the system being bypassed, as Pálmi and I did with the ice-making machines. Rationing forced enterprising men to resort to their own devices. In that respect it can be said to have led to corruption. It was asserted that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) maintained a fifty-fifty division rule between them in the committees that allocated various permits. I fear that such rumors had some basis in fact. To tell the truth, such arrangements still exist to some extent between political parties, and they are not improper in all cases. I sympathize with what Bjarni Benediktsson is supposed to have said: that if two men were equally qualified for a job, he would choose the man from his own party.

The problem is choosing the right men. A member of the Independence Party can of course be a good bank director. Too many positions, however, are handed out as political favors. For bank boards, for example, excellent people are often chosen, but they often have little experience of finance or business. Pressure is applied for this or that person to get a plum post. In some cases this leads to people being entrusted with tasks they cannot handle. Admittedly, political appointments to offices and jobs were even more widespread in earlier years than now, when the battles no longer stand between the cooperatives and the merchants.

In those days the Federation (Sambandið) and the merchants divided the market between them. One of the directors of the import office was Jón Ívarsson, a cooperative society manager. He was a very scrupulous man, and no one ever caught him at anything but honesty. I do not doubt, however, that he took good care that the Federation did not come out the loser in the rationing. Sverrir Júlíusson, the deputy director of the office, no doubt did just as well at guarding the interests of the Independence Party men and their clients.

Later the state of the economy changed, and with it the foreign currency situation, which made it possible to lift the restrictions. That began already with the government of Steingrímur Steinþórsson and continued under the Reconstruction Government (viðreisnarstjórnin), but it was not solely that government's doing, as is sometimes implied. It was only natural to reduce rationing and restrictions as the nation grew stronger. In that connection, however, it must also not be forgotten that the economic reforms of the Reconstruction Government rested to a considerable extent on extensive financial support from international institutions and the government of the United States.
"She Is Leaving the Country"

After my return home in June 1957 I worked on the construction of a high-voltage line from the transformer station at Elliðaár to the cement factory at Akranes. It was a very enjoyable job. For that work I had bought a special pole auger in the United States, which proved very useful.

In addition I attended to the many projects I have mentioned before. Some were time-consuming, like the ice production. In the evenings I worked myself to the bone on the house construction. The workday was therefore often long, and there was little time for the family.

I also tried to pursue my various hobbies, such as fishing and the outdoors. My father had bought the farm Klettur in Reykholtsdalur in 1945 and carried on extensive forestry there. He had also built a very good summer house there. The fishing was good in those days in Reykjadalsá. I went there with Dolly and the children. She, however, found fault with everything at Klettur — the weather was bad, the roads there poor, there was nothing to do, and so on. In fishing she had no interest. This disappointed me.

As mentioned earlier, Dolly told me she was expecting a child as our journey home to Iceland approached in the summer of 1957. Shortly after we came home she informed me that she had arranged with an obstetrician in Chicago to deliver the baby. She therefore wanted to go abroad to give birth, and in this connection had much to say about how primitive everything was in Iceland, the health service like everything else. I saw that it would be pointless to argue with her on this matter, and
decided to try to grant her wish despite the very great expense. The birth was expected around the middle of December.

In November Dolly began preparing for her trip. She then informed me that she intended to take the two children with her to the United States. She planned to stay with her parents for four months and said she believed this would be good for the marriage, the children, and herself. I flatly refused. Not only did I think it unwise to send two young children with a woman in her eighth month on such a long and arduous journey, but I also knew that the situation between Dolly and her mother would soon become intolerable once they got to Chicago, and that the presence of the children would hardly improve matters. Their noise and commotion had always irritated the old couple. I therefore told Dolly that I considered this ill-advised, not least for the sake of the children themselves. Moreover, I suspected that it could prove difficult to get Dolly back home to Iceland if she went away with the children. As far as I knew, she accepted my reasoning.

One evening the telephone rang shortly before midnight. I had fallen asleep but woke at the ringing. I was sleeping alone in my father's office, as mentioned earlier. A friend of mine was on the line and told me that Dolly was on her way to the airport with the children. I hurried there at once and arrived at the Loftleiðir terminal at the same time as she did. The children were with her, barefoot and poorly dressed. A crowd of people saw me take the children and carry them out to my car.

Dolly had taken the kids and the suitcases to a friend of hers earlier that evening while I stepped out. When I came home she said they were asleep. She herself said she was going to finish something before going to bed. After I had fallen asleep she fetched the children and set off for the airport. She had prepared everything carefully. My parents were not at home that evening, but for some reason Dolly blamed my mother for her failure to spirit the children away, and maligned her widely around town on those grounds.

Dolly was not deterred, however, and tried again to get tickets from Loftleiðir shortly afterwards. I prevented that by speaking with the airline's management. She then finally gave up her escape attempts.

We moved into the new house at Laugarásvegur 15 on December 15 with all the fuss that moving entails. It was a close call, for the next day, December 16, 1957, a son was born to us in the maternity ward of the National Hospital (Landsspítalinn). The birth went well.
The Stratagem Succeeds

Laugarásvegur 15 is a splendid single-family house. It is in the rear row of houses along Laugarásvegur, which I liked because there we were farther from the traffic. Under the main floor at the front is a double garage. From the United States I brought an electric garage door opener. It was one of the first in this country and was considered a great "luxury."

High steps lead up to the main floor. Into them I installed heating to melt snow and ice. That was considered no less remarkable an innovation. On entering, one comes into a foyer, and beyond it is a spacious hall. To the right one enters the bedrooms. Innermost is the master bedroom with its own bathroom, and off the corridor two children's rooms and another bathroom. From the hall one enters a large kitchen in the American style, even with both 220- and 110-volt outlets for the various American appliances we owned. At the end of the kitchen is a breakfast nook and a kitchen entrance. To the left from the hall one enters the living room with a large fireplace at its center, and finally from the living room into the dining room.

Beneath the main floor is a basement, which was only ready for carpentry when we moved in. A staircase from the hall was planned, but the stair opening was closed with a temporary floor. In it was a hatch so that one could get down into the unfinished basement.

The turn of the year often brings optimism. In January 1958 the situation at home seemed to me to improve. After Dolly came home to the new house from the maternity ward she was more cheerful and optimistic than before. Admittedly, the occasional unpleasant incident occurred. Several times I found the children home alone and crying when I came home for lunch. Dolly had then dashed off to the swimming pools (Sundlaugarnar) out of boredom and did not come home until much later. She later complained that I had been distant, indifferent, and cold during those first weeks after the birth of our third child. Dolly rarely mentioned such things until long afterwards. It also soon became apparent that my optimism was built on illusions.

In mid-February 1958 I went to the United States on account of my work. Three days after I arrived in New York I received a telephone call from the airport there. Dolly had arrived and had the three children with her. She could hardly get a word out on the phone for excitement. It was easy to hear that she felt she had accomplished a major feat.

Dolly said she had decided on the spur of the moment to go abroad because she had heard that I was being unfaithful to her. I am convinced that this was not the real reason, but rather that she wanted to show and prove that she could leave the country with the children. She had prepared the trip carefully and with good advance.
I could see that from her passports and her travel authorization. She had even had a telegram sent to herself from New York on the day I left. It read as follows:
Come at once with the children. Your Pabbi seriously ill in Chicago. Denni.

Dolly is said to have gotten a friend of hers on Long Island in New York to send her this telegram. She intended to use it if anyone questioned her movements or tried to stop her. She had managed to obtain tickets with Pan American from Keflavík Airport. I also discovered that she had carefully prepared the ground at home with the most incredible stories about me and my parents. According to them I was governed by my parents in each and every thing; she claimed that they were against her and that I was unfaithful to her, to touch only on the biggest points. In Iceland no one heard of her movements until the day after she left. In the days before the trip, little Jón had in fact often telephoned his grandmother and complained that he was home alone with his siblings. Dolly must then have been preparing the departure. Jón was six years old at the time.

I was deeply shaken by these latest events. I tried to get her to turn back at once. She barely deigned to answer me and would listen to no reason. On the trip I had, among other things, intended to consult doctors about my colitis. Dolly's journey abroad upended those plans. The doctor's visit was postponed and the abdominal attacks grew worse. The pains were as if a wedge had been driven through my middle. I sent my parents a telegram about how matters stood, that the children were safe and sound, and that I hoped everything would turn out all right. I promptly received a worried but unequivocal reply:

From this point on I cannot see that there is any way, or that anything can be right, except to settle this whole wretched business, to try to begin a new life, after repeated sacrifices for new attempts. To tell the truth, our one consolation – for your sake – was that this would then have to lead to it all ending with the two of you finally deciding to live your lives each for yourselves. I can see nothing else but that a complete divorce is the only thing that now comes into consideration – you must be able to finish your trip and see the doctors – that must not fail – but she of course continues on to Chicago. When you come home these

matters will of course be settled formally, and the ruling on child support in that regard must be followed – if she gets the children. Even if you two wanted to try to live together after this, it will be no life for you or the children. Through discord you have for the time being lost your health, and indeed all the conditions in the home are otherwise intolerable to any human being. Nor is there any question of sacrificing one's life for the children, for it does them outright harm that there is conspicuous discord between the parents – which they so often witness. [. . .] It often takes a tremendous effort to begin a new life, but sometimes it is the only feasible way. – [. . .] This is my conviction, and your mother's, after careful reflection – though of course it is difficult to give advice to others. But after long experience of what has happened time and again in your life together, the matter seems all but clear. – After deliberation I also considered it right to tell you this. Your mother sends you her greetings – and we pray God to go with you. – Your father

I could not bring myself to follow my parents' sound advice, but tried to the utmost. From New York I followed Dolly to Chicago in case it might serve to change her mind. She would not discuss any such thing and was thoroughly pleased with herself and her position. She could not be induced to say when she intended to return, or indeed whether she intended to at all. In the end I had to give up and leave my wife and children behind in the United States. I returned to Iceland after an absence of three weeks.

On coming home I made it my first task to send Dolly all the necessary airline tickets and asked her to come home. It proved fruitless. She answered that I would have to convince her that I would secure her future happiness. At the same time she pointed out to me that I could prove my love and care simply by moving out there to them. I saw no future in that and went nowhere. My hopes were shattered.
Eighth Chapter
DIVORCE AND THE BATTLE FOR THE CHILDREN

The marriage was hopeless and beyond saving. I gradually came to realize this. After Dolly's journey abroad, little else came into consideration but divorce. Yet other thoughts weighed on me no less. I found it extremely hard to accept that the children would be in Chicago. They deserved better than the insecure future and straitened circumstances to which I feared they would be condemned in their mother's keeping. I therefore kept trying to get her to come home with the children.

I did not feel well in the months that followed. I spoke of it with few people, though. The void that formed in my life I filled by working day and night. I had taken over the position of managing director of the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins) in December 1957, and a great deal of work came with it. The laying of the high-voltage line to Akranes was soon completed. That was the only project of Verklegar framkvæmdir in which I took part as an engineer. When Verklegar framkvæmdir was founded I had intended to work myself on the company's operations and projects. It turned out, however, that I attended only one board meeting before I moved to the United States at the beginning of 1955. After coming home I likewise did not take up full-time work for the company, but kept my seat on its board.

I corresponded with my wife during this time that we were apart. I told her that the longer she stayed in the United States, the more damage it would do to the relationship between us. In her letters, on the other hand, she acted as if there were nothing abnormal about our separation. Dolly lived at first with her parents, but as usual it soon came to a clash between her and her mother, and she then rented herself an apartment a short distance from them. I received two letters from her mother in which she said I must come out and fetch the children, for they were living in the utmost poverty. She told me that Dolly worked outside the home, was rarely at home, and left the care of the children to strangers. She herself said
she had no choice but to visit her grandchildren often so that they would get something decent to eat.

Our son was christened in Chicago in my absence. Dolly had told me that he was to be named Hermann Neil. Long afterwards I learned that he had been christened Steingrímur Neil. The baptismal certificate I have never seen. Neil was our third child.

Dolly saw a psychologist the whole time she was in Chicago. He wrote to me once and said he was about to travel to Europe. In the letter he asked me to come over to Copenhagen on a particular day for a consultation with him, for as he put it: "I believe that I have a complete solution to all your problems."\ I politely declined. I had had my fill of psychologists' miracle cures.

As the separation wore on, Dolly's letters became warmer and friendlier toward me. That was nothing new to me. It was always so when she had been away for some time, whether it was I or her mother who was involved. Then she could seem to want little more than to be reunited with the one she held dear from afar. When it came to the point, however, the story was always the same. As for me, matters stood quite differently. The more time I had for reflection, the more determined I was to divorce. I discussed that decision both with my parents and with friends, and all agreed that divorce was best for everyone. The worries centered on what would become of the children and on their welfare. I could not bear the thought of losing them.
Day and Night

During the time Dolly was in the United States with the children I worked a great deal in connection with two companies in which I had a share. These were Perlít hf. and Bruni hf., which unfortunately were not long-lived. Perlít is a name we gave to expanded perlite. Perlite is rhyolite and has the property that when it is ground and heated the stone expands and forms small, uniform spheres. Perlite spheres are light and fire-resistant. Perlite resembles pumice except that the uniform spheres make it more serviceable. Perlite is used in lightweight concrete, especially in tall steel-frame buildings. There was a considerable market for perlite in the United States.

The geologist Tómas Tryggvason was the first to draw attention to the fact that there is a fair amount of perlite in this country. Among other places, he believed there were good deposits in the so-called Prestahnjúkur on Kaldidalur, between Geitlandsjökull and Langjökull.
\ "I believe I have a complete solution to all your problems."

In 1955 a sample of the material had been examined in the United States and it seemed promising. The leading figure in these investigations was a certain Alfred Hedefine. He had, however, lost interest in the idea of processing when Bruce Gonser from Battelle, whom I have mentioned before, put me in touch with him in 1956. After that, the wheels began to turn once again.

Tómas and I, on the other hand, did not realize that Hedefine was in constant contact with representatives of the American State Department regarding these plans. Confidential documents from American archives, which Valur Ingimundarson has obtained and made available to the author of this book, show that officials of the department warned Hedefine against investing in Iceland because of the communists' participation in the left-wing government in 1956. I was entirely unaware of this extensive consultation between Hedefine and the American authorities.

During my visit to Iceland in the autumn of 1956, I discussed a possible extraction permit at Prestahnjúkur with my father, who had by then become prime minister. He was supportive and asked me to raise the matter also with Lúðvík Jósepsson, the minister of fisheries and commerce from the People's Alliance (Alþýðubandalagið). I went to meet Lúðvík, who declared his support, and subsequently the extraction permit was approved by the government, along with approval for road construction and the necessary works. All of this is meticulously recorded in the confidential documents of the American State Department, as strange as that may otherwise seem.

After my return home in the spring of 1957, I then pushed for the founding of a company to extract and export perlite from Prestahnjúkur. The founders were my colleagues at Verklegar framkvæmdir, along with Runólfur Þórðarson, my brother-in-law Sveinbjörn Dagfinnsson, and Tómas the geologist. To manufacture building components from the perlite we founded another company, Bruni hf. Later, Ásgeir Jónsson, who was one of the owners of the coal crane in Reykjavík, and Gunnar Guðmundsson, who runs the heavy-haulage company GG, joined the group of shareholders. In the United States, Alfred Hedefine founded the company Viking Minerals Inc. to bring the perlite to market in the West.

We began trial extraction from Prestahnjúkur. First we went with a bulldozer up to Kaldidalur and laid a rough road to the mountain, right by the source of the river Geitlandsá. Then we transported 100 tons of rhyolite and stored it in the coal yard. These transports were not only discussed in the so-called serious media but also made their way into the pages of the satirical magazine Spegillinn. There it was said that a "financially powerful limited company" had broken faith's monopoly on moving mountains by securing "the right of first refusal to a certain mountain, which until now has stood on Kaldidalur, but will not be standing there much longer."

Many are alarmed by this new venture and can see plainly, and through the mischief of it, that if this goes on for long, the whole country will be sold before it is over, and it would be better to sell it wholesale, as has been much discussed in recent years, rather than to use this cunning method for the sale.

Viking Minerals had experiments carried out on the utilization of the material, but the results were unfortunately not as good as we had hoped. The material was too variable in quality. Our partners believed they would have difficulty competing with the better perlite that was on the market in the United States. We therefore dropped the matter and dissolved the companies.

I worked hard on this project. Among other things, I walked from Kaldidalur down to Hvalfjörður with an engineer from the Road Administration (Vegagerðin) to examine possible road routes. Our idea was to transport the material along that route and out to Hvítanes in Hvalfjörður. The final version of the plan was to transport the rock by aerial cableway. We made extensive plans for the quarrying, transport, and sales. We invested about 100,000 krónur in the companies, which was a considerable sum.

Around the same time, Konráð Guðmundsson of Hótel Saga and Eyjólfur Konráð Jónsson, member of parliament, invited me to take part in founding a company to operate a health spa hotel in Hveragerði. Quite thorough studies were made, and for a long time the prospect seemed promising. In the end, however, nothing came of these plans. I myself had little involvement in these ideas except as a shareholder. I was employed full-time as director of the National Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins) and had largely set aside the entrepreneur in myself. The urge for enterprise found its outlet elsewhere. My work at the Research Council took all my time as the years went on. I ended up working less in business, engineering, and construction in Iceland than I had intended as a young man.
The Love of My Life

When half a year had passed since Dolly went to the United States, I decided there was nothing to do but ask for a divorce. I wrote to her that I would come over and we should settle our affairs. This was in August 1958. In that month an important change had occurred in my life that ruled out anything other than divorce. I had met another woman. When my wife unexpectedly came to Iceland a month later, I had fallen in love, for the first time in many years.

Guðlaug Edda Guðmundsdóttir was private secretary to Jakob Gíslason, director of the State Electricity Authority. Under him at that time were the State Electric Power Works (Rafmagnsveitur ríkisins), the electrical inspectorate, geothermal drilling, and more. In my work as director of the Research Council

(Rannsóknaráð ríkisins), I frequently had business at meetings with Jakob. Edda says that the girls at the office had remarked that engineers seemed on the whole to be good-looking men, and that this applied especially to one particular committee. I had a seat on it. At the first meeting, the first words passed between Edda and me. She came in with a tea trolley on wheels, looked at me and asked: "May I offer you coffee or tea?" I looked up and said: "Tea, please." That was all there was to it that time.

As I said before, I wrote off the marriage soon after Dolly left the country in February. At first I worked hard and kept to myself. As the summer went on, I went out more often to enjoy myself on weekends with my acquaintances and friends. We often went to the National Theatre Cellar (Þjóðleikhúskjallarinn), which had by then become a popular spot. Hótel Borg and the Independence Party House (Sjálfstæðishúsið) were also places we frequented. After a dance I sometimes invited a good group back to Laugarásvegur. It was all good-natured, though often lively, since there were great merrymakers in this group. These parties of mine were festivities among good friends, but by no means debauchery.

On an August evening I saw Edda at the Independence Party House and recognized her at once. She was there with her friends. I was in the company of the Clausen brothers and they introduced us. Edda is their cousin. My friends soon realized that I had taken a liking to this girl. They therefore tried, without success, to get her to join the group going to Laugarásvegur after the dance. She declined. I was somewhat restless over the following days, but the very next weekend we met again. That was at the National Theatre Cellar on August 31, 1958. Örn Clausen then managed to get her to come with us to Laugarásvegur along with a good group. It was still summer, so the night was bright. As the others began drifting off homeward, we were still sitting and talking together. I trusted this girl at once and confided in her about my marital difficulties. We both remember this, Edda and I, because she lost an earring somewhere on the floors of my home. It was made of silver and a great favorite of hers. We searched for it for a long time, but without success.

At the next meeting at Jakob Gíslason's office after that good evening, I presented Edda with new earrings, the most beautiful silver earrings I could find. This was the beginning of our acquaintance. I was thirty and she was twenty-one.

I was immediately captivated by Edda's looks and manner. She outshone other girls, being both shapely and elegant in all her bearing. I fell for her charms. There is probably no way to explain how such a thing happens. It is hard to put into words why one is drawn to another person. As our acquaintance grew closer, I thought ever more highly of this young woman. Edda was well balanced and dependable in each and every way. Jakob Gíslason, her boss, praised her to the skies for her diligence, precision, and goodnatured

intelligence. I heard the same from others. Our acquaintance deepened as time went on. Nevertheless, we took things slowly in many respects, since I was still married. I did take Edda out to dinner, and we had good times together. With every meeting, our mutual respect, admiration, and love grew still further.
Dolly Returns Unexpectedly

After I sent Dolly the letter to the United States in which I asked for a divorce, I heard nothing from her until the morning of September 25. As I was leaving home, I was handed a telegram that had been sent from New York the day before. It said simply:
On my way home. Dolly.

The message had a great effect on me. My first thought was to get word to Edda. That was easier said than done, because her family had moved into a new home where a telephone had not yet been installed. So I called Örn Clausen, as I always did when much was at stake, and got him to deliver a letter to her from me. I wrote it in haste and made many slips of the pen. Alongside the corrections of the scribbles I wrote "nervous" by way of explanation. I wanted to assure Edda that nothing would change between us despite my wife's arrival. The letter read as follows:

Dear Edda This morning I got the worst news I can remember. At 10 o'clock came a telegram: "Coming home" – Dolly. It was just as Pabbi said: "Since you have written to her not to come and that you want a divorce, you can be certain she will come." I have tried to reach you this morning. I don't want this to take you by surprise. Örn is going to run over with this letter. The plane arrives in half an hour. Dear Edda, when I am free of this foolishness of mine — and that shall be as soon as humanly possible — you will once again have no peace from me. I love you, my dear, more today than yesterday; and yet I thought it was not possible to love you more than I did yesterday. Your Denni.

Two hours after I read the telegram from Dolly, she landed with the children. I met them at the airport. Dolly looked quite well and was strikingly well dressed. The children, on the other hand, seemed to me pale and drawn. Jón stammered and had nervous tics. Herdís was withdrawn and shy of people, which she had never been before. I was very glad to see the children. As for Dolly, however, I felt little joy. Nor did I hold any hopes for the future of our marriage. I had become convinced that divorce was the only solution.

We did not really get back together; rather, we lived like two strangers in the house. Apart from my work outside the home, I spent much time on carpentry and other work on the house. I was pressing to get the basement into usable condition with a view to renting it out, and so I would often disappear after supper down through a hatch in the floor of the hall. It was while doing this carpentry that I best found time to think, and I grew firmer in my conviction that divorce was the only way.

I told Dolly of my conclusion and tried to discuss the matter with her. It was pointless. She let my words go in one ear and out the other, and even went so far as to threaten suicide if I divorced her. If she sensed any criticism, or if anyone mentioned her trip abroad, she was both astonished and scandalized. The letters her mother had written me she retrieved and put away in a locked drawer. Most of the letters Dolly herself had written me in those last months also disappeared.

After Dolly's return, I carefully considered the paths I could take to secure the children's safety and future. I was filled with dread at the thought of Dolly getting all of them. I had, however, little in hand with which to demand custody of them, and I feared that litigation would lead to great harshness and hostility. At the same time, I ran the risk that she would get custody anyway, and that I would be worse off for having tried. I felt certain that Dolly would rush away at the first opportunity and thus prevent me from following their upbringing. I therefore decided to try the path of negotiation.
"I Want a Divorce"

After fruitless attempts to discuss divorce, I wrote Dolly a letter. I handed it to her on October 10, 1958, about two weeks after her arrival in the country. The next day I left for a conference in Paris. In the letter I express the hope that she will read it, even though nothing had come of trying to talk with her in the preceding days, any more than at other times. The essence lay in these three words:
"I want a divorce." I said I would gladly resolve our affairs peacefully, because I did not want sympathy and goodwill to turn into bitterness and ill will. The letter continues:

I have tried to tell you, Dolly, that I no longer love you. Perhaps you are right that I have not done so for two or three years. To that it must be added that I no longer trust you, and the thought of living with you and being your husband strikes me as very repellent. With that in mind, I ask you to realize that I could never make you happy here in Iceland. I could neither fulfill your desires [. . .] nor be faithful to you.

I said I had had seven months to think things over on my own and had reached a conclusion after careful reflection. I was fully convinced that if we tried to go on living together, it would only destroy our lives and the children's.

I am ill, and I have been getting worse every day recently, with constant pain in both sides and through my chest, just as before in California, which was the most tormented time I have ever lived through. [. . .] In California I came close to losing my faith in life. I do not want that to happen again. I want to regain my former health and once more have something to live for.

Enclosed with the letter was a draft of divorce terms. Dolly later removed my copy from my desk and used it to submit a falsified version of the above letter in our custody case, which soon got under way. In the letter I offered Dolly full custody of our children, child support, alimony, and a house in the United States, and in addition her share of the house on Laugarásvegur, in return for the children being allowed to visit me at least every other year and my being permitted to visit them whenever I myself wished.

I love these children more than anything else. I do not want to destroy their lives by being an unhappy and nerve-worn father to them in a marriage with an unhappy and nerve-worn mother. I would, however, gladly keep at least one of them. That would be worth more to me than anything else I can imagine. But to reach a peaceful solution I am prepared to leave them all to you. More than that I cannot do.

I also argued that the children would be better provided for here at home, but that if there were no alternative to her taking the children to the United States, I considered it necessary that various conditions be met, both of a financial nature and for the purpose of enabling me to follow the children's upbringing. I planned to sell our house on Laugarásvegur and obtain a currency transfer in order to secure a house and sound finances for my family in the United States. The offer was contingent on such a currency transfer being granted.

In Paris my mind was occupied not only with the divorce but no less with my love for Edda. I had brought with me a photograph of her that I never tired of looking at and admiring. In the evenings I tried to put my feelings into words in letters:

Dear Edda! I cannot go to sleep without "talking" to you. [. . .] I sit here looking at you; I miss you, I love you. Oh, how wonderful it would be to have you here. Then the rain outside would turn to sunshine in my heart. What might you be doing tonight? [. . .] Oh, I long for you, my dear; what am I to do with myself? It would be wonderful to have you here. We would go out and enjoy ourselves, but not for too long, because we would look forward to being alone together, just you and I, I and you. (Poetic of me!) Long hair suits you well, but your hair is beautiful however it is, tousled or combed. This is the last sheet. How do I use it best? To tell you once more that I love you? Yes, I think so. I love you and I miss you, my darling. Your devoted Denni

Immediately after my return from Paris, I looked into the possibility of a currency transfer so that my offer to Dolly could stand. I was told that it was out of the question to have more than a small share of the assets transferred, in all likelihood only the legally mandated child support. Nor did Dolly show any spirit of reconciliation. In a letter from this time I describe my state of mind once it was clear that I could hardly provide for them in America.
I then [withdrew] my letter, for I felt that for the sake of my conscience I could never consent to Sara [Dolly] taking the children to the United States, into the miseries that would await them
there, not least since it had been shown that they would not be provided for financially.

Shortly afterwards I wrote to Dolly and proposed that she stay here at home with the children. I offered to let her live in our house and to provide for them so that they could live a respectable life. This was an attempt at a settlement on my part. It was never answered. We had long since ceased to live as husband and wife. I slept on a sofa in the living room and Dolly in the bedroom.
Suspicion and a War of Nerves

I told Dolly of my love for Edda immediately after her arrival in the country, when we discussed divorce face to face for the first time. No doubt it acted as oil on the fire of conflict that flared up in its wake. Yet I have never regretted that honesty. There was plenty of suspicion all the same. The following months were beyond belief, and those disputes fell not least on those who least deserved it, the children and Edda. She had to endure a great deal in the months that followed.

In the wake of my demand for divorce, one can say that everything went up in flames. Dolly repeatedly engaged in behavior that I felt strengthened my claim to custody of the children. She left them evening after evening and was away from home whole nights. She said she could not look after them any better than I looked after her. We also attended reconciliation meetings with the Reverend Jakob Jónsson. There I declared myself certain that the marriage was over. Dolly and I quarreled fiercely.

While I lived on Laugarásvegur, Dolly kept a watchful eye on all my movements. That did not, however, prevent me from meeting Edda now and then. As I said before, I worked a great deal in the basement of the house in the evenings. One evening I was painting in the basement when Dolly said she was going out. A girl was called in to look after the children. When I had finished painting, I decided to dash over to see a friend of mine in the west end of town, even though I was in my painting overalls. I stayed there about half an hour. When I came out together with him and several others, who had asked me to drive them to Hótel Borg on my way home, we found Dolly lying in the car. She had crawled into the trunk of the car earlier that evening in order to spy on my movements. There she had waited the whole time while I painted and visited my friend. This was during the period when we were attending reconciliation meetings with Reverend Jakob. She promised not to repeat this trick. Nevertheless, a few days later I came upon her laying a blanket in the trunk of the car. After
it became a rule with me to check the trunk every time I moved the car.

I worked ever more often at the office in the evenings or visited my friends in order to avoid being at home. I took my coat and walked out whenever things flared up. On one occasion Dolly broke four or five vases and a statuette. She had then fallen out with little Jón and I had meant to step between them. I then took the children to their grandmother. Every day I was on the verge of moving out. It was only at the pastor's urging that I postponed it until after Christmas. I rented an apartment at Lynghagi 4.

After I moved to Lynghagi at the turn of the year, I persuaded Edda to stay there more or less. From the beginning I took care to conceal nothing from her about my troubles in the marriage, which I regarded as a former marriage. Edda's arrival was not what made me decide to file for divorce. I had already settled that with myself. My love for her, however, made me even more resolute in my position. After we met, anything other than divorce was out of the question. Edda and I were determined to marry. My parents thought very well of that match.

In the wake of my moving out of the home, Dolly aimed her spears ever more at Edda and her family. On one occasion Böðvar, Edda's brother, found Dolly under the kitchen table in their mother's house. She had crawled in through a window from scaffolding that stood outside. Dolly was most likely looking for me, but neither I nor Edda was in the house. If we ventured to the cinema, we could just as well expect Dolly to be waiting outside accompanied by a photographer to take pictures of us. They were probably meant to serve as evidence in the custody case, which we both realized was brewing. In the litigation that followed, however, I never denied my relationship with Edda.

In my rented apartment at Lynghagi there was no peace either. Dolly talked her way in with the people on the lower floor and pressed against both windows and doors with peeping and loud noises. It happened that she sat outside the door of my apartment all night to try to catch Edda and me walking out together in the morning. On one occasion she called the police to the scene and expected them to write a police report on my adultery. The police, however, showed understanding that this was a private matter. Dolly nonetheless described this at great length in a letter to the Child Welfare Committee of Reykjavík (Barnaverndarnefnd Reykjavíkur). Unfortunately this was not the last time the police were called in.

These blows naturally put great strain on my new relationship with Edda. It did not help matters when her family became roughly entangled in the course of events, as I have described. Dolly showed there the extremes of her nature, but in

Edda, on the other hand, I found a balance and trust that I valued greatly. Naturally Edda often had a hard time and was anxious, since we could always expect the worst. Many would doubtless have retreated from the field, but Edda never flinched. She supported me without hesitation and thus stood by our vows of a shared future. That convinced me of her steadiness, faithfulness and love. I had gained a life companion.
"My Marriage"

In those autumn months of 1958 my father's government, the left-wing government, collapsed with great commotion. Shortly after the break-up of the government, further developments also began to unfold in my divorce case. That winter was a time of personal reckoning. My father was much preoccupied with finding explanations for what had gone wrong in the coalition. I was no less occupied with settling accounts with the events of recent years.
It is wholesome and perhaps necessary to come to an understanding of why my marriage to Sara Jane (Donovan) (Dolly) has failed. I intend to attempt to do so here below.

Thus began my self-examination on 19 typewritten pages. In one corner of the first page stands: "Written in Jan.–Feb. 1959 for my own instruction," handwritten in ink. The heading was simply "My Marriage," and there I traced my relationship with Dolly from our first acquaintance to the beginning of 1959. Much of what has been said about my marriage in earlier chapters is drawn from those pages. There I say in the opening words:

It is difficult to face the fact that the marriage has failed when three lovely and innocent children are involved. It is first and foremost their future that must be borne in mind, and which one must try to secure, when the account is settled.

I put this report down on paper to bring order to my thoughts about the marriage, Dolly and the children. In doing so I wanted to try to let reason and good sense prevail to the extent that it was possible. Naturally it was difficult, and in fact impossible, to keep emotions out of these matters. I stood in the middle of the dispute, and new events I recorded on paper as they happened. In one of the last sections of the report I say:

Now she has begun another activity in earnest. She intends to win over the children's minds by disparaging me in their hearing. She keeps harping on the claim that I do not love them, that I have run away from them, that I want nothing to do
with them, etc. She has also taken up working against their grandfather and grandmother in the same way, with the result that Jón hardly dares to go there for a visit.
My writings end with a short section that bears the heading: Conclusions.

In reality, conclusions are unnecessary. The conclusion was divorce. But why? Probably chiefly because all trust in the marriage is gone. Dolly has never trusted anyone, not her parents, not me, no one. One never knows what to expect from her; constant uncertainty. Little by little I have stopped trusting her and begun constantly to expect the worst. That, of course, is impossible in a marriage. Dolly is very unbalanced and given to extremes. She can be fine when everything is going smoothly, but as soon as any shift in the balance occurs, she goes to utter extremes and can be highly dangerous to herself and those close to her. Dolly always throws gasoline on the fire. I feel sorry for Dolly and wish her, with all my heart, happiness in the future. I am very sorry that I have not succeeded in making up to her what she has missed out on, as I had dreamed of doing. Unfortunately, what the psychologist, her former fiancé, said came true: I proved not to be man enough to control Dolly.
Indescribable Clashes

The divorce of Dolly and me was entered before the City Court of Reykjavík (Borgardómur Reykjavíkur) on 19 February 1959. A letter from the Reverend Jakob Jónsson was submitted stating that attempts at reconciliation had proved fruitless. I filed a claim for full custody of the children and offered to pay Dolly a specified sum monthly. Dolly did not appear until a week later and then presented her demands. She likewise demanded full custody of our three children, full child support for them, and a monthly allowance for herself. She furthermore reserved all rights in the case, since I had abandoned her and our children, "as well as on account of my conduct in that connection and in other respects". The case was referred to the Ministry of Justice (dómsmálaráðuneytið) and to the probate court.
While our divorce case was under way, the state of affairs between me and Dolly was inflammable. Many things happened then that I would rather forget.

Among them was that she took up with some American who worked for Ragnar Ingólfsson, who rented facilities for his business in the basement on Laugarásvegur. This relationship seemed to be a kind of revenge on Dolly's part for my relationship with Edda. The American later testified that he had begun to have second thoughts as time went on and had broken off the relationship out of fear of Dolly. I lived at Lynghagi and went to my work at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). I nevertheless saw Dolly and the children daily, since I attended to various things concerning their household. Among other things, I fetched the milk every other day. In this way I had the opportunity to talk with the children, but naturally this also invited the risk of clashes. And clashes there certainly were.

Despite everything that had gone before, I felt I was still getting to know a new side of my wife that I would never have believed she possessed. Some days I could hardly show myself without her flying at me. The most serious incident, and at the same time the best documented, can in fact be read about in police reports. Dolly claimed that I had tried to run her down and in effect reported me for attempted murder. It well illustrates the sorry state all our dealings had reached, and no doubt we both bore blame for that.

One morning when I came with the milk I was unusually early. I knocked for a long time, but since no one opened I made ready to deliver the milk by going up through the hatch from the basement. I had scarcely stuck my head up through the opening when Dolly came screaming out of the bedroom. I told her the truth, that I was early because I was on my way up to Hvalfjörður. Sveinbjörn Dagfinnsson and I had leased the river Brynjudalsá and were building a salmon ladder there. When little Jón heard this he was wild to come along. His mother would not hear of it. Without further ado she attacked me tooth and claw. I tried to restrain her by gripping her wrists, but that made bad worse. Jón had run out to the car and I meant to follow. Dolly then rushed to the telephone and was going to call the police, but I cut off the call and asked her again and again to leave it be and not make us into greater fools than we already were with constant calls to the police. She paid no heed to that. I then unplugged the telephone and went out.

Dolly, however, came after me in pajamas and a jacket but no shoes. She was in such a fluster that she stumbled on the red gravel. She nevertheless got to her feet and took up position in front of the car. I stopped. She then ran to the right-hand door, but all the doors were locked. I drove slowly off. She ran into the path of the car but moved aside at once when she felt it begin to move.
I drove away with Jón, since it seemed to me out of the question to leave him with Dolly in that state. On the other hand, I also considered it inadvisable to take him along

him with me against Dolly's will. After I managed to get Jón to agree to return home, I immediately telephoned Dr. Esra Pétursson, who had been treating Dolly, and asked him to take Jón home and try to calm his mother. That he did. Dolly, however, had run to the next house and called the police from there. They came to the scene and wrote a report based on her account. The next day I was called in for questioning. There were no further proceedings on the part of the police in this matter. Dolly told anyone who would listen that the explanation was that my father held virtually dictatorial power in the country, so that even the police were afraid of him. Dolly likewise declared it a fact that I had meant to kill her. Nothing less would do. In the police archives her testimony therefore bears the title: "Re: Man who drove at his wife. Suspect: Steingrímur Hermannsson." I can smile at this now, but laughter was certainly far from my mind in 1959.

Our custody case was referred to the Child Welfare Committee of Reykjavík (Barnaverndarnefnd Reykjavíkur), and it is safe to say that its handling bore a strong stamp of our bitter disputes. Accusations flew back and forth. I also had to demand an injunction against Dolly's attempts to sell household furnishings without my consent. She had advertised the items under a false name. When her lawyer came, together with Egill Sigurgeirsson, my attorney, to make an inventory of our household furnishings, she threw him out. By then various things had disappeared from the house, among them our table silver and valuable porcelain.

Ólafur Þorgrímsson then took over her case before the Child Welfare Committee. He tried to demonstrate that despite all the accusations we had made against each other, they were not confirmed in any reliable manner. This was a dispute between two fine individuals who had not had the good fortune to enjoy a happy marriage. It was our temperaments and our pride that were to blame for the fact that we found it harder to part ways than circumstances warranted. In this he flew directly in the face of Dr. Esra Pétursson's opinion on Dolly's mental health. Esra's conclusions, the lawyer said, were in strangely close agreement with my own conclusions on the same subject. If the psychiatric examination were to be given weight, a comparable evaluation of me would also have to take place to determine which of us was the healthier in this respect. A certificate concerning Dolly's mental health from Dr. Þórður Möller, which was at odds with Esra's assessment, was also submitted.

The Child Welfare Committee of Reykjavík delivered its conclusion in July 1959. Suffice it to say that the committee split three ways in its position. Its chairman, and one committee member besides, wanted the mother to receive custody on the condition that she remain in this country, at least for a period of one year, and be under supervision during that period. Two committee members proposed that I receive custody
of Herdís and Dolly custody of the boys. Finally, one committee member proposed that I receive custody of all the children.

One basic premise of the committee was that I had originated and initiated the divorce. I found this a most remarkable conclusion. It was based on the fact that it was I who moved away from home. No account was taken of the prior history. I could make no sense of this ruling. No doubt Dolly was not satisfied with the ruling either, since she was required to live in Iceland. I appealed it in a letter to the Ministry of Justice.
The Abduction of the Children

The Ministry of Justice (dómsmálaráðuneytið) decided to refer the case for ruling to the Child Welfare Council (Barnaverndarráð), the highest ruling authority in custody disputes. The scope of the case had by then already grown large. The case documents numbered 40, in numerical order, plus seven photographs of letters and six other documents, unnumbered, along with a transcript from the Reykjavík register of divorces.

The Child Welfare Council began its proceedings at the end of July 1959. We were once again given the opportunity to submit evidence in the case, and we both made use of it. A great many documents were thus added to the case files, and yet again new physicians were engaged to assess Dolly's health. Those examinations, however, came to an unexpected and abrupt end.

In the summer of 1959 I had feared that Dolly would try to leave the country with the children. The chairman of the Child Welfare Committee informed Dolly, at my request, that she was forbidden to do so until a final ruling on custody was in place. I also obtained a concurring ruling from the Ministry of Justice.

Despite these measures, word reached me that there was reason to believe Dolly intended to leave the country on 24 June. My mother-in-law had evidently taken at face value her daughter's tall tales about the wretched conditions in Iceland. She had come to the country and evidently had a role to play in the planned departure. I telephoned the office of the Pan American airline at Keflavík Airport to find out whether my family was on the passenger list of one of its planes. At first I got no answers, then wrong ones, but at last I managed to confirm, with the help of the police at Keflavík Airport, that Dolly and the children were on the passenger manifest. The police subsequently prevented their departure, by order of the Ministry of Justice. I requested that the American embassy be notified of this violation of the law, that the children's passports be examined, and furthermore that it be investigated whether the airline had been party to the matter.
Ten days later Dolly and her mother made two more unsuccessful attempts to get out of the country. In doing so Dolly broke a promise she had

given the ministry only a few days earlier. In the wake of this I demanded that the children be taken from my wife and their care entrusted to a specially appointed woman. A few weeks later the ruling of the Child Welfare Committee (Barnaverndarnefnd) came down, and thereafter all my energies went into pleading my case before the Child Welfare Council (Barnaverndarráð). The Ministry of Justice did not see its way to taking the children from Dolly, but responded to her repeated escape attempts by assigning the police to watch the house and appointing a nurse to be in the home as a guard. The police often kept watch from a car parked in the street. This attracted the undivided attention of the children in the neighborhood, and no doubt of others as well. These measures, however, were discontinued after about a month, despite my protests and warnings.

The Child Welfare Council was slow to deliver its ruling. On the morning of Friday 18 December 1959 I was awakened by a telephone call. At the other end of the line was a friend of mine, who told me that the house on Laugarásvegur appeared to be deserted. I threw on my clothes and went to the scene at once. There I found only two adolescent girls, in their twelfth and thirteenth years, who had often looked after the children. Dolly had gotten them to sleep in the house overnight and instructed them to turn on lights and open the curtains early in the morning so that someone would be seen moving about. They had, however, overslept. Dolly and the children were nowhere to be found. She had left the country on the first plane that morning. I put it this way in a letter I wrote the following day: that it "[may] truly be said that [the flight] approaches an organized child abduction".

Dolly had planned her departure carefully. This is best seen from the sequence of events recorded from witnesses when the case was under investigation by the State Criminal Investigation Police (Rannsóknarlögregla ríkisins). Statements were taken from everyone involved in the matter. Three weeks before the departure, Dolly had contacted one of her old water-ballet students, a nineteen-year-old girl, and asked for her assistance. Dolly told her that I refused to give my consent for her to leave the country with the children and that she "would therefore have to resort to tricks to get away with them," to quote directly from the police report. Dolly told the girl nothing about the Ministry of Justice's travel ban. The girl promised her help and settled her tax payments, which was a condition for being allowed to buy airline tickets in those years. She did not know when the journey was planned until the day before departure. Then she was tasked with booking tickets for herself and the children and picking them up shortly before closing time the same day. There the children were registered under false names at the girl's address, as Jónas Karlsson, Tómas Karlsson and Edda Karlsdóttir.
The girl also obtained her friend's permission for Dolly to use her name for the purchase of a plane ticket. Dolly likewise had her hair dyed, so as to

be unrecognizable. The plane tickets were all one-way to Copenhagen, except the girl's ticket, which was round-trip. The reason they flew to Copenhagen was that passports did not have to be presented when flying to the Nordic countries, any more than now. The flight departed from Reykjavík Airport with Iceland Airways (Flugfélag Íslands).

Dolly went out to the airport ahead, and the girl came after with the children. When they arrived, the girl took the children aboard the plane. She showed her passport unasked but presented only the tickets for the children. The children had been instructed to pretend not to know their mother, and they were absolutely forbidden to address her or call out to her under any circumstances. The children were told they would meet her in Denmark. Dolly stepped aboard just before departure, at 8:30. She showed a ticket bearing her friend's name but was not asked for a passport. She sat near the front of the plane, while the girl and the children sat in one of the rearmost rows. They can thus hardly have seen their mother during the journey. There were 27 passengers in all on the flight.

On arrival at the airport abroad, the girl was stopped on her way from the plane and asked whether the children were in her charge. She said they were. She was stopped again at passport control, and there she was asked whether the children's mother was traveling with them. She admitted it. Dolly was then fetched and taken in for questioning. Dolly had instructed the girl to take the children to the American Red Cross in Copenhagen if she herself were detained by the Danish authorities. She had foreseen that possibility. The girl carried with her a letter to the Red Cross from Dolly in which the organization was asked to take charge of the children. The organization was to send them by air to their relatives in the United States. Dolly had even given the girl 600 dollars for the fares should they be needed.

In Iceland I had immediately notified the authorities of the children's abduction. A call was placed at once to Iceland's ambassador in Copenhagen, asking him to make an attempt to stop the children and turn them back home. The Ministry of Justice issued that order. This failed. Dolly produced American passports at the questioning at the airport, and thereupon the Danish police declined to intervene in the matter. Dolly therefore flew on unhindered to New York with the children later that same evening, while the girl who had assisted her stayed one night in Copenhagen and flew back the next morning. She received money for her expenses from Dolly, but no other payment.

I was very unhappy about these latest events. It seemed to me that Dolly's flight could have been prevented if my wishes had been followed as regards surveillance. I therefore wrote a letter to the Ministry of Justice in which, among other things, I said:

As the ministry is aware, my wife, Sara, managed to flee the country with the children yesterday, despite the ministry's ruling that it is not permitted to take the children out of the country without my consent while their custody has not been decided. [. . .] The ministry did not comply with my aforementioned demand that the children be taken from their mother, but placed a police guard at the house and then hired a nurse to watch over them. These security measures were soon discontinued, despite my warnings . . .
In the letter I demanded that the ruling be "firmly enforced and nothing left undone to bring the children back home."

The Icelandic authorities continued their attempts to assist me. The Minister for Foreign Affairs summoned the ambassador of the United States to a meeting and explained to him how seriously the Icelandic authorities viewed the matter. What was pondered most was whether to demand that the children be sent back home. After extensive meetings, deliberations, and consultation with the American embassy, it was concluded that this would be pointless. The most likely response of the American authorities would be to refer the matter to a court in the place where the children were staying. That would then give rise to a new custody dispute in the United States. I decided instead to await the ruling that was expected from the Child Protection Council (Barnaverndarráð).
The Ruling of the Child Protection Council

After Dolly's departure, the lawyer Ólafur Þorgrímsson was appointed her spokesman before the Child Protection Council (Barnaverndarráð), as he had in fact already been. Egill Sigurgeirsson assisted me. The Child Protection Council delivered its ruling on 17 February 1960. It departed from the conclusion of the Child Protection Committee (Barnaverndarnefnd) that I alone had been to blame for the divorce. On that point it said:

It appears that a deep-seated disagreement arose between the couple early in their marriage. The husband, who was born and raised in Iceland, is said to have wanted the couple to make their home in this country. The wife, who was born and raised in the United States, is on the other hand said to have wanted their home to be in the United States. The couple appear not to have managed to resolve this disagreement between themselves, and from this fundamental disagreement there seem to have arisen quarrels of many kinds between them, which they have likewise not managed to settle. They do, however, appear to have made various attempts to come to

agreement, among other things by living for a time alternately in the United States and here in Iceland, and they have also, chiefly the wife, sought the help of doctors and other counselors on marital matters.

Here we come to the heart of the matter. In these words is crystallized what might perhaps be called the roots of the marital troubles between Dolly and me. Our temperaments did not match, and her instability served to magnify everything, this disagreement as much as any other. I could not imagine spending my life in the United States under those circumstances. Who knows, on the other hand, what would have happened if I had met another woman there and we had been well matched in every respect other than the question of where to live. There was no shortage of exciting job offers, and my future prospects in the United States were great. The cracks in my relationship with Dolly, however, ruled out all such speculation in my mind. I never saw sufficient reason to reconsider the firm decision to spend my life in Iceland, as I had always intended.

The Child Protection Council (Barnaverndarráð) took little account of the mutual accusations or the doctors' certificates, which it did not consider conclusive. The council reached the unanimous conclusion that Jón should stay with Dolly and Herdís with me. On the youngest child, Steingrímur Neil, it split. The chairman held that, because of the child's young age, strong arguments would be required before the child could be taken from his mother. The majority of the council, on the other hand, held that custody of the youngest child belonged to me. The majority considered that the mother had shown a lack of "a sense of responsibility for the welfare and safety of the children," and moreover that it seemed likely she could not provide for two children in the United States "except by working so much outside the home that she would largely have to entrust their care and upbringing to strangers or to public institutions." The council members also saw reason to fear that Dolly would evade supervision of the children's upbringing and might even sever contact with the father entirely. The Child Protection Council was in full agreement that such supervision was very important and considered it most desirable that "the lady settle here in this country," but did not make that a condition. I was not pleased that the children would be separated. Still, I was far more content with this ruling than with the earlier one.

A month later I obtained a formal separation from bed and board under Icelandic law. It was issued by the Ministry of Justice (dómsmálaráðuneytið) on 14 March 1960. There I was granted custody of the two younger children, while Dolly received custody of Jón in accordance with the council's ruling. At the same time I was ordered to pay child support for Jón and alimony to Dolly. With this the case came to an end here in Iceland.

After the ruling of the Child Protection Council I investigated still further whether I could claim my children back home, both with the assistance of the Ministry for Foreign Affairs (utanríkisráðuneytið) and on

my own initiative. Shortly after my wife's flight I turned to Thor Thors, Iceland's ambassador to the United States, with the aim of tracking down where Dolly was staying. Those attempts proved fruitless. Thor also spoke with the federal government, the State Department, in the United States, but received the answer we had expected: no assistance was to be had from the American government, since the matter fell within the jurisdiction of the state in question. I also spoke at length with the American ambassador in Iceland. He received me very well and said that an inquiry had shown that the divorce case had been handled lawfully in Iceland in every respect, that my wife's circumstances had been excellent, and that the embassy had nothing to complain of. The ambassador also said that he viewed my wife's flight with grave concern. He strongly advised me to seek the counsel of a good lawyer over in America and then press to have the ruling of the Child Protection Council (Barnaverndarráð) enforced.

Dolly finally made herself heard. She sent letters that were full of accusations against me. She said I completely lacked any sense of responsibility toward her and the children, and that I was letting them starve in the United States. With the help of the letters I found out where they had ended up. They were staying in a house or cabin that Dolly's family owned at Pompano Beach in Florida. In her letters she laid great emphasis on how badly the children were faring in terms of food, clothing, and other necessities. It seemed to me my duty to make yet another attempt to bring the children home.
Fetching the Children from the United States

At the beginning of August 1960 I went to the United States. In Tallahassee, Florida, I met the consul Hilmar Skagfield. I had contacted him at the suggestion of Þórarinn Þórarinsson, member of parliament and editor of Tíminn. At first I asked Hilmar to help me locate the children, but he soon took an active part in most aspects of the case. Our dealings grew into a good friendship, for Hilmar served me very well. Hilmar put me in touch with a lawyer named Jim Dye, who was also a pilot. The lawyer went through all the documents and came to the conclusion that I was fully within my rights in claiming the two children over whom I had been granted custody. I had Icelandic passports for them. With Jim Dye I flew from Tallahassee to Miami on 15 August in his small airplane, and there we went to see a deputy sheriff. My lawyer presented the case. After that, we obtained the deputy sheriff's assistance in enforcing the Icelandic ruling. We went to Dolly's home, where we found the three children. Dolly was at work.
The deputy telephoned her and announced that we had come to enforce the Icelandic ruling and to take the two younger children away with us.

I was greatly relieved to find my children safe and sound, and it also touched me how glad they seemed to see me. The joy, however, was not unmixed, and in truth I was in great inner turmoil. My lawyer laid heavy emphasis on everything being done according to the law. That meant that under no circumstances could I take little Jón with me. I had received the same advice from home, from the lawyers I had consulted. This was enormously difficult for me. I could hardly contain myself as I tried to explain to Jón that he alone was to stay behind with his mother. Naturally, there is no way for an eight-year-old child to understand such a thing. Jón wept bitterly and begged me to be allowed to come along to Iceland. Leaving him behind is one of the hardest things I have gone through in my life. I felt I could hear him crying all the way to the airport.

We hurried as fast as we could to the international airport in Miami, which was an hour's drive away. When we arrived, we checked when the next flight would be. I wanted to get out of the country as quickly as possible and not risk changing planes in New York. So I bought tickets for the first flight. It was to Cuba. As it turned out, the plane's departure was delayed. That proved fateful.

Dolly had not sat idle after the telephone call from the deputy sheriff. She turned directly to the county court and was told there that I had no ruling from that court in my possession. She immediately filed a complaint to have the Icelandic ruling invalidated and secured the assistance of the police to stop our departure at the airport. There I waited for the plane to take off, cursing its delay. I was naturally on edge, but thought mostly of keeping the children calm. Neil was only in his second year and surely had little understanding of what was going on. Herdís, on the other hand, was in high spirits and looked forward to going home and seeing her grandfather and grandmother. Shortly before the plane was due to take off, police officers arrived. They informed me that we were being detained; I was forbidden to leave the state with the children. The police also took the children into their custody. At that they became very frightened and distressed.

Dolly filed a claim before the county court for a full divorce under American law and for the invalidation of the Icelandic custody ruling. This led to the issuing of an order that the children be held until the matter had been resolved in the courts. Our children were placed in a foster home. I immediately filed a counterclaim before the court demanding that the Icelandic ruling be recognized and enforced. It was clear that
I had failed to recover the children without court proceedings in the United States. As was to be expected, these turned out to be both protracted and costly.

Two days after these events, the custody case had already reached the front pages of newspapers in Florida. Considerable coverage followed as the case unfolded. It made the front pages of daily papers all across the United States. Much was invariably made of the fact that I was a high-ranking official and a former representative of Iceland at the General Assembly of the United Nations. Hardly a news story was written, either, without the addition that I was the son of a former prime minister of Iceland. It was sometimes added that he had instigated the closing of the American military base in Iceland. Apparently, word had still not reached the United States that those plans had come to nothing.
Battling in the Courts

At first, Dolly's fight was about getting the children out of the foster home. She succeeded in that within a relatively short time. Her lawyers stressed that the sheriff had exceeded his authority by assisting me in recovering the children, since I had not had the ruling of an American court in hand. In the media over there, the sheriff reprimanded his deputy, who had supported my case, and acknowledged an error on the part of his office. The children therefore soon moved back to their mother.

The complaint she filed against me bore obvious marks of having been drawn up in the heat of the moment. In addition to demanding a divorce, the invalidation of the Icelandic ruling, and custody of the children, she accused me of coldness and lovelessness in the marriage, of a lack of financial support, and of "inhumane treatment" of my absent family. Dolly did not stop there, however. She also accused me of attempted murder by running her down with a car. The papers over there were fond of dwelling on this point. Dolly was referring to the events described earlier. In addition, she maintained that the ruling of the Child Protection Council (Barnaverndarráð) was invalid because my father had exerted political pressure to influence it. She also held fast to her accusations of large-scale infidelity on my part.

I hired a new lawyer to handle my case. His name is Lee E. Weissenborn, a most admirable man who conducted all the proceedings outstandingly well. We became good friends, and I also came to know his wife Judy well, as I lived in their home for a time. Weissenborn was prominent among the Democrats in that area and later sat in the state legislature for them.

It immediately became clear that the litigation would entail considerable expense. A vast number of documents from the Icelandic cases, witness testimony, and other records had to be translated. Legal costs were high, and it was expensive to stay in
