Florida while the court proceedings lasted. I also had to obtain unpaid leave from the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) for a period of four months.

Because of this great expense I applied for financial support from the Icelandic authorities. I sent a letter to Bjarni Benediktsson, the Minister of Justice, requesting state-funded legal aid, since this was a test case. It was to be determined whether an American court would recognize an Icelandic ruling. I set out my financial situation and the great costs that would accompany the final division of property before the probate court. I also called attention to the ministry's responsibility, since the watch kept on Dolly had been discontinued, enabling her to flee the country with our children. I made clear, however, that it was by no means my intention to criticize the ministry, for I had always been shown the utmost goodwill there. Bjarni responded favorably to the request and provided a considerable grant, although the request for legal aid was refused. I myself put substantial money into the litigation, and my parents contributed what was lacking. It may be said that this saved me from financial bankruptcy on that account.

During the trial Dolly added still more to the already long list of items in her complaint. She testified in court that she knew nothing of having had lawyers acting on her behalf in Iceland, and likewise denied being aware that she had been a party to any divorce or custody case in Iceland. She asserted moreover that she had been entirely unaware of the Ministry of Justice's travel ban, let alone that she had known of any warnings over an attempt to violate it. She said she had no memory of having spoken with its staff to get the travel ban overturned, or of the Ministry of Justice at all. She also said she could not remember by what route she had flown from Iceland to the United States.

Dolly said in the witness box that my father and I had made her life unbearable, and that furthermore it was quite impossible to live in Iceland since it was a communist state. My father, she said, she believed to be a communist. The prime minister of the government now in power, however, she declared was not a communist, since he had been in the opposition when my father was prime minister.

It was easy to produce documents that disproved Dolly's statements and discredited them. It did, however, require gathering evidence and a great deal of work, since all the documents had to be translated. My testimony was entirely consistent with what I have already set down in these pages. I confirmed in court that I had been unfaithful to my wife at the end of 1958, but said that by then we had in fact already parted ways. In addition, the Clausen brothers, Sverrir Scheving and Ragnar Ingólfsson, testified about Dolly's relationships with other men before the formal divorce took place. From the litigation and the testimony there were

regular news reports published in the papers. The Miami Herald said the trial clearly illustrated the difficulties of international disputes of this kind: "There is no agreement on the facts of the case." Every assertion and the whole course of the marriage were fought over.

Despite the extensive press coverage in the United States, the Icelandic media published nothing about the custody case or the court proceedings in the United States. My brother-in-law Sveinbjörn Dagfinnsson got in touch with the editors of the newspapers. The editors all agreed that the dispute was my private affair and that it would not be covered except with my permission. Morgunblaðið even cancelled the publication of a news story the paper had already written. Matthías Johannessen, editor of Morgunblaðið, collected all the clippings and news items that reached the paper and gave them to me. The Icelandic dailies regularly received such mailings from the United States. Matthías also told me that the editorial office had received a very spiteful letter from Dolly. I deeply appreciated this considerateness on the part of the media here at home. I doubt that matters would be handled the same way in some quarters today, though Morgunblaðið still has an unchanged policy in this respect. For that the paper deserves praise.
The End of the Battle

At the outset my lawyers believed that, judging by precedents in the State of Florida, there was a reasonable chance of victory. The fact that the case pitted a foreign man against an American woman, however, considerably reduced my chances of winning. In February 1961, when the litigation had lasted nearly six months, the court ruled that the Icelandic ruling did not apply in the case. After that ruling it became clear to me that the odds of winning the case were very small. The main witness hearings took place in March of the same year, and then followed a long and difficult wait for the judge's final decision. I prepared myself for defeat.

I was not present when the judgment was delivered on 16 November 1961, about 15 months after I made my attempt to fetch the children from the United States. More than three years had passed since I first demanded a divorce from my wife, and for over two and a half years of that time I had loved another woman. All that time we had been unable to marry because of the marital fetters I was still in under American law. At last I received a full divorce. That ruling was most welcome.

After going over the evidence in the case, the court confirmed in most respects my account of the marriage and the conflicts that accompanied it. Dolly had at the outset consented to living in Iceland but done little to make it possible. The court recounted the occasions on which she either refused to come to Iceland or left the country

without my knowledge. The judge also came to the conclusion that by the time my relationship with Edda began, the marriage had in reality been over. The outcome therefore rested in no way on my alleged infidelity. It was not considered proven that Dolly had been unfaithful. It may be said that the court reached a conclusion about the causes of the divorce similar to that of the Child Protection Council (Barnaverndarráð) before it. Its position, however, was far harsher toward Dolly and in some respects one-sided. This was based, among other things, on the law of the State of Florida that a wife was obliged to follow her husband to wherever he wished to make a home for the family:

The court is of the opinion that the causes of the divorce were the wife's repeated opposition to the husband's firm decision that the home should be in Iceland. Under the laws of this state the husband has the right to establish the family's home, and it is the wife's duty to live with him there. During the whole time that the parties to the case lived together in Iceland, the wife, who is an ingenious and determined individual, fought fiercely against this becoming permanent. The wife's opposition to living in Iceland manifested itself in extreme criticism of Iceland and Icelanders, criticism of the husband's family and friends, opposition to building a home in Iceland, threats to take the children and return to the United States, fits of temper, and constant quarrels. This conduct of the wife constitutes exceptional cruelty toward the husband, who could not be induced to buy peace with his wife by abandoning his native land, family, and friends.

The judge also considered it obvious that after I announced in the autumn of 1958 that I wanted a divorce, it had been clear to both parties that a court case would follow. Thereafter, both parties had sought to gather various pieces of evidence and to record events that they believed would serve them in such litigation. It was described how Dolly had more than once hidden herself in the car, and how I had called on my friends as witnesses to her leaving the children alone at night or having overnight guests. The court saw no reason to take any of this evidence into account in its ruling, since the separation had in reality already become a fact by the time these events occurred.

The judge considered it evident that we were both fully capable of raising the children. Custody judgments in Florida, however, contained few examples of anything other than the mother receiving full custody. The circumstances of the case were not deemed weighty enough to change that. Dolly was therefore awarded custody of all the children. I, on the other hand, was awarded generous visitation rights, as it was phrased. The judgjudge
decided that the children could stay in Iceland during the summers. However, demands were made for high sureties to guarantee that I would return the children at summer's end.

On the basis of documents submitted from the Icelandic tax authorities, child support payments were determined. Dolly actually put forward unsubstantiated claims that my income was enormous. The judge disregarded those words. Support for each child was set at 40 dollars a month. Dolly was not awarded any separate alimony, but I was ordered to pay her legal costs, about 1,200 dollars in all. The judge also ruled that our property in Iceland should be divided in half.

The outcome did not surprise me, though I would have preferred it to go the other way. It takes a great deal for children to be taken from their mother and permission granted for them to be taken out of the country, where the court cannot supervise their upbringing.

To tell the truth, I was satisfied with most other aspects of the ruling. I felt Judge Farrington had acquainted himself well with all the facts of the case and dealt with the dispute objectively. His conclusion regarding the troubles in the marriage was very much in my favor. Most important, however, was that I was granted very extensive visitation rights with the children, and the court also intended to supervise their upbringing in the United States. Dolly was forbidden to take them away without the court's consent. Admittedly, she soon disregarded that provision — as a matter of course, I am tempted to say. At least, little in that regard surprised me.

It is no exaggeration to say that the difficulties in the marriage and the dispute over my children weighed heavily on me for years. Shortly before the ruling was announced in the United States, an acquaintance of mine remarked that he was glad that I would now hopefully start talking and thinking about something else. This was surely said thoughtlessly. Yet there was probably a grain of truth in it. I did not burden my acquaintances with my worries after that.

The years with Dolly are a period of my life that I had not intended to revisit. Yet it would never occur to me to say that I wished I had never met her. Then the children I have in the United States, whom I love dearly, would never have come into being. I would probably also never have met Edda, and my whole life would have gone a different way. Life is a single whole. The past cannot be changed, and one cannot exclude one part without losing everything. No single strand of it can be left out. That is why it is not done in this book.

The children were at the center of these disputes as time went on. Yet I also find it valuable to know that in this turbulent storm I nevertheless tried, again and again, to give the relationship with Dolly a chance. In hindsight
I perhaps did so too often, but for the children's sake I had to be convinced that every avenue had been exhausted. And I was.
The Relationship with the Children

The most precious thing in what followed, apart from my new life in Iceland, was how well I managed to maintain a good relationship with the children. In fact, their bond with me is much stronger than with Dolly, even though they remained with her in the United States. This applies especially to the two older ones, Jón and Herdís.

The very first summer after the ruling was handed down, Jón stayed with me in Iceland, then Herdís, then Jón and Neil together, and so on in turns. This greatly strengthened their ties to Iceland. That applies not least to Jón. I could sense that he wanted to be nowhere else. He was very attached to his grandfather and grandmother. The children often stayed with them on Tjarnargata and at the summer house at Klettur in Borgarfjörður. Mamma's thick rice porridge was a special favorite of Jón's, just as it famously was of mine. We went on mountain trips and fishing trips, and I taught the boys to cast a fly. They do it very well. Edda took the children under her wing like a mother during those summers. She has been a good friend of theirs ever since, and they turned to her with many things, both their joys and their sorrows.

The children's visits, however, were rarely free of trouble. Every spring Dolly came up with some new demands and regularly delayed their departure. She often demanded higher child support on these occasions. I therefore frequently had to turn to my lawyer out west and pursue my cases there before the courts. In this way the knot was always untied, and usually at no cost to me. Still, this brought unpleasantness, which I was admittedly used to but the children were not. Yet they grew accustomed to these troubles, which repeated themselves every year, and showed incredible equanimity.
Dolly's Fate

At first Dolly seemed to want to sever my ties with the children and forbade them to write to me. Soon, however, she changed her mind. Neil was of course too young, but Jón could write, having turned nine, and Herdís, who was six, drew pictures. I still have all these letters and drawings in thick bundles.

Dolly soon met a former soldier, married him, and took the name Murrey. He owned a house in Ithaca in New York State. They moved there, and thereby out of the jurisdiction of the court in Florida. In doing so she violated

against the court order, and various troubles arose from it. I was instructed to send the children's support payments to the court, but she could not collect them there. This was not resolved until the case had gone before a court in New York State. There she made one of her many attempts to have the support payments raised. The proceedings, however, ended quickly with the ruling from Florida being upheld. In some ways I found it better to have the children in Ithaca, a short distance from New York. It was then easier for me to visit them on my travels. I did so quite often and had enjoyable times with them.

Unfortunately, Dolly's second marriage soon came to an end. This Murrey is said to have been difficult to live with. Between the two of them everything went the same way as it had with us before. The marriage blew up with a great commotion. One day he was gone and has not been heard from since, as I understand it. I do not even know whether they are formally divorced. Dolly gave Murrey a terrible account in her letters. However, I never knew how much stock could be put in those descriptions. The children do not want to talk about him. Dolly kept the house undivided and has rented it out to students, earning some income from it.

I believe Dolly took fairly good care of the children, at least provided for their most basic needs. However, there were sometimes considerable clashes between them. I saw that in letters from them and indeed also in what Dolly wrote. She even asked me several times to intervene. I never did, as it was not clear how I could. In particular, her relationship with Neil sometimes turned bad. There could be fights and great commotion. She blames her second husband for these relationship problems. I do not think it likely, however, that he bears all the blame.

I last met Dolly when Jón, our eldest son, got married here in Iceland in 1981. She attended the ceremony. No trouble came of it. Some time earlier it had come to light that Dolly had not managed to sell the silver tableware that had disappeared from our house during our married years. She had hidden it with a friend of hers. The set is for twelve people and was a wedding gift to us. Edda and I decided to give Dolly this silver while she was here. I think she appreciated it greatly. At least she wrote me a lovely thank-you letter after returning to the United States. She still writes to me now and then, expressing worries about or satisfaction with one of the children, or making grand statements about the United States and how communists in disguise are undermining everything there.
Jón

As mentioned before, Jón benefited from coming to Iceland the very first summer after the divorce. After finishing his university studies in the United States, he worked for the State Architect of Iceland (Húsameistari ríkisins) here at home for a year. He lived then with his fiancée in the basement apartment at Tjarnargata 42. They then moved to California. He has done well there. He runs his own architecture firm in Redwood City, not far from San Francisco.

Jón has the same hair color as I. He is very orderly and precise, careful with money, and organized down to the last detail. He is a fine athlete and cycles in particular. He rides dozens of kilometers every day to keep himself in shape. He has cycled across the length and breadth of California and several other states. Jón is exceptionally meticulous. He was a great tinkerer as a child and can devote enormous amounts of time to pondering the tasks before him. That could drive me crazy, because I am by nature much more impatient. Jón very quickly got the hang of casting a fly. His precision showed in the way he would instantly pull the line back up if there was the slightest flaw in the cast, even though I taught him that this might scare the fish. If he knew of a salmon in a pool, he could likewise show incredible patience when I would long since have given up and gone looking elsewhere.

Jón always did very well in school. He was admitted to the renowned technical school, the Massachusett Institute of Technology. He completed a B.S. degree in architecture and mechanical engineering with excellent grades in 1974 and received a good scholarship for a master's program in architecture at the university in Eugene, Oregon. While Jón was at MIT I visited him several times. At least once we all went, the children and I, skiing in the mountains of New England. In the summer of 1973 Jón stayed in Iceland and worked for the architects Guðmundur Kr. Guðmundsson and Ólafur Sigurðsson.

Jón took advantage of being both an architect and a mechanical engineer and specialized as such in energy-saving design. He immediately got considerable work on such projects. In California there are strict rules about energy use in buildings, both in heating and cooling. He established his own firm, and the building inspection authorities frequently referred home builders to him when energy-efficiency requirements were not being met. Jón also specialized in renovating old houses. He takes all the time needed to find the most beautiful solutions in each case. That serves him well, because in the area where he lives it is forbidden to alter old houses except with special permission, and the alterations must blend well with their surroundings. He has even had to design
a house around protected redwood trees, and he accomplished it masterfully. Beautiful architecture can be a pure work of art.

Jón soon took up painting and is quite a good painter. Among other things, he has held an exhibition here in Iceland, at Gallerí Borg, where he sold several pictures. I myself own works by him, and I find his pictures very beautiful. He always has a sketchpad in his hands and sketches nearly everything he sees. He cultivates his passion for salmon fishing by painting salmon flies.

In Oregon Jón met Lotte, a girl of German descent. They were married in the Catholic church in Reykjavík in 1981. Jón and Lotte have two sons, Bryan Johannes and Stefan Steingrímur. Johannes is the name of Lotte's father. Bryan was baptized in Iceland. They never use their second names, since their pronunciation is not within everyone's reach in the United States. Jón and Lotte place great emphasis on their sons' upbringing and sent them to a strict Catholic school.

They bought their house and remodeled it entirely on their own. Jón has received a special award for the work, and their house has been featured in a respected architectural journal out west. The renovation is like a work of art.
Herdís

Herdís came here the second summer after the divorce. I believe the divorce and the marital difficulties between Dolly and me weighed most heavily on her in her younger years. She was at an especially sensitive and impressionable age. She has told how, during the first weeks after arriving in Iceland, she was suspicious of Edda and of her grandmother and grandfather because of the pictures Dolly had painted of them. Herdís and Edda soon became good friends, however. Just like Jón, Herdís grew attached to her grandmother and grandfather and often stayed with them on Tjarnargata.

Herdís did not get along well with her mother. As soon as she turned eighteen and was free to travel, she decided to come to Iceland. This was against her mother's wishes, but Herdís was determined and had her way. When she arrived at the airport, however, she received a harsh welcome. Her mother had called and reported that her daughter was carrying drugs and should be stopped. Nothing was found despite a thorough search, but the trip was delayed by several weeks. Little needs to be said about what a miserable experience this was for an eighteen-year-old girl. Suspicion of drug smuggling is not taken lightly in the United States.
Herdís, however, did not lose heart and made it to Iceland despite these

setbacks. She then lived with us for three and a half years. For most of that time she worked at Landsbankinn (the National Bank of Iceland). Herdís wanted to pursue further education, and I supported her in that decision. She went to study in Oregon, where her brother Jón was, and graduated from university there with a degree in public relations. She did well in her studies.

Herdís was a beautiful child and is a striking woman. She keeps her red hair color better than her brother Jón. Herdís is now a homemaker in Santa Monica, California. She has a fine husband, Cary. They did not meet until she was 35 years old. He is a few years younger than she and was a department manager at the fashion store Sachs. His father and brother, however, are both lawyers. At Herdís's urging he threw himself into his studies and is now preparing for the bar exam. Cary says his wife takes wonderful care of the home, and she knows everything under the sun about healthy eating. She has introduced me to various things in that field.

Herdís and Cary have two lovely sons, Adam Jónas and Eiríkur Haraldur. She often calls Edda their grandmother. We attended their baptism in the United States. Dolly was not there. The younger son is developmentally disabled, which places great strain on the household. At two years old he had the development of a six-month-old child. Scans showed that the ventricles of his brain are abnormally large.

Herdís is determined and good at speaking her mind. She has truly needed that to secure the necessary help for her son. She has gotten him in with the most skilled specialists at the university hospitals in California. She will not hear any mention of the boy being placed in an institution.
My relationship with Herdís has always been especially good. Iceland and the United States have tugged at her heart all her life.
Neil

Neil stayed longest in his mother's home. He was unruly and difficult for his mother — or they for each other. In his teenage years he could be said to have been in constant rebellion. Dolly was forever writing that I should do this or that, tell him one thing or another. She said she had no control over Neil, but that he respected me.

Neil came here with his brother every other summer except the first year. Then Jón came alone. He never spoke Icelandic. There was some discord between the brothers, but it was probably no more than is usual. Neil was a good fisherman and a tremendous athlete. Among other things, he won many awards in diving. His mother decided that he should

a place on the United States Olympic team and took the matter into her own hands. That led to him quitting competition. He did, however, earn some income from giving diving exhibitions. Edda and I once saw him perform. He seemed to me to be very skilled. Judging by his trophies, I could well believe he might have earned a spot on the Olympic team. He is also a strong swimmer and for a time did sailing. He gave all of this up in some kind of rebellion.

Neil resembles his mother the most of the three children. He has certain traits of her temperament but is fortunately better balanced. He clashed at one time with his stepfather, and there were often confrontations between them.

Neil is determined and handy. I think, however, that he is a loner and shuts himself off by burying himself in work. Perhaps he gets the work instinct to some extent from me. When Neil was a teenager he was very busy building model airplanes and made fireworks and firecrackers of all kinds. Both are pursuits I dabbled in during my own childhood. As I have said before, I was once reprimanded for nearly setting fire to the Ministerial Residence (Ráðherrabústaðurinn). For Neil it went worse. He was arrested.

It happened when the police knocked on the door because of Dolly's traffic violations. According to newspaper reports, she testified that the police officers had threatened to kick the door in. Neil was carrying a large firecracker when mother and son went to the door, and he was arrested as a result. Dolly told a reporter that her son had felt the home and his mother were threatened. Neil was put behind bars, and high bail was demanded for his release. Dolly, meanwhile, fought her battle in the local papers, where she was called "a well-known critic of the school system," and blamed communists for the situation Neil was in. They were poisoning the minds of youth and trying to dissolve society by instilling criminal tendencies in young people through propaganda in schoolbooks!

During the proceedings it emerged that Neil made bombs out of light bulbs, gunpowder, and model-airplane fuel, which he had radio-controlled model airplanes release from a great height so they would explode in the air. He was finally released with a warning.

Neil first completed a degree in biology but then decided to go into dentistry like his maternal grandfather. He earned a fine degree from Cornell University. He moved away from his mother to Florida, where he worked at first at a large dental practice and then independently. Neil bought a large station wagon and outfitted it as a dental office. He drove the car between retirement homes and offered his services. He soon had a great deal to do, worked his fingers to the bone, and earned a decent living.
Neil bought a small and rather shabby house. It happened that his house was broken

twice into his place, which was more than he could bear. He then resorted to old know-how and built a burglar-alarm system that consisted of firecrackers or percussion caps going off if a window or door was opened in his absence. This was meant to drive off unwelcome visitors. By this point in the story he had taken up with a girl named Dabbý. They fell out badly and he threw her out. She responded by reporting him to the police for having explosives in his possession. The police sent an army of men to the scene, a helicopter and everything to go with it. In the United States, householders have shot visitors by mistake and every other child seems to have access to a gun. But there is general uproar if "bombers" are so much as mentioned. They are considered terrorists.

The police stormed into Neil's home and photographed the burglar-alarm system. They also found a canister where Neil had kept leftover gunpowder. He was charged with possession of explosives, which is no trivial charge in the United States. It made no difference that the girl withdrew her accusation.

Misfortune, however, had not stopped pursuing Neil. I advised him to turn to Lee Weissenborn, who had handled my affairs in the United States. He was prepared to defend him for 15,000 dollars. I offered to pay a good part of that. Neil, however, chose another lawyer, who had been recommended for cases of this kind. He cost 12,000 dollars, and I paid a little over half of it. The lawyer advised him to plead guilty, and he would then negotiate a light sentence. Neil agreed to that.

When it came to sentencing, however, it turned out that the lawyer had completely neglected the case and no agreements were in place. Neil was sentenced to nearly two years in a correctional facility. This whole affair was outrageous, and Neil was badly treated. I paid the fees of a lawyer who undertook to appeal the case. He worked well but did not succeed in getting the case taken up by the appeals court. The court held that nothing new had come to light in the case.

A correctional facility is, however, quite another matter than imprisonment in the United States. Neil was placed in a good facility in Alabama. In fact there was an excellent correctional house near his home, but since it is right next to a military base, the authorities thought it inadvisable to house a "potential terrorist" there! Not all foolishness is alike. During his stay, Neil studied law and intended to have himself cleared before the courts.

Neil was released for good behavior when he had served a little over half of his correctional sentence. For a long time he intended to sue the lawyer who had betrayed him, but I managed to talk him out of it. Neil got a good job at a dental practice. But it was still not all over. Acquaintances of his were keeping for him a safe with various documents he wanted to store

in a safe place. I find it most likely that he wanted to keep them away from their mother. When he went to retrieve the documents, however, it turned out that the safe had been opened. He became furious and threatened to report the matter to the police. His acquaintances, however, beat him to it and reported him for violent behavior. He was on probation and could not even be caught speeding without risking having to go back inside. This ended with Neil having to serve the six months he had remaining.

Dolly has been consumed by this affair. She moved to Florida from Ithaca and has been living in Neil's house. I do not know whether that has been for the good, though I believe she means well. Every now and then I receive letters from her asking me to intervene when things have come to a head between her and Neil. Among other things, she complained that he had thrown her out and thrown her clothes in the trash. She had to retrieve them from the dump. He is not without a temper, any more than his mother.

I last saw Neil in January 1997. He looked very well. He is still unmarried. Neil has had more than his share of misfortune, but he is both dependable and trustworthy. I have full confidence that he will do well as a dentist once he is free of this trouble. I believe Herdís took the divorce hardest at first. As time passed, though, I think it left the deepest wound in Neil. Dolly, however, blames her second husband for everything that has gone wrong in the children's lives.
Neil was released this past June. He immediately got a job at the same dental practice and seems content with his lot.
An Unexpected Epilogue

Shortly before this book was ready for printing, I ran into an old acquaintance of Dolly's and mine at the birthday party of a mutual friend. She said she had heard of my planned biography and had been reminded of me. She had in her possession a large envelope of letters that Dolly had asked her to keep in the fall of 1958. What the letters contained she did not know, but they had been in her keeping for forty years and I was free to have them, as so much time had passed. She said she felt no obligation toward Dolly, because when Dolly had come to Iceland to attend the wedding of Jón, our son, she had shown no interest in reclaiming the letters from storage.

I collected the envelope from this good woman's home. It turned out that these were letters that had passed between me and Dolly in 1958, after she left the country with our three children. In them I try to get her to come to Iceland, while she writes to me about her circumstances and the children's in the United States. In

the same envelope, however, were also the letters from Dolly's mother, which she sent me without her daughter's knowledge that same year. After Dolly came to Iceland in the fall of 1958, they disappeared from a locked drawer, as mentioned before, along with most of the letters Dolly had written me that year. Dolly evidently did not destroy them, as I had thought, but placed them in this storage.

I searched high and low for these letters during our custody dispute. They contain the only recorded testimony of the opinion of Dolly's mother that it would be best for the children to grow up with me in Iceland. She called Dolly's absences merely a "vacation" and assured me that she would in the end return to Iceland. In her first letter she said:

These wonderful children belong with you in Iceland. You know, Denni, that Chicago, or any big city, proves very hard on [children] if they do not have their parents and [do not receive] proper care. [...] My opinion is that it is best for the children's health and happiness that they stay with their parents in your home in Iceland.

Dolly's mother stressed emphatically that her daughter should not learn of her writing. She repeats this again and again in the letters and asks me to send my replies to my father-in-law's dental office. At the trial she could not be persuaded to repeat what the letters said. There she told an entirely different story. In the later letter, however, she speaks even more categorically about where the children should live and says it makes no difference whether Dolly can be persuaded to live in Iceland. In the letter's conclusion she says:
If she does not adapt, or cannot, you will be forced to take these precious children into your care and let them enjoy good fortune and good treatment in Iceland.
These were the words in her mother's writings that stung Dolly most sharply, as may well be imagined.

When I read these letters now, I find in them first and foremost confirmation of my account of my separation from Dolly in 1958, as it has appeared on these pages, in the custody case in Iceland and in the court proceedings in the United States. The question inevitably arises, though, whether these letters from Dolly's mother would have changed the course of events or the custody rulings here at home or in the United States. Such speculation, however, leads to no conclusion, and I blame no one for how things turned out. It would serve no purpose anyway.
Chapter Nine
RESEARCH, MARRIAGE, AND WRESTLING BOUTS

A short while ago, the man who has been managing director of the State Research Council left his post, and a new man has now taken over his duties. He was chosen from three applicants, all of whom are doubtless well educated, but it is pure coincidence that the one chosen for this position is the son of the prime minister.

I was appointed managing director of the State Research Council (Rannsóknaráð ríkisins) as of December 1, 1957, in my thirtieth year. My appointment was not received in silence by the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) newspapers, any more than the other works of the left-wing government. The chief complaint was that a scientist should have been hired for the job. The other applicants were Guðmundur Pálmason, a geophysicist and an acquaintance of mine from the chess scene at the Gymnasium, and Magnús Magnússon, a physicist and later professor.

To answer the criticism of my appointment to the office of managing director of the Research Council, I wrote an article that I intended to publish in Tíminn. In it I said I did not intend to "answer the nagging and sniping of the Independence Party papers directed at me, and especially at my father," but rather wished to answer the many people who had sincerely asked me: "What is the Research Council?" In the article I discussed the council's field of work, the duties of its managing director, and the lack of facilities for research in the country.

I have this article in manuscript, and there one can see that I intended to end it with a quotation from the words of a "fine citizen" who wished me "success in the job, so that the 'scandal sheets' would attack [me] for my own deeds, and not for being my father's son." My father has evidently read the article over, made various suggested changes in the margins, and proposed that the ending
should not be about me but about the future of research and its facilities in Iceland. His suggestion for the closing words went like this:

To tell the truth, it seems to me that this matter is so large, and such a shared interest of the entire nation, that it should be possible to make a joint effort on it, raised above the basest considerations of hatred and vindictiveness.
By the time the article was finished, the newspaper coverage had probably blown over, and I took the course of making no reply at all. At least there is no sign that it ever appeared in Tíminn.

I doubt that the harshness of Icelandic politics has at any other time been greater than during the left-wing government. I was critical of the government's work and policies, as appeared in my correspondence with my father during these years, and felt progress was slow on various reform issues. He, too, was not entirely satisfied and had his hands full holding the government together. He wrote to me in a letter:

Regarding the politics, I must say this: Of course you are right that it is going only middling well. I always expected that when I began working with these two parties. It is not comfortable holding this together. Now the Independence Party men are organizing strikes, and most foreigners consider that the strangest phenomenon that has ever occurred.

These words of my father touch on the worst excesses in the conduct of the opposition during these years, one of the strangest affairs in Icelandic political history. The leaders of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) used their influence in the labor movement and organized strikes with the aim of nullifying the government's attempts to keep inflation in check. In this way they intended to bring down my father. The Cold War was at its height and the atmosphere was charged with a rancor that, in certain men, approached hatred. It was as if the nation's welfare and prosperity were unhesitatingly to yield to the short-term interests of the conservatives.

Fair-minded men in the Independence Party saw their fault in this matter. In the biography of Ólafur Thors, Matthías Johannessen quotes Jónas Haralz as saying that what Ólafur regretted almost most in his political career was "that the Independence Party and its advocates had encouraged, or even actively worked toward, strikes in order to bring down this left-wing government." Jónas adds that:
"Bjarni Benediktsson said that it had been justifiable, because the life and future of Iceland had been at stake, so perilous was the government's policy in security and defense matters."

It has always seemed to me that people have ventured onto thin ice in politics when the end justifies the means. From there it is a short step to justifying any violence whatsoever. The judgment of Jónas H. Haralz is unequivocal. He was economic adviser to both my father and Ólafur Thors. He spoke well of Ólafur but said the strike actions had been "both foolish and underhanded at once, and built on great short-sightedness." I do not consider that an unfair judgment.
At the Research Council

My first acquaintance with the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) was not especially encouraging. My predecessor in the post of managing director of the Research Council was the distinguished scientist Þorbjörn Sigurgeirsson. He left for other duties at the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands). Þorbjörn's office was a cubbyhole on the third floor of what was called the Industries Department Building (Atvinnudeildarhúsið). To get into the office one had to walk through the small but ornate office of the botanist Ingólfur Davíðsson. In the room intended for my use there was a wreck of a desk, two shabby chairs, and a small cabinet. Papers took up most of the space. They lay in piles everywhere; the desk was barely visible and the floor was covered as well. There was no filing system. I do not doubt that Þorbjörn found what he needed, but this was very far from the kind of order I wanted to have.

The Research Council consisted of three men. Its chairman was Björn Sigurðsson of Keldur, a gentleman in bearing and manner and the Icelander who has come closest to receiving a Nobel Prize in science. He defined the so-called slow virus infections. Maedi and visna in sheep were his main research subjects, along with paratuberculosis. Björn's findings on the course of these diseases have proved of inestimable value in later years in research on AIDS and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, to name a few examples. The AIDS virus appears closely related to the maedi/visna virus, which turned out to be one and the same.

Alongside Björn on the Research Council sat the engineer Ásgeir Þorsteinsson and the geologist Tómas Tryggvason. The council was appointed according to nominations from the three largest parties in the Althingi (Alþingi). I thought that a bad arrangement, one that bred distrust and hampered the council's work. After the untimely death of Björn of Keldur in 1959, it so happened that the third seat remained vacant until the law on the Research Council was changed in 1965.
This old Research Council was established by law in 1940. Pálmi

Rector Hannesson had held a seat there from the beginning until his death in 1956, and Emil Jónsson, later a government minister, was on the council for the first three years. No others had held seats there. Rector Pálmi was one of the pioneers behind the founding of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). My father once told me that Pálmi had mentioned that he would very much like me to become managing director of the Research Council when I came home from my studies. This never came up, however, in my conversations with Pálmi.

The role of the Research Council, as defined in the law, was to work toward strengthening research in the service of the country's industries and to advise the government. When I took up my duties, the council's most extensive task was assisting the Ministry of Industry (atvinnumálaráðuneytið) with the overall management of the University's Industries Department (Atvinnudeild Háskólans). The University's Industries Department was divided into three divisions: an agricultural division, a fisheries division, and an industrial division. The council was a kind of board for it and dealt with almost everything under the sun: equipment purchases, hiring, salary matters, and the institution's housing affairs. In addition, it dealt with various matters referred from the ministry, gave opinions on legislative bills, and so forth. It also granted foreign parties research permits here in Iceland, gave opinions on individual research projects, and provided advice relating to them.

I felt the work of the Research Council could be made more focused. One of my first tasks was to set up an archive. To assist me I obtained Glúmur Björnsson, office manager at the State Electricity Authority. Glúmur had a good head for figures and was very knowledgeable about everything concerning office administration. We created a filing key, and I read up considerably on that discipline. I chose a key in the decimal system. It was used throughout my time at the Research Council, and it and these documents can still be consulted at the National Archives (Þjóðskjalasafnið). When the flood of paper, which had drifted about with little order, had been arranged systematically, it filled two large filing cabinets.

I was interested in modernizing the operations of the Industries Department with technology, even if only in a small way. I therefore bought dictation machines for the division heads. I was accustomed to using such a machine to dictate letters and other material that secretaries then typed up. This was considered a great novelty but met with mixed success. There was only one secretary at the institution at that time. She came to me and complained bitterly about Halldór Pálsson in the agricultural division. He was an extremely fast talker and more often than not would dictate onto the tape at full speed and then say: "No, I'm going to change this," and begin the same spiel all over again. The secretary was on the verge of giving up completely. The outcome was that Halldór went back to the old methods.

Soon I began trying to get myself out of the cubbyhole assigned to me and to look for a better office in the Industries Department's premises. The Research Council agreed with this, but it was no easy matter, for the building was packed full.

After considerable maneuvering and deliberation it was decided to move the industrial division's building-materials research into rented premises. In this way two good rooms were obtained for the managing director, meeting facilities, and a secretary, on the east side of the north end of the building on the ground floor. A reception area and a room for the cashier and bookkeeper were also arranged.

The heads of the divisions were a hand-picked crew. Jón Jónsson was head of the fisheries division, which was located in Borgartún. He became the first director of the Marine Research Institute (Hafrannsóknastofnun). Halldór Pálsson, who later became director of agriculture, was over the agricultural division, and Óskar B. Bjarnason was over the industrial division. The cashier and bookkeeper were one and the same man, Pálmi Pétursson. Haraldur Ásgeirsson was over the industrial division's building-materials research. He resigned a few years later and set up an independent operation but was hired as head of building research again when it became an independent division.
A new generation of scientists

In practically every room of the Industries Department Building (Atvinnudeildarhúsið) worked men who were a pleasure to get to know. They were full of drive and went incredibly far on enthusiasm alone. Almost without exception they threw themselves body and soul into their work and were well aware how enormously important their work was for the nation. Perhaps that made it sting all the more how limited a response it met with. Nearly all of them had one problem in common. The conditions for research in Iceland at the end of the 1950s were primitive, in a word. In some fields our scientists were little better off than the pioneers who earlier in the century had accomplished great feats single-handedly and with scant resources.

Around and after the Second World War, Icelanders began to pursue more disciplines than the old professional fields and went abroad to study the social sciences, engineering, and the natural sciences in increasing numbers. Copenhagen was no longer the center of Icelanders' higher education. More went to the United States, Britain, Germany, and elsewhere.

Gradually, small groups of scientists formed here in a few fields, for instance in marine research, research related to agriculture, chemistry, building construction, and the natural sciences. In the 1950s, conditions for research were admittedly better than when Bjarni Sæmundsson rowed out in an open rowboat to collect samples. Many of our leading scientists, however, still had to cope with being alone in their specialty and sometimes had little to lean on but the example of the pioneers. It is in fact incredible how many of these men accomplished great works under austere conditions.
When I came to the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð), marine research was among the best provided for.

Since the sea is our livelihood, it was considered more necessary to pursue that research than other kinds. About 20 employees worked on it. Other departments were smaller. Many well-educated individuals who came home in those years after rewarding studies abroad were disappointed by the facilities that awaited them. Little funding could be obtained for scientific work.

Many could be named from that tough band of scientists who worked at the Industrial Research Department (Atvinnudeildin) in those years. Björn Jóhannesson, a kinsman of mine from Skagafjörður, was a soil scientist. He later went to the United Nations and worked there on development matters. Among other outstanding individuals one may name Björn Sigurbjörnsson, permanent secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture (landbúnaðarráðuneytið), and Ingvi Þorsteinsson, who later became my brother-in-law. They worked in the agricultural division. In the fisheries division one may name Jakob Jakobsson, who later became director of the Marine Research Institute (Hafrannsóknastofnun). In the industrial division there were men such as Guðmundur E. Sigvaldason, who is director of the Nordic Volcanological Center (Norræna eldfjallastöðin), Jóhann Jakobsson, who later became head of the division, and Sverrir Scheving Thorsteinsson, my comrade and friend. Many more would of course deserve to be named for their scientific work and remarkable contributions, for this was a good team even though it was not large in number.

In 1960 I hired Inga Lára Guðmundsdóttir, sister of my wife Edda, as secretary of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). She proved extremely dependable and was a model employee in every respect. Inga Lára still works half-days at the Research Council as a department head. She is married to Ingvi Þorsteinsson, the natural scientist mentioned earlier.
The Left-Wing Government Bursts

The left-wing government collapsed at the end of 1958, at about the same time as my first marriage. It proved to be the last government headed by my father. He was in many ways to be pitied in that coalition. He had to hold together a government in which sat old arch-enemies from within the left-wing movement, from the ranks of the communists and the social democrats. In addition, some of the Progressive Party members were not convinced of the sincerity of the coalition partners. This became especially noticeable as the coalition wore on. Economic matters then became an ever greater source of dispute.

The left-wing government contended not least with difficult economic conditions during its time in office. The country's industries were on the verge of grinding to a halt when it took power, and various major projects were in jeopardy. As previously recounted, the government achieved considerable success in obtaining loans abroad for those projects. Among them were the Sog hydroelectric plant (Sogsvirkjun) and the cement factory

at Akranes. In addition, funds were allocated to the electrification of rural areas and the construction of fish-processing plants, twelve trawlers were purchased, and considerable sums were devoted to housing loans and home construction for the general public.

The state of the national economy was in fact not at its best when the left-wing government took over. The catch had failed and the terms of trade had worsened, and moreover the structure of the economy and the currency situation were far from what would have been ideal. Of this I was convinced, and I wrote to my father when the government was being formed. I wanted to completely overhaul the currency regime and increase economic freedom:

To me it seems necessary to establish a correct exchange rate, preferably a floating one. Then necessities ought to be made free, though with a modicum of price controls, while placing import controls on that fishing-boat currency rubbish. This whole thing needs to be turned around back home.

The left-wing government abolished the so-called fishing-boat currency scheme but introduced an extensive system of transfers in its place. With that, the multiple exchange-rate system was abolished in Iceland. The People's Alliance men (Alþýðubandalagsmenn), however, could not be persuaded to undertake a radical overhaul of the economy. By the autumn of 1958 it was clear that measures would have to be taken if inflation was not to get out of hand.

My father asked the Federation of Labour (Alþýðusambandið) to convene a special congress that summer to discuss the necessary measures, but this was refused. The federation's leaders could not be persuaded to move up their scheduled congress, which was to be held late in the autumn. Consultation with the labour movement was essential, because the coalition agreement stipulated that its approval had to be sought in the shaping of economic policy. Many have wondered that my father should have agreed to such a provision, and some have even considered it the most fateful mistake of his political career. He held the view, however, that a responsible labour movement ought to play a substantial role in shaping society. He set out that ideal in a letter to me half a year before the formation of the left-wing government:

In many countries, e.g. the Nordic countries and elsewhere, the labour unions [have] their own economists who determine, after careful study, whether the economy can pay more without contracting and harming the workers with less work. The labour unions of Iceland will reach this stage before very long — perhaps by way of great misfortunes and chaos and difficulties — but

it will come, mark my words, and nothing is more necessary than [to] hasten this development. The working people of Iceland must become responsible — and they will not become so unless they, [that is] their agents or representatives together with the farmers, govern every now and then.

This strikes me as well said and very wise. My father had great faith in cooperation between the labour movement and the farmers' organizations in national affairs before the formation of the left-wing government. In my judgment he was ahead of his time in his attitudes in this respect. It led him, however, to overestimate the labour movement's willingness to hold a left-wing government together. The Federation of Labour (Alþýðusambandið) failed and voted down the necessary economic reforms at its famous congress, where my father himself spoke in favour of the proposal.

I am firmly of the opinion that the collapse of the left-wing government was more consequential than is generally acknowledged. One may say that with it ended the only serious attempt ever made in Iceland to give the organizations of wage earners direct participation in the governing of the country. Since the days of the left-wing government, such ideas have not been raised. No one has wanted to end up in my father's shoes at the Federation of Labour congress of 1958. The only thing comparable to this in later years is the cooperation in the run-up to the National Reconciliation agreements (þjóðarsáttarsamningarnir) of 1990. That, however, was more an accord between the government, the employers, and the labour movement than a case of the institutions of the labour movement having direct influence on government policy-making. In this respect, politics in Iceland has developed differently from Scandinavia and Britain since the end of the Second World War. There, large social democratic parties with strong ties to the labour movement have ruled the roost. In Iceland, the left has always been its own worst enemy.
Viðreisn takes power

With the coming to power of the Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkur) and the Social Democratic Party (Alþýðuflokkur) in 1959, the longest-lived coalition of the republican era was formed. Ólafur Thors initially headed this government, and it took its name from its programme, Viðreisn ("Reconstruction"). This government also marked a turning point in the history of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). In its wake, the party remained out of government longer than at any time before or since — twelve years.

At first, the economic measures of the Viðreisn government overshadowed all other public debate. The currency was devalued and purchasing power reduced accordingly. These were unpopular measures. On the other hand, it seemed to me of great importance that various restrictions on business were lifted and economic freedom increased. I had long been

of the opinion that it was overdue. Truth be told, however, I had scarcely begun to involve myself in national affairs when all this was happening, and I took little part in public debate. My mind was occupied with science, research, heavy industry, and power plants.

Early on, the Viðreisn years were hard going for the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) in parliament. It seemed to me that its members of parliament were slow to find their feet and often went overboard in their criticism. Their argumentation often struck me as unfocused. They opposed practically everything the Viðreisn government did, as is unfortunately the general custom in Icelandic politics. I considered this dubious, and thought it would lead only to the party stagnating in its policies and its ways of working. I disagreed with the parliamentary group on important policy areas, and felt that the Progressives' refrain was all too often that the party could not be made co-responsible for anything that this wicked government did. I supported the Viðreisn government, for example, in its plans for heavy industry in Iceland, which I considered a direct continuation of the left-wing government's policy. I argued for a responsible opposition.

Not everyone thought the parliamentary group too rigid. Within the young Progressives' organizations, a strong and numerous group of radicals came onto the scene. To them the parliamentary group seemed too timid in its opposition to the government. The erosion of the public's living standards, rising inflation, and the government's conservative policies were grist to their mill. This group wanted to define the Progressive Party as a radical left-wing party and the chief adversary of the conservatives. They made the slogan "Anything is better than the conservatives" ("Allt er betra en íhaldið") their motto. That way of thinking had always had strong roots in the hearts of Progressives. Various party members wanted to proceed more cautiously than the radicals.

These conflicts were reflected in the fact that the party's youth movement split into two opposing camps during these years. Clashes frequently occurred in elections to positions of responsibility. For this reason, people were routinely rounded up for meetings and new members multiplied rapidly. In Reykjavík, the Association of Young Progressives (Félag ungra framsóknarmanna) had become the second most numerous political association in the country by the early 1960s. I myself did not take a direct part in party work at first and stood apart from these factional struggles.
Turmoil at the Research Council

The Viðreisn government's coming to power changed nothing about my position at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). I remained on good terms with Gylfi Þ. Gíslason, the Minister of Education, who had signed my letter of appointment in the days of the left-wing government. This peace held, at least most of the time. Gylfi was an enthusiastic Minister of Education, handled his affairs well, and exerted himself in every way. He

could nevertheless be impetuous, both in thought and in speech. When he lost his temper it was as if his tongue could by no means keep up with his swift-flying mind, and he would stumble over his words.

When I came to the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð), Glúmur Björnsson had been assigned to compile an overview of the funds flowing to research in this country. Glúmur was an exceptionally numerate and reliable man. The work had nonetheless been somewhat delayed. I immediately set to work on these investigations and soon took this project largely upon myself. From then on it became a regular part of the Research Council's work to publish overviews of the development of research and experimentation in Iceland. The Research Council issued reports with this information and still does. The first report came out in 1960 and was called The Development of Research and Experimentation in Iceland from 1950–1960. It showed that only 0.3 percent of the national product in Iceland went to these fields, while in the Nordic countries their share was nearly three times higher, and in the United States and Britain close to five to six times higher, to name a few examples.

The findings attracted a great deal of attention. The Minister of Education, Gylfi Þ. Gíslason, reacted furiously, considered it little short of slander, and said the report was "not calculated to enhance the reputation of Icelanders among other nations." He delivered a scolding speech in the Althing in which he called the comparison questionable and said it was no wonder that we lagged behind other industrialized nations. At the same time, however, he criticized the industries and companies for their low contributions to research and said he realized that state funding would have to be increased. Following this, I compiled a memorandum in consultation with the Research Council. It contained further justification of our findings and of the definition of research funding. My reply was sent to all members of parliament.

This made Gylfi even angrier. He telephoned every member of the council and poured bloody abuse over them. He also had the study repeated in rough outline, adding expenditures for all kinds of practical projects such as drilling for hot water and other things of that sort. In this way he managed to raise the figures considerably. This misunderstanding of Gylfi's stemmed first and foremost from the fact that he did not grasp the definition of research and experimentation, which perhaps was not to be expected.

We had pored long over what should count as research and what should not, and had consulted research councils elsewhere in the Nordic countries. We thought it most natural to use the international definition, whereby research is only that which aims at the acquisition of new knowledge. Thus a survey of rock strata in geothermal areas would count as research, but by no means the drilling for hot water that builds on the results of such stratigraphic studies.

I believe that everyone who studied this matter thoroughly was convinced by our arguments, for it is a fundamental principle of international comparison that the results between countries be comparable. The Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) stayed its course and still publishes these reports, which gradually became more detailed. The definition remains the same. At the same time, we Icelanders still lag far behind other nations as regards research and development. Funding for research has nevertheless increased little by little. I believe it is now around one percent of the national product.

In fact, one may say that it was not the state that had most cause to be ashamed of these findings. The shortage of research funding was attributable not least to the fact that in Iceland virtually no money came from the industries themselves. Abroad, companies are very large participants in research activity.

Partly in light of this finding, I pushed to have ten percent of companies' income exempted from tax if it was devoted to research under their own auspices or at public research institutes. That was granted. Abroad, tax concessions have in many places given rise to flourishing research in the business sector. I was disappointed, however, with the outcome here at home. Companies responded little or not at all. As time passed I in fact lost sight of this provision, and I understand it was removed in one of the numerous amendments that have been made to the tax laws. Indeed, tax relief for investment in research has once again become one of the principal causes of the Icelandic Research Council (Rannsóknarráð Íslands), as my old workplace is called today.

I remember only one other incident in which a shadow fell over my collaboration with Gylfi Þ. Gíslason during the fourteen years he was my superior as Minister of Education. On one occasion, as often before, I was to have a meeting with Gylfi and arrived at the appointed time at the Government Offices. When more than an hour had passed beyond the scheduled meeting time, I left, leaving behind a note to the effect that I could not be bothered to warm the benches of the Government Offices. Gylfi telephoned the moment he received the message. He was half offended by this missive. I answered defiantly, saying that I had sat there far past the meeting time and could not shirk my other duties with such idleness. Nothing further came of this. Our frictions likewise had no lasting consequences, and in fact we never discussed them at our meetings.

I never became as close a collaborator of Gylfi's as my father had been, and we were on opposite sides on various issues of the Viðreisn years. Matters came to a head especially over the question of membership in the European Economic Community (Efnahagsbandalag Evrópu) when an application for associate membership came onto the agenda. Gylfi was at the forefront of the pro-Europeans there. My father spoke well of Gylfi as long as their paths ran
together, and Gylfi has often spoken warmly of my father. I believe Gylfi also regretted that their paths parted.

Gylfi is a brilliantly intelligent man and well read. This showed more often than not in his work, both inside parliament and out. He seems to have kept his working vigour nearly undiminished into recent years. He has regularly sent me articles he has written for Nordic publications. They bear clear witness to his gifts and keen breadth of vision.
Building up facilities for research

To remedy the lack of facilities for research activity in the country, the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) emphasized two things, in addition to promoting increased funding. One was to reorganize the working environment of research with new legislation on the Research Council and the research institutes of the industries; the other was the planning and construction of a new research campus. At Keldnaholt, 48 hectares of land had been allocated to the Research Council, the office of the Director of Electric Power (raforkumálastjóri), and the University of Iceland (Háskóli Íslands). Jakob Gíslason, the Director of Electric Power, had taken the initiative in securing it. He is among the more remarkable colleagues I have had. Jakob was quiet and measured in all his bearing, deeply thoughtful and resourceful. My dealings with Jakob also proved fateful, for it was in his offices that I met my wife Edda, as related earlier.

I set to work at once preparing the construction work at Keldnaholt. Two of the country's most esteemed architects were engaged to design the campus, Skarphéðinn Jóhannsson and Sigvaldi Thordarson. They were superb professionals, artistic to their fingertips, and highly entertaining. They had one great flaw, however: unpunctuality. When the building committee had once again been kept waiting for them and a quarter of an hour had passed beyond the announced meeting time, I sent the committee members away. A quarter of an hour later the architects came storming in. They asked whether there was not supposed to be a meeting. I replied that it was over. I had adjourned the meeting once the academic quarter-hour had elapsed. They grew very angry, and Sigvaldi outright lost control of his temper. I told them that they had been engaged for this job and were obliged to show up on time. From then on, meetings would be adjourned once a quarter of an hour had passed beyond the announced meeting time. They stormed out. Skarphéðinn telephoned later that day, however, and apologized. After this they generally arrived on the dot.
Skarphéðinn I knew well and valued highly. He designed my house on Laugarás and assisted me with the drawings for my house at Arnarnes, where

I still live. In his work he emphasized simplicity and purity in the interplay of building and surroundings. There his knowledge of Icelandic nature came fully into its own, for he was a great outdoorsman. Skarphéðinn passed away before his time. His works made him the "master builder of learning and science," as I have put it before.

In preparation for the construction at Keldnaholt, research campuses in the Nordic countries were visited. I managed to obtain a good grant from the United Nations cultural and scientific organization, Unesco, for the journey. It was made in 1962. Besides me, the architects came along, as did Jakob Gíslason and representatives of the departments that were to be located at Keldnaholt. This trip was extremely instructive. We visited research campuses both at Blindern in Oslo and at the Technical University in Trondheim, at Otaniemi near Helsinki, and in Denmark. All the facilities in Norway were excellent, but we found the visit to Finland the most instructive. The architects in particular were beside themselves, and no wonder. The buildings were both well designed and exceptionally beautiful.

The Finns were hospitable and invited us, among other things, to a sauna at their research centre. There they had three kinds of bathhouse: a dry sauna, a wet sauna, and a smoke sauna. The latter was heated with wood and all the walls were soot-black. One did not need to sit there long to become smeared with soot. The fourth sauna was a kind of laboratory where human heat tolerance was studied under various conditions.

Jakob and I were invited into the smoke sauna. When we stepped out of the haze, before we knew it two formidable strapping women had seized us in their paws and slapped us flat onto wooden benches. There was no reasoning with them, as they spoke nothing but Finnish. They set about massaging us so vigorously that every limb creaked. I took it in good part, but I can still picture the look of embarrassment on Jakob's face as he was hauled up onto the bench. Finally the viragoes filled sizeable buckets of water and dumped them over us as we lay there.

When we had at last managed to rinse off the soot, we were invited, naked, into a lounge where the Finns sat in groups. There beer and other refreshments were brought to us by charming Finnish girls. We were little accustomed to liberality of this sort. I took it in good part, but Jakob was utterly mortified. Everything proceeded decorously, however. A detailed report was written about this trip, but the sauna adventures received scant mention.

The first building at Keldnaholt was occupied in 1965. It was erected for the agricultural department. The Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) had a kind of general oversight of the construction, and I sat on the building committees for the houses. Early on, the work was hampered by the fact that no funding was available. In the legislation on

the University Lottery (Happdrætti Háskólans), it is stipulated that 20 percent of its revenues shall go to the state treasury. This is the so-called licence fee, which is still in force and was from the very beginning meant to go to research for the benefit of the industries. The treasury, however, appropriated these funds for other projects. I took this matter up with the Minister of Education and wanted the licence fee put into the building fund of the University's Department of Applied Sciences (Atvinnudeild Háskólans). He received this quite favourably, but the matter nonetheless seemed to make little headway. Among other things, I obtained loan capital from the Unemployment Insurance Fund (Atvinnuleysistryggingasjóður) so that construction would not come to a halt. It was not until I had discussed the matter with Magnús Jónsson, the Minister of Finance, that my idea for the disposition of the lottery money was accepted. His support was decisive. With this money the research campus at Keldnaholt was largely built.

After a handsome building had been erected for the Agricultural Research Institute (Rannsóknastofnun landbúnaðarins), premises were built for the Building Research Institute (Rannsóknastofnun byggingariðnaðarins) and finally the Industrial Research Institute (Rannsóknastofnun iðnaðarins). It had been planned that the University's Faculty of Engineering would also be housed at Keldnaholt, but the university obtained additional land west of Suðurgata and decided to keep all its activities in one place. I well understood that point of view. It would certainly have been beneficial, though, for the research institutes and the engineering faculty to be in close proximity.

The Director of Electric Power's construction plans also came to less than had been intended. The office of the Director of Electric Power was split up, and Jakob Gíslason became Director of Energy (orkumálastjóri). Keldnaholt did not become the great national centre of research that was aimed for at the outset. Nevertheless, the development there was one of the most important steps ever taken toward providing facilities for research activity in the country. I took great pleasure in participating in this work.
International cooperation in the making

As was common among administrative institutions in Iceland, participation in international cooperation was extremely limited when I began work at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). I was very keen to change this. In my first years at the Research Council, foreign contacts accordingly increased greatly. First, ties were established with the research councils elsewhere in the Nordic countries, which had a forum for cooperation, Nordforsk. I attended the annual meetings of that organization and thus came into contact with many excellent leaders of research activity in the Nordic countries. That often proved very useful.

Robert Major was the director of the Research Council of Norway. We became great friends. Robert later became a kind of adviser on the organization of research activity in this country, together with the head of the science committee of the Economic Co-operation

and Development Organisation in Paris, that distinguished man Dr. Alexander King. They both came to Iceland more than once. Among other things, they delivered the keynote addresses at a major conference which the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) convened on the organization of research in 1961. Robert also came often on his own. He was a great outdoorsman and we frequently went on mountain trips together. We climbed Herðubreið and Kerlingafjöll together and cast for fish in Grímsá, in Seyðisá, on Arnarvatnsheiði, and elsewhere. On fishing trips he was so eager that he didn't think it worth getting into his sleeping bag; instead he lay down on top of it and was out in the river before five in the morning.

Soon the Minister of Education asked me to be one of Iceland's two representatives on a committee on higher education and science at the Council of Europe (Evrópuráðið) in Strasbourg. Various fine men sat on it who became good friends of mine. Among them I can name Ármann Snævarr, university rector, Snorri Hallgrímsson, professor, and Magnús Már Lárusson, university rector. My acquaintance with Ármann in particular became close.

After meetings we usually dined in the French manner, with excellent wine, at one of the small but good restaurants that abound in the city. Then we walked back to the hotel. When the meal was over, Ármann would often want to head in one direction and I in another. My suggestion always prevailed and always proved right. I have long considered myself to have a good sense of direction, whether in cities or in the mountains. Once, admittedly, we spent two hours on the way because we came to the river that runs through Strasbourg and had to take a long detour to reach the hotel. The direction, however, had been exactly right!
My acquaintance with Ármann proved extremely important to me when I, the engineer, was appointed Minister of Justice in 1978. I then often sought advice from Ármann, who never failed me.
Thrown into the Progressive Party

My entry into politics came about so suddenly that I can almost put an exact date on its beginning. It was in October 1962. Edda and I were then busily preparing for our wedding. She worked as a flight attendant for Loftleiðir and was away on a flight at the time. Representatives of the Association of Young Progressives in Reykjavík (Félag ungra framsóknarmanna í Reykjavík), FUF, got in touch and wanted to meet me. I was in fact well aware of what they had in mind. Within the association there had been fierce disputes, and battles as never before in every election for the board and offices.

Örlygur Hálfdanarson led the radical wing among the young Progressives and served as chairman of their national federation, SUF. He was a highly competitive man and placed great emphasis on securing his position by backing a supporter of his for the leadership of FUF. Some dug in
their heels, and in the end everything was tied up in a hard knot. An agreement was then reached between the factions to get me to take the chairmanship for one year.

My parents were abroad, and I invited the group to the house on Tjarnargata. I opened the meeting by arguing that it would not be right for me to take on the chairmanship. I would turn 35 the following summer, and the party's rules provided that the age limit stood at 36. I made little headway with my guests. It made no difference what I put forward; everything was contradicted and turned into its opposite.

We sat for a long time, and at last I was asked whether I wasn't going to offer them anything. I then brought out a whisky bottle that my father kept in a cupboard. Then the game began to heat up. Various trials of strength got under way, and no less wrestling. Among others I wrestled with Eyjólfur, son of Eysteinn Jónsson, chairman of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). That bout ended with us crashing into a beautiful standing lamp in the living room. It toppled over. The shade, which was made of glass, escaped undamaged, but the same could not be said of the stand. It broke at the base. The wrestling produced no decisive result, but the outcome was that I took on the chairmanship. I formally took office on 13 October 1962.

I am convinced that Þráinn Valdimarsson, who was the party's executive director, played a very large part in this reconciliation within the youth movement. He himself says that he spoke many times with my father during those years about whether I could be persuaded to take up political work. This interest stemmed from the fact that he knew some of my co-workers from the Fertilizer Plant (Áburðarverksmiðjan), older men who had grown up with the working culture of the countryside and never let a task slip from their hands. They are said to have described me as the only man who was never seen walking; instead I always ran between work areas. These stories were somewhat exaggerated. Þráinn likes to recall that he usually received the same answer from my father to his overtures. It went something like this:
If Steingrímur is needed in Icelandic politics, his part will come to the fore. On the other hand, you can fully trust that I will neither encourage nor discourage him from such work.
Þráinn therefore chose to take other routes.

By getting me into the leadership of FUF, Þráinn Valdimarsson succeeded in bringing me into politics. No one bore more responsibility for that than he.
