Nor was it long before he helped bring about my taking a seat on the party's central committee and after that on its executive board. Þráinn likewise threw his weight behind things when it was necessary
to convince me to stand for parliament. He was a true shaper of destiny in my political life.

Þráinn was also one of my best collaborators in party work after I was chosen for leadership there. He was an invaluable worker, has an incredible memory, and his conscientiousness is as dependable as night following day. He is one of the greatest judges of character I have ever known and took great pains to get to know people. I believe Þráinn knew every active Progressive across the whole country by name.

Þráinn chose to retire in 1983 after 36 years of work for the party. Since then he has enjoyed life with his family, swims and plays golf most days, in addition to dissecting social issues to the marrow at daily coffee gatherings with a group of his contemporaries from politics and business. I take great pleasure in playing golf with Þráinn from time to time. He is one of the few from my work in the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) whom I still meet fairly regularly.

I never had any inclination toward work in other parties, and my participation in the Progressive Party came about of its own accord. I don't think I ever formally registered in the party. At the outset, though, I was firmly determined not to be drawn into politics. As I have said before, I had held that view ever since childhood. Nevertheless, I had a keen interest in public affairs and frequently attended meetings on such matters, not least among the young Progressives. Often I could not hold my tongue and contributed my own views to the discussion. This chatter of mine, however, by no means meant that I was contemplating a career in politics. Nor, in fact, was the chairmanship of FUF intended as a step on that path — at least not on my part.

Indeed, my main worries in the days that followed concerned not the Association of Young Progressives but a broken lamp and a wedding. The standing lamp was a particular favorite of my mother's. I therefore hit upon the plan of repairing it by slipping a smaller tube inside the stand where the blow had struck it, and in that way I was able to reinforce it. Soon after my mother came home, however, she began to remark on how strangely the lamp was leaning. A short while later she gave me the lamp. It stands in the dining room at home as a kind of monument to the beginning of my political career. I still don't know whether my mother suspected how things really stood. She knew I had invited a group over, because I accounted for the whisky bottle as soon as my parents returned home. But I never told her that I had broken the lamp. Edda must have been startled when she came back from her flight. Her husband-to-be, who had always sworn off all politics, had become chairman of the second most populous political association in the country.
"Will You Marry Me?"

The divorce and the battle over the children colored my private life more than anything else during my first years at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). There is no knowing how I would have come through that ordeal had it not been a foregone conclusion that Edda and I bound ourselves all the more tightly together the more we were beset. I valued Edda's steadfastness especially highly, not least because of my earlier experience. When a formal divorce from Dolly was obtained in the United States, we began to think about our wedding. It took place just under a year later, on 19 October 1962, only about a week after I was elected chairman of the young Progressives. We were married quietly at the home of the Reverend Jón Guðnason, who among other things had served at Prestbakki in Hrútafjörður. The wedding was simple and beautiful. It took place at ten in the morning in the presence of my parents and Edda's mother. After the ceremony, the closest relatives were invited for champagne and kransakaka. In the afternoon we flew off toward London on our honeymoon.

While the legal proceedings with Dolly were under way, Edda had been living in her parents' home. The house on Laugarásvegur was soon put up for sale, since it was subject to division in the divorce case. I therefore lived in my old room in my parents' house on Tjarnargata. Edda and I nevertheless spent more time together than this suggests. We went most places together and, among other things, attended a dance course where we learned the latest steps, the cha-cha-cha and the tango. By the time we married she had left her position as private secretary to Jakob Gíslason, the director of electric power affairs, and had become a flight attendant with Loftleiðir. She therefore stopped a little over half a year after we married. It was an unwritten rule that married women did not serve on flights. That soon changed, though, like so much else.

Edda was born at Laugarvatn in Árnessýsla, where her mother's family had lived for several centuries. Her grandmother was Ingunn Eyjólfsdóttir, who was descended in a direct line from Högni, a member of the law council (lögréttumaður) at Laugarvatn. Edda's grandfather was Böðvar Magnússon, a farmer at Laugarvatn and a staunch Progressive. He was captivated by Jónas of Hrifla's vision of district schools, and Ingunn and Böðvar gave their land for the District School at Laugarvatn (Héraðsskólinn á Laugarvatni). That proved fateful, because Guðmundur, Edda's father, took a position there as a teacher and met Hlíf, her mother, who was one of the couple's eleven daughters. Guðmundur and Hlíf moved to Reykjaskóli in Hrútafjörður shortly after Edda was born. Her father was headmaster there, and there she grew up. Edda had a happy childhood in the lively and nurturing environment of the school community. She learned to read over her big brother's shoulder at the age of four, could swim by five, and swam nearly every day from then on. The story goes that once guests had

come to Reykjaskóli, among them a girl the same age as Edda. A swimming outing came up in conversation, but the visiting girl turned out to be unable to swim. Edda said straight away that so was she. Her father thought this a pity and needless modesty. The story, on the other hand, describes Edda very well. She did not want this new friend of hers to seem the lesser person.

Edda had two older brothers: Böðvar, who has already figured in this story, and Gísli Ölvir, who died at the age of 23. Edda also has a sister one year younger than herself, Inga Lára. They have always been very close. Inga Lára worked as my secretary at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð), as mentioned earlier, and is one of the best co-workers imaginable. She is quick-witted, clear-headed, and swift at every task. As children the sisters were usually dressed alike, and their favorites were beautiful party dresses — salmon-pink taffeta dresses and blue velvet dresses. It can be difficult, however, to stay dressed up in one's childhood years. On 17 June it was the custom for guests to go swimming. Once, in her excitement, Edda forgot herself and dove in wearing the blue velvet dress. She then had to sit and watch the dress dry for the rest of the day while her sister paraded in hers.

Impulsiveness, however, was by no means characteristic of the Edda I came to know, fell in love with, and married. That young woman surpassed others in elegance and refinement. She is good to talk to and a steadfast friend. Edda is exceptionally hospitable, warm and sincere with strangers, and loyal to her friends and family. Yet she does not parade her feelings, and she deals with difficulties in private. Edda is a strong woman and a good mother.

In every matter she is both firm and true in her convictions. Edda can be very determined and yields nothing to me in arguing a case when she chooses to. On rare occasions we have quarreled hard, as happens, but it has always smoothed over quickly. She is generally quicker than I am to make peace. Edda is an extremely good dancer. She has an artistic bent, plays the piano, and paints in her spare time.

Guðmundur, Edda's father, died of cancer at only 55 years of age. I therefore never knew him. Edda wrote a fine essay about her father in the book Faðir minn skólastjórinn (My Father the Headmaster). Her mother, Hlíf, lived alone with her children after her husband's death. She obtained a plot in Álfheimar and built a home for the family. This she did admirably. Hlíf is a remarkable woman and exceptionally high-spirited. She is approaching ninety, plays bridge every week, and is seldom more in her element than when dancing. When the divorce case between Dolly and me was at its height, it took a toll on everyone around me. Edda's mother was naturally worried about the situation and the conflicts her daughter had suddenly become caught up in, barely twenty years old. As time passed, however, it became clear to everyone
that Edda and I were serious about our relationship. From then on my mother-in-law and I formed a good relationship, which truly endures still.

Our honeymoon began in London, where a party was thrown for us at the embassy at the invitation of Ambassador Henrik Sv. Björnsson. From there we went to Paris, where we stayed at an old, dignified hotel close by the Arc de Triomphe, where it was said that de Gaulle had often stayed before he became president. In Paris we were also invited to a party at the embassy. Pétur Thorsteinsson was then ambassador in Paris. Neither party was at our request; the ambassadors had simply heard of our travels. We were touched by this unexpected and princely welcome.

From Paris we went on to Rome, where we spent three days. We walked the city from end to end, as far as the days allowed. In Rome we rented a small two-seater Fiat sports car and drove south along the Italian peninsula to Sorrento, which lies directly opposite the island of Capri, a short way south of Naples. There is a celebrated rocky coastline there and great natural beauty. When we got out onto the road from Rome, we stopped the car to have a bite. I have always been suspicious of pasta and hardly consider it food, so we got ourselves hamburgers. They were dripping with olive oil. Whether the oil or the meat was to blame, we both got upset stomachs. It took us a full twenty-four hours to get over the consequences of this pickiness of mine.

From Sorrento we made excursions to nearby places — the city of Naples, Pompeii, Herculaneum, and Capri. I had gotten into the swing of filming and have many reels from that trip. In the evenings we danced in glamorous nightclubs and Edda appeared at her loveliest. She has herself said that she never took as many clothes with her on any other trip.

From Italy we flew to Frankfurt, from where our route lay to Karlsruhe for a meeting of the Council of Europe's committee on education and science. On the way there a remarkable incident occurred. I had intended to rent a cheap Volkswagen for the journey, but no such car was to be had. So we took the plunge and chose a Mercedes-Benz sports car. It was exceptionally powerful and responded delightfully when you stepped on the accelerator. Between Heidelberg and Wiesbaden there was a stretch of the autobahn called the death mile because of how many accidents had happened there. The traffic was heavy and fast, but suddenly it came to a standstill. I had time to slow down, but then saw in the mirror a red car approaching at terrifying speed. The driver slammed on his brakes when he finally realized, but lost control of the car, which shot off the road. Before I knew it, it was heading straight back up onto the road — now directly at the side of our car, the side where Edda was sitting. Fortunately I stepped not on the brake but on the accelerator

at that moment. A gap of about two car lengths had formed ahead of us, and the sports car shot forward. I don't remember whether I touched the bumper of the next car in front before I managed to stop. The red car grazed past just behind our car and hit the barrier separating the lanes of the autobahn. It flew over this two-meter-high defensive wall like a gymnast doing a somersault and landed on its wheels on the other side. The last thing I saw was the driver looking around, dazed. Fortunately there was no oncoming traffic in sight. I have no doubt that it is thanks to that powerful Mercedes-Benz that we are alive. Admittedly, one could say that if we had been in a Volkswagen we would have been far behind the red car when this happened — but that is another story.
After coming home we moved into our first home, a small but cozy attic apartment in Sólheimar. And work took over.
A Young Progressive

I took the young Progressives' organizational work firmly in hand and immediately set about reorganizing the activities of FUF together with my fellow board members. We went through the membership roll and brought it up to date. It contained various people who had long since passed the age limit and moved on to the party associations of older members; others had left the party, and the occasional man was even deceased. A program of activities for the year was published, and monthly meetings were decided upon. They were usually held on the Progressive Party's (Framsóknarflokkurinn) premises at Tjarnargata 26, where we had facilities in the basement. The meeting format was changed so that guests sat at a round table and spoke from their seats instead of going up to a podium. This brought about greater participation in all discussion and better attendance.

The chairmanship was an enjoyable time and in fact lasted two years, as I was re-elected despite my age. There were various fine men there, and the board was very energetic. Its members included, among others, Jón Aðalsteinn Jónsson, later a wholesale merchant, who was treasurer, and the broadcasters Páll Heiðar Jónsson and Kári Jónasson, news director at the State Broadcasting Service (Ríkisútvarpið).

In those years a powerful group, or clique, took shape within the young Progressives' associations. Besides part of the board, it included men such as Kristinn Finnbogason, who was managing director of Tíminn for many years, Jón Abraham Ólafsson, Matthías Andrésson, Grímur Jónsson, Páll Jónsson, and Óðinn Rögnvaldsson, to name a few. These were all men of tremendous drive, willing workers and determined.
Kristinn Finnbogason was the one of these comrades-in-arms whose path ran longest

alongside mine in the party. He was in many ways a remarkable man. Kristinn was large in stature and a heavyweight in everything he did. In his younger years he was an electrician in Austur-Húnavatnssýsla, very radical and even rumored to lean toward communism. After he moved to Reykjavík he started up business ventures of various kinds and did quite well. He then joined the young Progressives' associations. Kristinn was a true friend to his friends, and for them he would do anything. He was a princely host and served food and drink generously — so much so that guests had their hands full getting through the refreshments and walking upright afterwards.

If Kristinn took a dislike to people or counted them among his enemies, he was hard as flint and did not spare strong words. In such dealings he always made his presence felt and bore down on his opponents with all his weight. Kristinn and I became good friends and shared many memorable moments together, both in the bustle of politics and outside it. Among other things, we were fishing companions for many years. Kristinn died before his time.

The Viðreisn years were oil on the fire of our young men's idealism, for contentious issues were many, devaluations were frequent, and ideas about joining the European Economic Community (Efnahagsbandalag Evrópu) kindled love of country in our breasts. It was fun to work in politics in those years. The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) won record support, and all party activity was on the upswing. There we certainly did not want to be found wanting.

When I came home from the United States, my ideas were in various respects at odds with the Progressive Party's policy. I had enormous faith in the possibility of setting more strong pillars under the Icelandic economy and considered cooperation with foreign parties promising to that end. The party was to a large extent suspicious of foreign investment, which I strongly advocated. Many had doubts about the freedom of the market system. I considered it inevitable and firmly supported the initiative of individuals in those things they could manage. In the party I was sometimes considered too much of an individualist for these reasons.

I was certainly not among the most radical in the ranks of the young Progressives, and it can no doubt be said that I was further to the right than the great majority of party members in those Viðreisn years. Yet I was at the same time a firm supporter of the cooperative ideal, and of equality in education, health care, and welfare. These views I hold still. I have always believed that society has a duty to provide everyone with a minimum standard of living. Those who come out the losers in life's struggle must have hope of getting back on their feet. I also thought it natural and right to harness the cooperative movement or the state for larger undertakings and investments that were beyond the power of individuals. In short, I supported
welfare state with a mixed economy. What was considered right-wing extremism a good thirty years ago is considered leftist heresy now.
The Stance on Europe

The first major political undertaking was not far off. We prepared ourselves and the party, both openly and behind the scenes, for the party congress and the parliamentary elections that were held at the beginning of summer 1963. There had been considerable discussion about the European Economic Community (Efnahagsbandalag Evrópu, EBE) and Iceland's possible membership in it that winter, following Britain's application to join the community. The British were among our most important trading partners. The Reconstruction Government (Viðreisnarstjórnin), and especially some of its ministers, spoke strongly in favor of so-called associate membership for Iceland in the EEC. Gylfi Þ. Gíslason was foremost among them. Young Progressives organized a variety of discussions, and a large conference was held on the European Economic Community, which in our judgment was the issue of issues.

At the conference I gave a talk on the free movement of capital and labor. There I came to the conclusion that there was perhaps more reason to fear an exodus of young Icelanders than an influx of foreign labor. I placed the greatest emphasis, however, on the point that "we Icelanders could ourselves create rapid economic development and living standards comparable to the best in our neighboring countries." We would fare best when we were not muzzled by policies that others decided.

At the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) congress that spring, we put forward a strongly worded resolution stating that membership in the Economic Community was out of the question. I remember that Eysteinn Jónsson felt this was too strongly worded and wanted to soften the tone. We refused that outright, and I went to the podium more than once to present our case. The matter ended with a vote, and we prevailed.

I think it can be said that at this congress my position on Iceland's membership in a community of European states crystallized at once. It remained unchanged throughout my political career. The resolution read as follows:

The most fateful issue for the nation in the coming elections will be the position of the Icelandic authorities regarding negotiations with the European Economic Community. The Progressive Party has from the beginning emphasized that tariff and trade agreements should be sought with the European Economic Community. On the other hand, no one any longer doubts that the government par-

ties are aiming at some kind of Icelandic membership in the EEC, even if something else is being suggested now, before the elections. Associate membership in the EEC, as the government itself has defined it in its report and its arguments, would lead to foreign control over the nation's principal industries and resources. With that, its independence and nationhood would be placed in direct peril.
We considered this resolution a major victory and celebrated it at my home in Sólheimar until morning.

Eysteinn, however, usually had his way in the party. The Federation of Young Progressives (FUF) regularly held a kind of discotheque in its quarters in the basement of the party office on Tjarnargata. These became especially popular gatherings. Morgunblaðið, however, reacted furiously with great invective directed at us. It said there that Steingrímur Hermannsson was responsible for brainwashing innocent youngsters. I found this very unfair, since perfect orderliness prevailed and the whole operation was exemplary. The articles nevertheless led to Eysteinn and the party leadership becoming skittish about these gatherings. The youth evenings were discontinued, and the kids went back to hanging around the snack shops.

The Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) succeeded in making the European question one of the main issues of contention in the 1963 parliamentary elections. In that campaign I gave my first political speeches and wrote articles for the newspapers. I had no trouble criticizing the Reconstruction Government. In my view, it had failed in one of the principal goals of its policy. Inflation had gotten out of hand. I also had growing doubts about an economic policy built on "a suitable level of unemployment." I made industry and economic affairs my topic ever more often:

Our economy is unfortunately unbalanced, and therefore the economic policy that may perhaps work for nations of millions with highly diversified economies is not at all suited to us here. This has been proven in recent years. It takes nothing more than the herring catch being larger than in an average year, with the consequence that capital increases in the country, and then everything comes unhinged, the cost of living rises faster than ever before, and the government can do nothing about it.

I criticized the Reconstruction Government in speech and in writing. I have, however, never considered it wise to base my arguments first and foremost on abuse of the opponent. I chose rather to be optimistic and positive and to emphasize what I and my party could do better for the future of the nation.
The 1963 elections were my father's last elections. He had planned to withdraw from politics, but the European question was decisive in his standing for one more election.

When I look back, an obvious parallel appears between my father's last election campaign and my own last elections in 1991. In both, the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) emphasized opposition to the European Community. Our arguments were almost the same. I still believe that a small state like Iceland has both a unique culture and special interests to protect. We would be mere hangers-on in a European union of states. It is naivety to claim otherwise. In both of these elections, the supporters of European integration maintained that the matter was not really on the agenda. In 1963 the argument was that British membership in the community was uncertain, and in 1991 negotiations were said not to be imminent.

This vigorous election campaign of ours in 1963 reflected the fact that, as time went on, the years in opposition had in some ways done the party good. There was time to attend to the party's internal organization and work. Many joined the Progressives. The party's activities became very vigorous, especially among the younger men, and the party won its greatest electoral victories in its history. In the 1963 elections the Progressive Party received 28.2 percent of the vote and gained two members of parliament. The Reconstruction Government (Viðreisnarstjórnin) narrowly held on. The Progressives' increased support could doubtless be traced to distrust of the government, its neglect of the interests of wage earners, its stance on the European Community, and its indifference in welfare matters. Many considered the government right-leaning and serving the interests of employers and foreign monopolies.
Chapter Ten
A NEW BEGINNING

Edda and I laid the foundation for our own home at Arnarnes in 1964. We had actually already secured the plot in 1960. Arnarnes had previously been a farm. A farmer lived there who was mentally ill. He was one of three brothers. The story was told of the farmer that he had been displeased with the intrusion that occurred when the British set up fortifications on the point. So every evening he went out and spread cow dung on all the roads the soldiers used. In the end they gave up. The proud army of the British Empire fled the dung stench of the eccentric crofter rather than the rain of German bombs.

My father often walked through this area on his rambles. The seashore at Arnarnes is especially beautiful. On one of his first outings, the old man of the farm came wading toward him with a hayfork raised. My father was fortunately quick to twist the weapon out of the farmer's hands and managed to talk him down. The old man then made a special exception for my father's walks; he was allowed to roam the point. The occupant's brothers eventually had him declared legally incompetent, and Páll Magnússon, a lawyer, was engaged to divide the area into building plots. Páll deserves most of the credit for the plots being as equal in size as they are, and for there being no road along the shore, as had previously been planned. He was the father of Pétur, who was one of my card-playing companions for many years, as mentioned before.

Pétur pointed the plots out to me when they were all still available, apart from a few plots that Páll's family intended for themselves. I wanted to buy five plots and discussed it with my father, since I did not have enough money. He thought very poorly of that idea and advised me against it. He said I might well profit from such speculation, but that it would chiefly bring me worries and other material cares. My father was very much opposed to speculation, and I let
be said. If I had bought the five plots I could have built practically for free, since plot prices increased tenfold in a short time.

Edda and I had some money to begin building the house on Mávanes, as the street was called. I had received half of what remained when Laugarás was sold, though debts had admittedly weighed heavily against it. My father also lent me one million, which was a considerable sum. I took out a bank loan for what was still lacking, and I certainly benefited from having kept up payments on my earlier loans for Laugarás. In those borrowings I no doubt benefited from my father. These unindexed loans for Arnarnes largely burned up in the inflation of the Reconstruction years.

I made all the preliminary drawings for Mávanes 19 and, among other things, built a plastic model at 1:50 scale so the house could be visualized. At that point no basement was planned. The architect Skarphéðinn Jóhannsson went over the work and made all the working drawings. He also proposed various changes, some of which I took into account. I had very firm opinions about how the house should be. It turned out that it was more expensive to fill in the foundation than to finish a basement. I therefore designed an office, a sitting room, and a storage room there, as well as a boat shed that soon became my workshop, since no boat ever materialized.
The Last Company and the First Computer

Around the same time as we began building the house, events came to a head in what remained of my involvement in business. I had already parted ways with the ice production, and by 1963 the position of Verklegar framkvæmdir hf. had become difficult and the company's finances were strained. Three projects had gone rather badly financially: the construction of the Post and Telephone building in Kópavogur, Hallveigarstaðir in Reykjavík, and a salmon ladder in Langá. By this point all the founders except Ólafur Jensson had in effect ceased working for the company quite some time earlier. We still held our shares, however, and attended the annual general meeting once a year. The difficulties seemed about to be resolved when the company was entrusted with building the new police station and the building of the Science Institute of the University of Iceland (Raunvísindastofnun Háskóla Íslands). We believed that with this it would be possible to turn the operation around.

Our hopes were not fulfilled. There was a considerable loss on the construction of the new police station, and the Science Institute building did not prove the windfall for the company that had been hoped. Verklegar framkvæmdir hf. ultimately could not cover its debts. A composition with creditors was negotiated in 1965. All the founding partners took part in the settlement. We lost the money

we had put into the company, and in addition a good number of personal guarantees that we had undertaken fell upon us. I believe the settlement was carried out honorably, and none of us went bankrupt because of it.

My drive for activity and my ideas found an outlet in other projects once my involvement in running businesses ended. I had seen computer technology take its first steps during my studies in the United States, as I have recounted earlier. After coming to Iceland I continued to follow this development, though from a distance. I have always been fascinated by devices and new technology. This stayed with me in my work at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). In the minutes of the council from 19 October 1963, under the item "electronic calculator" (rafeindareiknir), it says:

The managing director put forward the idea of whether the State Research Council should try to take the plunge and bring such a calculator to this country. It seems obvious that sufficient work is arising in the country for one such machine, and it is really a matter of sink or swim.

I was assigned to look into the matter further and took it up with the University. There was no good word yet for these new devices, and under the item "rafreiknir" I reported on the progress of the matter at the council's next meeting. The outcome was that the first mainframe computer was leased from IBM. This marked the beginning of the University Computing Centre (Reiknistofnun Háskólans), which has been a pioneer in computing in this country. It was apparently Sigurður Nordal who proposed the excellent word tölva, which should be declined like völva (prophetess). It was hard to say which phenomenon was wrapped in greater mystery, the ancient prophetesses or the new computers.
The Most Expensive Ptarmigan Hunt in History

I pursued outdoor life and mountain trips as much as I possibly could while I was at the Research Council. I knew of little better than going skiing when the weather was good, and if a weekend was free, the wilderness had my whole heart. I had spent untold hours restoring an old Dodge Weapon, an American military jeep of the larger type. Among other things, I had fitted it out for mountain travel so that one could sleep in it on narrow benches. My travel companions, however, usually chose a tent over these sleeping quarters, so I often slept alone in the vehicle.
In late autumn 1963 one of those irresistible days dawned, on 11 November, to be precise. As so often when the urge to travel was in

me, I rang up Sverrir Scheving, who had been my travel companion ever since our secondary-school days. I had a hunting permit not far from Stíflisdalur, where Einar Ágústsson, later minister for foreign affairs, owned land. So I called Sverrir shortly before noon and got him to come ptarmigan hunting with me. He rarely hesitated when travel was involved.

We had no sooner reached the hunting grounds than we got the vehicle stuck. We had intended to cross the ice-covered Kjálká river, just above where it flows into Stíflisdalsvatn. We knew it as a harmless brook that in summer one can practically wade across in slippers. There had been frost for several days, and we examined the sheet of ice, which seemed to us quite thick. But when we were nearly all the way across, we broke through thin ice. There had been an air pocket underneath. So we sat stuck in the ice sheet, which reached above the middle of the wheels and was about a foot thick. We could not budge the vehicle at all.

The vehicle had a powerful winch, and we set to work in earnest trying to pull ourselves out by hooking it around a telephone pole that was nearby. The winch did not fail, but the same could not be said of the pole. It had begun to lean alarmingly when we finally gave up, and the telephone line to Reykjavík was on the verge of snapping. Equally fruitless was hammering away at the ice sheet with a crowbar and sledgehammer, though we struggled at it for a good while. The vehicle sat as stuck as before, and Sverrir and I agreed that this method had been tried to the full, especially as dusk was falling in earnest.

We decided to try to reach a telephone. Sverrir soon found an unoccupied house, which he broke into and found a rural party-line phone. He rang on the country line, and the one who answered was the provost at Þingvellir. Sverrir told him how things stood, that we were stuck, cold, and wet. He asked the clergyman to call Gunnar Guðmundsson, owner of heavy machinery at GG þungaflutningar, on our behalf. That worked. Gunnar was my comrade from the perlite adventure. A great gentleman and a famously strong man.

We had grown weary waiting for help by the time Gunnar arrived on the scene. He was in a jeep not unlike mine, well equipped and with an enormous winch. But nothing could budge the jeep in the river. It sat stuck as never before. We postponed further operations until morning and went back to town, leaving things as they were.

Gunnar and I set out again on an expedition the next morning with two vehicles. He drove a ten-ton GMC truck with a ten-ton winch, a derrick, and every possible piece of equipment. It was one of the most powerful vehicles in his fleet. We were dumbfounded when we came to Kjálká. It had broken up, and an ice dam had formed below the spot where the vehicle sat. The river had turned into a lake surrounding the vehicle. Nothing of it stood above the water except the driver'
s cab. A massive slab of ice had settled onto the hood and had also slid through the windshield and lay across the steering wheel. Every window in the vehicle was broken.

Gunnar and I decided to try to get the vehicle out before further damage occurred. The truck, however, had difficulty getting into position because of the rising water, and Gunnar wanted to try to reach it from the other bank. He therefore drove up along the river, intending to cross it higher up, but as luck would have it, the truck slid sideways into the river where it was quite deep. Needless to say, water immediately got into the diesel engine. Gunnar thus had no choice but to shut the vehicle down. We were once again forced to head for the settlements for further assistance.

We returned with two trucks with winches and traction mats, and we got Sverrir to come in his Weapon jeep, and I also asked him to bring a boat. Sverrir was surprised at first but procured a rowboat from Tómas Tryggvason, a geologist. When Sverrir arrived he understood what we needed the boat for. The vehicle was almost completely submerged in the river. I rowed out to it to get a line onto it. The bumper was so deep that I was half underwater fastening the winch cable. It was now easy to pull it out of the river, as the ice was gone. Gunnar's truck, however, sat firmly stuck in the riverbed and was on the verge of tipping onto its side. To recover it we therefore had to use both of the other trucks. One pulled while the other held steady with a taut cable so the monster would not go over on its side.

In the end both vehicles were towed to the city, mine completely without windows. I set to work in earnest repairing it. Once the water had been drained out of it and new oil put in, it roared to life as if nothing had happened. It took some time, however, to dry the vehicle out. The only things that were completely dry were Sverrir's and my shotguns, which we had hung on hooks in the corner of the driver's cab that stood above the water. But we never got a single ptarmigan.
The Surtsey Eruption

Great blows fell in quick succession in those November days. On the fourteenth of November, a fishing boat from Vestmannaeyjar reported columns of steam rising from the sea southwest of Heimaey. An undersea eruption had begun. Every available aircraft was immediately booked for sightseeing flights over the eruption site. I got a ride on a plane of the Civil Aviation Administration (Flugmálastjórn). It was unforgettable to see the black column rising toward the sky. This sight was doubtless what inspired the geologist Sigurður Þórarinsson to the name of the island that rose up, Surtsey. He took it
in Völuspá, and it was aptly put, for it seemed evident that Surtur was stoking the fire, and doing so vigorously.

In the Industrial Research Building (Atvinnudeildarhúsið) there was naturally a great commotion, no less than elsewhere, since many of the nation's leading natural scientists were gathered there. The country's geologists all wanted to get to the eruption site. I immediately became considerably involved with the eruption and research into it. Two or three days after the eruption began, Pétur Sigurðsson, director of the Coast Guard (Landhelgisgæslan), called me. Several scientists had by then contacted him asking for a patrol vessel for scientific research. Pétur asked whether I couldn't arrange for them to travel there together on one ship instead of each demanding a ship of his own. This led me to initiate the establishment of a committee whose task was to organize the research activities on Surtsey, the Surtsey Committee (Surtseyjarnefnd). It later became the Surtsey Society (Surtseyjarfélagið). I became its chairman and in fact still am.

The day after the eruption began, a representative from the American embassy called me. He said that a man had come to him with credentials from the United States Congress who was desperate to get out to the eruption site. I told him to send the man to me. Before I knew it, a giant of a man who spoke with great flair had walked into my office. This was Professor Paul Bauer, slightly tipsy as was his custom when traveling; one of the finest gentlemen I have ever known.

I called the Coast Guard, which promised to take him along to the eruption site if he came to Vestmannaeyjar. He was therefore put on the first flight, and everything worked out perfectly: when Bauer arrived at the dock, the Coast Guard vessel was just pulling in. The Surtsey eruption did not disappoint him, and neither did the people of Vestmannaeyjar. In the Islands he found men after his own heart and the right company for celebrating scientific achievements. When Bauer drank, the whisky was counted not in glasses but in bottles.

After his return to Reykjavík, a journalist from Alþýðublaðið got an interview with Bauer. There he recounted his travels and his admiration for the country. He also praised me to the skies and concluded by saying that "men like that ought to exist in the United States." We became friends for life.

Paul Bauer was a professor at American University in Washington, in addition to becoming an adviser to the United States Congress. He was a distinctive and strong personality. Bauer was big and heavy, stiff in his gait, and walked with a limp. He had volunteered in the Korean War and was sent to the South Pole, though I cannot imagine what military significance that had. There he went skiing and had a bad fall. He always bore the marks of it and limped ever after.

Professor Bauer, or Páll as we sometimes called him, was a geophysicist by training. However, he never finished his doctorate. His father was a major businessman in Massachusetts. He owned numerous companies there when the Great Depression struck, among them a fishing company and a distribution company for printed matter, to name just a few. Paul returned home to help with the business and gave up his studies. He managed to save the distribution company while most of the rest went bankrupt. He later came to own it, became wealthy, and was finally able to entrust its management to others on his behalf. With that he could devote himself to his burning interest in geology and other sciences. This interest drove him to Iceland.

Paul became a great admirer of the country from his very first trip and often came here two or three times a year. He also became a great benefactor of research on Surtsey and elsewhere. He had a small science fund in the United States which he called the Bauer Scientific Trust. He distributed considerable sums from it every year. He soon realized that this money would often go further here than in the United States, and we benefited greatly from that. Among other things, a research shelter was built on Surtsey which was christened Pálsbær in his honor. He also supported various promising Icelanders in their graduate studies.

Bauer enjoyed hunting and fishing. Among other things, I invited him salmon fishing and goose hunting. On one occasion we were fishing in Svartá. I went out and cast, since he had trouble standing in the river. When I had hooked a salmon on the fly, I called him over to me. I have never seen anything like his antics in playing a salmon. The swings and the showing off were tremendous, but in the end the fisherman fell flat on his stomach into the river. I of course reacted immediately and managed to get the giant of a man out. It is one of the greatest exertions I have ever attempted. Bauer was still holding onto the rod, which I pried away from him before I helped him ashore. There I settled him in the jeep. He asked me only one favor, to give him whisky, and drank half a bottle down before my eyes. I had no time to follow the fate of what remained in the bottle, for I ran back down to the river and landed the salmon. Bauer reminisced about this incident for many years afterward and called me his lifesaver. Not because I pulled him out of the river, but because I had whisky in the car.

I introduced Bauer to my parents. He achieved the distinction of being one of the few men who was allowed to help my mother with the kitchen work. We were then staying at the summer house at Klettur in Borgarfjörður. He insisted on being allowed to teach her his own salmon recipe. He crushed cornflakes and mixed them with butter and lemon juice and spread it on the fish, which he then fried
in the oven. We called this "salmon à la Bauer" and still eat it sometimes for variety.

Bauer was an exceptionally generous man. On my trips to the United States I usually stayed with him when I was in Washington, D.C. Once I called him before setting off on such a trip and the conversation turned to whether Edda would come along. I said we could not afford it. The day was hardly over before we were handed a ticket for Edda that Bauer had paid for. We stayed with him on that trip and then went to Florida at his invitation. It was a very enjoyable stay.

In 1964 I went with Guðmundur Sigvaldason and Unnsteinn Stefánsson to Duke University to discuss scientific cooperation in connection with Surtsey. After that trip Bauer invited us to the Bahamas, to the island of Bimini, off the Florida coast. It was a very memorable trip. Unnsteinn could not make it, but Guðmundur and I went. There I caught my biggest fish, a 524-pound swordfish. A model of that creature's head hangs on my wall in the basement. The Miami Herald saw fit to run a story on this catch of mine and made much of my name, which it specifically noted was not made up. The journalist added at the end of his article that it would be no small thing for me to go home to Iceland and be able to say: "You should have seen the swordfish I caught. It was as long as my name."

Bauer always stayed at Hotel Saga on his trips to Iceland and always ordered three bottles of whisky the moment he checked into the hotel. After I had become a member of parliament, there was once a great commotion. He said he had heard through the pipes in the bathroom that Russians in a room on the floor above were involved in a conspiracy to assassinate me. The divine spirits doubtless played their part in that story. His weakness for drink was his most dangerous enemy. Konráð, the restaurateur at Saga, finally managed to get him to bed, and I slept soundly. Professor Bauer died in January 1977.
The Reorganization of Scientific Research

The organization of research activities in the country was soon taken up after I began working for the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð). There was in fact great need for it, as the structure had become old and outdated in many respects. I worked on this a great deal as managing director of the State Industrial Affairs Committee (Atvinnumálanefnd ríkisins). I regarded it as fundamental to the future and advancement of research in Iceland.

The State Industrial Affairs Committee was established by a parliamentary resolution proposed by my father. He also became its first chairman. When he became prime minister in 1956, Vilhjálmur Þór took over the chairmanship. As I

have mentioned before, I travelled a good deal on the committee's behalf during my later stay in the United States. That was mainly on account of heavy-industry investigations and meetings with potential partners about operating an aluminium smelter. The Industrial Affairs Committee (Atvinnumálanefnd) became the formal heir to the various ideas about heavy industry that I and others had aired and worked on in the years before its establishment.

After I joined the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) I immediately began working for the committee. That was no coincidence. Þorbjörn Sigurgeirsson, my predecessor at the Research Council, had been executive director of the Industrial Affairs Committee ever since its founding. I took over that task like the others.

When the left-wing government left office, this story reached a turning point. The Viðreisn government took the heavy-industry issues onto its own desk and wanted as little as possible to do with the Industrial Affairs Committee. It did not, however, go so far as to abolish it. The committee therefore continued to meet and regarded as its main task the reorganization of research activity in the country. Once that work was completed it dissolved itself, since it received no new assignments from the government. This can probably be held up as a model where committees without tasks are concerned.

The last meeting of the Industrial Affairs Committee was on 21 October 1964. It then passed the following resolution with the votes of Vilhjálmur Þór, Davíð Ólafsson and Eggert G. Þorsteinsson, but against the dissenting vote of Einar Olgeirsson, who did not want to abolish the committee:

From the very beginning, the Industrial Affairs Committee considered one of its main tasks to be preparing legislation on research in the service of the industries. That work was completed in 1962. Since then the committee has received no matters for consideration; the present government has directed them elsewhere. The committee therefore sees no reason to operate as matters now stand.

The Viðreisn government did in fact revive the State Industrial Affairs Committee in a new and more extensive form, but that is another story. A bill on the reorganization of research affairs was finally introduced in the Althingi and passed, with minor amendments, in 1965. In its wake a large Research Council was established, on which sat, among others, seven members of parliament elected by the Althingi, along with representatives appointed by the research institutes and from the business sector. This was meant to strengthen understanding of research and its importance in the Althingi and among employers. Both were lacking. Under the law, the Minister of Education chaired the Research Council himself. It, however, elected a five-member executive committee and ceased to handle the day-to-day management of the University's Industrial Research Department (Atvinnudeild Háskólans). After this, the role of the Research Council consisted in

advising the government on the strengthening of research. In addition it dealt with the budgets of the research institutes in consultation with their directors and the state budget officer. The Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) was to handle foreign relations, and its role in promoting research on the utilization of the country's natural resources was specifically stipulated.

The Industrial Research Department (Atvinnudeildin) was split up into semi-independent research institutes, which were given the names Agricultural Research Institute (Rannsóknastofnun landbúnaðarins), Industrial Research Institute (Rannsóknastofnun iðnaðarins), Building Research Institute (Rannsóknastofnun byggingariðnaðarins), Marine Research Institute (Hafrannsóknastofnun) and Fisheries Research Institute (Rannsóknastofnun fiskiðnaðarins). They all received independent three-member boards on which a representative of the business sector had a seat. The purpose of this new arrangement was not least to increase the institutes' contact with operating companies, which was far too limited. I myself wanted to increase the institutes' independence still further. I stressed that they should be allowed to earn their own revenues and dispose of them according to their own policy. I also wanted them to have full authority over the hiring of staff and over negotiating pay and terms, within a certain framework. This was not approved. The latter point in particular was seen as problematic. I recall many meetings with that remarkable man, Gunnlaugur Briem, permanent secretary of the Ministry of Industry (atvinnumálaráðuneytið), at which he pounded the table and said it was out of the question that the research institutes be given licence to blow up the state's wage system.

The Research Council was placed under the Minister of Education, while the research institutes each went under their own ministry. By then the Ministry of Industry had been split up. I wanted the Research Council to come under the Prime Minister's Office, where a special department of science would be established. That proposal I had from the foreign advisers, Robert Major, the Norwegian, and Alexander King at the OECD. This was not achieved.

There is no doubt that these changes were important and strengthened all research activity in the country. Some things, however, did not turn out as well as intended. For example, the participation of members of parliament in the Research Council was not of much use. Their presence on the council was supposed to lead to increased appropriations. In that they proved rather useless.

The executive committee laid down the main lines of the Research Council's work. Chosen for it were Davíð Ólafsson, director of fisheries, Jónas Haralz, economist, Magnús Magnússon, professor, and my good old acquaintances Helgi Bergs, engineer, and Sveinn Björnsson, who was then director of the Technological Institute (Iðntæknistofnun). This was an industrious executive committee. Magnús was elected chairman and served in that role until 1972. Our collaboration was excellent. He had been one of three applicants when I
secured the managing director's position. Magnús and I are good acquaintances and friends.

As the years passed there were naturally changes of personnel in the executive committee. Others who sat on the committee while I was at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) were Jón Skaftason, member of parliament; Bjarni Bragi Jónsson, later an economist at the Central Bank (Seðlabankinn); Haraldur Ásgeirsson; Ellert B. Schram, member of parliament, later editor of DV and president of the Icelandic Sports Federation (ÍSÍ); Ingvar Gíslason, later minister of education; Sigmundur Guðbjarnason, professor and later rector of the university; and Sveinn Guðmundsson of Héðinn. Sveinn Björnsson took over the chairmanship from Magnús. Sveinn sat on the executive committee longer than anyone, the whole time I was at the Council after the new legislation was enacted. Sigmundur Guðbjarnason then took over the chairmanship from him in 1975.
Negotiations with Alusuisse

In the autumn days of 1997 everything threatened to boil over because of my interest in environmental matters — or my meddling in that field, as some chose to call it. In that skirmish I appeared to be almost the only Progressive Party man (framsóknarmaður) who had doubts about the value of heavy industry and new aluminum smelters. The tables had well and truly turned since the time I went against the party leadership, spoke in favor of power plants and industrial works in Iceland, and took a seat on the negotiating committee for the aluminum smelter at Straumsvík. That I certainly did in the Viðreisn years.

Soon after the Viðreisn government took power, Jóhann Hafstein, the minister of industry, appointed a new heavy-industry committee. It took over the tasks of the Industrial Affairs Committee (Atvinnumálanefnd) in that area. Only trusted Independence Party and Social Democratic Party men were appointed to it, under the leadership of Jóhannes Nordal, governor of the Central Bank. I was, of course, not in that group. Everything I had previously worked on in these areas landed on the committee's desk, both work done on behalf of earlier governments and at the Research Council. In many respects the committee members did their work well. Politics, however, excluded me from the inner circle in this endeavor. I did not enjoy the confidence of that government.

The committee's most extensive task was the negotiations on the construction of an aluminum smelter in Iceland. Jóhannes Nordal traveled to meetings with the various parties on both sides of the Atlantic who had shown interest in the matter, most of whom I had met before. The diatomite in Mývatn, an oil refinery, and much else were also dealt with. I was soon summoned to the committee's meetings for consultation, and in some of the matters I was rather deeply involved, such as the construction of the diatomite plant (Kísilgúrverksmiðjan) at Mývatn. That matter had in fact been on the desks of the Research

Council along with many others. I also remember meetings about the construction of an oil refinery. In that connection a young American oil magnate from Texas, Baron Kidd, came to this country. The minister of industry wanted to treat him well. The ministry asked me to take the guest and his entourage, together with some of my own companions, fishing in the Víðidalsá river. That I did with pleasure. On that fishing trip, besides Kidd and his wife, were Vilhjálmur Lúðvíksson, my colleague at the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð), and Jón Hjartarson, merchant at the Húsgagnahöllin furniture store. We became great fishing companions. It turned out to be a most enjoyable trip. Kidd stayed in touch for quite a while afterwards. The salmon fishing was good, but we did not haul an oil refinery ashore on that trip. I sometimes think of that now with relief, and at the same time I marvel that some people should be reviving that bad idea. At the time, though, I spoke forcefully for establishing an oil refinery and criticized the naysayers. I believed the oil industry could become the foundation and basis for chemical industries of many kinds.

When it had become clear that the Swiss aluminum company Alusuisse was serious about entering negotiations on building an aluminum smelter here in Iceland, the winds shifted as far as my part was concerned. Members of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and socialists had by then been keeping up questions and motions in the Althing (Alþingi) about aluminum agreements. Eysteinn Jónsson, among other things, put forward a motion to establish a special parliamentary committee on the matter. It was shelved by the government's representatives. The government realized, on the other hand, that it was important to have an advocate within the Progressive Party.

I was invited to take a seat on the negotiating committee at the end of 1964. At first this took me by surprise. I could not help being somewhat suspicious, as appears in my letter to my friend Runólfur Þórðarson a few weeks later:

At first it struck me as rather odd that I should be placed on this committee. I suspect that it was first and foremost for the purpose of getting some Progressive Party man in there, so that it would be harder for the party to say that it had been completely bypassed.

Within the Progressive Party this was a sensitive matter, for not everyone there was taken with the idea of an aluminum smelter. No doubt it did nothing to quiet the critical voices that the party was in hard opposition. It was clear to everyone that I favored these projects. Various members of parliament from the party let it be understood that they were only moderately pleased with my committee work.
Eysteinn Jónsson was gloomy about the matter. About these voices I say in the previously mentioned letter:

I laid strong emphasis on it, when this came up in conversation, that I would naturally take part there only as managing director of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) and as an individual who has spoken quite considerably for this cause.

It was never requested in plain words on the government's part that I speak for the aluminum industry within the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). Presumably, though, it was expected that this would happen. I frequently attended meetings of the parliamentary party in order to report on the progress of the negotiations, and tried to present their advantages and to reduce unnecessary negativity among the members of parliament. That did not soften the tone of all the opponents of the matter. I also gave talks in many places and believe that the great majority of younger men favored the harnessing of hydropower and agreements on heavy industry.

The negotiating sessions were many and extensive. They were held variously in Reykjavík, Switzerland, London, or New York. A large American law firm was retained for legal counsel. It was also necessary to consult with the World Bank (Alþjóðabankinn), since it was expected to finance the necessary power plant at Búrfell. On the Swiss side there were two chief negotiators: the company's chief executive, Meyer by name, and its technical director, Müller. The Swiss were extremely meticulous. Every single detail of the agreements was scrutinized, and some were taken up again and again. That was at times rather tiring. Once a conclusion was reached, however, they stood by their word. I believe that has proved to be the case ever since.

Hjörtur Torfason, who is now a supreme court justice, was our legal adviser in addition to the American law firm. I liked Hjörtur well. He was both conscientious and precise. Punctuality, however, was not his strong suit. I remember one occasion when we were on our way to catch a flight and Hjörtur had not arrived. We had begun to grow very restless, and the aircraft doors had already been closed, when they were opened again and in stepped Hjörtur with his bag in his arms. This was not a unique occurrence where he was concerned.

In connection with these meetings there were usually grand dinners. I ate many delicious steaks on those evenings and made sure they were cooked rare, which was a great favorite of mine at the time. The Swiss crowned their meticulousness when it came to choosing the wine to go with the food. There was no cause to complain about the selection.
When the negotiations were reaching their final stage, Jóhann Hafstein, the minister of industry, invited the negotiating committees to dinner at his home, where

The Swiss were the guests of honor. Among the guests was also Prime Minister Bjarni Benediktsson, Ólafur Thors having by then passed away. When the Swiss left around eleven o'clock, I expected to head home as well. Then Bjarni called me over and asked me to speak with him. We sat down apart from the others and had a very informative conversation. Bjarni had a very distinctive voice, slightly pinched, and was a favorite of impressionists because of his peculiar manner of speaking. He was gray-haired, with a noticeably large head, and would hunch his shoulders slightly when he emphasized his words.

Bjarni was delightful company. Among other things, he was curious to know what the household atmosphere had been like in my childhood home, especially whether my father had talked about politics at the dinner table. I told him I could never remember that happening. "I'm glad to hear that," Bjarni then said. "My wife Sigríður sometimes scolds me for telling her so little about what is happening in politics. So it was the same in your home."

We then discussed politics. At one point I brought up the electoral system. I told Bjarni that I was strongly in favor of single-member constituencies and believed they would lead to greater stability in Icelandic politics. He said he agreed with me on that. "However, the wheel will not be turned back. Single-member constituencies will never be adopted in this country."

Bjarni Benediktsson was unquestionably a great leader and a decisive minister. He showed his strength in those years when he took over the leadership of the government and reached an accord with the country's labor movement when everything was heading toward major conflict. The personal trust between Bjarni and Eðvarð Sigurðsson, chairman of Dagsbrún, weighed heavily there, I believe.

Naturally, I disagreed with Bjarni about many things. He was an Independence Party man and very hard-line. The Independence Party (Sjálfstæðisflokkurinn) in those days, however, had not yet become the great free-market liberal party it is now. I could therefore accept much in his politics, not least in those years. I favored cooperation with the United States and believed that in defense matters it had been sensible to conclude the defense agreement after the war. I did agree with my father, however, that the military should leave once a secure peace had been established. In that respect, one might say I did not go as far as Bjarni in defense matters. To him they were an article of faith, not an opinion.
A Skillful Negotiator

Jóhannes Nordal was chairman of the negotiating committee on heavy industry. We therefore got to know each other well. He was quick-witted and swift to identify the main point in every matter. Jóhannes is ambitious and devoted himself to the negotiations. I found him to be an outstanding negotiator.

Jóhannes was a light-hearted and entertaining companion. He has quite a temper but also good self-control. He liked to sit down with a drop in his glass after difficult meetings and discuss matters. It was always in great moderation, though. These conversations were often most interesting, for Jóhannes is well read and widely knowledgeable. I liked him.

Jóhannes enjoyed ideal circumstances for attending to the negotiations and his other interests. He was a governor of the Central Bank (Seðlabankinn), and in those days it was considered no crime for bank governors to attend to whatever was thought to serve the public good. I actually believe the bank also bore a substantial share of the costs of Jóhannes's travels in connection with the aluminum negotiations. No objections were ever raised to this. Meetings were frequent in the heavy-industry committees under his leadership, and it seemed to some that he spent more time on those matters than on the business of the Central Bank. Within the bank, however, he had everything his own way. A member of the Central Bank's board of directors once put it this way: that I, at least, did not attend to the bank at the same time as I attended to environmental matters. Whatever may be said of the governance of the bank and its affairs during Jóhannes's time as governor, the same words could most certainly be applied to his work on heavy-industry matters.

After our negotiations with the Swiss were concluded and construction was beginning, relations with their negotiators remained good. Several more meetings were held, including in Switzerland. Our wives were even invited along. For many years the Swiss also invited Jóhannes and me to fish in Þverá. Edda and I thus got to know Jóhannes and his wife Dóra well, and we often went on salmon-fishing trips with them. Jóhannes is a fine fisherman who fishes only with a fly, and Dóra is in fact fully his equal in that regard.

Many counted Jóhannes among the Social Democrats (Alþýðuflokkur men) at first. Gylfi Þ. Gíslason appointed him governor of the Central Bank and they were great friends. When the left-wing government of Ólafur Jóhannesson came to power in 1971, Jóhannes nevertheless kept his position as chairman of the negotiating committee on heavy industry, though Iceland's negotiating committee was then given the name Committee on Energy-Intensive Industry (Nefnd um orkufrekan iðnað). By then Jóhannes had surely become the Icelander most versed in negotiations of this kind, and he performed well, so his elevation was not without reason. Jóhannes has always had a reputation for being a civil servant loyal to his masters.

It has mattered little which government has been in power at any given time; Jóhannes has done the bidding of them all and always enjoyed full confidence. As the years passed, other tasks were therefore added to his desk besides the heavy-industry negotiations and the governance of the Central Bank (Seðlabankinn). He became chairman of the board of the National Power Company (Landsvirkjun), and thus the country's principal interests in heavy-industry matters were united in one man.

In 1986 a new law on the Central Bank was passed. I was prime minister and took part in putting the finishing touches on the bill together with Matthías Bjarnason, the minister of commerce. It contains a provision that bank governors are prohibited from taking on duties outside the bank. Jóhannes strongly opposed this provision. In the end, an exemption was made for the governors then in office. That was done first and foremost so that Jóhannes would not have to step down from the board of Landsvirkjun.

After I took a minister's seat, I came to know Jóhannes's merits as an adviser. I think few people realize the extensive advisory role that the Central Bank played for most of that time. The bank was, not least, an advisory institution for the government. When I was minister of fisheries, the Central Bank governors Jóhannes Nordal and Davíð Ólafsson were among my chief advisers in all measures to keep the fishing industry running. Davíð had been director of fisheries for many years. We met often, for in those inflation years everything seemed to be heading for the rocks at roughly quarterly intervals. The Central Bank then intervened in many places and took heavy blows.

When I was prime minister in the years 1983–1987, Jóhannes often came to my office to review the state of economic affairs. I found that very useful, for he was knowledgeable and had a clear overview. We used this period, among other things, to loosen various restrictions, since we believed we were getting a grip on inflation. Many people forget how important the steps taken in those years were. In later years Jóhannes and I drifted apart and he put less emphasis on his advisory role. I think he was not much taken with the national-reconciliation government. He became more of a free-market man with the years, and our dealings gradually diminished. Perhaps it was to avoid disagreement.
Foreign Influence for Good and Ill

The aluminum agreement did not pass through the Althingi (Alþingi) without a stir. In the run-up to the negotiations, the opposition had finally succeeded in securing the establishment of a parliamentary committee that operated without direct participation in the actual negotiations. Despite my arguments in the Progressive Party's (Framsókn) parliamentary group, all its members of parliament cast their votes

against the bill, except two who abstained, Björn Pálsson and Jón Skaftason. I believe the deciding factor here was the strict discipline Eysteinn maintained over the parliamentary group. He always pressed very firmly to ensure that no one broke ranks in major matters. This was a legacy from Jónas frá Hriflu, who is the father of party rule in Iceland. I adopted a much more flexible policy in this regard after I became chairman of the party.

Agreement was reached only on the Búrfell power plant. The Progressive Party's (Framsókn) conditions for a foreign-owned aluminum smelter were that the construction should not lead to inflation and overheating; that the balance of settlement across the country should not be disturbed; that the agreement with the foreign party should be compatible with the independence and interests of the nation; and that the foreign company should be subject in all respects to Icelandic law. "The Progressive Party considered that none of these conditions was fulfilled," says the party's history about the aluminum agreements. In addition, much was made of the fact that the company was sold energy at a very favorable price.

I, on the other hand, was pleased with the aluminum agreement and my part in the matter. Few party members, though, endorsed that publicly until some time had passed. With the construction of the aluminum smelter at Straumsvík, one might say that my decades-old dream of harnessing hydropower for heavy industry in Iceland had finally come true.

I was not, however, uncritical of "foreign encroachment in Iceland," as it was sometimes phrased. During my student years in the United States, my eyes had certainly been opened to the importance of international cooperation and free trade in many fields. But my faith in Iceland and the Icelanders grew no less. I became convinced that loyalty to the cultural heritage and the language was among the most important things to nurture if the nation wished to govern itself at all. The words and ideals of Rector Pálmi Hannesson and my father's odes to the homeland claimed an ever larger place in my heart. I recalled this in a speech in which I described my outlook:

In all likelihood there are others in this room who heard the late Pálmi [Hannesson] speak in the assembly hall of the Gymnasium (Menntaskólinn), in his very beautiful and memorable way, about the importance of our history, language, and culture for the independence of this nation. I remember that his words often seemed to me extreme then, tinged with needless national chauvinism, but over the years I have learned to understand that they contained a great truth.

My acquaintance with the United States strengthened my faith in Iceland and Icelandic culture. In 1964 I was therefore one of those NATO supporters who backed the demand that the so-called "Yank television" (kanasjónvarpið) be restricted to the military base. That demand appeared

in the petition of the "60 voters," as famously happened. Among the sixty petitioners, men of learning and the arts were prominent, including: Bjarni Jónsson, suffragan bishop; Guðlaugur Rósinkranz, director of the National Theatre; the Reverend Sigurbjörn Einarsson; Kristján Eldjárn, curator of national antiquities; and the writers Gunnar Gunnarsson, Halldór Laxness, and Sigurður A. Magnússon, as well as the poet Tómas Guðmundsson. Also in the group were Ragnar Jónsson of Smári and Styrmir Gunnarsson, then chairman of Heimdallur and later editor of Morgunblaðið, but people from the world of politics were otherwise not prominent on the list. The reactions were not long in coming; some rejoiced eagerly while others responded angrily.

I would sometimes link the aluminum issue and the petition together in my speeches when I wanted to explain my position on foreign investment. The television issue involved cultural arguments that belonged less in the aluminum-smelter debate, it seemed to me. In a memorandum from this time I set out the reasoning for this position. There I first raise the point that we Icelanders would doubtless not be an independent nation if the loyalty of the Icelandic common people to the cultural heritage had not united them in the struggle for independence. On the other hand, I consider increased international economic cooperation a natural development and "harmless" if pursued with caution. It reads:

No instrument, however, is more dangerous to the distinctive culture of a small nation than unrestrained foreign television. Such foreign investment is therefore far more dangerous to the nation's independence than investment in an individual industrial enterprise, even one many times larger.

In this debate it naturally weighed heavily that Icelandic television had not yet been established. It is certain that the State Television (Ríkissjónvarpið) became a reality sooner than it otherwise would have because of the debate over the expansion of the Yank television. Around the time it began broadcasting, the military reduced the reach of its own transmissions. The Yank television was fenced in, just as the soldiers had been before.
Incessant Trips Abroad

When I think back to this time, it feels almost as if I always had one foot abroad. If I was not at meetings about the aluminum agreements or heavy-industry matters, it was because of the Nordic scientific cooperation or on behalf of the science committee of the Council of Europe (Evrópuráðið). In the 1960s such trips counted almost as privileges, and those who had business beyond the country's shores were regarded with envious eyes. Often, though, this envy was based on a misunderstanding. Even though these could often be enjoyable trips, they were
no less exhausting and naturally entailed long absences from the family.

In fact, one international committee remains unmentioned. Soon after I came to the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð), the minister of education had also appointed me Iceland's representative on the science committee of the Organisation for European Economic Co-operation, the OEEC, which later became the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in Paris, the OECD. I sat there for the twenty years I held the position of director at the Research Council. Informative meetings were held in this committee, and my membership in it served me well at the Research Council. Among other things, the organization's science division was engaged to carry out an assessment of research activity and its organization here in Iceland.

When I arrived at my first meeting of the science committee, Hans Andersen had recently become Iceland's ambassador to the OEEC. We knew each other slightly from my time at the United Nations, and naturally I paid him a visit. His wife Ástríður was not at home. Hans received me warmly and invited me out to dinner after the meeting. Then he invited me to his home and brought out a bottle of Drambuie liqueur. The bottles multiplied, for despite my repeated attempts to say goodbye, he would not hear of my leaving. Hans was lonely and rather melancholy. He clearly found it good to have the chance to recount his troubles. Morning was approaching when I finally made it to the hotel. I could not stand the sight of Drambuie for a long time after that.

From 1964 to 1968 Einar Benediktsson was embassy counselor in Paris. We were well acquainted. Once when I came to Paris, his wife Elsa was in Iceland. Einar invited me to stay with him, which I accepted. That evening we decided to explore the Paris nightlife. I owned, and still own, a little book by the famous American journalist Arthur Buchwald called "Paris After Dark." It is the best guidebook to the restaurants and nightspots of Paris I have ever come across, and it was a kind of bible of mine in those matters. We visited many good places on the Left Bank, not least jazz clubs. Late in the night we came to an elegant club not far from the Arc de Triomphe and knocked on the door. A young woman answered and said the place was closed to all but members. Then her eyes fell on me; she fell silent and quietly asked Einar in French whether I might perhaps be one of the Kennedys. Einar replied at once that this was indeed so, but that it must on no account get out. We were immediately let in and shown to seats of honor. We took care, of course, to speak English for the rest of the night. The girl had evidently not been able to keep our secret, though, judging by the service. We were waited on hand and foot as if kings were passing through. We sat there a good while and enjoyed being in the limelight.

In good moments I have reminded my friend Einar of that night and thanked him for his excellent guidance through the Paris nightlife. He has long been a complete teetotaler and is not especially grateful to me for this praise.

On my trips to Paris I sometimes bought clothing for Edda, especially dresses and coats. I liked to shop at the same place, a small and tasteful shop on the Rue de Madelain near the Opera. Every time I came there I was received with open arms. There was a young shop assistant there who resembled Edda in both height and figure. I always had her try things on. It did not hurt that she was very helpful in showing me beautiful clothes that were not outrageously expensive. These clothes always fit perfectly once I got home, and I received much praise for my good taste. Edda still wears at least two beautiful evening coats from those years on festive occasions, since all of this has come back into fashion.

In the work of the Council of Europe (Evrópuráðið) committee, I usually found personal acquaintance with individual committee members more useful than the meetings themselves. They were held twice a year. One was held in Strasbourg and the other in one of the member states of the council. In this way I got to various places that were interesting to visit. Edda frequently came along after we were married. The council's rules were that a fixed travel allowance was paid according to information from a travel agency, but participants were permitted to seek cheaper solutions. Edda thus often came along for little money. We have fond memories from many such trips, for example from Paris, Greece, Cyprus, and Turkey, though the subjects of the meetings are long forgotten to me. I also remember a meeting held in Florence. There Ármann Snævarr and I made the rounds of the many art museums and toured the ancient, famous city.
Feuds Among the Young Progressives

I had managed to calm the waters among the young Progressives (framsóknarmenn) in Reykjavík during the two years I served as chairman of the association. At the end of that period, in 1964, I also believed I had negotiated a peaceful succession. Far from it. The meeting at which the change of board was to take place was at first sparsely attended. Once it had been called to order, however, a large group stormed in, took over the meeting, and overturned the entire agreement. I do not know whether Örlygur Hálfdanarson was behind it. He made a special point of standing up to thank me for a flourishing tenure. Nonetheless, his men then secured themselves a majority in the board election.
It was a turbulent autumn. Those who counted among the more moderate part of the young
