Progressives wanted to remove Örlygur and worked for the election of Jónas Jónsson, later director of agriculture, to the chairmanship of the Young Progressives' Federation (SUF). Örlygur, on the other hand, intended to stay put with the support of the more radical faction. Matters came to a head at the federation congress held at Blönduós in September 1964. Attendance was large, speechmaking at its peak, and idealistic fervor ran high. I was among those who thought it was time for Örlygur to step down from the chairmanship. He parried the blow, however, and won the elections.

Örlygur was well suited to leadership and ambitious. We were thus cut from the same cloth in those respects, and it is of course a story old and new that ambitious men in that arena end up in collisions. Örlygur and I were no exception. He lost interest in political participation over the years, though, and it may be that he quit because he felt his advancement was not fast enough. It may also be that he had grown weary of the constant squabbles within the youth movement. Örlygur and I have become good friends over the years, and I hold him in high regard for his publishing work and his many endeavors.

One incident from the Blönduós congress stayed with me for a long time, and it had little to do with the chairmanship election. There was considerable merrymaking, as tends to happen, and some poured down quite a lot. I was staying at the hotel and went to bed before the night was far advanced. An hour later a large group came into the hotel and began carousing there, to my great vexation. I nevertheless managed to fall asleep, but early in the morning who should appear but Pétur, father of the brothers Már and Páll Pétursson of Höllustaðir. Már later became a district court judge and Páll a government minister, as is well known. Pétur laid into me with fierce reproaches for having knocked Már down during the night. I was utterly baffled but could hardly get a word in for the commotion. Már had drunk quite heartily that evening and remembered nothing of the circumstances, but woke up beaten and swollen in the morning. For some reason he was convinced that I was responsible. Shortly afterwards he sent me a hymnal with references he thought fitting. I took these accusations to heart but did not know how I could clear myself. Before long, however, witnesses came forward and this unfortunate misunderstanding was laid to rest. Már apologized to me and we became good friends. He is endowed with many fine qualities but cannot touch wine. Már later became chairman of the SUF and was considered one of the party's most promising young members. He also often contributed constructively at various meetings. In those early years of ours in politics, more people would probably have bet on Már attaining a minister's office than his brother Páll.
In the arena of the young Progressives there soon emerged a hard-bitten group of young men whose conduct made these clashes of the early Restoration years (viðreisnarárin) pale in comparison.
A Candidacy in the Offing

As early as 1964, various people from the West Fjords had begun broaching with me the idea of taking over my father's leadership role in the constituency, even though three years remained until the parliamentary elections. I, however, dreaded following in my father's footsteps. Indeed, one could put it as strongly as to say that I was opposed to the idea of running in the west.

In Reykjavík, interest also awoke in my standing for candidacy. This was especially the case among my colleagues within the Young Progressives' Association (FUF). A large group of them met at a meeting held in an assembly hall on Skólavörðustígur. There it was resolved to push for me to be placed on the party's list in Reykjavík. Þórarinn Þórarinsson, editor of Tíminn, and Einar Ágústsson, later foreign minister, then held the top two seats.

Þórarinn was a politician of the old school. He was a good speaker and had extensive knowledge of politics at home and abroad. He was most at ease as editor of Tíminn, where his skill with the pen came into its own in inspired writings about the obvious virtues of the Progressive platform and in sharp attacks on the party's opponents. He was also very interested in and knowledgeable about foreign affairs. Some remarked, though, that Þórarinn did not venture far beyond the editorial offices.

Einar Ágústsson was in many respects a different kind of man. He was imposing in stature and bearing, very popular, and an excellent speaker. Einar was a first-rate candidate and had achieved outstanding results running for the Reykjavík city council. He was, however, sensitive to criticism and thin-skinned, and not as industrious as Þórarinn once in parliament. He was only moderately grateful for these candidacy ideas of my supporters.

I saw no reason to do anything other than speak with Þórarinn and Einar directly. I soon sensed that they were not particularly eager to have me on the list. Some interpreted this as their fearing competition from me. Perhaps they considered it likely that I would later challenge them for the top seats. For me, however, the deciding factor was that I was moving house to Arnarnes, which lies in the Reykjanes constituency. I reckoned this would be used against me in Reykjavík, even though I was a born-and-bred Reykjavík man — something neither Þórarinn nor Einar could boast of.

There was also some discussion of whether I would want to run in Reykjanes with Jón Skaftason. That I wrote off immediately. It did not seem right to me to break the tradition that the second man on the list should be from Suðurnes, since Jón himself lived in Kópavogur. He had been radical in his younger years but underwent a complete transformation

after he entered parliament. Jón was considered one of the most right-leaning members of parliament of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) and one of the few who supported the aluminum smelter agreements. He was popular in his constituency but rather held back in his dealings with voters and lost his parliamentary seat before all was said and done. For a time the Progressive Party had no member of parliament in the Reykjanes constituency.

Around the same time as this was happening, the people of the West Fjords pressed harder than before for me to run there. The people of Strandir did not hold back either. Ólafur Einarsson at Þórustaðir was especially persistent. I discussed these matters with my father, who said he understood my doubts and wished himself to have as little influence as possible on this decision. I thus stood alone and had to make up my mind one way or the other.

While I was torn between declining and letting things run their course, I was engaged to deliver various talks at meetings out west. Pétur Þorsteinsson, the cooperative manager at Bíldudalur, organized them. I strongly suspect this was done with deliberate intent. I still have the letters that passed between us about my candidacy, in which his words of encouragement alternate with my misgivings. The first meeting was held at Patreksfjörður on Saturday, 23 May 1964. There I spoke about future policy in social affairs. I still have the speech on the cards from which I delivered it. It appears to have been quite thorough. The next day I gave a similar address at Bíldudalur. These speeches were in fact no isolated occurrence, for that year I gave such talks widely around the country at party festivals known as district gatherings (héraðsmót), and many of the speeches I still have. The decision on a candidacy, however, was not made that year or the next, which was nonetheless just as busy with district gatherings throughout the West Fjords and indeed more widely around the country.
A Young and Promising Man

I became active in the Progressive Party through my chairmanship of the FUF, soon took a seat at meetings of the central committee, and from 1963 sat regularly at meetings of the executive committee, in addition to being in regular contact with the leadership. I was also frequently engaged to deliver talks at gatherings or meetings around the country and to handle other tasks thought to be of benefit to the party. Some of them proved more consequential than others.

On a mild autumn morning in 1965, Eysteinn Jónsson telephoned me at the crack of dawn, as was his habit. He had met a young and promising man who he said would be an asset to the party, a newly graduated political scientist from Manchester. Eysteinn also said something to the effect that I was well suited to introduce him to the party's policies, since I came from the ranks of the educated and was among the party's future leaders. I readily agreed to the errand.

I telephoned the young man and we arranged to meet at the Grill at Hótel Saga. He was slim but slightly round-faced, dressed in a suit in the latest fashion. His hair was fair and grown well down over his ears. His locks were carefully combed as if by prescription, and enormous eyeglasses framed his face. He spoke with a distinctive voice that the nation has long since come to know. The young man was Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson.

We got along well. That winter we met regularly and discussed national affairs at this same place, which overlooks a large part of the capital. The fare on the table was also always the same, waffles with jam and cream, and we both drank tea. I found it enlightening to talk with Ólafur. I sensed at once that he was well informed; he was driven and had self-confidence that would have sufficed for an entire battalion. He had a lively interest in politics. That winter he was in fact working on a study of the Icelandic system of government and its development. So it was no wonder that social and political matters dominated our conversation.

Ólafur Ragnar was articulate and at times eloquent. Whether we discussed the issues of the day, fundamental principles, or political ideologies, it seemed to me that our ideals coincided in many respects. He was certainly radical in his views, but that did not displease me, for at the same time he was a great believer in the cooperative movement and a youth-association man in spirit. Ólafur Ragnar was also a staunch teetotaler. I am inclined to think his views were in almost perfect harmony with the youthful ideals of Jónas from Hrifla.

Ólafur Ragnar had studied in England and had much to tell. He was animated about the ferment taking place among students. I listened to his accounts with attention and was caught up in them. Numerous ideas were in the making, and many of them struck me as interesting. This was the beginning of the stirrings that have since been associated with the '68 generation. They did not in fact spread to Iceland until some time after these conversations of ours took place — if one can speak at all of the flower revolution having managed to take root in this country.

I am convinced that these meetings weighed heavily in Ólafur's decision to join the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn). I have sometimes put it this way: that I was given the task by the party chairman of bringing Ólafur Ragnar into the Progressive Party, only to serve the role ten years later of ushering him out on behalf of the then chairman, Ólafur Jóhannesson. I think I managed both reasonably well. And Ólafur Ragnar suffered no harm from it. But that is another story.

At one point in our conversations Ólafur Ragnar asked frankly what hopes he could entertain of advancement and a future in the Progressive Party. I was most positive and encouraged him at first to take part in the work of the younger

members. Ólafur, however, let it be understood that he considered that too much of a youth club and that his ambitions aimed higher. I soon gathered that he wanted to work more seriously on shaping the party's organization and policy. I said I had nothing against that. Yet I also marveled at how quickly he intended to climb the ladder of advancement to leadership in Icelandic society. He allowed himself no rest in that regard. This surprised me, for I was fifteen years older and uncertain about my own plans for the future. I had still not made a decision on the candidacy questions that had been the subject of considerable discussion.

In the latter part of the winter, Ólafur Ragnar spoke frequently of his prospects of running for the party in elections. I was in no position to promise any solution to that matter. I did, however, mention the third seat in Reykjanes as a possibility. There I had in mind that Jón Skaftason held the first seat and it was assumed that a man from Suðurnes would occupy the second. Ólafur did not think this offer held much advancement. He has seldom cared for intermediate moves in such a chess game. He aimed higher.
To Shrink Back or Take the Leap

I could not really blame Ólafur Ragnar for making ambitious demands about a place on a candidate list. I made such demands on my own behalf. As Christmas 1965 approached, more people threw their weight behind my running in the West Fjords constituency. In the end I entertained the idea of standing for election but made it clear that I would run only in the first or second seat. In the West Fjords the nomination method then in use was that a 30-member committee decided on the list. It was elected at the constituency assembly. The nominating committee met at Ísafjörður in September 1966. The outcome there was the one best described in a letter from Ólafur Einarsson of Þórustaðir, dated 13 September 1966.

In short, the results were, as you of course know, that Bjarni [Guðbjörnsson, bank manager] was elected to the 1st seat, Halldór [Kristjánsson of Kirkjuból] to the 2nd seat, and Steingrímur Hermannsson to the 3rd seat with 21 votes. I know, Steingrímur, that I need not point out to you that I and various others were not pleased with this outcome [. . .] I hope you will bear well in mind that the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) needs you and other young men of dedication. I reminded people at the meeting of what it would have been worth for the party when your father and Ey-

steinn Jónsson came there as young men with active minds and hands; and we have the same need now for such a thing to repeat itself. I will let this suffice for now, and though we in the West Fjords constituency did not have the good fortune to see the list arranged otherwise, I hope that you will attend more to the interests and outlook of our party, and give less weight to the position that in the end had to be taken among us.
Ólafur sent the letter with a neighbor of his who was traveling to the city. I promptly mailed him a reply which said, among other things:

I heard already on Sunday morning of the results of the meeting, and I was then and there determined to decline this offer of the third seat, and I felt I had a clean record in doing so, for I have always stressed that I would not accept such an offer. As it happened, however, the party leadership intervened before anyone spoke with me, and since then there has been much discussion and thought about this here in the south. I cannot say what the outcome will be.

Among those in the party leadership who exerted themselves were the executive director Þráinn Valdimarsson, who worked energetically on the matter; Helgi Bergs, who was secretary and strongly urged me to run; and the party chairman Eysteinn Jónsson. Though it was not yet clear what the outcome would be, I explained my reasons further to Ólafur in the aforementioned reply:

Some may regard it as arrogance on my part not to accept at once the offer of the third seat on your list. I hope you will not. Admittedly it gives me no particular pleasure to be the alternate of the two men who have been chosen for the first and second seats. They are both fine men, of that I have no doubt, but neither of them is the kind of political leader whom I would take pleasure in working for. I would gladly take the third seat if ahead of me there were a man, or men, whom I could look up to, even if in that case the prospect of a seat in parliament were far smaller.

I faced a difficult decision. As often before in such circumstances, I chose to set my thoughts down systematically on paper in order to weigh the pros and cons. On four numbered pages I work out what my decision should be. I calculated precisely, from the results of the last two elections, how support would need to shift between parties for the third seat

could be won. That seemed to me unlikely. There were two reasons. I considered it likely that a good deal of personal support would be lost when my father and Sigurvin, who had been second man on the list, retired from parliament. Secondly, I considered it "very doubtful" that the two top men on the list would attract new votes. Indeed, I thought that, all else unchanged, it was more likely the party would lose a seat.

I also pondered what the chances were that I would get a safe seat in the West Fjords later if I took the third seat in this election. That I considered unlikely, since the first and second men were only just past fifty and neither appeared to be on his way out. Nor was there any likelihood that I would be moved to a safe seat elsewhere after this election; in addition there would be considerable expense in the candidacy, lost wages, and I would forgo all extra work. I reckoned the candidacy would require a good deal of time, since the party's representatives had done little or nothing in the constituency for a long while. I also disliked the thought of being an alternate member of the Althing — or, to quote the memorandum:
In a few words, it seems to me that I would be nothing but an errand boy here in the south, a kind of draft horse for the "locals' list" in the West Fjords.
Yet I also raised the negative sides of refusing this offer. These I considered to be both personal and party-related.

If I decline the third seat it will doubtless be seen as a kind of arrogance on my part, and in all likelihood I would thereby be finished in politics, though in itself that matters little. On the other hand, it could come to pass that the party would lose a parliamentary seat in the West Fjords if energetic work is not done there, and few people in most places trust the party's candidates there to do the work that is necessary. Though it is in fact doubtful whether I can change that picture, I would no doubt be blamed if things went badly, and for the party it would be an enormous blow and would more or less guarantee the continued rule of a conservative government in the country. Of these points I care nothing about the former, but consider the latter quite serious.
It cannot be said that my conclusions bore witness to any eagerness to run:

From what is set out above I come to the conclusion that it is out of the question to accept the offer of the third seat in the West Fjords, if one looks first and foremost at my own interests or prospects of advancement in this connection. On the other hand, the difficulties this may pose for the party are a serious matter, and so it is only a question of whether I ought to take this on for those reasons.
A New Beginning

After the outcome of the custody case was settled, more calm and order soon came into my life. I did not, however, recover from the colitis until after several years. I also learned from this experience. I hardened, whether for better or for worse, and I learned that compromise and moderation are good rules in human relations.

While the struggle lasted I often sought strength in good books. My father's bookcase was a precious treasure to me. Not least, I read a great deal of poetry. I have remained faithful to it ever since. I always have a book of poems on my nightstand. There are few things I find better than ending the day reading poetry. Metered verse has always been more to my taste than free verse. There are exceptions, though. Hannes Pétursson and Matthías Johannessen, for example, stand high in my esteem.

Through my difficulties I had also come to know my parents from a new side. That acquaintance was beneficial and invaluable. The letters from my father taught me that I was not alone in having known hard times. His advice was always sound. In one of his letters he put it this way:
Everyone must endure and be tried, and does not become a man before that. No one can be wished a path always strewn with roses, but only that he be man enough to bear adversity.

My father sent me these lines when Dolly had called off our wedding at Christmas 1950. Much of what he wrote to me then proved a rich store in the years that followed. My parents had been through a great deal, and perhaps I can say it was good for me to come to know that story. In this way I benefited from their life experience and could better work through my own. My father was almost a fatalist where difficulties were concerned.

In all my long experience I long ago came to the conclusion that: "All is best as it is." The only thing we can do is neither bend nor break. It often grows so dark that everything seems hopeless to us, everything
pointless, but we keep going, and after some time all is bright again. – This is the experience of all who have endured and been tried and have withstood the ordeals.

During this period I probably worked longer days than ever before. Great expense accompanied the litigation. I cannot deny that I found the work restful and a distraction for the mind. Perhaps in those years I established a pattern of life in which I have been fixed ever since. I need to have plenty to occupy me. Even at the summer house at Klettur I am happiest doing carpentry or planting trees. Then again, this trait of character has perhaps marked me all my life.

The house Edda and I were building at Arnarnes rose quickly and well. I earned a good income when everything was counted, and a considerable part of it went into the house. What made the biggest difference, though, was probably that I worked on it myself until my back nearly broke. When we moved in, in March 1966, only one of the five bedrooms was finished, along with the living room and kitchen. The rest was unfinished, with dust everywhere.
A beautiful son had been born to us in August 1964. He was christened Hermann. Once we had settled in at Mávanes, a delightful daughter, Hlíf, was born to us. We had become a full-fledged family.

The first year after we moved in went into finishing the upper floor, but the basement and the final fittings took about ten years. This time must surely have been hard on Edda and the children. I worked long hours away from home and traveled a great deal both within the country and abroad. When I came home in the evening it was just long enough to grab a bite to eat. Then I was in my work clothes and off building. In 1965 I spent 1,500 working hours on the house, according to my books. That is nearly half a man-year, as every evening and every weekend went into the carpentry. This work was of course added on top of other work and projects. I therefore saw precious little of my family in those years, if one may put it that way. I did nearly everything in the house myself after we moved in, except the masonry. The electricians, my friends from the Fertilizer Plant (Áburðarverksmiðjan), helped me wire the house for electricity.

I was content in the work, for while building I often had the chance to reflect on life and on the tasks of the morrow. It was a relaxed engineer and a happy family man who planed the timber and cut the wood to size in this new house. I had come onto a new footing in life. I was married to a wonderful woman whom I loved, and a long-yearned-for peace had settled over our home life.

I also felt relief when I thought of the children I had in the United States. I had not lost my contact with them as I had feared. I had given up all business dealings and attended to my work at the Research
Council as best I could, to my great pleasure, while also finding time to pursue my many interests and hobbies. I felt I was sailing calmer waters than before.

To an outsider, it seemed that little could disturb the unbreakable equilibrium of home life in this young family. Those who knew us best, however, may have noticed that political work was becoming ever more prominent as time went on. I had begun to turn my thoughts ever more often to my future in that arena as I stood at my carpentry in the bedroom wing or the basement in the evenings. Before the house in Mávanes was fully finished, things had indeed come to a head in those matters. I accepted third place on the list of the Progressive Party (Framsóknarflokkurinn) in the Westfjords and believed that this would settle the candidacy disputes there. Nothing could have been further from the truth.

Those who followed politics closely also discerned that among young Progressives a hard-bitten group of left-leaning rebels was emerging onto the scene, with Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson at its head. This group was later named after Möðruvellir, and it fell to me to deal with them on behalf of the party leadership. I had extended a little finger toward participation in politics, and soon the whole hand was gone.

And what no one could know was that in the accounts of the Research Council (Rannsóknaráð) there also lurked a time bomb that would explode with a loud bang at about the same time as I was gathering strength for battles in the political arena. Soon the peace was well and truly over.
EPILOGUE

The book that here comes before the eyes of readers is the first part of the biography of Steingrímur Hermannsson. The work as a whole is based on numerous interviews with Steingrímur himself, his family and friends, colleagues and opponents. It is built on a wealth of documents in his possession: diaries, letters and personal notes, along with newspaper articles, speeches and other public material, as well as books and other sources related to the subject.

Steingrímur read the manuscript in part and in full at least four times and proved generous with suggestions on all manner of things, whether facts, content, language or style. Steingrímur's family has supported me from the first day, and the contribution of Edda Guðmundsdóttir has weighed heaviest there, with no disrespect to the others. Hermann Steingrímsson and Hlíf Steingrímsdóttir read the manuscript in draft, and Guðmundur Steingrímsson and Dagfinnur Sveinbjörnsson read it both in its original version and at the final stage. Pálína Hermannsdóttir willingly granted access to her photo collection, which was a valuable asset.

Steingrímur's companions and friends have been an invaluable source of information, suggestions and confirmations of particular details concerning this first part of his story. With some I recorded interviews on tape; others I met at short meetings or simply consulted by telephone. Among those who have been helpful, whether in matters large or small, are: Ármann Snævarr, professor; Árni Árnason, director; Bjarni Guðnason, professor; Björn Þorláksson, lawyer; Halla Hauksdóttir, medical laboratory technician; Haukur Clausen, dentist; Haukur Jónasson, physician; Helgi Bergs, former member of parliament and bank director; Matthías Johannessen, editor; Már Pétursson, lawyer; Ólafur Þ. Þórðarson, member of parliament and teacher, who recently passed away; Runólfur Þórðarson, engineer; Þráinn Valdimarsson, executivedirector,
and Örn Clausen, lawyer. They are all offered my warmest thanks, though none of them can in any respect be held responsible for the information found in this book or its presentation.

My family has been my strictest critic in all my writing through the years. This book is no exception. My grandfather Gunnar Steingrímsson read the manuscript carefully and contributed much of value. Mamma and Pabbi, Bergþóra Jónsdóttir and Eggert Gunnarsson, have read the manuscript many times over, and my brother Gauti is probably one of the best collaborators imaginable in all matters of text processing. My sister Valgerður endures the sorry fate of still being considered the teenager of the household despite having become a young lady of seventeen. She has assured me that even Generation X can enjoy the biographies of politicians. Last but not least, my maternal aunt Kristín Jónsdóttir, Icelandic-language scholar and office director in the Ministry of Education (menntamálaráðuneytið), read the manuscript in full in two versions and a considerable part of it in the third. After each reading I received from her a multitude of suggestions and comments on structure, content and presentation that I could not imagine having been without.

Sverrir Jakobsson, historian, read the manuscript in full with his characteristic precision and incredible breadth of vision. Even though I have known Sverrir for many years, he regularly manages to catch me off guard with his superior knowledge of practically everything between heaven and earth. Kristrún Heimisdóttir, lawyer, read the work in full in what was supposed to be its final version. Her comments were not only invaluable but led to a complete reshuffling of the first four chapters of the book. Valur Ingimundarson, historian, contributed to the work previously unpublished documents that he had obtained in American archives. He deserves all the credit for this valuable find. Heimir Þorleifsson, historian, kindly gave permission to publish pictures from Saga Reykjavíkurskóla, and Eygló Stefánsdóttir at the photo archives of DV and Tíminn provided good assistance in gathering pictures. Sigríður Rögnvaldsdóttir has overseen the publication on behalf of Vaka-Helgafell. I thank her especially for good cooperation, useful comments and careful proofreading.

From this enumeration it may be gathered that I am a rich man. A biographer could not imagine a better group to lean on during the making of a book. Conversations with this group and my other friends have kept me alive through the writing, the reshuffling of chapters, the rewrites and the read-throughs, which have become more numerous than I care to remember.
Dagur B. Eggertsson
